t: Lenin's critique of the Proletkult and its implications for China's cultural construction
zh: 列宁对“无产阶级文化派”的批判及其对我国文化建设的启示
paras: Yang Yinyin asks what Lenin's struggle against the Proletkult (the "proletarian culture" current led by Bogdanov) can teach China about cultural construction today. The article treats the Proletkult as a representative form of cultural nihilism. It argues that Lenin's critique remains instructive for developing socialist culture with Chinese characteristics and for building a strong cultural nation, and it links this to Xi Jinping's calls to oppose cultural nihilism and to carry forward Chinese culture through "creative transformation and innovative development".

The article first reconstructs Lenin's criticism in four parts: Machism as the philosophical error behind the Proletkult, its "independentism" towards the Party, its nihilism towards cultural heritage, and its "closed-door" sectarianism towards practice and the people. It draws on Bogdanov, Lebedev-Polyansky, Pletnev, Lunacharsky and others, and on Lenin's writings, letters and marginal notes, including the 1920 resolution on proletarian culture. A final section derives four lessons for China today.

Yang's core argument is that each Proletkult error had a Leninist answer. Against Machism's "elements" and claimed neutrality, Lenin asserted the Party-mindedness of philosophy and the guidance of Marxist theory. Against demands for "complete autonomy", he placed the Proletkult organisations under the People's Commissariat for Education and the "general direction of the Russian Communist Party". Against the slogan that the past is poison, he insisted that proletarian culture must absorb and remake all that humanity has produced, including bourgeois specialists and old intellectuals. Against laboratory-style culture-making, he held that culture comes from the practice of the people, including peasants and intellectuals. Yang adds that the Proletkult was not uniform: Lunacharsky and Bogdanov accepted inheriting the past, but only after proletarian ideology had been established, which Yang says wrongly separates two processes that should run together.

Yang draws four lessons for China: guide cultural work with Xi Jinping Thought on culture; strengthen the Party's centralised leadership over propaganda and ideological work, including its "cultural leadership"; hold to both the "soul" of Marxism and the "roots" of excellent traditional Chinese culture, while learning openly from other cultures; and root culture in the people. On the last point Yang criticises current closed-door and elitist tendencies, citing repetitive television fantasy plots and elite-oriented literature, and calls for better public cultural services. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Lenin's polemics with Bogdanov and Pletnev, and of how they are used to frame current Party cultural policy.
quoteEn: Critically inheriting the historical cultural heritage and establishing a new proletarian culture are not two separate, successive processes, but can be advanced simultaneously.
quoteZh: 批判继承历史文化遗产与建立新的无产阶级文化并非先后割裂的两个过程，而是可以同步推进的关系。

glossary.explanation: A Russian movement of the revolutionary years, centred on the Proletarian Culture organisations (Proletkult) and led by Alexander Bogdanov, which sought to create a distinctly working-class culture independent of the past and of the Party. Lenin criticised it in 1920 and after.

In Chinese official discourse, a label for attitudes that wholly negate a nation's traditional culture or its own cultural path. Xi Jinping has repeatedly criticised it since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

The body of Xi Jinping's ideas on culture, formally presented in 2023 as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It is treated in official discourse as guidance for cultural and ideological work.

The Party's claimed authority over the direction of culture and ideology, linked to the Gramscian notion of hegemony. Xi Jinping stressed it at the June 2023 symposium on cultural inheritance and development.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.explanation: An official formula for handling traditional Chinese culture: reworking its content and forms to suit present needs, rather than either discarding or simply reviving it.

t: The philosophical foundation of Marx's revolution in the theory of the modern state and its contemporary value
st: An examination centred on The German Ideology
zh: 马克思现代国家观革命的哲学奠基及其当代价值——以《德意志意识形态》为中心的考察
paras: Li Yingrui asks what The German Ideology contributed to Marx's theory of the modern state and whether that theory remains valid 180 years later. The article argues that the materialist conception of history, first set out systematically in this work, provided the philosophical basis for a revolution in how the modern state is studied. In Li's account, it also yielded the first reasonably complete and systematic statement of Marx's state theory, which the author holds is still explanatory today.

The article has three parts. The first treats the materialist conception of history as a new worldview and methodology, examined at three levels: ontology, epistemology and axiology. The second reconstructs four theses on the state in The German Ideology, tracing them through the Holy Family, the Communist Manifesto, Capital, the Civil War in France and the Critique of the Gotha Programme. The third draws out the present-day value of these ideas for socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Li argues that Marx grounded the state in practice and material production rather than in speculative premises such as the Hegelian absolute spirit. This is the core of the shift from a Hegelian to a materialist approach. The author states that the modern state arose from the division of labour and from "pure private property", and that it has a dual character: it performs social functions but is essentially a class instrument and an "illusory community". It will be replaced by a "real community" once production develops, and the proletariat must first seize political power. Li also stresses the diversity of modern state forms. On this view, Marx and Engels distinguished the capitalist modern state from the new socialist state of the dictatorship of the proletariat, and China's system is presented as its Chinese, contemporary form.

Li concludes that Marx's state theory is scientific, practical and open, and that claims it is outdated are mistaken. The author calls for three tasks in further deepening reform: holding firm to the Four-sphere Confidence and rebutting distortions of the socialist system, using problem-oriented institutional reform to adapt the relations of production to the productive forces, and putting social fairness and the people's wellbeing at the centre of modernizing national governance. Read the original if you want a close Chinese reading of The German Ideology as the foundation of Marxist state theory, and an example of how that theory is tied to current Party discourse on institutions and governance.
quoteEn: The construction of Marx's theory of the modern state took the materialist conception of history as its scientific worldview and methodology, and the emancipation of human beings with the proletariat as their main agent as its theoretical and practical theme.
quoteZh: 马克思现代国家学说的建构过程，是以唯物史观为科学的世界观和方法论，以实现无产阶级为主体的人的解放为理论主题和实践主题

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party discourse calling for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It was articulated in the early 2010s.
The official name for China's current model of socialism, associated with Deng Xiaoping and reform and opening up. Party theory presents it as Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions.
A Marxist term for working-class rule in the transition from capitalism to communism. In Chinese discourse it is linked to the formula of the people's democratic dictatorship.

glossary.zh: 国家治理体系和治理能力现代化
glossary.pinyin: guójiā zhìlǐ tǐxì hé zhìlǐ nénglì xiàndàihuà
glossary.literal: modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity
glossary.explanation: A goal set by the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). It refers to improving the institutions of the state and the capacity to run them.

t: The contemporary situation and clarification of Lenin's theory of imperialism
st: From the perspective of the dialectical relationship between politics and economics
zh: 列宁帝国主义理论的当代境遇与澄清——以政治与经济的辩证关系为视角
paras: Xiao Bin and Zheng Yongliang take up a charge made by a number of Western scholars: that Lenin's theory of imperialism over-emphasises economics and neglects geopolitics and the theory of the state. The authors argue that this charge rests on a misreading of historical materialism, and that returning to Lenin's method remains necessary for understanding present-day imperialism, including the post-2000 expansion of US-led capitalism.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the political and economic sides of Lenin's theory: the political hegemony contained in imperialism's economic features, the revolutionary potential in its parasitism and decay, and Lenin's critiques of Hobson, Hilferding and Kautsky. The second surveys Western criticisms: Leo Panitch and Sam Gindin, John Willoughby, Vivek Chibber, Ashman and Callinicos on 'state instrumentalism'; and Noonan, Morgenthau, Schumpeter and Waltz on 'economic reductionism'. The third offers a reply and restates the method.

The authors' central move is to argue that critics split politics from economics mechanically. They hold that Lenin saw imperialism as a structural fusion of the state with monopoly capital, citing his remark that the state merges ever more closely with the capitalist alliances, and not as simple state subordination. They also hold that Lenin stressed the relative independence of politics. On the post-1945 'informal empire', they accept that it rests on state coordination through Bretton Woods, NATO and cultural industries. They maintain, however, that its base is still highly financialised monopoly capital, so stressing state 'autonomy' alone slides into political voluntarism. The authors then draw four methodological lessons: historical materialism applied to a new stage; a totalising political-economy critique; the dialectic of necessity and contingency, structure and agency; and the rise from the abstract to the concrete.

The authors conclude that a new theory of imperialism should refine state theory and geopolitical analysis without abandoning Lenin's core categories of monopoly, finance capital and capital export. These should be examined under financialisation, globalisation, informatisation and neoliberalism. They warn that abandoning the totalising method leads either to political idealism that reduces everything to state power, or to fixation on fragmentary phenomena such as derivatives, digital technology and cultural discourse. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist defence of Lenin against Western state-centred and realist critics, and a detailed account of the critics' arguments.
quoteEn: Lenin's theory of imperialism is far from outdated; its dialectical, historical and totalising core of political-economy critique remains an indispensable intellectual guide for constructing a scientific contemporary theory of imperialism.
quoteZh: 列宁的帝国主义理论非但没有过时，其蕴含的辩证的、历史的、总体性的政治经济学批判内核，依然是构建科学的当代帝国主义理论不可或缺的思想指南

t: The determination of time in Marx's theory of value
zh: 马克思价值理论中的时间规定
paras: Pan Yuwen asks what role time plays in Marx's theory of value at a moment when algorithmic management, affective and creative labour, and the blurring of work and life are putting the labour-time standard under strain. The article argues that time is not a neutral, natural yardstick in Marx. Pan contends that Marx offers a critique of time as a historically produced and socially coercive measure, one that remains explanatory under digital capitalism.

The article first reviews three readings of the "value–time" problem: the traditional reading, the New Reading of Marx, and Autonomism. It then reconstructs how time became the measure of value in classical political economy, from the Physiocrats through Adam Smith and David Ricardo. Finally it returns to Marx's account of socially necessary labour time, the "temporalisation" of labour and the "crisis of measurability", and applies these to digital capitalism. Thinkers engaged include Rubin, Sweezy, Backhaus, Postone, Negri and Hardt, Foucault and Sohn-Rethel.

Pan argues that the traditional reading treats time as a technical unit, the New Reading plays down labour time in favour of value-form analysis, and Negri and Hardt reject "time-as-measure" as a flaw in Marx. Each, in Pan's view, misses Marx's critique. Pan reads Marx's dual definition of abstract labour, as physiological expenditure and as a purely social relation, as the key to the problem. Concrete labour becomes abstract labour time through a process of temporalisation, illustrated by Taylorism, which sets the time a task "should" take. Socially necessary labour time therefore does not record pre-existing labour. It produces abstract reality and disciplines labour towards the demands of valorisation. On this reading the "crisis of measurability" is a recurrent feature of capitalist production, not a novelty of immaterial labour, and Pan holds that it does not refute Marx. Immaterial labour, Pan says, extends temporal domination by turning all of a worker's time into potential surplus labour time.

Pan concludes that Marx's value theory contains a deeper critique of time than either the New Reading or Autonomism supplies. Abstract value-time, detached from natural and lived time, is presented as a mechanism of abstract domination over labour and life. Pan treats this critique as a resource for understanding and resisting contemporary temporal domination and for rethinking the real possibility of free time. Read the original if you work on value theory, the New Reading of Marx, Autonomism or the political economy of digital labour and want a detailed argument that socially necessary labour time is a mechanism of domination rather than a neutral measure.
quoteEn: Socially necessary labour time is not only a historically constructed measure of value but, more importantly, the key mechanism through which capital exercises abstract domination and disciplines labour and life.
quoteZh: 社会必要劳动时间不仅是一种历史性建构的价值尺度，更是资本实施抽象统治、规训劳动和生命的关键机制。

t: Rethinking the consistency of Marx's and Engels's philosophical thought
zh: 马克思恩格斯哲学思想一致性再思考
paras: An Qinian takes up the long-running claim that Marx's and Engels's philosophies differ fundamentally or even oppose each other. The article argues that this "Marx–Engels opposition thesis" is untenable and that their philosophical thought is wholly consistent. In An's view, most defenders of consistency have simply stressed their close collaboration, whereas a targeted theoretical rebuttal built on their own texts remains underdeveloped.

The article first sets out two representative versions of the opposition thesis: Georg Lukács's History and Class Consciousness (1923), and the American Marx scholar Norman Levine's work from the 1970s and 1980s, with brief mention of Terrell Carver. It then makes two moves: it argues that the thesis conflicts with the historical record, and that it rests on misreadings of Marx. It ends by suggesting what a fuller account of their unity would require.

On the historical record, An notes that Engels criticised abstract materialism for setting nature against humanity in 1844, before Marx's Theses on Feuerbach. Both men said they were in full theoretical agreement from 1844, and The German Ideology, which they co-wrote, develops the practice-centred view. Engels's account of labour in the transition from ape to human, and his 1890 statement on the decisive role of production, are cited as evidence that he never abandoned that view. For An, the main misreading is to treat Marx's criticism of old materialism as a rejection of it. Marx wrote that it understood reality only as object, and An reads "only" as meaning that he accepted the material world as independent of human will. Marx therefore viewed the world from two angles, matter and human practice. Labour in Capital is itself a material exchange between natural forces, so practice does not contradict a materialist ontology or the dialectics of nature. The difference in emphasis arises because Marx had to found historical materialism, centred on human emancipation, while Engels later defended dialectical materialism against neo-Kantians and Dühring.

An concludes that the two did not oppose each other but each developed different aspects of shared ideas. He adds that Soviet and Chinese philosophers have not yet built a systematic theory unifying practical materialism, dialectical materialism and historical materialism. He links this task to the ecological crisis, the "one-dimensional man" and the risks of artificial intelligence. He also links it to Xi Jinping's account of Chinese modernization, which he says calls for a philosophy combining humanism with scientific rationality. Read the original if you want a detailed textual rebuttal of Lukács and Levine, or an account of how Chinese philosophers frame the unity of practical and dialectical materialism.
quoteEn: Thus it is not that Marx's and Engels's philosophical thought stands in opposition; rather, at different times and in response to different practical needs of struggle, each chose and elaborated different aspects of a shared body of ideas.
quoteZh: 可见，不是马克思恩格斯哲学思想相对立，而是他们在不同时期从不同的斗争实践需要出发，分别选取共同思想中的不同方面加以阐发。

glossary.explanation: An official concept promoted under Xi Jinping describing China's own path of modernization. Its stated features include a huge population, common prosperity, balanced material and cultural-ethical progress, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development.

The Marxist theory of history, which explains social development through material production and social relations. Chinese philosophers treat it, with dialectical materialism, as the core of Marxist philosophy.

t: The scientific meaning, constraints and realisation path of common prosperity in spiritual life
st: A reading based on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
zh: 精神生活共同富裕的科学内涵、制约因素及实现路径
zhSub: 基于《1844年经济学哲学手稿》的解读
paras: Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) statement that material poverty and spiritual poverty are both alien to socialism, Li Suxia and Zhang Xun ask what Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 can contribute to understanding common prosperity in spiritual life. They argue that the Manuscripts, where Marx first used the phrase "spiritual wealth", already contain a coherent picture of such prosperity, grounded in the opposition between labour and capital. The authors present this as having present-day significance for Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first defines the concept; the second identifies what constrains spiritual common prosperity under capitalism; the third sets out how it can be realised. A short conclusion places Marx's approach against ancient Greek and modern philosophy and links it to the coordinated development of material and spiritual civilisation. Throughout, the authors rely closely on passages from the Manuscripts on estranged labour, private property, Hegel and the French workers' associations.

On the concept, the authors hold that spiritual common prosperity means the completeness of human life-expression, realised through labour, social interaction and the satisfaction of spiritual needs. It also means a harmonious relation with nature, which Marx calls humanity's "inorganic body", and a dialectical unity of content and form, reached through critiques of German classical philosophy and Hegel. On constraints, they identify estranged labour, private property and the logic of capital. Estranged labour in four forms impoverishes workers' spiritual life; private property makes society's spiritual life materialistic; capital's logic makes collective spiritual life hypocritical, through dehumanising domination, the hoarding and squandering of wealth, and a rigid division of labour.

For realisation, the authors derive three conditions from Marx: securing free time for the proletariat, sublating private property, and uniting the proletarians. They summarise this as a sequence of criticising estranged labour, sublating private property and uniting the proletarians. They conclude that this sequence points from estrangement to freedom and from the individual to the common. Read the original if you want a close, text-based Chinese reading of the 1844 Manuscripts used to ground the Party's current language of spiritual wealth.
quoteEn: As an important work in the formation of Marxist philosophy, the Manuscripts creatively put forward a logic for common prosperity in spiritual life: critique of estranged labour, sublation of private property, and union of the proletarians.
quoteZh: 《手稿》作为马克思主义哲学形成过程中的重要著作，创造性地提出了精神生活共同富裕“异化劳动批判—私有财产扬弃—无产者联合”的逻辑思路

glossary.explanation: The official Party label for China's path of development, stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is said to coordinate material and spiritual civilisation, among other features.
A goal of shared affluence for all, treated in official discourse as an essential requirement of socialism. Here it is extended from material to spiritual life.
The Chinese rendering of Hegel's and Marx's Aufhebung: a process that negates something while retaining and elevating its positive elements.
Marx's concept in the 1844 Manuscripts of labour under capitalism that confronts workers as an alien power. It is estranged from the product, the activity, species-being and other people.

t: Marx and Engels's twofold critique of capitalist civilization
zh: 马克思恩格斯对资本主义文明的双重批判
paras: Starting from Xi Jinping's remark that capitalist civilization rests on a system of capitalist exploitation and cannot overcome the barbarism within it, Chen Gaohua and Zhou Hang ask how Marx and Engels themselves criticised capitalist civilization. They argue that the critique has two sides: the violent expansion of capitalist civilization abroad, and the barbarism it produces inside capitalist society. Capitalism, in their reading, is a civilization that is at once civilized and barbarous.

The article first reconstructs Marx and Engels's criteria for calling a society civilized, drawing on their reception of Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society. It then treats the two critiques in turn: expansion through colonies, slavery and the world market, and the condition of workers under capital. The authors confine their account to the European capitalism of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and they do not treat it as all forms of capitalism or of human civilization. A short conclusion extends the argument to digital capitalism, ecological crisis and neo-colonialism.

On the criteria, the authors say Marx and Engels did not take civilization to mean reason, refinement or technology. They defined it by social relations: a society counts as civilized when the division of labour, exchange and commodity production are fully developed, and capitalism pushes all three furthest. On expansion, the authors cite Marx on India, Turkey and China and on slavery as the pivot of modern industry. In this reading, civilizing rhetoric masks plunder and monopoly, and colonies show the hypocrisy that is veiled at home. On internal barbarism, the authors argue that the "civilizing" of capital turns domination into contractual, legitimate and hidden order. Progress enlarges capital's power over labour rather than enriching workers, so that, as Marx put it, the more civilized the worker's product, the more barbarous the worker.

The authors conclude that Marx and Engels exposed the capitalist civilization of their time as a unity of civilization and barbarism, and they claim that recognising this breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. They say the contradictions persist in new forms: algorithmic and platform exploitation, ecological crisis, and technological, financial and cultural hegemony that draws developing countries into new dependency. Only by seeing through capitalist civilization's hypocrisy, they argue, can civilizations overcome estrangement and conflict through equal dialogue and mutual learning. Read the original if you want a close, text-based account of how Marx and Engels used "civilization" and "barbarism", set in the context of current Chinese debates over civilizations.
quoteEn: The more capitalist civilization advances, the more the workers in capitalist society sink into an uncivilized condition of poverty.
quoteZh: 资本主义文明愈发进步，资本主义社会中的工人就愈陷入贫困的非文明境地。

glossary.explanation: In this article, the historical social form of European capitalism in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, defined by developed division of labour, exchange and commodity production, and spread through colonial expansion.
In Engels's use, drawing on Morgan, the stage of clan society without class oppression. The article also uses the term for the barbarous, violent features that persist within civilization.

t: A historical-materialist interpretation of spatial ethics
zh: 空间伦理的历史唯物主义阐释
paras: Li Jiali asks how spatial ethics, meaning the ethical values built into the spaces people produce, can be grounded in historical materialism. The author argues that space is a product of human practice rather than a neutral container. On this basis Li presents China's rural revitalization strategy, the people's city concept and the community with a shared future for mankind as answers to the problem that go beyond Western spatial theory.

The commentary opens with the new urbanization drive and the goals of the 15th Five-Year Plan outline, which Li reads as a people-centred spatial ethics. It then notes that Western spatial production theory, critical urban theory and spatial justice theory expose alienation but, in Li's view, neglect the human subject. Marx and Engels wrote no dedicated treatment of space, but Li finds spatial factors in their critique of capitalism: the labourer's body, town and country, and the world market.

The core argument has three steps. First, the real individual is the logical premise, since space gains an ethical character only through practice, and ethics unfolds at three scales: bodily, urban-rural and global space. Second, social being is the objective basis of content. Ethical demands arise from concrete conditions, such as the body as an instrument of capital, structural urban-rural divides and unequal relations between core and periphery. Third, the free and all-round development of the human being is the value goal.

Li concludes that clarifying the premise, basis and goal of spatial ethics lets space confirm human essential powers and unites theory with practice. The 15th Five-Year Plan goals for countryside, city and world are described as grounded in real needs and as a critique and transcendence of the capitalisation of space. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars frame spatial theory within historical materialism and current planning language.
quoteEn: The rich content of spatial ethics is not the simple application of some universal, abstract moral scheme at different scales, but the concrete transformation of the particular social being of each level of space into the realm of ethical consciousness.
quoteZh: 空间伦理的丰富内容并非某种普遍抽象的道德图式在不同尺度上的简单套用，而是各层次空间中特殊的社会存在向伦理意识领域的具体转化。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept associated with Xi Jinping since the early 2010s. It calls for common security, shared prosperity and openness in international relations.
A national strategy announced in 2017 to develop the countryside through industry, ecology, governance and living standards.
A concept of urban development, promoted by Xi Jinping, holding that cities are built by the people and for the people.
The outline of China's national economic and social development plan for 2026–2030.

t: Why stand first? Rethinking "Marxism is the unity of standpoint, viewpoint and method"
st: A reconsideration of the priority of standpoint in Marxism
zh: 为什么首先是立场？
zhSub: 对“马克思主义是立场、观点和方法的统一”的再思考
paras: Zhao Jiwei asks why, within the familiar formula that Marxism is a unity of standpoint, viewpoint and method, standpoint should come first. The article answers that standpoint is the "soul" and commanding element of the other two, and that the proletarian and people's standpoint is the premise on which Marxism's scientific and revolutionary character rests. Zhao presents this as a response to Western tendencies to weaken or dilute that standpoint.

The article opens by criticising several Western positions. These are radical-left thinkers such as Jacques Rancière and Antonio Negri, who replace the proletariat with plural subjects; Western Marxism, which rejects the dictatorship of the proletariat; and scholars who treat Marxism only as philosophy. Three sections follow, each tied to a question: standpoint and values (whom Marxism serves), standpoint and method (how the world is understood), and standpoint as the link between science and revolution (how the world is changed). The evidence includes the Communist Manifesto, The German Ideology and Capital, and comparisons with Adam Smith, Ricardo and List. It also draws on Bernstein, Rosa Luxemburg, Habermas, the Paris Commune, Lenin, and the Chinese Communist Party.

Zhao argues that Marxist viewpoints, including historical materialism and the theory of surplus value, are theoretical expressions of the proletarian standpoint rather than neutral knowledge. Bourgeois economics and philosophy that claim neutrality are said to defend capitalism, so the same object analysed from different standpoints yields different conclusions. On method, Zhao holds that contradiction analysis and class analysis serve the aim of overthrowing exploitation. Detached from standpoint, they become abstract tools, as in Bernstein's treatment of surplus value or Habermas's recasting of economic crisis as an administrative problem. Method in turn gives standpoint cognitive tools and practical routes, such as the mass line, and tests it in practice. Zhao reads the Paris Commune's failure as a case of unclear theoretical standpoint, and presents reform and opening up as a contemporary example of scientific and revolutionary unity under a people-centred standpoint.

Zhao concludes that standpoint is the "soul", viewpoint the "body" and method the "application", and that their unity must have standpoint as its axis. Only by holding to the proletarian and people's standpoint can viewpoint stay scientifically oriented and method serve human emancipation. Without it, the article warns, theory hardens into dogma or degenerates into a narrow sectarian movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist-theory argument for the priority of class standpoint, including its critique of Western Marxism and post-Marxist thought.
quoteEn: Standpoint is the "soul", viewpoint the "body" and method the "application"; their unity is concretely the unity of the proletarian standpoint, viewpoints that serve proletarian emancipation, and methods that fulfil the proletariat's mission.
quoteZh: 立场是“魂”，观点是“体”，方法是“用”，三者的统一具体表现为无产阶级的立场、为无产阶级解放服务的观点和实现无产阶级使命的方法的统一。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese Party theory for taking the fundamental interests of the broad masses as the starting point of theory and policy. The article treats it as continuous with the proletarian standpoint.
A Chinese Communist Party method of work associated with Mao Zedong, summed up as 'from the masses, to the masses'. It involves gathering popular views and turning them into policy.
The policy course begun in China in 1978 that introduced market-oriented reforms and opened the economy to the outside world.

t: The three-dimensional innovation of the Marxist worldview and methodology in contemporary China
zh: 当代中国马克思主义世界观和方法论的三维创新
paras: Following the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025), which called for upholding and applying the worldview and methodology of contemporary Chinese Marxism, Liu asks in what ways that worldview and methodology represent an innovation on Marx's own. The article argues that the innovation has three dimensions: it is epochal (shídàihuà), national (mínzúhuà) and popular (dàzhònghuà). Liu presents the "six musts" as the concentrated expression of this worldview and method.

The article is organised in three sections, one for each dimension. The first traces how Marx and Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping each analysed their own epoch. The second takes up the Second Integration, the combination of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture. The third examines how theory is made accessible to ordinary people, drawing on the Yan'an period and on present-day media.

Liu argues that epochal innovation comes from answering the questions of the age. Marx grounded the concept of an epoch in the contradictions of modes of production, Lenin in imperialism, Mao in war and revolution, and Deng in peace and development. For Xi's era, Liu pairs each of the "six musts" with a classical Marxist counterpart, for example people-centredness with the mass view of history and global vision with "workers of all countries, unite". On the national dimension, Liu claims Marxism and traditional culture converge on materialism, on practice (set against the Western speculative tradition) and on human development, and that each "must" fuses a Marxist idea with a Chinese one, such as the "people as the foundation" tradition. On the popular dimension, Liu holds that the people-centred character of Marxism underlies the whole set, and calls for building on Yan'an methods such as Ai Siqi's Mass Philosophy, audience-specific communication, and online and local-cultural carriers.

Liu concludes that the three innovations are complementary. The first gives theory its contemporary content, the second gives it a distinct cultural character, and the third lets the people accept and own it. Together they are said to make the theory more vital and to root it more deeply in China. Read the original if you want a systematic Party-theoretical account of how the "six musts" are linked to the Second Integration and to the popularisation of Marxism in China.
quoteEn: Making Marxism national does not mean simply blending its basic principles with Chinese culture. It means keeping Marxism as the guide and promoting the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional Chinese culture.
quoteZh: 实现马克思主义民族化不是将马克思主义基本原理与中华文化简单糅合，而是坚持以马克思主义为指导，推动中华优秀传统文化创造性转化、创新性发展。

glossary.literal: six things that must be upheld
glossary.explanation: A set of principles in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) that summarise the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought. They are: put the people first; be self-confident and independent; uphold fundamental principles and break new ground; adopt a problem-oriented approach; apply systems thinking; and have a global vision.

Xi Jinping's formulation, stressed since 2021–23, that the basic tenets of Marxism must be combined with fine traditional Chinese culture. It complements the first combination, with China's concrete realities.

t: The mode of existence of modern humans and its transformation in the perspective of the critique of political economy
zh: 政治经济学批判视域中现代人的存在方式及其变革
source: Social Sciences in China (中国社会科学), 2026 no. 6
paras: Starting from the claim that Chinese modernization requires the modernization of the human being, Huang Zhijun asks three questions: who the modern human is, in what fundamental way modern humans exist, and how the transformation of that mode of existence can be grasped at the level of practical principle. The article argues that Western Marxists, working with Marx's concept of alienation, offered a forward-looking but ultimately purely theoretical critique. In Huang's reading, Marx instead follows the logic that the sublation of self-alienation takes the same path as self-alienation itself, and this logic yields both a critique and a real prospect of change.

The article first compares three answers to what a modern human is: Adam Smith's self-interest, Hegel's self-consciousness, and Marx's production of exchange value. It then examines the modern mode of existence in three spheres taken from Marx's critique of political economy: the mode of material production, the mode of social interaction, and the mode of spiritual life. It next sets out how each sphere might be transformed and closes with implications for the modernization of the human being.

Huang's central move is that Smith grasps the human through things and Hegel through spirit, while Marx finds the inner measure of modern humans in the production of exchange value, an alien yardstick that rules over them. In material life, ends and means are inverted, and the division between productive and non-productive labour reflects the capitalist's standpoint. In social interaction, money and credit exert an abstract domination. In spiritual life, labour is split between a reified, profit-oriented form and a non-alienated form. Huang argues that the conditions for overcoming these predicaments are created by the same epoch that produces them. Material life would move towards common production, social interaction towards a new system beyond money and credit, and spiritual life towards the satisfaction of individual needs and all-round development.

Huang concludes that Marx surpasses Smith's and Hegel's idealist accounts and that change must rest on new modes of production and interaction, so that people move from subordination to a position as subjects. For the modernization of the human being, Huang draws three implications: a people-centred approach, a community with a shared future for mankind, and spiritual abundance for the people, so that development moves from the realm of necessity towards the realm of freedom. Read the original if you work on Marx's critique of political economy, alienation theory or the philosophical foundations of Chinese modernization and want a systematic Marxist account of modern human existence.
quoteEn: Examining the transformation of modern humans' mode of existence in the perspective of the critique of political economy, by the logic that the sublation of self-alienation takes the same path as self-alienation, we find that the material and spiritual conditions modern humans need to escape their universal predicament are created by the very epoch that generated that predicament.
quoteZh: 在政治经济学批判视域中，按照“自我异化的扬弃同自我异化走的是同一条道路”的逻辑来考察现代人的存在方式变革，我们可以发现现代人摆脱普遍性困境所需要的物质条件和精神条件，正是由生成这种困境的时代造就的。

glossary.explanation: The official Party-state formulation of China's own path of modernization, prominent in official discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
The idea in Chinese official and academic discourse that modernization is essentially about transforming people's qualities, capacities and ways of living, not only the economy.
The rendering of Hegel's and Marx's Aufhebung: to negate, preserve and raise to a higher level at once.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy and civilisational concept of international cooperation and shared global governance.

t: The threefold core meaning of practice as the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy
zh: 实践作为马克思哲学基石的三重核心要义
paras: Hu Bo asks what makes the concept of practice the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy and what it contains. The article, published in Guangming Daily in May 2026, argues that Marx's philosophical revolution consists in placing practice at the centre of a complete system, and that practice is the key to understanding human essence, the formation of the real world, and human freedom and emancipation. Hu identifies three closely linked core meanings: practice as the human mode of life-activity, as the foundation of the real world, and as the true force that transforms it.

The article is organised in three sections matching these dimensions: an account of human nature, an ontological and world-view account, and a theory of emancipation. Hu draws mainly on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology and Capital-era passages on labour. Idealism, old materialism and religious theology serve as foils throughout.

In the first section, Hu holds that practice differs from animal instinct because it combines two attributes: thinking initiative (purposes and plans guide action) and sensuous reality (subject, object and means are all real, so ideas can be realised). Practice is therefore neither pure mind nor mindless matter. Hu also stresses its purposiveness, with a final purpose in the freedom and emancipation of all humanity. The second section argues that nature in the human sense and society are products of generations of practice, so idealism, which makes spirit the origin, and old materialism, which reduces the world to mechanical matter, both miss the real basis of history. The third section claims that practice is the force that changes the world, so philosophy's task becomes changing it rather than merely interpreting it.

Hu concludes that emancipation requires a two-way movement between theory and reality: thought must press towards reality, and reality towards thought. This means shifting from speculative justification to concrete, historically specific programmes, which Hu sees in Marx's empirical study of capitalism. It also requires practitioners to be consciously guided by truth rather than partial desires or narrow experience. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style exposition of the practice concept in Marx's early philosophy and its link to emancipation, as presented in a Chinese Party-press venue.
quoteEn: Practice serves as the mediating bridge between human inner thought and the external sensuous world, and its fundamental mechanism for creating reality lies in realising the interaction and mutual transformation of ideas and sensuous objects.
quoteZh: 实践作为连接人的内在思想与外部感性世界的中介与桥梁，其创造现实的根本机制就在于，它实现了思想观念与感性对象的相互作用与转化。

t: On the wealth attributes of lucid waters and lush mountains
zh: 论绿水青山的财富属性
paras: Liu Yan takes up Xi Jinping's claim that "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets" and asks what it means that lucid waters and lush mountains (green mountains and clear waters) are at once natural, ecological, social and economic wealth. The article argues that this claim of multiple wealth attributes is the foundation of the idea. In Liu's reading, it extends Marx's category of wealth in an ecological direction and goes beyond the limits of Western economics.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical meaning of the claim through three dimensions of wealth: its essence, its content and its measure. The second treats the dialectical logic by which the different forms of wealth coexist and convert into one another. The third discusses the theoretical value of the idea for reconstructing the view of wealth, with attention to accumulation, distribution and the inheritance of wealth. Liu draws on Marx's Critique of the Gotha Programme, the Grundrisse and Capital, and on texts collected in the Selected Works of Xi Jinping on Ecological Civilization.

Liu makes three main moves. First, wealth is defined as an advanced form of productive forces consistent with green development, with high-quality ecological products and services answering the people's need for a better life, and with a measure that reflects the contribution of resources and the environment. Second, conversion from green mountains to "mountains of gold" rests on three unities: the historical and the theoretical, science and value, and possibility and actuality. Liu traces three stages of understanding since reform and opening up: trading green mountains for gold, wanting both, and seeing that green mountains keep producing gold. Third, the article contrasts this with Western modernization, which it describes as relying on resource extraction and as oriented to capital accumulation, and with "zero growth" and "degrowth" theories (Jason Hickel and Kohei Saito are named). Liu says these theories treat growth and protection as incompatible, whereas the Chinese idea seeks their mutual conversion.

Liu concludes that the claim points to a new path of accumulation through green and low-carbon development, with innovation-driven growth and intensive rather than extensive models. It makes ecological justice a principle of distribution, covering fairness within and between generations. It sets prosperity and the flourishing of human civilization as the aim of wealth inheritance, through the integration of production, living and ecology. Liu presents it as a basis for Chinese modernization and as a reference for other developing countries. Read the original if you want a close account of how current Party ecological theory is tied to Marx's concepts of wealth, use-value and the measure of wealth.
quoteEn: Lucid waters and lush mountains are at once natural and ecological wealth, and social and economic wealth.
quoteZh: 绿水青山既是自然财富、生态财富，又是社会财富、经济财富

glossary.zh: 绿水青山就是金山银山
glossary.en: lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets
glossary.literal: green waters and green mountains are mountains of gold and silver
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping, first stated in 2005, holding that ecological protection and economic development are mutually reinforcing. It is a core principle of the Party's ecological civilization policy.
The official term for the Party's path of modernization, presented as distinct from Western models. It includes harmony between humanity and nature as one of its features.
An official goal and framework in China that places environmental protection within the overall development strategy. It is also the title of the Xi Jinping selected works cited in the article.

t: The threefold core meaning of practice as the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy
zh: 实践作为马克思哲学基石的三重核心要义
paras: Hu Bo asks what makes practice the cornerstone of Marx's philosophy and what distinguishes it from all earlier philosophy. The author argues that the revolutionary change Marx achieved lies in placing the concept of practice at the base of a complete philosophical system. According to Hu, the concept carries three closely linked determinations: a theory of human essence, a theory of the foundation of the world, and a doctrine of human liberation.

This short theoretical piece in the Guangming Daily has three sections, one for each determination. The first treats practice as the human mode of life-activity. The second treats practice as the basis on which the real world arises and develops. The third treats practice as the real force that transforms the world. Hu draws mainly on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Theses on Feuerbach, and contrasts Marx with idealism, old materialism and theological accounts of creation.

In the first section Hu says that, for Marx, free and conscious activity is the species-character of humans, unlike the instinctive behaviour of bees or spiders. Practice combines two attributes: thinking initiative, which includes purposiveness and an ultimate aim of universal human freedom and liberation, and sensuous reality, which turns ideas into actual things. In the second section Hu argues that nature as humanised nature and society as the sum of social relations both come from practice. Idealism reduces the world to spirit and old materialism reduces it to mechanical matter, and Hu holds that both lack a theory of practice. In the third section Hu contends that practice makes humans the makers of their world, so philosophy's task becomes changing the world rather than only interpreting it. Hu also reads Marx's line that reality must strive towards thought as requiring theory to be turned into concrete programmes. It also requires practitioners to act consciously on truth rather than on partial desires.

Hu concludes that Marx's doctrine moved from speculative argument for human freedom to a practical approach, which set concrete aims and paths for liberation under capitalism. The dynamic unity of theory and practice depends on agents who consciously follow truth. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese restatement of the standard Marxist-philosophical reading of practice, as it appears in the Party press.
quoteEn: Practice is the mediating bridge between people's inner thought and the external sensuous world, and its basic mechanism for creating reality lies in realising the interaction and transformation between ideas and sensuous objects.
quoteZh: 实践作为连接人的内在思想与外部感性世界的中介与桥梁，其创造现实的根本机制就在于，它实现了思想观念与感性对象的相互作用与转化。

t: Historical laws and the historical subject from the perspective of historical materialism
zh: 唯物史观视域中的历史规律与历史主体
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 14 April 2026
paras: This short commentary asks how historical materialism relates objective historical laws to the people who make history. Wang and Wu argue that the scientific character of the theory lies in the dialectical unity of the two: laws give social change its direction and necessity, while the people, as the historical subject, are the material force that recognises, applies and realises those laws.

The article is organised into three pairs of unity: the constraint of laws and the initiative of the subject; the necessity of laws and the subject's capacity to choose; and social progress and the free and all-round development of the human being. It draws mainly on Marx and Engels, including the 1859 Preface, Engels's idea of the resultant of many wills, and Marx's three stages of human development.

In the authors' account, laws set a boundary of possibility, since practice cannot overleap the limits of the productive forces or the sequence of social formations. Within that space, the subject's cognition and choices shape the path, form and pace of development. Class position affects how different classes understand and act on laws, so class struggle becomes part of how they unfold. Choices that accord with laws advance society, while those that violate them are eventually corrected by historical necessity. Laws are not fate; they come alive only through the practice of millions.

The authors conclude that the realisation of laws and the development of the subject are mutually reinforcing. Greater understanding of laws lets people align relations of production with the productive forces and the superstructure with the economic base, speeding progress. Freedom is thus not escape from necessity but, in the authors' phrase, necessity that has been recognised. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese textbook-style statement of how law and agency are reconciled in historical materialism.
quoteEn: Historical law is not fate; it can only come alive through the practice of hundreds of millions of people.
quoteZh: 历史规律不是宿命，它必须通过亿万人的实践活动才能“活”起来

t: "Human–AI synergy" and the transformation of forms of labour
zh: “人智协同”与劳动形态的变革
paras: Zhu Hongwei, writing in the China Social Sciences Journal (April 2026), asks how large AI models are changing labour. The article begins from the State Council's opinion on the "AI+" initiative, which calls for new forms of human–machine collaboration. Zhu argues that AI is shifting from tool to "collaborative subject", which frees workers for creative labour but also lets the logic of capital penetrate production and creates interlinked systemic risks.
The piece first describes the new forms of collaborative labour. It then sets out three risks of capital's penetration and closes with three institutional responses.

Zhu holds that human–AI synergy builds on the strengths of both sides, opening a \"missing middle\" of tasks neither can do alone. Living labour remains the only source of value, since intelligent machines are objectified knowledge and fixed capital that raise efficiency without creating new value. The three risks follow from this: gains captured by capital and technical elites, which Zhu says produces \"intelligent poverty\"; labour substitution and worker \"deskilling\", with a structural mismatch between scarce high-end and surplus low-end jobs; and flexible work that conceals capital's domination, leaving gaps in rights protection.

Zhu calls for institutional innovation to regulate capital and steer the technology. Proposals include curbing the disorderly expansion of AI capital, distribution by data contribution, ethical review of AI, technical support for weaker groups, and digital-literacy training. The aim is \"co-evolution\" that serves human development. Read the original if you want a short Marxist account of AI-era labour that rests on the labour theory of value and fixed capital.
quoteEn: The basic fact that "human–AI synergy" labour has not changed is that capital's domination over labour has not fundamentally changed; flexible, free and diverse ways of working merely disguise that domination.
quoteZh: “人智协同”劳动没有改变的基本事实是，资本对劳动的支配没有发生根本性改变，灵活、自由与多样化的劳动方式只是对支配的掩饰。

glossary.explanation: A term the author uses for labour in which people and AI systems work together as partners. It extends the official phrase "human–machine collaboration".
A State Council initiative to integrate AI into the economy and society. The opinion on deepening its implementation is the article's starting point.
Marx's term for labour actually being performed by workers, as against labour stored in machines and other products. The article treats it as the only source of new value.

t: Free time and human digital existence
zh: 自由时间与人的数字化生存
paras: This short commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2026, asks how digital technology affects free time, which Wen Quan treats as the key condition for people's free and all-round development. Wen argues that digital technology holds real potential to release people from necessary labour, but that, fused with the logic of capital, it fragments, accelerates and empties out time.

The piece moves in three steps. It first sets out Marx's view of time as "the space for human development" and of free time as leisure plus time for higher activity. It then examines the potential and the predicament of free time in the digital age, drawing on Nicholas Negroponte's Being Digital. Finally it considers how free time might be rebuilt.

In Wen's account, automation, remote work and online learning widen the forms free time can take. Yet "digital labour" quietly turns life time into production time: work messages arrive at night, and platforms convert users' browsing and likes into data for profit. Algorithms on the production side drive delivery workers towards "self-exploitation", while consumption-side recommendation feeds produce "filled" rather than self-determined time. Wen reads this time alienation as an extension of capital's logic, so attention should shift from the technology itself to the social relations and power structures in which it is embedded.

Wen calls for vigilance against virtual time displacing real creative practice and against "digital addiction". The author also proposes institutional safeguards for workers' time rights, a fair allocation of time and a narrower digital divide. Wen concludes that, with technical progress, institutional protection and awakened time-consciousness, free time can be freed from digital capital, so that people "dance with bits" rather than being devoured by them. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist reading of platform labour, algorithms and leisure that is organised around Marx's concept of free time.
quoteEn: Free time is not only fragmented and encroached upon in quantity; in quality, too, it has fallen from a space for self-development to a free resource for capital's valorisation.
quoteZh: 自由时间不仅在“量”上被碎片化切割和侵占，在“质”上也从发展自我的空间沦为资本增殖的免费资源。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term for time beyond necessary labour, covering leisure and time for higher activity such as study, art and social life. In Marxist theory it is the measure of wealth and the basis of all-round human development.

A concept in critical digital studies covering paid and unpaid activity that produces value for digital platforms, including users' data-generating behaviour. The article uses it to describe life time being turned into production time.

glossary.literal: free and comprehensive development of the human being
glossary.explanation: A Marxist ideal of a society in which individuals can develop their capacities fully. It is a stated goal of socialism in Chinese official theory.

t: The idea of human emancipation in The German Ideology
zh: 《德意志意识形态》中人的解放思想
paras: This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2026, asks how Marx and Engels treat human emancipation in The German Ideology. Yang argues that the work completes a revolution in the conception of history and moves emancipation away from abstract moral appeals or changes of ideas. It places emancipation within the objective laws and practical process of social development.

The article proceeds in four steps. It starts from the premise of the "real individual", then turns to the division of labour, private property and alienation. It next discusses the growth of productive forces and the revolutionary proletariat, and ends with the "genuine community" and the free and all-round development of the individual.

Yang's central argument is that emancipation must be examined through material production and social relations rather than through self-consciousness or an abstract human essence. In this account, the involuntary division of labour and the private property it produces turn labour into an alien power, and the worker, the capitalist and the relations between people are all alienated. Emancipation requires highly developed productive forces and world-wide intercourse. Capitalist large-scale industry creates universal alienation but also the material and subjective forces to overcome it, above all the proletariat. The result Yang describes is "autonomous activity" and a genuine community, in contrast to the illusory community of class society, in which individuals gain freedom through their association.

Yang concludes that the idea combines a revolution in the view of history with a lasting practical movement. It remains, the author says, a basic theoretical resource for criticising capitalist modernity and for exploring humanity's future. Read the original if you want a brief, orthodox Chinese overview of how The German Ideology links the real individual, alienation and communism.
quoteEn: Human emancipation ultimately shows itself in the free and all-round development of individuals in a future society, an emancipation from the \"one-sided person\" to the \"all-round person\".
quoteZh: 人的解放归根到底表现在未来社会个人的自由全面发展上，是由“片面的人”到“全面的人”的解放。

t: From the critique of religion to the critique of fetishism
zh: 从宗教批判到拜物教批判
paras: This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in April 2026, asks how Marx's early critique of religion relates to his mature critique of fetishism. Zhu argues that the two are continuous: religious critique was the starting point and model, and the critique of fetishism is its culmination, in a sense a radicalised version of it.

The article follows Marx's path from the 1840s to Capital. It covers his place among the Young Hegelians, the 1843 Introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, On the Jewish Question, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, and the theory of fetishism in the 1857–58 manuscripts and Capital.

Zhu's central move is to treat the theory of alienated labour as the bridge. Marx saw religion as alienation of human essential powers, and found the same structure in the state and in capitalist production, where the worker's product confronts him as an alien power. Later Marx distinguished commodity, money and capital fetishism, and the article cites the 'automatic fetish' of M–C–M′. Zhu holds that fetishism resembles religion but is more fundamental and concealed, because it is an objective illusion rooted in capitalist relations of production, a 'secular religion'.

Zhu concludes that Marx's philosophical revolution was a continuing critique, not a new system. It asks where abstract powers such as God, value and capital come from, and it exposes ideologies that present historical social relations as eternal natural order. Real emancipation, Zhu says, requires changing the relations of production that keep generating fetishes. Read the original if you want a concise outline of the continuity between Marx's early alienation theory and his theory of fetishism.
quoteEn: Fetishism is not a subjective illusion but an objective one, rooted directly in the particular nature of the capitalist mode of production.
quoteZh: 拜物教不是主观错觉，而是客观错觉，直接根植于资本主义生产方式的特殊性质。

t: The fetishism dilemma of the digital age and how to resolve it
zh: 数字时代的拜物教困境及其破解思路
paras: Zhang Huaming asks why people come to treat algorithms, data and platforms as mysterious, autonomous powers, even though these are products of human labour. The commentary argues that this "digital fetishism" is a new form of Marx's commodity fetishism. It hides real power relations and exploitation behind digital symbols, and Marx's critical method can demystify it.

After recalling Marx's account of commodity fetishism in Capital, Volume I, the article identifies three layers of digital fetishism: data, algorithms and platforms. It then sets out how to critique them and closes with institutional proposals.

Zhang holds that data value comes from users' unpaid "digital labour", while the exchange of "free services" for data only appears equal. Algorithms, on this account, are not neutral. They carry the stance of their authors and the intentions of capital, and they extend control over couriers, consumers and public opinion. Platforms present themselves as public infrastructure while concentrating capital and exploiting small producers such as couriers and drivers. The chain "commodity–money–capital" thus becomes "data–algorithm–platform capital", and the core remains that relations between things mask relations between people.

Zhang calls for "demystification" through the labour theory of value, for recognising users as digital labourers, and for restoring human agency. Proposed measures include exploring public ownership of data through public data pools or data trusts, independent algorithm audits, recognised worker status and social insurance for platform workers, and making giant platforms public, like utilities. Zhang stresses that the aim is not to reject technology but to make it serve people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a concise Marxist-political-economy treatment of digital capitalism and platform labour, with concrete policy proposals.
quoteEn: Digital fetishism has not gone beyond Marx's critical framework; it has merely evolved the fetishistic chain of \"commodity–money–capital\" into a new form of \"data–algorithm–platform capital\".
quoteZh: 数字拜物教并未超越马克思的批判框架，它只是将“商品—货币—资本”的拜物教链条，演进为“数据—算法—平台资本”的新形态

t: Engels's historical-materialist interpretation of the "ideological battlefield"
zh: 恩格斯对“思想战场”的唯物史观阐释
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 1 April 2026
paras: Wei Qiang, a professor at Chongqing University, asks how Engels's 1855 study The Armies of Europe, written at Marx's request during the Crimean War, treats what the author calls the "ideological battlefield" (sixiang zhanchang). Wei's thesis is that, although the phrase is not an explicit term in Engels's text, it runs through it as an analytical thread. Armies' ideas, discipline, cohesion and morale, Wei argues, are social forms of consciousness shaped by mode of production, class relations and tradition. On this reading Engels widened military struggle from armed confrontation into a total contest between material and spiritual forces.

The short commentary first sets out the historical occasion: the war made Europe's armies of about two million men open to comparative study. It then follows three themes in Engels's text: national military characteristics, discipline, and morale and will. Examples include French, British, Russian, German and Austrian forces, with the British stand at Inkerman cited as a case. The piece closes by drawing a lesson for contemporary military affairs.

Wei's central claim is that Engels grounds the ideological battlefield in social being. National traits such as French dash, British tenacity or Russian passive obedience are, in Wei's account, products of civilisation level, economic structure and political system, and not racial endowments. Engels's contrast between feudal discipline based on corporal punishment and bourgeois discipline based on contract and duty to the state is read as reflecting different relations of production. Multinational Austria shows, for Wei, that coercive discipline without shared interests breaks down under strain. Morale is presented as ideological identification turned into combat power, the political awareness of whom one fights for, which can offset material inferiority.

Wei concludes that, whatever the technology, war's agent remains human beings, and that the initiative on the ideological battlefield is as important as on the armed one, or more fundamental. Winning hearts, holding ideological leadership and cultivating spiritual cohesion are described as lasting core issues of military struggle. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese reading of Engels's military writings that stresses morale, discipline and ideology, and want to see how it is tied to present-day military ideological work.
quoteEn: The ideological battlefield is not an abstract, fragmented spiritual space, but a special field rooted in material social relations.
quoteZh: 思想战场不是抽象、断裂的精神空间，而是植根于物质社会关系的特殊场域。

glossary.explanation: The author's label for the contest over ideas, discipline, identification and morale within and between armies. It is the author's analytical construct, not a term Engels used explicitly.

t: Lenin's thought on strengthening the Party's political development and its contemporary value
zh: 列宁关于加强党的政治建设思想及其当代价值
paras: Yue Kui asks what Lenin contributed to the idea of the Party's political development (dang de zhengzhi jianshe), and what it offers the Communist Party of China today. The article argues that, although the classical Marxist authors did not use the term, Lenin's practice in leading the Russian Bolsheviks produced a coherent set of principles. Yue presents these as a creative development of Marxist party theory and as a theoretical basis for the Chinese Party's current work.

The article first notes that the 19th Party Congress (2017) placed political development first among the Party's building tasks and that the 20th Party Congress (2022) made it the lead for all Party building. It then reconstructs Lenin's thought under four headings: the Party's supreme leading position, ties with the masses, a stable leadership group with a core, and a correct political programme with strategy and tactics. It also treats iron political discipline. The final section turns to three present-day lessons.

On leadership, Yue reads Lenin's idea of the Party's "general leadership" and his claim that the dictatorship of the proletariat is the proletariat's leadership in politics as placing political leadership above all other forms. On the masses, Yue stresses Lenin's call to work wherever the masses are, including in reactionary trade unions and bourgeois parliaments, and his criticism of "Left" communists who withdrew. Yue also cites his view that a party's treatment of its own mistakes is the surest test of its seriousness. On leaders, Lenin is said to reject both the cult of personality and nihilism about leaders' roles, while requiring a stable leadership group with a "first violin". Yue presents Lenin's demand for "iron" discipline and obedience to the central organs as a condition for winning and holding power.

Yue draws three lessons for the present. The Party must be upheld as the "supreme political leading force", a formulation written into the Party Constitution at the 20th Party Congress. The Two Upholds, which Yue reads as inheriting Lenin's "iron discipline" and leader authority, must be put into practice. And "the people's hearts are the greatest politics", which Yue links to closed-loop mechanisms for responding to public needs, such as assessment based on the public's sense of gain and security. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-theory scholar reads Lenin's texts on party leadership, discipline and the masses to support current Party-building doctrine.
quoteEn: In Lenin's view, the stability of the Party's leading core is the fundamental guarantee of its vitality and fighting capacity and bears directly on its governing capacity and its vanguard character, so the Party's leadership group must remain highly united and stable.
quoteZh: 在列宁看来，党的领导核心的稳定是党的生命力和战斗力的根本保证，直接关系党的执政能力和先进性建设，党的领袖集团必须保持高度团结稳定。

glossary.explanation: A strand of Party building concerned with political direction, loyalty to the central leadership and political discipline. The 19th Party Congress in 2017 placed it first among the Party's building tasks.

The official demand to uphold the authority of General Secretary Xi Jinping as the core of the Party Central Committee and the Central Committee's centralised, unified leadership. It has been stressed since 2018 as a basic political requirement.

glossary.zh: 党是最高政治领导力量
glossary.pinyin: dǎng shì zuìgāo zhèngzhì lǐngdǎo lìliàng
glossary.explanation: A formulation from the report to the 20th Party Congress, written into the revised Party Constitution. It asserts that the Party's leadership extends over all state organs, the military, and social organisations.

glossary.en: the people's hearts are the greatest politics
glossary.literal: popular support is the greatest politics
glossary.explanation: A slogan of Xi Jinping's era holding that popular support determines the Party's survival. It is used to justify a people-centred approach to governance.

t: Marx and Engels on Party-spirit cultivation in the proletarian party and its implications
zh: 马克思恩格斯无产阶级政党党性修养思想及其启示
paras: Zang Xiuling takes up the question of what Marx and Engels said about cultivating "Party spirit" (dangxing) in a proletarian party, and what this means for the Communist Party of China today. Writing against the background of the Fourth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2025) and the study campaign on the central Party's eight-point regulations, Zang argues that Marx and Engels, though they used the word "Party spirit" only three times, set out a coherent early framework for it. In this reading, the framework is the intellectual source of the Chinese Party's own conception of Party-spirit cultivation.

The article first defines Party spirit as a party's essential, class-based attribute, and Party-spirit cultivation as the long-term self-remodelling of members. It then arranges Marx and Engels's scattered statements under four headings: political, theoretical, disciplinary and moral cultivation. Evidence comes from the Communist Manifesto, the rules of the Communist League and the First International, Engels's "On Authority", the Paris Commune, and the struggles against Bakunin, Lassalle, Proudhon and Weitling. A final section draws practical lessons for Party members.

Zang argues that political cultivation is the core. It covers a standpoint serving the great majority, a direction that links immediate and final goals, the authority of a centralised leadership, a correct programme, and the "two most radical ruptures" with traditional property relations and ideas. Theoretical cultivation rests on a scientific worldview that keeps the party pure and turns a class "in itself" into one "for itself". Disciplinary cultivation combines intra-party democracy with centralism, serious Party life, and enforcement through supervision and recall, as in the Commune. Moral cultivation means selflessness, loyalty and the status of "public servant", protected in the Commune by universal suffrage and workers' wages for officials.

Zang concludes that Party spirit does not persist automatically over time or grow with rank, so cultivating it is a lifelong task. Following Xi Jinping, Zang recommends that members place political cultivation first and study the classics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Members should also uphold the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, apply democratic centralism, and cultivate the virtues of serving the people, loyalty to the Party and personal probity. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese reading of Marx and Engels's party-building texts and the way it is tied to current Party discipline and ideology campaigns.
quoteEn: The Party spirit of proletarian party members does not continue spontaneously with the passage of time, nor does it grow naturally as their posts rise.
quoteZh: 无产阶级政党党员的党性不会随着时间的推移而自发延续，也不会随着职务的提升而自然增强。

glossary.explanation: The essential, class-based attribute of a party, and by extension the standpoint and discipline expected of its members. In Chinese Communist discourse it is used for both the Party's character and individual members' loyalty to it.
The long-term effort by members to raise their political awareness, theoretical level, discipline and morality. It is a standard theme of Party education in China.
A formula adopted in 2022 affirming Xi Jinping's position as the Party's core and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought.
A slogan calling on Party members to uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Party Central Committee and the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.
The organisational principle of Communist parties that combines internal discussion and election with binding obedience of lower bodies to higher ones and of the minority to the majority.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions.

t: On the new form of scientific socialism in the twenty-first century
zh: 论二十一世纪科学社会主义的新形态
paras: Wu Haijiang asks what historical position Chinese modernization occupies in the development of scientific socialism and what kind of theoretical narrative should accompany it. The article argues that Chinese modernization has opened a new form of scientific socialism for the twenty-first century. In Wu's account, this form rests on the achievements of a developed socialism with Chinese characteristics, aims to surpass contemporary capitalism, and looks towards the next stage of socialism.

The article first traces scientific socialism through three historical forms. These are the Marx–Engels conception tied to mature Western capitalism and the Paris Commune, the twentieth-century practice in Russia and China, and the present form. It then examines why Chinese modernization can claim to create a new form, looking at the difficulties it has resolved, the era in which it unfolds, and its innovations in path, theory, institutions and culture. The last third turns to narrative and to building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system of scientific socialism, covering its necessity, its basis, its methods and three priority areas.

Wu contends that the new form answers three long-standing problems. The first is how to position socialism against capitalism: Wu describes a socialism that grew outside the capitalist system, uses markets and other capitalist instruments, and keeps its own goals. The second is how to avoid the ills of Western modernization, through a modernization of a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical balance, harmony with nature and peaceful development. The third is how to defend the socialist system, through a people-centred stance, the Party's overall leadership, and reform and opening up. Wu also reads the "two great trends", the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and changes unseen in a century, as the setting that links China's questions with the world's.

Wu proposes building an autonomous knowledge system of scientific socialism guided by three methodological pairs: criticism with construction, upholding fundamentals with innovation, and subjectivity with openness. Its priorities should be the new possibilities opened by Chinese modernization, the social effects of digital and AI-driven technological revolution, and new features of contemporary capitalism such as financialization. The aim is a Chinese model of scientific socialism for the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Party theorists periodise scientific socialism and frame a research agenda around Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: It is a socialism that grew outside capitalism, boldly makes use of everything in capitalism that can be used, and gradually gains a relative advantage over capitalism.
quoteZh: 它是一种外生于资本主义，并且大胆利用资本主义一切可以利用的东西、逐步取得对于资本主义的相对优势的社会主义。

glossary.explanation: The official concept of China's path to modernization, which the Party presents as distinct from Western models. It is characterised by a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical balance, harmony with nature and peaceful development.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's theory, path and system since the reform era, combining Marxism with China's national conditions.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, associated especially with Xi Jinping and the Chinese Dream.
The policy begun in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping of economic reform and opening to the outside world.

t: The three perspectives on the concept of productive forces in Marx and Engels
zh: 马克思恩格斯生产力概念的三重视域
paras: Marx and Engels never fixed a single definition of "productive forces", although the concept runs through their political economy, historical materialism and scientific socialism. Zhang Lin and Fu Guowei argue that the concept must be read in context, as a theoretical grasp of real material production rather than an abstract category. Their thesis is that three perspectives – political economy, historical materialism and scientific socialism – each use it differently, yet are united in the mission of interpreting and changing the world.

The article takes each perspective in turn and then draws out lessons for the present. The first part covers the labour-productivity analysis in Capital and the 1857–61 manuscripts. The second covers the German Ideology and the 1859 Preface on the "sum of productive forces" and social revolution. The third covers the idea of "new productive forces" and the social nature of productive forces. A final section applies these ideas to new quality productive forces.
