They argue that the Manifesto is both the programmatic document and the theoretical model for constructing such a system. Existing scholarship, the authors say, has mostly catalogued and explained the Party's theoretical innovations, so a return to the classic text is needed.

The article has four parts. It first presents the Manifesto as a theoretical programme, a party declaration and a banner for spreading Marxist discourse. It then examines the logic and style by which the text constructs that discourse, followed by its themes, main line and methods. The last part considers the Manifesto's role in the worldwide spread of Marxism and its meaning for the Communist Party of China.

The authors' central claim is that discourse serves theory, and that the materialist conception of history underlies the whole discourse system. On this basis the Manifesto ties discourse to class interests, treats the proletariat and its party as the subject of discursive struggle, and rebuts bourgeois charges on private property, education, 'eternal truths' and the family. Its theme is 'human emancipation', its main line is communist revolution, and 'class' is its starting category. Four methods are drawn out: unity of logic and history, of critique and construction, of construction and dissemination, and of the general and the particular, the last shown by the prefaces to later editions. The authors also credit the text's declaration form, short paragraphs, rhythmic historical narration and first-person voice for its persuasive force.

The authors conclude that the Manifesto's translation and circulation, which Plekhanov and others testified to, show how discourse wins over the masses and shapes party-building. They propose that the Party's discourse has followed the Manifesto's analysis of social contradictions, passing through the themes of revolution, construction, reform and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation as the principal contradiction changed. The people-centred wording of each period is, in their account, a continuation of the Manifesto's value stance. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theory reading of the Manifesto as a model of discourse construction and of how Chinese scholars link it to current discourse innovation.
quoteEn: The publication of the Manifesto marked the great beginning of the proletariat's seizure of leadership in the realm of ideas and public opinion.
quoteZh: 《宣言》的发表标志着无产阶级夺取思想舆论领域领导权的伟大开端。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese theory for the concepts, categories and modes of expression through which Marxist theory is presented and spread. Building it is treated as a task of Chinese social science.
The Marxist view that the mode of material production shapes social structure and consciousness. The article treats it as the foundation of the Manifesto's discourse.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official goal of restoring China's national strength and standing. It is the current theme in the Party's official historical periodisation.

t: Socialization of production, human development and the self-preservation of capital: an analysis based on Marx and Engels on the role of capital
zh: 生产社会化、人的发展与资本的自我保存——基于马克思恩格斯关于资本作用论述的分析
paras: Wang Zhongru takes up the question of how Marx and Engels understood capital, arguing that popular views of it are often distorted. The author notes that the well-known passage on capital's willingness to commit any crime for 300 per cent profit is a quotation Marx took from T. J. Dunning, and that it is often wrongly treated as Marx's own judgement. Wang's thesis is that Marx and Engels saw capital as a historically necessary carrier of the socialization of production and a material precondition of all-round human development, and that its disappearance is also its 'self-preservation'.

The article has five sections. It begins with the misreadings of capital, then examines capital as a carrier of socialization (of the means of production, of labour forms and of products). It next treats capital and human development, then the extinction of capital and the meaning of 'self-preservation'. It ends with the historical experience of socialist states, from Lenin's New Economic Policy to reform and opening up, and with the role of capital in the socialist market economy. The evidence is drawn mainly from Capital, the Grundrisse, Engels's Anti-Dühring and Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, and Lenin on cooperatives.

Wang argues that Marx and Engels combined moral critique with scientific critique, and that capital's destruction of small production and its cooperative labour created social labour and productive forces that individuals could not reach alone. Human development shows a paradox in which social relations grow richer while the individual becomes more one-sided, a contradiction capital cannot resolve. Reading Marx's Grundrisse passage, Wang holds that capital's extinction means abolishing its character as a relation of domination while keeping the factories, machines and land. Violence plays only a secondary role, and it is capital's own contradictions and the growth of science that bring about its end. Wang claims that the Soviet and Mao-era practice of eliminating capital and small production by force failed, and that no better carrier of socialization has yet been found.

Wang concludes that capital cannot be abolished until a more effective carrier exists. Under the Communist Party's leadership in China, the author says, capital serves human development and does not dominate production, so Western left critiques of capital cannot simply be applied to China. Citing Xi Jinping, the article calls for bringing out capital's positive role while controlling its negative effects. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's close reading of Marx and Engels that is used to justify private capital under socialism, including the argument about Lenin's cooperatives and Soviet history.
quoteEn: As an important carrier of the socialization of production, capital cannot be abolished until humanity has found a more effective carrier.
quoteZh: 资本作为生产社会化的重要载体，在人类找到更有效的载体之前，是不能废止的。

glossary.explanation: The official description of China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining market mechanisms with public ownership and Party leadership.
The policy launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping that introduced market reforms and opened China to foreign trade and investment.
Lenin's policy from 1921 that replaced War Communism and allowed private trade and small-scale capitalism under state control in Soviet Russia.

t: The political logic of techno-feudalism as an expression of the nature of capital, and its critique
zh: 技术封建主义表征资本本质的政治逻辑及其批判
source: Socialism Studies (社会主义研究), 2025 no. 3
paras: Liu Yanfeng and Tu Liangchuan take up the thesis of "techno-feudalism", advanced by Western scholars such as Yanis Varoufakis and Cédric Durand, and ask what it reveals about the nature of capital in the digital age. They argue that big technology firms such as Amazon, Google and Facebook, by monopolising platforms, data and algorithms, have returned capitalism to a feudal-like structure of hierarchy, dependence and exploitation. The article's aim is to clarify the concept, expose its logic and take a critical stance towards it.

The article opens by contrasting traditional feudalism with its "hyper-modern" form along four lines: land gives way to data as the key means of production, overt coercion to concealed exploitation, landlords to tech giants, and serfs to "cloud serfs". It then proceeds in three main sections: digital labour (gig work, "play labour" and the move from "cloud proletarians" to cloud serfs), technological monopoly power (platform capital, self-legitimation, algorithmic control), and data production at global level (cloud rent, data reproduction, data colonialism). A closing section offers reflections and policy proposals.

Liu and Tu contend that platforms function as fiefs: workers and firms must obey platform rules and pay rent or share profit to gain access. Gig work offers formal flexibility but fragments labour and subjects workers to algorithmic rating and surveillance. Activities that feel like play, such as content sharing, are said to generate value for platforms, turning users into "digital tenant farmers". Platforms extract "cloud rent" from advertisers, merchants and users, and present monopoly as innovation, openness and sharing. Globally, the authors describe data colonialism, in which developed countries and tech giants exploit data from developing countries, leaving the latter in a "semi-colonial, semi-feudal" digital dependency.

The authors conclude that understanding and limiting the technological power of the tech giants is key to a fairer, more open society. They propose strengthening antitrust supervision (stricter merger review, mandatory opening of platform interfaces and data), raising workers' rights (legal recognition of platform workers, algorithm transparency, working-time limits), and building a global data governance framework (data localisation, unified protection rules, regulated data circulation and trading). Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist treatment of the techno-feudalism debate, with its policy recommendations on platform monopoly, gig labour and data sovereignty.
quoteEn: Techno-feudalism has likewise used cloud capital to replace capitalism.
quoteZh: 技术封建主义也借助云资本取代了资本主义

t: Althusser's reconstruction of the "problematic" of Marx's epistemology and its limits
zh: 试论阿尔都塞重塑的马克思认识论“总问题”及其局限
paras: Tan Yong examines Louis Althusser's attempt to reconstruct the epistemological "problematic" (总问题) of Marx's thought. Althusser formulated it as the question of which concepts and conceptual systems allow one to think the elements of a structure, their structural relations and the effects of that structure. Tan argues that this formulation is partly justified, because it fits Marx's texts and the logic of German classical philosophy, but that it cannot stand as Marx's fundamental problematic.

The article has three parts. The first tests Althusser's formulation against Marx's texts, looking at the object of knowledge, the conceptual tools and the link between them. The second places it in a sequence running from Kant's "how is knowledge possible" to Hegel's "how is a scientific system of truth possible", and then to Althusser's question. The third sets out the limits. Tan draws on Adorno and Alfred Sohn-Rethel for much of the critique.

In the first part, Tan argues that Marx treated capitalist society as a structured organism and built new concepts such as surplus value and the value form to analyse it. Marx's dialectical materialism and his method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete then tie these concepts to reality. In the second part, Tan reads Kant as limited by the transcendental subject and the subject–object model, and Hegel as idealist, minimising the human subject and ignoring society. On this reading, Althusser's question marks Marx's advance over both: it brings in history, society and structural thinking. In the third part, Tan names three limits. The question leaves out practice beyond "theoretical practice", meaning mental labour. It is confined to a structuralist way of thinking and so neglects the unity of the logical and the historical. And it does not address Marx's guiding principle that social being determines social consciousness. Tan holds that Sohn-Rethel's "real abstraction", with money as the bridge to abstract thought, answers this principle better.

Tan concludes that Althusser's reconstruction widens the field of research on how Marx's epistemology broke with Kant and Hegel. In Tan's view, it commits the error of taking a part for the whole, and the true problematic of Marx's epistemology still needs further study. Read the original if you work on Althusser, Marx's relation to German classical philosophy, or Sohn-Rethel's real abstraction and want a Chinese critique of structuralist readings of Capital.
quoteEn: The question Althusser poses, namely which concepts and conceptual systems allow one to think the elements of a structure and their relations, does not touch the guiding principle of Marx's epistemology at all.
quoteZh: 阿尔都塞提出的“用何种概念和何种概念体系人们可以思考结构的各个要素及其关系”这一问题，根本没有触及马克思认识论的主导原理

t: On Daniel Brudney's normative interpretation of alienation in the young Marx
zh: 论布鲁德尼对青年马克思异化问题的规范性阐释
paras: Zhang Zuliao examines Daniel Brudney's reading of alienation in the young Marx. Brudney does not deny the traditional historical-materialist view that changing the mode of production is the basic route to overcoming alienation. He adds a normative claim: the degree to which alienation is overcome should measure the justice of a society. Brudney justifies this claim through a Rawlsian method, reflective equilibrium. Zhang argues that the justification fails at key points. Reflective equilibrium cannot work as a self-sufficient method, and Brudney's conception of the person as "concern" is metaphysical. On this account the project ends in the foundationalism Rawls opposed.

The article has four parts. The first reconstructs Brudney's reordering of the four determinations of alienated labour in the 1844 Manuscripts. The second sets out his idea of mutual concern and "structural friendship", drawing on the Comments on James Mill. The third explains how Rawls's constructivist framework, the original position joined with reflective equilibrium, is supposed to keep a conception of the person open to revision. The fourth part assesses Brudney's use of it. Zhang takes Rawls's own constructivism as the benchmark for judging whether Brudney's justification works.

Zhang reports that Brudney puts alienation from labouring activity first, ahead of alienation from the product. In this reading alienation becomes a failure of relations between subjects, in which people produce "for" one another and for the species. Brudney also rejects the assumption that communism requires the overcoming of material scarcity. Zhang then argues that in Rawls reflective equilibrium operates only inside a wider structure. The conception of the person there is distilled from public political culture and stays provisional. Brudney has no original position and does not say what the "features" of time, place and culture are. His conception of concern is derived from a metaphysical notion of human nature, so it cannot be revised by reflection. Brudney himself concedes that readers "must find a given conception of the person".

Zhang concludes that Brudney's scheme produces only limited "reflection" without real "equilibrium". It is a weakly constructivist foundationalism, which may explain his preference for the young Marx over the mature one. Zhang still credits the attempt with restoring a normative dimension to the young Marx that had been greatly underestimated. Zhang adds that even refined reflective equilibrium introduces historicity only to a limited degree. How a normative standard can be joined with historical materialism remains, in Zhang's view, a task for Marx studies and political philosophy. Read the original if you work on the normative reading of Marx, on alienation, or on Rawls–Marx comparisons and want a detailed internal critique of Brudney's method.
quoteEn: Reflective equilibrium is not a self-sufficient method of justification; only within a more holistic structure of justification can it provide a fairly thorough reflection on, and weighing of, the conception of the person.
quoteZh: 反思平衡并非自足的证成方法，必须在更为整体性的证成结构中才能对人的观念提供较为彻底的反思和权衡

t: A critique of the technological positing (Gestell-like "setting-up") of digital capitalism
zh: 数字资本主义的技术摆置批判
paras: Xie Yazhou asks how capitalism "sets up" human society through technology, and what is distinctive about this under digital capitalism. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, Xie argues that the "artificial intelligence" promoted by digital capitalism is a technological imaginary that leaves no room for the daily labour through which people build their lifeworld, and that it is an expression of capitalism's inherent technological force.

The short essay begins from the commodity as Marx described it, then moves to the structure of capitalist production, and finally to the digital stage. It draws on Marx, Kant and Gilbert Simondon, and on the idea of a "real abstraction" in commodity exchange.

Xie's central claim is that capitalism sustains itself not by producing ever more commodities but by maintaining a "world of things" through which its synthetic, abstract mechanism operates. Value turns relations between people into relations between things, so capitalism rests on a thing-to-thing structure (inter-objectivity) rather than a subject-to-subject one (inter-subjectivity). Digital technology, in Xie's account, turns all objects and subjects into code. It lets capitalism posit things at a higher level and become a self-planning "transcendental subject". On this basis Xie says daily life now depends more on phones and data identities than on trust or love.

Xie concludes that the world planned and posited by this "transcendental subject" is a world of things, not a human one, and that the key task is to return the world to human beings. Read the original if you want a short, philosophically oriented Marxist critique of AI and digital capitalism that combines commodity theory with Kantian and Simondonian ideas.
quoteEn: Capitalism sustains its life not by producing more and more commodities, but by using commodity production to maintain its synthetic abstraction mechanism and its creative effects.
quoteZh: 资本主义不是通过生产越来越多的商品来维持自己的生命，而是通过商品的生产来维持其综合抽象机制及其创造效应。

t: Digital capitalism: intertwined transformation and predicament
zh: 变革与困境交织的数字资本主义
paras: This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how digital capitalism should be understood and criticised with Marxist tools. Shi argues that it is the capitalism of the information age, not a rupture with capitalism's tradition. It releases productive potential while deepening economic polarisation, alienated labour and governance problems.

The piece has three parts: the historical emergence of digital capitalism, a historical-materialist critique of it, and the practical predicaments it produces. It draws on Marx's remarks on historical economic forms, on production in general, and on the Rhodes passage, and gives examples from platform work.

In Shi's account, data, platforms and algorithms are absorbed into capital's valorisation and accumulation. The logic of capital, the wage-labour position of workers and the tendency towards new inequality are therefore unchanged. The article claims that the digital mode of production is a historical product, that "general data" plays the role Marx assigned to production in general, and that platforms are a shell through which capital controls global industrial chains that still depend on the real economy. Shi identifies three predicaments: users produce data but cannot control it or share in its returns; the anarchy of production deepens through algorithmic opacity and weak regulation; and both wealth polarisation and worker impoverishment intensify. For the latter two, the article cites figures on the market share of the top ten technology firms and on the wealth share of the bottom half of humanity.

Shi concludes that criticism must return to the material basis of production, expose "digital fetishism" and break data monopolies so that technology serves human liberation rather than capital accumulation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar applies classical categories to platforms, data and gig labour.
quoteEn: Digital capitalism is the capitalism of the information age, and by no means an abrupt rupture with the capitalist tradition.
quoteZh: 数字资本主义是信息时代的资本主义，而绝非脱离资本主义传统的断裂性突变。

glossary.explanation: A term for capitalism restructured around data, platforms and algorithms. Here it is treated as a continuation of capitalism, not a new system.
The author's coinage, modelled on Marx's 'production in general', for the abstract category of data that governs digital production, exchange and consumption.
An extension of Marx's commodity fetishism to data and platforms, which are said to hide the social relations and real-economy basis of capital's control.

t: Contemporary Western digital capitalism in the perspective of historical materialism
zh: 唯物史观视域中的当代西方数字资本主义
paras: This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks how contemporary Western digital capitalism should be understood. Lan argues that it is not merely capitalism applying a new tool. In Lan's account, digital, network and intelligent technologies have produced a new mode of capitalist control, exercised through digital platforms that allocate production factors and govern the circuit of accumulation. Lan calls for a return to historical materialism and the critique of political economy.

The piece moves through three headings: changes in the factors of production, the transformation of the mode of production, and platforms and the new monopoly. It sets digital capitalism against earlier industrial and finance capitalism, drawing on Marx's Capital and on the work of Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean.

Lan's central claim is that data and computing power have joined land, labour-power, capital and credit as factors that decide whether firms survive. Just as banks gained control through credit rating in the late nineteenth century, platforms now do so through data, traffic and computing power, integrating individual firms into platform-run industrial chains. Lan also contends that digital capitalism leaves wage labour in place but turns stable employment into gig and outsourced work, so that firms shed the legal protections and workers bear the risks. A few giant platforms, in this reading, become monopolies above both workers and industrial capitalists, and Lan notes that Varoufakis and Dean call this 'technofeudalism', which they treat as a metaphor.

Lan concludes that Marx's intellectual legacy still has analytical force and that historical materialism and the critique of political economy remain tools for analysing and criticising digital capitalism. The piece ends with Marx's remark that theory becomes a material force once it grips the masses. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist framing of platform capitalism and its link to the technofeudalism debate.
quoteEn: Digital capitalism has not fundamentally changed the capitalist relation of wage labour, but it has turned stable employment into an unstable gig economy and outsourcing economy.
quoteZh: 数字资本主义并没有彻底改变资本主义的雇佣劳动关系，但让稳定的雇佣关系变成了不稳定的零工经济和外包经济。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory that material production and social relations shape historical development. Chinese authors use it as a basic method of analysis.
Marx's project, found in Capital and its preparatory manuscripts, of criticising capitalist economic categories and relations.
A term used by Yanis Varoufakis, Jodi Dean and others for a monopolised digital order in which platforms hold power over firms and users. Lan says it is a metaphor, not a literal return to feudalism.

t: Human–machine collaboration under large-model production and changes in the labour process of digital capitalism
zh: 大模型生产下的人机协作与数字资本主义劳动过程变迁
paras: Huang Zaisheng asks whether human–machine collaboration in the era of large-model (generative AI) production, which digital capital presents as a reconciliation of humans and machines, is freeing workers from digital servitude. Drawing on labour process theory and Marx's political economy, the article argues that such collaboration is essentially the latest round of capital's \"accelerated mechanisation\" to raise labour productivity. It contends that the supposed \"re-humanisation\" of work is an ideological gloss, and that collaboration brings a distinctive form of deskilling.

The article is organised in four parts. The first traces how collaboration emerged and takes three practical forms: intelligent assistants, \"digital employees\" and general-purpose AI agents, followed by its dynamic evolution. The second examines the \"re-humanisation\" narrative in three respects: work content, free time and the results of labour. The third analyses four mechanisms of deskilling: substitution of mental labour, the erosion of the skill premium, a paradox in generating complex cognitive ability, and over-reliance on AI. A short conclusion follows. Huang draws on empirical studies such as a call-centre study and creative-writing experiments.

Huang's first move is to read the collaboration narrative as a new way of manufacturing consent. Digital capital promises to relieve workers of repetitive tasks, yet still needs cheap global labour for data cleaning and algorithm supervision, which the author calls \"ghost work\". Citing Marx on free time, Huang argues that capital turns freed time into surplus labour and that gains in productivity accrue to capital rather than to workers, who face \"time poverty\" and dependence on platforms. The second move concerns deskilling. AI tools level performance between novices and experts, which dissolves the skill premium. Heavy use of digital employees also cuts off the practice through which complex cognitive abilities develop. Because large models statistically recombine existing knowledge, over-reliance dulls creativity and could lead to \"model collapse\".

Huang concludes that human–machine collaboration raises the productivity of digital capital and produces an unprecedented \"digital prosperity\", while knowledge workers suffer deeper deskilling beneath a surface of humanised conditions. Even if workers became \"cyborgs\", the human–machine hybrid would remain an object of extraction as long as capital controls the key means of production for large models. The author expects workers to become \"digital poor\" and the biggest losers of the AI wave. Read the original if you want a Marxist labour-process critique of generative AI that draws on recent empirical studies of workplace AI use.")
quoteEn: In view of this, the claim that human–machine collaboration promotes the "re-humanisation" of labour content is merely an ideological rhetoric by which digital capital deliberately beautifies and "naturalises" the capitalist application of intelligent machines.
quoteZh: 鉴于此，所谓人机协作推动劳动内容“再人性化”的说法只不过是数字资本刻意美化“自然化”智能机器资本主义应用的一种意识形态说辞而已。

t: On Marx's critique and transcendence of Ricardo's political economy
zh: 论马克思对李嘉图政治经济学的批判与超越
source: Journal of Hebei University of Engineering (Social Sciences Edition), online first, 23 June 2025
paras: Yuan Jinqiu and Liu Jie ask what Marx's critique of David Ricardo actually achieved and why it still matters. They answer that Marx's political economy is a revolutionary break with classical political economy, not a continuation of Ricardo. They present this against two modern challenges: Böhm-Bawerk and Samuelson, who reject the labour theory of value, and Schumpeter, who treats Marx as Ricardo's heir. In the authors' view, both fall back to Ricardo's level or below.

The article has three parts. The first traces four stages in Marx's reading of Ricardo: rejection under Feuerbach's influence (Paris Notebooks), strong endorsement (The Poverty of Philosophy), initial doubt (London Notebooks), and full critique and transcendence (the manuscripts of 1857–63 and Capital). The second examines Marx's treatment of Ricardo's value theory, rent theory, international trade, accumulation and view of machinery, drawing mainly on Theories of Surplus Value. The third compares their methods.

The central argument is that Marx resolved the "two difficulties" of Ricardo's system. The first is how the exchange of capital and labour fits the law of value. The authors say Marx answered it with the two-fold character of commodities and labour, and the concept of labour-power. The second is how equal capitals yield equal profits. Marx answered it by distinguishing surplus value from profit and value from price of production. Marx's absolute rent, the authors add, rests on landed monopoly and agriculture's lower organic composition of capital. They suggest that platform economies reproduce a variant of this rent. On method, they argue that Ricardo's abstraction was incomplete and ahistorical, treating bourgeois relations as natural, while Marx used historical materialism and dialectics. These include ascending from the abstract to the concrete and the unity of the logical and the historical.

The authors conclude that Marx's critique of Ricardo and the formation of his own political economy were one process. They hold that it exposed the historical transience of capitalism and the conflict between socialised production and private ownership. They add that its ultimate purpose is to give scientific grounds for proletarian revolution and a path to communism and human emancipation. Read the original if you want a detailed, stage-by-stage account of Marx's relation to Ricardo, or a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Schumpeter and of neoclassical critiques of the transformation problem.
quoteEn: The process by which Marx came to know Ricardo is at one with the process by which Marx's political economy took shape.
quoteZh: 马克思认识李嘉图的过程与马克思政治经济学的形成过程相统一。

t: From the philosophy of practice to practical materialism: Cieszkowski, Hess and Marx
zh: 从实践哲学到实践唯物主义：切什考夫斯基、赫斯与马克思
paras: How did the young Marx move from Hegelianism to practical materialism? Lin Zhao and Fan Xingxing take up one thread that Hiromatsu Wataru identified in this transition: the Young Hegelian critique of Hegel's philosophy of history by August von Cieszkowski and Moses Hess. Marx never discussed either in his published work, and Engels left them out of his account. The authors argue that both men developed a 'philosophy of practice' that prepared Marx's turn, but remained trapped inside idealism, so Marx's practical materialism is a real break rather than a continuation.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Cieszkowski's Prolegomena to Historiosophy (1838) and its link between philosophy of history, philosophy of the future and philosophy of practice. The second turns to Hess, from The Holy History of Mankind to The European Triarchy and On the Essence of Money, and his critique of modernity and his socialism. The third asks what it means for Marx to replace 'philosophy' with 'materialism', by asking what was wrong with the philosophy of history and what the philosophy of practice still lacked.

In the authors' account, Cieszkowski made practice the 'synthesis' of Hegel's system and opened the future to knowledge and action. Hess brought the argument down to subjective spirit and the present, and added French socialism and a critique of private property. Both, the authors argue, stayed inside the 'mystical shell' of Hegel's dialectic. Cieszkowski dealt only with spiritual elements and had no historical subject. Hess kept a V-shaped narrative of paradise, suffering and a new Jerusalem, and treated bourgeois modernity as simply evil. Marx, by contrast, grounded history in civil society, the mode of production and the critique of political economy, and identified the proletariat as the subject that modern industry and property relations produce.

Lin and Fan conclude that practice becomes scientific only when it is understood through its material preconditions. At that point the philosophy of practice turns into practical materialism, which they also call a theory of proletarian revolution. They suggest that Marx and Hess parted ways, on this view, because of this difference, with Marx heading toward scientific socialism and Hess toward Zionism. Read the original if you study the Young Hegelian background to Marx's thought, or want a Chinese reading that sets Cieszkowski and Hess against Marx's break with philosophy.
quoteEn: Only when this material activity is understood as the precondition does the philosophy of practice turn into practical materialism, and only then is the scientific grounding of communism complete.
quoteZh: 只有理解了这个作为物质活动的前提，实践哲学才转变为实践唯物主义，共产主义的科学化才宣告完成

t: The world-historical logic in Marx's theory of fetishism
zh: 马克思拜物教理论中的世界历史逻辑
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 13 October 2025
paras: Sun Jia asks how Marx's theory of fetishism can explain the course of world history and the fate of human subjectivity. The short newspaper essay argues that history can be read as the continual remaking of forms of dependence. In this reading, humans demystify and master natural forces while falling under social forces that they create and that become independent through reification.

The article traces Marx's thinking from the 1842 Bonn Notebooks, where he excerpted de Brosses on fetish worship, through the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology and the Grundrisse to Capital. It then turns to the ethnological notebooks of 1879–82 and closes with a brief note on digital technology.

Sun's central distinction is between two kinds of fetish. The natural fetish of early societies is 'destructible': when it fails to satisfy desire, its worshippers smash it. The commodity, money and capital fetishes of capitalism are 'indestructible', because they are reified social relations and part of the whole system of exchange. Sun links this to the three forms of dependence in the Grundrisse: personal dependence, personal independence resting on dependence on things, and the free association of individuals. Scientific revolution ends mystified dependence on nature, but capitalism re-naturalises social relations, so demystification must now be directed at society.

Sun concludes that the free association of individuals is the historical direction in which social forces return to conscious human control, at a higher level than the early blood-based community. Algorithmic authority, data worship and artificial intelligence myths are presented as new forms of modern fetishism. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-language account of how fetishism theory is being used to read world history and digital technology.
quoteEn: Human history is not only a history of the development of the productive forces or of class struggle, but also a history of continuous struggle with the 'fetish'.
quoteZh: 人类历史不仅是生产力发展史或阶级斗争史，也是一部与“物神”持续斗争的历史。

t: Marx on the relationship between "history" and "world history"
zh: 马克思对“历史”与“世界历史”的关联性阐述
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 13 October 2025
paras: Jiang Haibo asks how Marx, in his Economic Manuscripts of 1857–58, understood the relation between national "history" and the overall process of "world history". Jiang argues that Marx redefined both categories through the critique of political economy, escaping the Eurocentrism the author attributes to Hegel's view of world history as the unfolding of spirit. The result, in Jiang's reading, is a dialectical unity of the two.

The short article first traces how the category of "history" changes with the mode of production. It then examines how history and world history are linked, and ends by assessing the contemporary value of this idea.

Jiang contends that in pre-capitalist societies, natural economy, feudal landholding and guild restrictions kept history closed and local. Capital's drive for surplus value broke these limits, pulling all peoples into the world market, reorganising production factors globally and ending separate national narratives. The global division of labour created by large-scale machine industry ties the two categories together. National history becomes a partial expression of the whole, while world history supplies the conditions for overcoming local limits. Jiang adds that national differences feed the diversity of world history, and that Marx, though critical of colonial brutality, acknowledged its transformative role. Modern China's path from the Opium War to the 1911 Revolution is offered as an example.

Jiang sets Marx against two opposed Western tendencies: a nationalist view of history that equates it with national history, and a globalist view that denies national particularity. Marx's approach, Jiang says, supports a historical understanding that unites nationality and universality. Jiang also holds that his idea of a "human wholeness" is consistent with a community with a shared future for mankind, which the article presents as a contemporary development of Marx's thought. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic account of how Marx's 1857–58 manuscripts are linked to current Chinese foreign-policy language.
quoteEn: "History" and "world history" form a dialectical unity, and the national narrative of "history" is a partial manifestation of the overall process of "world history".
quoteZh: “历史”与“世界历史”是辩证统一的整体，“历史”的民族性叙事是“世界历史”整体进程的局部呈现

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for cooperation among states on shared global problems while respecting different development paths.
In Marx's usage, the process by which capital's expansion links separate national histories into a single world-wide history. The author contrasts this with Hegel's idealist conception.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: "The Poverty of Philosophy": which philosophy, which poverty? The last metaphysics and Marx's critique
zh: “哲学的贫困”：什么哲学?什么贫困?——最后的形而上学与马克思的批判
source: Journal of Huaqiao University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2025 no. 3
paras: Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy answers Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty, yet Marx never says directly what he means by "philosophy" or by "poverty". Lin Jinlong takes up this gap, which the author says scholarship has long neglected. The article proposes that Proudhon's thought is the "last metaphysics", the final effort of the metaphysical tradition after Hegel's system dissolved. On this reading, the poverty Marx names is both an original poverty and a final one.

The article first reconstructs Proudhon's "economics-metaphysics" through five features. These are his idea of "science", his claim that economics is concrete metaphysics, his "natural history of labour", his series of economic categories, and his defence of small private property. It then examines the role of "God" in Proudhon's text and his ambivalent debt to Hegel. Next it sets out Marx's critique of Hegel and of Proudhon, and ends by placing Proudhon alongside the Young Hegelian "ideologists" of The German Ideology.

Lin argues that Proudhon borrows Hegel's dialectic as antinomy and series, but rejects Hegel's "absolute idea" and replaces it with an "infinite" God. Marx, in Lin's account, finds that Proudhon reduces the dialectic to a bare thesis and antithesis. Proudhon also treats categories such as division of labour, machinery, monopoly and taxation as a logical sequence detached from history. His "economic evolution" therefore takes place "in the mystical embrace of the absolute idea". Lin concludes that Proudhon uses Hegel against Hegel and only swaps one "God" for another, which Lin names as the root of philosophy's poverty. He is "last" because he advanced beyond the German ideologists by seizing the dialectic and joining reason with experience. He is "original" because he remains within the idealist conception of history.

Lin concludes that the "philosophy" criticised is Proudhon's attempt to unify reason and experience within Hegelian conceptual dialectics. The "poverty" is the failure of metaphysics to renew itself from within. Proudhon's "unity of experience and reason" is contrasted with Marx's "unity of the logical and the historical", which is anchored in labour as sensuous, objective activity and in real history. Historical materialism, Lin holds, ends classical metaphysics as a closed system and offers a new periodisation of the history of philosophy. Read the original if you want a close comparison of Proudhon's and Marx's texts and a reading of Proudhon as post-Hegelian metaphysician.
quoteEn: Proudhon tried to use Hegel's method to summon a new "God" and then used this new "God" against Hegel's "absolute idea". The result is merely Hegel set against Hegel, so he naturally could not escape the bonds of the Hegelian system.
quoteZh: 蒲鲁东企图借用黑格尔的方法召唤一个新的“上帝”,再用这个新“上帝”反对黑格尔的“绝对观念”,因而其最终结果不过是用“黑格尔”反对“黑格尔”,自然不能摆脱黑格尔哲学体系的束缚。

t: Reflections on deepening research into the basic principles of Marxism from a knowledge-system perspective
zh: 深化马克思主义基本原理研究的知识化思考
paras: Responding to the new requirements the Party Central Committee set in November 2024 for the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project, Zhang Yunfei asks how research on the basic principles of Marxism can be deepened by building a "knowledge system" for the field. The article, published in Ideological and Theoretical Education in 2025, argues that this system should become a Chinese-style, world-class component of China's independent knowledge system of philosophy and social sciences. Zhang's answer is that the knowledge system has to be defined by a clear object of study, a distinctive research paradigm, a balanced set of resources and a concrete disciplinary mission.

The article has four parts. It first defines the object of study of Marxism, of Marxist philosophy and of the basic-principles knowledge system. It then sets out a research paradigm of holistic, integrated and comprehensive study. Third, it discusses three kinds of resources: Marxism itself, fine traditional Chinese culture, and foreign philosophy and social science, including Western social thought and world Marxist currents. The last part assigns the knowledge system three functions: strengthening scientific belief and ideals, supporting the innovation of ideological and political theory courses, and serving the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Chinese modernization.

Zhang holds that the object of study is the universal laws of development of nature, society and thought. These laws are not the object of dialectics alone: Marxist philosophy supplies the worldview and methodology, while political economy, scientific socialism and the other branches uncover the laws. The knowledge system is then the knowledge-form expression of the basic principles, and it takes in the discipline, academic and discourse systems. For the paradigm, Zhang says Marxism's wholeness derives from the wholeness of its object. Research must also integrate Marxism with its sinicized forms, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and must bring together field-specific strands such as Xi's ecological civilization thought. On resources, Marxism is the main body, tradition is a historical-cultural source reached through the Two Integrations, and foreign thought serves as a reference, to be neither swallowed whole nor dismissed.

Zhang concludes that the system must turn scientific knowledge of the "two inevitables" into firm belief and ideals. It must also reshape textbook structure and teacher competence and the methods of teaching, and it must generate a "socialism knowledge system" and a "modernization knowledge system" for Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed view of how a leading Chinese Marxist theorist links the discipline of basic principles, ideological and political teaching and the project of an independent knowledge system.
quoteEn: In short, the knowledge system of the basic principles of Marxism is the knowledge-form expression and knowledge-form outcome of those basic principles.
quoteZh: 简言之，马克思主义基本原理知识体系是马克思主义基本原理的知识化表达和知识化成果。

glossary.explanation: Formula associated with Xi Jinping: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities (the first) and with fine traditional Chinese culture (the second).

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions.
Official term for China's path of modernization, presented by the Party as distinct from Western models.
The Marxist thesis that the demise of capitalism and the victory of socialism are historically inevitable.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义理论研究和建设工程
glossary.pinyin: Mǎkèsīzhǔyì lǐlùn yánjiū hé jiànshè gōngchéng
glossary.en: Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project
glossary.explanation: A national project launched in 2004 to compile textbooks and promote research and teaching in Marxist theory.
Compulsory courses in Chinese schools and universities that teach Marxism and Party ideology; basic principles of Marxism is one of them.

keywords: Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project

t: Marx and Engels's fourfold critique of Russian populism and its scientific method
zh: 马克思恩格斯对俄国民粹主义的四重批判及其科学方法
paras: How did Marx and Engels respond to the Russian populist claim that Russia could bypass capitalism and move directly to socialism? Ji and Wang argue that their response was a sustained, four-part critique, aimed at what the authors call the theories of village-commune superiority, Russian revolutionary advantage, the peasantry as revolutionary subject, and a non-capitalist path. The authors present this critique as a model of scientific method for confronting erroneous currents of thought today.

The article takes each of the four targets in turn, drawing on Marx and Engels's polemics with Herzen's successors and with the revolutionary populists Lavrov, Bakunin and Tkachev. Texts discussed include Engels's writings on Russia's social question, Marx's letter to the editors of Otechestvennye Zapiski, his correspondence with Vera Zasulich, and the 1882 Russian preface to the Communist Manifesto. Each section pairs a populist claim with the analytical method the authors see Marx and Engels using against it: historical, comparative, class and dialectical analysis.

On the commune, Ji and Wang report that Marx and Engels treated communal land ownership and the labour artel as forms found at low stages of development across many peoples. In their reading, the survival of these forms showed Russian backwardness, and the commune carried an internal duality of common arable land and private plots that drove its decay, which the 1861 reform accelerated. Against Tkachev, Engels argued that socialist revolution presupposes both bourgeoisie and proletariat. He also argued that the tsarist state served the nobility and that exploitation by nobles, usurers and speculators already resembled capitalist relations. Against reliance on the peasantry, he stressed peasant isolation and weakness, citing the quickly extinguished Spanish rising organised by Bakunin.

Ji and Wang conclude that Marx and Engels did not deny a non-capitalist path but analysed it dialectically. The commune could not generate anything new from itself, and communal property was disappearing. Russia's chance of skipping the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism depended on a Russian revolution complementing proletarian revolution in the West. The authors add that Engels continued after Marx's death to call for struggle against populists everywhere, and they hold that this critique offers methodological guidance for criticising mistaken social trends now. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of the Marx–Engels debate with Russian populism and of how that debate is used as a method for ideological critique.
quoteEn: Marx and Engels's critique of Russian populism not only vividly displays the scientific method and distinctive wisdom with which they fought various currents of thought, but also offers methodological guidance and experience for our present work of criticising erroneous social trends.
quoteZh: 马克思恩格斯对俄国民粹主义的批判不仅生动展现了他们与不同社会思潮斗争的科学方法和独特智慧，也为我们当今的错误社会思潮批判工作提供了方法指导和经验借鉴。

t: The temporal horizon of Marx's dialectics and its historical significance
zh: 马克思辩证法的时间性视域及其历史意义
paras: Liu Shaoming asks how temporality conditions the appearance of dialectics in Marx's philosophy, a question the author says existing scholarship has not addressed. Earlier studies, Liu notes, stress the consistency, internal unity or mutual interpretation of dialectics and history, but do not show what Marx's temporality does for dialectics. The article argues that a phenomenological 'original time' in Marx's theory is the condition under which the dialectical subject, its negativity and its basic forms become manifest.

The article begins by contrasting dialectics (which privileges mediation and negation) with phenomenology (which privileges immediate givenness), and argues that the two can be combined. Drawing on Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty and Marcuse, Liu reads Marx as performing a transcendental reduction that returns individual, nature and society to sensuous practical activity. Three sections then take up three temporal horizons: simultaneity, futurity and the historical field. A final section compares Marx with Hegel.

In Liu's account, simultaneity unites subject and object, and individual and society, in one practical activity, so that the true dialectical subject is 'individual–society–nature'. Futurity, expressed in survival and reproduction, self-confirmation and the pursuit of truth, brings out primordial difference and self-negation. The historical field, in which past, present and future are unified, is where the negation of the negation and the unity of opposites appear; Liu treats the latter as derived from the former, using the relation of productive forces and relations of production as an example. The three horizons are said to form a methodological and a real unity.

Liu concludes that Marx inherits Hegel's concepts of subject, negativity and historicity, but surpasses Hegel's 'non-temporal' dialectics. Hegel's absolute spirit is, in this reading, abstract, its negativity feigned and its future already fixed, and his concept is placed above time. Marx's temporal dialectics supplies a real basis for the subject, its motive force and its forms, and so becomes a tool for criticising reality and exposing the 'eternal present'. Read the original if you work on Marx's dialectics, phenomenological readings of Marx, or the Marx–Hegel relation and want a detailed argument built on Husserl, Heidegger and Marcuse.
quoteEn: Marx used the phenomenological method to make dialectics appear on a temporal foundation, going beyond the exclusion of temporality in Hegel's dialectics and thereby providing a basis of appearance for the reality of dialectics.
quoteZh: 马克思用现象学方法将辩证法在时间性基础上显现出来，超越黑格尔辩证法对时间性基础的排斥，从而为辩证法的实在性提供了显现基础。

t: Marx's transcendence of Feuerbach's doctrine of "sensuous intuition" and the formation of historical materialism
zh: 马克思对费尔巴哈“感性直观”学说的超越与历史唯物主义的生成
paras: Engels called Feuerbach an intermediate link between Hegel's philosophy and the Marxist standpoint. Li and Xu ask why Marx's transcendence of Feuerbach's "sensuous intuition" should be seen as a key step in the formation of historical materialism. They argue that existing scholarship oversimplifies the question: it stresses either Feuerbach's abstract "species-essence" or his reliance on sensuousness, and so obscures how the two aspects of his doctrine fit together.

The article is a history-of-ideas reconstruction in three parts. The first examines how Feuerbach criticised Fichte's "intellectual intuition" and Hegel's philosophy of spirit in order to build his own doctrine. The second explains why the young Marx, from his legal studies in Berlin through the Rheinische Zeitung and the Paris Manuscripts, drew on Feuerbach. The third shows how the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology went beyond him.

On the authors' reading, Feuerbach answered Fichte's split between the transcendental and empirical self by making a sensuous subject with real needs the starting point. He answered Hegel's self-moving concept by holding that sensuous objects can be grasped only through species-thinking. Marx's early difficulties were the opposition between what is and what ought to be, and Hegel's "logical, pantheistic mysticism" on material interests. Feuerbach's ideas helped Marx with both, and with his critique of alienated labour and money in the Paris Manuscripts. The authors then argue that Marx came to see sensuous intuition as merely theoretical. The Theses replace it with "objective activity", that is, practice, and define human essence as the ensemble of social relations. The German Ideology develops this into a theory of comprehensive production, with five forms of production, and into a theory of relations of production. On this account the world Feuerbach intuits is in fact a historical product, and no transcendental species-essence is needed to explain illusory ideology, which the authors trace to the naturally arising division of labour.

The authors conclude that moving beyond Feuerbach was necessary for Marx to unify thought and being in practice and to create a scientific theory of history. That theory could also propose abolishing capitalist private ownership, which a moral critique of alienation could not do. Read the original if you want a detailed account of the Fichte–Hegel–Feuerbach–Marx line of development and of how the Paris Manuscripts, the Theses and The German Ideology relate to Feuerbach.
quoteEn: Only by thoroughly transcending Feuerbach's doctrine of "sensuous intuition", creating a scientific theory of history and letting it genuinely affect objective reality, can a scientific path to the identity of thought and being be found, and philosophy truly be realised.
quoteZh: 只有彻底超越费尔巴哈的“感性直观”学说，创立科学的历史理论并发挥其对客观现实的真正影响，才能找到实现思维与存在相同一的科学路径，进而真正实现哲学的现实化。

t: Marx's historical and class consciousness in examining the transformation of money into capital
zh: 马克思考察货币转化为资本的历史意识与阶级意识
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (Makesi zhuyi lilun xueke yanjiu), 2025 no. 3
paras: Liu Jingdong asks how Marx's account of the transformation of money into capital, and of labour-power becoming a commodity, supplies a framework for understanding both the birth of capital and its world history. The article argues that Marx's critique of capital and of political economy rests on an organic unity of historical consciousness and class consciousness. In Liu's reading, this unity lets Marx explain the shift from traditional to modern modes of production and expose the exploitative essence behind apparently free and equal exchange.

The article draws mainly on Volume 1 of Capital (Part Two, 'The Transformation of Money into Capital'), on Volume 2's chapter on the circuit of money capital, and on Marx's 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts. It has four sections. The first treats money becoming capital as the precondition of the move from traditional to modern production. The second treats the emergence of capital and the free worker. The third examines the social conditions of the circuit of money capital and the new class relations. A short conclusion follows.

Liu makes three main moves. First, the author contrasts simple circulation (C–M–C, aimed at use-value) with the circulation of capital (M–C–M′, aimed at self-expanding value), and treats the capitalist as 'personified capital' driven only by surplus value. Marx's contradiction in the general formula is resolved, Liu says, only by labour-power becoming a commodity, whose use creates more value than it costs. Second, labour-power can be a commodity only where workers are free in a double sense, which is the historical result of primitive accumulation separating producers from the means of production. Marx's remark that this condition 'contains a whole world history' is read as having both a temporal and a spatial meaning. Third, in the circuit M–C…P…C′–M′ the purchase of labour-power looks like a fair contract, yet the author argues that it conceals exploitation. Bourgeois economists such as McCulloch miss this because of their class position and non-historical thinking, in Liu's account.

Liu concludes that Marx identified the commodity status of labour-power as the social-historical condition for money to become capital, and so traced the mechanism of transition from traditional society to modern capitalism. By piercing the 'veil' of free and equal exchange, Marx, on this reading, reached his judgement that capitalist commodity production is an epoch-making mode of exploitation. The article also treats the way labour and the means of production are combined as a basic criterion for distinguishing social formations. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reading of Capital Volumes 1 and 2 that stresses the unity of historical method and class standpoint in Marx's critique of capital.
quoteEn: Based on the organic unity of historical consciousness and class consciousness in his critique of capital and of political economy, Marx outlined the basic forms of the birth history and the world history of capital.
quoteZh: 马克思基于资本批判和政治经济学批判的历史意识与阶级意识的有机统一，勾勒了资本的诞生史和资本的世界史的基本形态。

t: The "Schulz factor" in the transformation of the young Marx's philosophical thought
st: An examination based on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
zh: 青年马克思哲学思想变革中的“舒尔茨因素”探析——基于《1844年经济学哲学手稿》考察
paras: Shao Yu takes up the "Schulz factor": Marx's extended quotations from Wilhelm Schulz's Die Bewegung der Produktion in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, especially Notebook I. The question is what problem led Marx to "material production", and what role and limits Schulz had in the young Marx's philosophical change. Shao argues that Schulz supplied empirical material and a viewpoint from material production, but that Marx's concerns were already formed and he read Schulz from a Feuerbachian standpoint.

The article first reviews earlier scholarship, from Cornu and Rubin to Japanese and German studies and recent Chinese work. It then goes through Marx's quotations in two places: the chapter "Wages", on workers' poverty, and the chapter "Profit of Capital", on competition between large and small capitalists. In each case Shao sets Marx's context beside the original context in Schulz. The article ends by assessing the factor's role against Marx's earlier engagement with poverty and with Feuerbach.

In Shao's reading, Marx and Schulz share a target: political economy that treats the worker as a labouring animal and offers average wages as evidence of progress. Shao argues that Marx goes further, tracing poverty, alienated labour and the concentration of capital to private property. For that reason Marx judges wage increases and wage equality, as in Proudhon, to be inadequate reforms. Schulz, by contrast, looks to state-led reform and the growth of free time and spiritual life. Shao calls this an abstract "spiritual production" close to Hegel's philosophy of history, whereas Marx holds that civil society determines the political state and that private property must be abolished in social reality.

Shao concludes that the Schulz factor had a direct and an indirect effect. It gave Marx an empirical angle for criticising political economy. It also pointed to a way beyond Feuerbach's intuitive materialism, towards historical materialism. Its effect was limited, however. Marx had been thinking about worker poverty and real freedom since the Rheinische Zeitung period, and Schulz mainly reinforced principles he already held. Read the original if you study the formation of Marx's historical materialism or want a close text-based comparison of Marx's excerpts with Schulz's original arguments.
quoteEn: Schulz speaks of "material production" mainly for the sake of "spiritual production", and the road to social change he adopts is one of abstract change in ideas.
quoteZh: 舒尔茨讲“物质生产”主要是为了“精神生产”，他所采取的社会变革之路是一种抽象的思想变革之道。

glossary.explanation: Marx's theory that history is shaped by material production and the social relations built on it. The article traces its formation in the mid-1840s.

t: The normative content of Marx's idea of human emancipation and its historical unfolding
zh: 马克思人类解放思想的规范性内涵及其历史性展开
paras: Lin Yuchuan takes up an open question in Chinese research on Marx's political philosophy. Is the political philosophy found in Marx's early writings the same as the one implicit in his critique of political economy and historical materialism? If it is, how should the continuity be understood? Lin's answer is that human emancipation is the core proposition of Marx's political philosophy. It is normative, and its normative content becomes more concrete and historical over time without being abandoned.

The article has five parts. It first establishes human emancipation as the central proposition, tracing it from Marx's early writings through the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period to the later works. Lin then defends its normative character against the view, illustrated by Hans Kelsen, that historical materialism excludes norms. Next, the article sets out four levels of normative content across Marx's career. Finally it examines the mature period and closes with brief remarks on the present.

Lin argues that Kelsen sets up a false opposition between the a priori and the empirical. Historical materialism can accommodate norms once ideas are allowed to act back on the economic base, and norms can be abstracted from empirical facts. On Lin's reading, Marx's early claim that emancipation returns the human world to human beings was derived from the alienation of civil society, not from a purely a priori premise. The four levels are: equal respect and freedom (the Rheinische Zeitung period); conditions for each person's full development, distinguishing political from social emancipation; the emancipation of labour for the proletariat; and an association of free individuals. Lin holds that the critique of exploitation and alienated labour in Capital deepens the early ideas and does not break with them. He therefore rejects readings that base Marx's mature political philosophy on a non-normative concept such as the division of labour.

Lin concludes that human emancipation is an era-specific proposition. While humanity remains in the stage of 'dependence on things' and wage labour persists, it takes the form of the emancipation of labour, or the proletariat's social emancipation. In that long stage it breaks down into sub-questions such as winning power, ownership reform, democracy, equality and distributive justice, and rights protection. Lin holds that these can approach Marx's ideal only if grasped from the standpoint of labour's emancipation. Human emancipation is thus presented as a historical mission to be completed through staged tasks. Read the original if you work on Marx's political philosophy, on the normative versus historical-materialist readings of Marx, or on Chinese debates about the unity of the early and mature Marx.
quoteEn: Marx's early abstract idea of human emancipation was not simply discarded in his mature period, but returned at a higher level in a more concrete and richer form.
quoteZh: 马克思早期抽象的人类解放思想，在其成熟时期并没有被简单地抛弃，而是以更具体和丰富的形式实现了更高层次的复归

t: The emancipatory character of Marx and Engels's view of morality
zh: 马克思恩格斯道德观的解放性特质
paras: This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2025, asks what distinguishes Marx and Engels's view of morality. Wang and Wan argue that it has a clear emancipatory character, expressed in three ways: moral critique contains intellectual emancipation, moral practice points to institutional emancipation, and the moral ideal pursues human emancipation.

The article takes the three dimensions in turn. It first examines four targets of Marx and Engels's moral critique, then their revolutionary practice, and finally their ideal of the liberation of humanity. Each dimension is defined briefly and supported with classic formulations from Marx and Engels.

On critique, Wang and Wan say Marx and Engels exposed religious morality as illusory, Hegel's morality as idealist, feudal hierarchical morality as base, and bourgeois morality as hypocritical. They cite Marx's debates on the law on thefts of wood and the formally free labour contract concealing surplus-value exploitation. On practice, the authors argue that the historical materialist case against capitalism leads to the proletarian revolution. They list the means: developing productive forces, class struggle, party-led workers' movements and the "two ruptures". The proletariat is the agent, and its revolutionary moral qualities are stressed. On the ideal, emancipation has an individual side (free individuality, socialised means of production, the end of the old division of labour, shorter necessary labour time) and a species side (reconciliation with nature, society and oneself).

The authors conclude that the three elements form one whole. Critique clears away ideological obstacles, practice creates material conditions, and the ideal supplies value orientation and goals for both. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style outline of how Chinese scholars present Marxist moral theory as an emancipatory framework.
quoteEn: Moral critique clears away ideological obstacles to realising the moral ideal, moral practice creates the material conditions for it, and the moral ideal in turn provides value orientation and goals for moral critique and practice.
quoteZh: 道德批判为道德理想的实现扫除思想障碍，道德实践为道德理想的实现创造物质条件，而道德理想则为道德批判和道德实践提供价值导向和目标指引。

glossary.explanation: Chinese shorthand for the Manifesto's call for the most radical rupture with traditional property relations and with traditional ideas.

t: Research on Marxist ethical thought must foreground the "question of standpoint"
zh: 马克思主义伦理思想研究要突出“立场问题”
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 23 October 2025
paras: In this short commentary in Chinese Social Sciences Today, Li Peichao argues that studying Marxist ethical thought requires grasping its standpoint, viewpoint and method, and above all its standpoint. Li holds that the standpoint is a value standpoint: it concerns for whom moral criticism and defence are made and whose freedom, justice and dignity are pursued.

The piece has three parts. The first defines the value standpoint as the essence of Marxist ethics. The second explains why it must be settled first, by contrasting Marxism with other currents in the history of ethics. The third draws consequences for building a Chinese Marxist ethics.

Li contends that from Marx's early essay on choosing a profession through to his critique of capitalism, the standpoint stays constant: that of the proletariat and the people. It is neither that of a "minority elite" nor "value-neutral". Many Western currents, in Li's account, leave aside people's concrete historical existence and develop ethics as a refined, inward-looking intellectual exercise, such as debates over the trolley problem that ignore its causes. Li argues that such "standpoint-free" ethics covertly expresses a standpoint of withdrawal from real moral relations and conflicts of interest. For Li, viewpoint and method only embody and justify the standpoint, and separating them from it turns Marxist ethics into abstract knowledge.

Li calls for a discipline system, academic system and discourse system of Marxist ethics with Chinese characteristics, built on the Two Integrations and serving Chinese modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Li rejects borrowing Western paradigms or using them as the test of whether Marxist ethics is valid. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese ethicist links the people's standpoint to the project of an indigenous Marxist ethics.
quoteEn: The value standpoint is the fundamental question; viewpoint and method embody and substantiate it, and one cannot discuss them apart from the value standpoint.
quoteZh: 价值立场是根本问题，观点和方法是对价值立场的体现和论证，不能离开价值立场来谈观点和方法。

glossary.explanation: Formula associated with Xi Jinping: combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture.
The official term for China's own path of modernization, promoted by the Party leadership since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of national revitalisation, tied to the Chinese Dream and to a national centenary target of 2049.

t: Political-philosophical implications of Marx's distinction between "the property of the individual" and "private property"
st: An examination based on the Economic Manuscripts of 1857–58
zh: 马克思区分“单个人的财产”与“私有财产”的政治哲学启示——基于《政治经济学批判（1857—1858年手稿）》的考察
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2025 no. 4
paras: Tu Liangchuan asks what Marx's distinction between "the property of the individual" (单个人的财产) and "private property" in the 1857–58 manuscripts (the Grundrisse) contributes to political philosophy. The article argues that, although Marx was analysing forms of production before capitalism, the distinction follows his method of reading earlier forms in light of the developed one. In Tu's reading it criticises capitalist "property appropriation" (财产占有) and looks forward to a communist ideal of "property ownership" (财产所有) that serves all-round individual development.

The article has three main sections plus a conclusion. The first traces how individual property in the general conditions of production, mediated by the community, dissolved into private property through the Asiatic, ancient and Germanic forms of ownership. The second examines how bourgeois property rights, presented as freedom and equality, become a power of domination, drawing on Hegel's link between property and freedom and on Marx's critique. The third turns to Marx's picture of "social individual ownership". The conclusion links the distinction to common prosperity in the course of Chinese modernization.

Tu's central move is to separate a right (the individual's use of the conditions of labour) from a power (capital's command over others' labour). Under capitalism, the supposedly equal exchange between capital and labour hides the separation of labour from its objective conditions. In this account, workers' surplus labour becomes capital's surplus value, so that "the product appears as the property of another". Tu argues this is a basic condition of capitalist production and not an accident. Against it, the individual's property is described as non-closed and non-exclusive: it consists in the "common social productive capacity" and in a "social individual ownership" that unites social appropriation with individual ownership.

Tu concludes that abolishing capitalist private ownership and building communist social individual ownership would return property to being the material basis of human essential powers and of free individuality. The article presents common prosperity as the political restoration of this positive content and as a historical-materialist critique of capitalist appropriation. For Tu, Marx's distinction offers a theoretical reference for judging ownership questions in modern political philosophy and a guide for building the mechanism of "property enjoyment" under common prosperity. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of property in the Grundrisse or on how Chinese scholars link it to common prosperity.
quoteEn: The capitalist mode of production is in essence a set of social relations and a mode of power and domination founded on property rights.
quoteZh: 资本主义生产方式本质上是以财产权为基础的社会关系和权力统治模式。

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's own path of modernization, promoted by the Communist Party since the early 2020s. It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A goal of shared wealth for all the people, stressed in Party policy and since 2021 as a central objective of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

A Chinese rendering of Marx's idea of a post-capitalist form of ownership. The article reads it as uniting common appropriation of the means of production with individual ownership of what labour produces.
The article's term for the capitalist relation in which owners of capital take possession of others' labour and its products. It is contrasted with "property ownership" (财产所有).

t: Confirming the essence of artificial intelligence from the perspective of historical materialism, and its significance
zh: 唯物史观视域下人工智能本质的确证及其意义
source: Studies on Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2025 no. 6
paras: Liu Tongfang asks what artificial intelligence (AI) fundamentally is, as a premise for thinking about the human–machine relationship. The article argues that AI can be understood by borrowing the way Marx analysed the essence of things, especially the human essence. On this view AI is a 'human-like' being: an externalisation of human knowledge and rational capacity, but not equal to human intelligence and not capable of fundamentally surpassing it.

The article opens by tracing Western philosophical views of essence, from Plato and Aristotle to a 'universal' essence (Hobbes, Spinoza) and a 'particular' essence (Feuerbach). It then reconstructs Marx's treatment of the human essence, from the species-essence of the 1844 Manuscripts to the Theses on Feuerbach's 'ensemble of social relations'. The second section applies this method to AI through three questions: what distinguishes AI from other beings, how it came about historically, and what its real properties are. The third section draws out the significance of this determination.

Liu makes three claims. First, as the 'brain' of automated machine systems, AI is the externalised, objectified form of human knowledge, which Liu links to Marx's account of machinery as the 'organs of the human brain'. Second, its emergence is a necessary stage in the development of the productive forces, extending the automation of manual labour to part of mental labour. Third, AI both exceeds and does not exceed human intelligence. It outperforms individuals in specialised, data-driven tasks, but it stores the knowledge of humanity as a whole. It also lacks the bodily needs and life experience from which human intelligence arises, and it lacks practice, in the sense of purposeful transformation of the environment to meet a subject's needs.

On this basis Liu argues that AI's capacity for emancipation and its alienating effects are internally linked. Under capital's logic, AI shortens necessary labour time but deepens exploitation and produces a 'useless class'. Liu's reading is that the negative effects stem from capitalist control and use, not from AI itself. Following Marx, Liu rejects both radical progressivism and conservative romanticism and calls for neither utopian myths nor fantasies of catastrophe. AI is described as a material basis for human liberation, not a 'divine' being beyond humanity. Read the original if you want a Marxist-philosophical argument on AI's essence that draws on Marx's texts on machinery and the human essence.
quoteEn: AI is only an enhancement of human rational capacity and does not itself possess the life experience and practical capacity that come with the human body.
quoteZh: 人工智能只是对人的理性能力的增强，其本身并不具有人类躯体所带来的生命体验与实践能力。

t: Time and the remainder of the system: Schelling's philosophy of the "Ages of the World"
zh: 时间与体系剩余：谢林的“世界时代”哲学
paras: Wang Ding asks how a post-Kantian philosophical system can unite its beginning (the "One") with its completed whole (the "All") when that beginning must be immediate. The article's thesis is that the solution of Schelling's early period and of Hegel turns the beginning into a "remainder" of the system. In Wang's reading, Schelling's later philosophy of the "Ages of the World" (Weltalter) tries to repair this through a critique of time and a rebuilt "metaphysics of time".

The article has three parts. The first sets out Hegel's three requirements for a system and Schelling's objection to Fichte's "self-positing of the I". The second takes up Schelling's 1827 lectures on the system of the ages of the world and his critique of time. The third examines the distinction between "principle" and "cause", the role of God, and the problems that remain. Wang also disputes readings of Schelling by Xian Gang and Markus Gabriel.

Wang argues that Schelling objected to Fichte because self-consciousness cannot ground the conditions of its own existence. After Fichte, the beginning became a law that recurs at every level of the system. That law, however, is a bare fact (Dass) which the system cannot absorb, so the "ouroboros" structure never closes. The same law also strips the system of real time, because everything becomes an ever-present "now", or eternity. Wang reads Schelling's response as a "Möbius-strip" folding back on the law itself, asking what lies before and after the "now".

Wang concludes that Schelling therefore introduces "cause" (Ursache) as distinct from "principle". The cause explains why the ideal outweighs the real, a relation that is willed rather than necessary. On this reading, God appears as the cause of the "better", which restores teleology. Wang presents the "system of the ages of the world" as a historical, ontological and teleological metaphysics, not mysticism. The article ends with open questions: where the ground of a given highest ground lies, whether the world can give itself meaning, and, if not, where one could now go beyond it. Read the original if you follow German idealism, Schelling and Hegel, or debates about system, history and meaning in philosophy.
quoteEn: To complete the system, the system's beginning became the system's own "remainder": a "fact" that makes the "All" possible while never itself entering the "All".
quoteZh: 为了完成体系，体系的开端成了体系自身的“剩余”，成为了让“全”得以可能而自身永不进入“全”的“事实”。

t: The ontological construction of sensation and its contemporary effects: a new reading of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
zh: 感觉的存在论建构及其当代效应：《1844年经济学哲学手稿》的新解读
paras: Bao Jin and Huang Jing take up the young Marx's account of sensation in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. They argue that it is usually read as a Feuerbachian anthropological materialism and dismissed as immature. In their reading, the account is first of all ontological. Marx accepts Feuerbach's principle of sensuous objectivity but builds the practical structure of sensation on "sensuous activity", and this breaks with the basic framework of metaphysics.

The article has four sections. It first contrasts Hegel's treatment of sense-certainty in the Phenomenology of Spirit with Feuerbach's critique in Principles of the Philosophy of the Future, and with earlier empiricism. It then examines the objective relations of sensation in the Manuscripts, and Marx's reworking of Feuerbach's concepts of passivity and passion. It ends by tracing contemporary effects of Marx's account, drawing on Byung-Chul Han, Eva Illouz, Bernard Stiegler and Herbert Marcuse.

The authors argue that Feuerbach treated sensation as something ready-made and never asked how it comes to exist. Marx transforms Feuerbachian "passivity" into passion, a driving force that takes hold of its object, so that passivity and activity form a dialectical unity. With the help of MEGA2, the authors stress Marx's distinction between appropriation (Aneignung), possession (besitzen) and having (Haben).
