Marx answered with the labouring estate, which at this stage was still a speculative category and not yet the historical and practical proletariat. Cheng suggests that once popular sovereignty rests on that estate as the people's subject, the principle of the dictatorship of the proletariat is close at hand. Read the original if you want a short, text-based account of how the early Marx's break with Hegel's theory of the state is reconstructed from the Logic–philosophy of right relationship.
quoteEn: But whether monarch, bureaucratic estate, landed estate or commercial estate, as private estates within civil society none of them can safeguard the public interest of the state; they can only defend their own private interests, even turning public goods to private ends.
quoteZh: 但是，无论君王、官僚等级、地产等级还是工商等级，作为市民社会中的私人等级，他们都不能维护国家公共利益，都只会维护各自私人利益甚至化公为私。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist concept for rule by the working class during the transition to socialism. In Chinese Marxist theory it remains a core principle of the state.

t: The construction and transcendence of "moral politics": Rousseau, Hegel and Marx
zh: “道德政治”的建构与超越：卢梭、黑格尔与马克思
paras: Zhang Dang asks how modern political philosophy has dealt with the separation of morality from politics, and how Marx's thought resolves the difficulty. The article argues that Rousseau diagnosed this separation and proposed rebuilding "moral politics". It holds that Hegel refined the project through his distinction between "ethical life" and "morality", and that Marx went beyond both by tracing the problem to property relations.

The article follows a genealogy in three parts. It begins with Hobbes's and Locke's accounts of the state of nature and of property, and with Rousseau's critique of them. It then covers Rousseau's "general will" and his programme against inequality, followed by Kant's shift after the French Revolution and Hegel's assessment of Rousseau. The final part takes up Marx's 1843 Rousseau notes, his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, his historical-materialist method and his critique of political economy.

Zhang's central claim is that Rousseau and Hegel both work from will and reason and both accept the legitimacy of private property. For that reason, the author says, Rousseau ends up defending property as "sacred" while attacking inequality. Hegel's "ethical politics" in turn leaves unresolved how the ethical state becomes real, and risks formalism. Marx, in this reading, borrows Rousseau's democratic ideas to criticise Hegel's "state formalism" and calls for a "true democracy". He treats individuals and communities as products of material production and forms of intercourse. The author gives special weight to Marx's distinction between private property based on the producer's own labour and private property based on exploiting others' labour, which is said to expose the confusion behind Rousseau's position.

Zhang concludes that Marx dissolved the gap between morality and politics by locating its root in private ownership and the state that protects it. The route beyond it, in the article's account, is for the proletariat to act as the revolutionary subject. It would rebuild economic forms and social institutions, and restore "individual ownership" on the basis of associated labour. The author presents this as a scientific practical guide towards reducing the wealth gap and achieving real democracy and equality. Read the original if you are interested in the Rousseau–Hegel–Marx lineage in political philosophy, or in how Marx's property theory is used to answer the moral-political question.
quoteEn: Marx put forward a new social principle that goes beyond the principle of particularity, and thereby deeply resolved the root of the predicament of "moral politics".
quoteZh: 马克思提出了超越特殊性原则的新社会性原则，深刻破解了“道德政治”困境产生的根源

glossary.explanation: The article's term for Rousseau's project of grounding the political order in moral principle, notably the general will, in response to the split between morality and politics in modernity.
The article's label for Hegel's attempt to go beyond "moral politics" by anchoring freedom in the institutions of the ethical state (Sittlichkeit) rather than in subjective morality.
Rousseau's volonté générale, the universalised will of the community aimed at the common good, which he distinguishes from the mere sum of particular wills (the "will of all").
A phrase from Capital describing the property relation Marx expected to follow the negation of capitalist private property, based on cooperation and common possession of the means of production.

t: Reinterpreting Heidegger's practical philosophy
st: A supplement to Volpi
zh: 重解海德格尔实践哲学
zhSub: 对沃尔皮的一种补充
paras: Franco Volpi's reading of Heidegger's relation to Aristotle became a model for studying Heidegger's practical philosophy, yet Liu Mingfeng argues that Chinese scholarship has mostly introduced it without critical reflection. The article sets out Volpi's work, identifies its gaps, and offers a supplement. Liu's thesis is that Heidegger's practical philosophy begins not in the analysis of Dasein in Being and Time but in the early Freiburg 'hermeneutics of facticity', which the author holds to be a practical philosophy in its own right.

The article places Volpi within the 1960s revival of practical philosophy in Germany and follows his main works, from Heidegger e Aristotele (1984) to the 1989 essay on the homology between Being and Time and the Nicomachean Ethics. It then turns to Heidegger's 1922 'Natorp Report', the early Freiburg lectures and the 1923 course on the hermeneutics of facticity. Liu also discusses Jacques Taminiaux, Gadamer, Jean-Luc Nancy and Adorno as comparison points.

Liu credits Volpi with showing that Dasein exists first as praxis and production rather than theory, and that Heidegger 'ontologizes' Aristotle. Volpi's focus, however, falls on the Marburg period after 1923, and Volpi never takes up the hermeneutics of facticity, even after the early lectures were published. The author reads that hermeneutics as the appropriation of one's present situation through interpretation, which draws in Aristotle as a historical source. Following Gadamer's and Volpi's method of analogy, Liu compares this appropriation with Aristotelian phronesis, the choice of right action in a concrete situation. Liu adds an 'internal' argument: in the 1921–22 lectures Heidegger unites philosophy and hermeneutics as the self-interpretation of factical life, which makes philosophy itself a lived practice.

Liu concludes that the hermeneutics of facticity is a practical philosophy, but a formal one. Because it is a circle of life interpreting itself, it can offer no external guidance or norms. Its significance, in Liu's view, lies in grounding the primacy of the concrete situation and in giving ethical action an authentic orientation. Liu defends Heidegger's refusal to prescribe norms by comparing it with Adorno's view that no standard of the good life is possible in a wholly corrupt society. Read the original if you work on Heidegger, Aristotle or Gadamer and want a critique of Volpi that draws on the early Freiburg lectures.
quoteEn: We are confident in declaring that the hermeneutics of facticity is practical philosophy.
quoteZh: 我们有信心宣称实势性诠学就是实践哲学。

t: Marx and Engels's theory of civilization and its contemporary value
zh: 马克思恩格斯的文明理论及其当代价值
paras: As civilization has become a high-frequency term and a scholarly hotspot, Zhang Sanyuan argues that clarifying it requires "returning to Marx". Marx and Engels never wrote a dedicated treatise on civilization, but Zhang contends that historical materialism is itself a genuine, scientific theory of civilization. The article sets out to reconstruct that theory and show its guiding role in the civilizational logic of Chinese modernization.

The article has four parts. It first outlines four periods in the formation of the theory (from the early 1840s to Engels's late writings) and then presents five principles for interpreting it. It then sets out the theory's core content, its distinguishing features, and finally its contemporary value, drawing mainly on The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto, Capital and Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State.

Zhang holds that the five interpretive principles are the people-centred, critical, thoroughgoing, processual and holistic. The core claim is that civilization originates in "the production of the immediate means of life", develops as an open process, follows the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and has human emancipation and all-round development as its theme. Zhang argues that the theory unites the ideal with the practical, class character with humanity as a whole, criticism with construction, and system with development. In this reading it exposes capitalist civilization as a unity of civilization and barbarism, and rejects idealist, "hero" and single-line views of history in favour of multiple paths.

Zhang concludes that the theory is not outdated. In the article's account, it grounds the communist ideal, points toward a universal happy life, and supports building a community with a shared future for mankind. It also underpins confidence in civilizational self-awareness under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zhang presents Chinese modernization, through the Two Integrations, as a creative application that surpasses the capital-centred Western civilizational outlook. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese interpretation of Marx and Engels on civilization and its link to the official idea of a new form of human civilization.
quoteEn: Although Marx and Engels never wrote a dedicated treatment of civilization, their \"new worldview\" aimed at \"changing the world\", namely historical materialism, contains a rich and profound theory of civilization; one may even say that historical materialism is itself the true, scientific theory of civilization.
quoteZh: 马克思恩格斯虽然没有专门论述过文明问题，但在他们以“改造世界”为目的的“新世界观”即唯物史观中却有着丰富而深刻的文明理论，甚至可以认为，唯物史观本身就是真正的、科学的文明理论。

glossary.explanation: The official Party formulation of China's path of modernization, elaborated since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as distinct from Western modernization.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: An official phrase claiming that Chinese modernization creates a civilizational form different from and, in the official account, higher than Western modernization.
The official principle of integrating Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. The second integration was added in 2021–2023.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy and theoretical concept of global cooperation and shared interests, promoted since 2012–2013.

t: The four perspectives in the construction of Marx's theory of mental production
zh: 马克思精神生产理论建构的四重视域述论
source: School Party Building and Ideological Education (学校党建与思想教育)
paras: Bi Tianliang and Deng Chunyu take up Marx's category of "mental production" (精神生产), which he developed while building his theory of communist society and the all-round development of the human being. Existing scholarship has studied its meaning, formation, features and contemporary value; the authors argue that the theory is best grasped as a whole through the several perspectives from which Marx constructed it. Their thesis is that four perspectives together make up the theory: the division of labour, the critique of political economy, the totality of social production, and the all-round development of the person.

The article is a research essay with four numbered sections, one per perspective. It moves from a historical account of mental production under successive forms of ownership, through Marx's typology of productive and unproductive mental production against Smith, Say and List, to the place of mental production within the system of social production, and finally to its value for individual development. It closes with a short statement of the theory's present significance.

In the authors' reading, Marx grounded mental production in historical materialism by tying it to the division of labour: it became a distinct sphere once mental and material labour separated, and under capitalism it is industrialised and subordinated to capital. Drawing on the Marxian distinction, Bi and Deng present "productive" mental production as that which creates surplus value for the owner of the conditions of production (Milton's writing of Paradise Lost is the example), whereas free, "unproductive" mental production is outside capital's logic and requires disposable free time. They then argue that Marx placed mental production in a system of four kinds of production: of human beings, material goods, ideas and social relations. Material production fundamentally determines it, yet it reacts back and has relative independence and uneven development, as with art. Finally, drawing on the Grundrisse, the authors link mental production to the stages of human dependence, in which capital turns it into an instrument of surplus-value creation and of money-worship and hedonism, and to its free form as a basis for all-round human development.

The authors conclude that these four perspectives amount to the outline of Marx's theory of mental production and a weapon in establishing historical materialism. They contend that clarifying them rebuts Western scholars who reduce Marx to "economic determinism" or linear productive-force determinism. They also hold that the theory helps diagnose the "spiritual pathology" behind contemporary economic and social problems, helps people overcome spiritual crises and promotes common prosperity in spiritual life. Read the original if you want a concise systematic overview of how Marx's mental production theory is organised, and of how Chinese scholars link it to current ideological and cultural work.
quoteEn: Examining the history of mental production from the perspective of the social division of labour forms a main thread for understanding Marx's theory of mental production.
quoteZh: 从社会分工的视角考察精神生产的历史，构成了理解马克思精神生产理论的一条主线。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term for the production of ideas, consciousness and cultural products such as law, religion, philosophy, science and art. Chinese scholarship often renders it as 'spiritual production'.
A Chinese policy goal of shared wealth for all, prominent in Party discourse since the 2010s. Here it is extended to the sphere of spiritual or cultural life.

t: A political-philosophical project on war and peace: Marx's sublation of Rousseau
zh: 战争与和平的政治哲学筹划:马克思对卢梭的扬弃
source: Teaching and Research (教学与研究), 2025 no. 3
paras: Lan Yang asks how Marx's historical-materialist account of war and peace was formed through a sustained dialogue with Rousseau, and what this means for a world the author describes as undergoing deep change. The article argues that Marx sublated Rousseau's contract-theory framework: he kept its dialectical insight but moved the analysis from human nature and the state to the capital logic of modern society.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Rousseau's treatment of war and peace in four steps: the roots of war in human nature, the paradoxical condition of the state, possible routes to peace, and the evaluation of wars. The second sets out four ways in which Marx criticised and went beyond this model. The third draws out the contemporary implications of that sublation, ending with a reference to Xi Jinping's call for a community with a shared future for mankind.

In Lan's reading, Rousseau traced war to private property rather than to human greed and proposed peace through republics, ultimately small ones, and defensive alliances. Lan calls this a state-centred approach resting on an abstract view of human nature. Marx replaced the abstract natural individual with the real individual in material production, so that war becomes the intensified form of power relations arising from modes of production and distribution. Marx also treated the state paradox as an expression of civil society's divisions and located the antagonisms of the modern world in the logic of capital. Lan identifies three forms: class opposition, a hierarchical international structure, and recurrent struggles for hegemony. They correspond to class wars, colonial wars and wars of hegemony. Political emancipation alone cannot end the cycle of war and peace, so Marx pointed to abolishing private ownership of the means of production and a free association of individuals, with socialist forces as the practical route. He also replaced general moral condemnation with criteria for distinguishing just from unjust wars.

Lan draws three lessons. Conflicts need historical, totalising analysis rather than abstract concepts such as human nature, the state or "universal values". Hegemonism remains the main obstacle to peace, and Lan cites protectionism and trade wars used by a few countries against emerging ones. A new international political and economic order that breaks the "centre–periphery" pattern is urgently needed. Lan presents building a community with a shared future for mankind as the practical outcome and as the world-historical significance of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Rousseau and Marx on international relations, and an example of how such theory is tied to current Chinese foreign-policy language.
quoteEn: Marx held that war in fact originates in the relational structures and patterns of distribution that real human beings form in the process of material production.
quoteZh: 马克思认为战争实际上源自现实的人在物质生产过程中所形成的关系结构和分配模式。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny for humankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for cooperative, multilateral international relations and shared security and development.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's long-term national goal of restoring China's strength and international standing, central to Xi Jinping's political discourse.
The Chinese rendering of Hegel's Aufhebung: to negate something while preserving and elevating its valid elements.
A term from Marx and Engels's German Ideology for people understood through their actual material activity and social relations, as opposed to abstract human nature.

t: The historical-materialist road to "universal world history"
zh: 通向“普遍的世界历史”的唯物史观之路
paras: Wu Hongzheng asks what "universal world history" (universal history) means in Kant, Hegel and Marx, and what the concept offers for Marxist world-history theory in the twenty-first century. The article argues that Marx broke with the idealist versions of the concept. In Marx's historical materialism, universal world history is communism, reached through "universal intercourse" that sublates the particular interests of single nation-states and the barriers between civilizations. Wu presents this as a theoretical basis for the new categories of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, namely a community with a shared future for mankind, a new form of human civilization and common values of all humanity.

The article has three parts. The first compares the three thinkers' answers to the question of where the world and humanity are heading. Kant's answer is contractarian: a cosmopolitan constitution and a league of nations for perpetual peace. Hegel's is theodicy: the absolute spirit moves from the Oriental to the Germanic world. Marx's answer is materialist and aims at human liberation. The second part sets out Marx's critique of idealism, drawing mainly on The German Ideology. The third part gives the principles of universal world history as Marx understood it.

Wu's central claim is that idealist universal history has only the form of universality, not its substance. For Wu, the "thought in the form of universality" is the ruling ideology of a class or nation that presents its particular interests as common ones. Wu argues that today "universal values" play this role: unilateralism, zero-sum thinking and de-globalization are pursued under their cover. Marx located the real ruler of world history in capital and in the "domination–subordination" relations of production it creates, which grew out of manufacture and merchant capital. Wu draws three conditions from Marx. First, a "universal class", the proletariat, must form, and this is how the cyclical pattern of one particular class replacing another can be escaped. Second, the productive forces must develop to a high level, so that universal intercourse becomes possible. Third, the domination–subordination relations must be broken, as with the town–country opposition, and private ownership must disappear.

Wu concludes that Marx's path shows how humanity can sublate national particular interests and build cooperative, win-win relations of intercourse. In Wu's view, "building a community with a shared future for mankind" is the new content that twenty-first-century Marxism gives to universal world history. If states build win-win relations of production on the basis of common values of all humanity, Wu argues, humanity can partly escape the capital-dominated order and move towards communism. Read the original if you want a Marxist philosophy-of-history reading of Kant, Hegel and Marx that links "universal values" and the community with a shared future for mankind to Marx's critique of ideology.
quoteEn: Under capitalist private ownership, people are ruled less by the "abstract domination of ideas" than by the "abstract domination of capital".
quoteZh: 在资本主义私有制下，与其说是人们受到“观念的抽象统治”，毋宁说是人们受到“资本的抽象统治”。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping has promoted since 2012–2013 as the Chinese vision for international relations and global governance.
A formula introduced by Xi Jinping in 2015 (peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom). Official discourse presents it as an alternative to Western "universal values".

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A phrase used in official discourse since 2021 to describe the civilizational significance of Chinese modernization.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and two opposed conceptions of rights
zh: 马克思的《黑格尔法哲学批判》与两种对立的权利观
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 6
paras: Wang Xueqiao asks what Marx's unfinished and unpublished manuscript Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right shows when read through the question of rights. The article argues that the manuscript is organised around two opposed conceptions: a state-based conception of rights, represented by Hegel, and a civil-society-based conception, which Marx establishes by overturning Hegel. Although the critique appears to concern rights at the level of the state, Wang holds that its direct purpose is to ground rights in civil society. On this reading it opens the construction of Marx's historical-materialist conception of rights.

The article has four parts. The first distinguishes the two conceptions and notes that the German Recht, rendered in Chinese as law, right, rights and statute, should not be reduced to law, since many economic rights in civil society do not take legal form. The second examines Marx's critique of Hegel on monarchical, executive and legislative power. The third traces how this critique led to the historical-materialist conception of rights, drawing on the 1859 Preface, The German Ideology and Critique of the Gotha Programme. A short conclusion follows.

Wang's central claim is that the separation of civil society from the state makes the two conceptions possible, and that the key question is which kind of right is more fundamental. Hegel, in Wang's account, starts from the logical Idea and treats the state as the actuality of the ethical Idea. Marx reverses this: family and civil society are the presuppositions of the state, and rights arise from the 'material relations of life' rather than from the state or from a social contract, which Wang says distinguishes him from Rousseau. Wang then draws three consequences. Rights are legitimate only through their basis in civil society. The gap between rights that ought to exist and rights actually held can only be understood from civil society and property relations. The historical development of rights follows the forms of the division of labour and of ownership.

Wang concludes that Marx's reading directs inquiry into the basis of rights to civil society, and that establishing the civil-society-based conception was the theoretical precondition for his historical-materialist theory of rights. Wang adds that Marx's notion of civil society widened from the narrow sense of bourgeois society to the whole of human history, so that his view of rights is not confined to the bourgeois case. Read the original if you study Marx's early critique of Hegel, the philosophy of rights, or how Chinese legal scholars link the 1843 manuscript to historical materialism.
quoteEn: The establishment of the civil-society-based conception of rights was the theoretical precondition for the construction of Marx's historical-materialist conception of rights.
quoteZh: 基于市民社会的权利观的确立是马克思的历史唯物主义权利观得以构建的理论前提。

t: Generative AI and a new field of inquiry into the value movement of digital capitalism
zh: 生成式人工智能和数字资本主义价值运动新论域
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 1
paras: Huang Zaisheng asks how generative AI, of which ChatGPT is the best-known example, reshapes the value movement of digital capitalism: its production, realisation and distribution of value. Working in a Marxist political-economy framework, the article argues that a form of "AI capitalism" is beginning to emerge. In Huang's account, generative AI produces abundant digital wealth, but under what the author calls "Silicon Valley private ownership" it also sharpens the inherent contradictions of the system.

The article is organised around four sets of questions. It examines commodity production and consumption, the labour process under human–machine collaboration, capital accumulation under competition among large models, and threats to the capitalist order of production. It draws on Marx's discussions of machinery, the relative surplus population and accumulation, and on examples including GPT-3, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Midjourney and crowdsourcing platforms.

Huang makes three main moves. First, generative AI opens a new stage of digital production: synthetic data eases data scarcity, pre-trained large models generalise machine productivity, and AI-generated content automates content creation. Digital capital thereby gains what the author calls exclusive ownership of "means of cognition". Second, human–machine collaboration changes digital labour unevenly. Unpaid user labour gains in value, crowdsourcing splits into a threatened micro-labour segment and a better-rewarded creative one, and platform workers gain somewhat better conditions. Meanwhile large models are said to create "surplus proletarians" and entrench oligopoly through a "computing-power monopoly". Third, accelerating AI undermines the conditions of capitalist order. It erodes digital capital's "spatio-temporal fix" and the absorption of living labour, and it strains the copyright regime that secures the value of knowledge commodities. It also intensifies conflict between platform firms and bourgeois states over power and ideology.

Huang concludes that smart machines do not end digital labour, since collaboration frees people for more creative work. Yet the author holds that the contradictions of digital capitalism are becoming harder to reconcile. Only by going beyond the logic of capital, fundamentally changing the platform system and exploring the construction of "digital socialism" can AI benefit all and digital labour be liberated. Read the original if you want a Marxist political-economy reading of large models that covers commodities, labour, accumulation and state–capital power, together with a Chinese academic view of AI capitalism.
quoteEn: Only by going beyond the logic of capital, thoroughly transforming the platform system of digital capitalism and exploring the construction of digital socialism can AI benefits for all and the liberation of digital labour be truly realised.
quoteZh: 只有超越资本逻辑，彻底变革数字资本主义平台体制，探索建设数字社会主义，才能真正实现AI普惠和数字劳动解放。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese and international Marxist scholarship for capitalism organised around data, digital platforms and algorithms. Here it is the object of analysis rather than an official category.
The author's label for an emerging stage of digital capitalism in which production, exchange and distribution are increasingly run by AI systems.
A concept associated with David Harvey: capital relieves overaccumulation crises by expanding geographically and deferring returns over time. The article applies it to digital capital.
The author's term for workers made redundant by AI-driven automation, linked to Marx's idea of the relative surplus population.
The article's name for a socialist alternative to platform-based digital capitalism. It is not defined in detail.

t: A reading of the final part of Capital: "Revenues and their sources"
zh: 《资本论》终篇“各种收入及其源泉”读解
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2025 no. 3
paras: Marking the 130th anniversary of the publication of Volume III of Capital and of Engels's death (1895), Gu Hailiang offers a close reading of Part VII of Volume III, "Revenues and their sources". Gu argues that this part is the closing part not only of Volume III but of all three theoretical volumes of Capital, and that it gathers the logic of the whole work.

The article traces the theme chronologically and then by topic. It begins with Marx's first treatment in the 1861–63 manuscripts and his shift of Volume III's theme from "capital and profit" to the configurations of the process as a whole. It then follows Part VII chapter by chapter: the trinity formula, the analysis of the production process, the "semblance of competition", production and distribution relations, and the classes. It ends with three general points on the significance of Part VII as a conclusion.

Gu's central reasoning is that wages, profit, interest and rent appear to spring from labour, capital and land, but that ownership of these factors only entitles owners to shares in a value already created. In Gu's account, all such revenues are transformed shares of surplus-value, which is the product of unpaid labour by wage-workers. Total surplus-value sets the limit on the sum of profit, interest and rent. Distribution relations, Gu stresses, are the reverse side of production relations and share their historical and transitory character. The classes of wage-workers, capitalists and landowners are defined by what they own. Gu also reads Part VII as completing the move from the abstraction of the "direct production process" to the concrete forms of capital in the process as a whole, and as extending the labour theory of value and the theory of surplus-value: the dual character of labour, the organic composition of capital, realisation in reproduction, and the transformation of value into prices of production.

Gu concludes that Part VII reveals how the mystified forms of revenue conceal the real source of value and surplus-value, and that it brings Capital's theoretical logic to completion. The reading also credits Engels's editorial work on the unfinished manuscripts, including the short opening of the final chapter on classes. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Marx's manuscripts of 1861–65 lead into Part VII and how a Chinese Marxist economist interprets its place in Capital.
quoteEn: The reading of Part VII of Volume III above shows that it is not only the "final part" of Volume III but the "final part" of the three theoretical volumes of Capital.
quoteZh: 以上对《资本论》第三卷第七篇的解读说明第七篇不只是第三卷的“终篇”，更是《资本论》理论部分三卷的“终篇”。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term in Capital Volume III for the vulgar-economic scheme land–rent, capital–interest, labour–wages, in which each factor appears to generate its own revenue. Marx treats it as a mystified surface form of capitalist relations.

glossary.en: configurations of the process as a whole
glossary.literal: the forms/configurations of the total process
glossary.explanation: Marx's formulation of the theme of Volume III, in which production and circulation are considered together. It includes the concrete forms capital takes, such as industrial, commercial and interest-bearing capital and landed property.

t: Platform capitalism and the industrial reserve army
zh: 平台资本主义与产业后备军
source: Contemporary Chinese Marxism Studies (当代中国马克思主义研究), 2024 no. 2
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the Brazilian scholar Ildeli Colombini (the Chinese name is a transliteration; the original spelling is uncertain). It asks how work organised through digital platforms should be understood in Marx's terms. The author argues that existing research is largely descriptive or too broad, and so misses new concrete forms of the subsumption of labour and of the formation of the industrial reserve army.

The article has four parts. It first surveys the literature on platform work, from the uncritical "sharing economy" to critical notions such as uberization, on-demand work and platform capitalism. Two theoretical sections follow, on formal and real subsumption and on the reserve army, drawing on Capital and Marx's unpublished sixth chapter. A conclusion closes the piece. Examples range from ride-hailing and delivery (Uber, Ifood, Loggi) to engineering, design and care platforms (Turing, Upwork, Care.com).

Colombini makes two central moves. First, platforms produce surplus value rather than a feudal-style rent, as the "digital feudalism" thesis holds. Formal subsumption arises because self-employed drivers, designers and programmers are separated from the conditions of their work. Real subsumption arises through algorithmic management, which extends and intensifies work, individualises tasks and pay, hides its rules from workers, and uses user ratings to push competition and "subordinate self-management".

Second, because workers return to the market after each task, platforms fold the reserve army into active work itself. The author calls this a new sub-category of Marx's floating reserve army, with competitive pressure constant rather than cyclical. This also internalises the struggles of the unemployed, which may unite employed and reserve workers and explain the rise in platform-worker organising. Colombini stresses this is only a possible new fissure, as platform owners seek new ways to split the two groups. Read the original if you want a Marxist account of platform labour built on subsumption and the reserve army, set against "digital feudalism" and precarity theories.
quoteEn: Digital platforms no longer strictly separate employed workers from the reserve army but merge the two, because after each task workers must again look for work to earn what they need to live.
quoteZh: 数字平台不再严格区分在职工人和后备军，而是将这两类工人合并在一起，因为在每次活动结束后，工人都会再次寻找工作，以获得维持生计所需的报酬。

t: The historical basis of production and the logical starting point of exchange: on the research and presentation processes in Marx's theory of the value-form
zh: 生产的历史基础与交换的逻辑开端：基于马克思价值形式理论研究与叙述过程的探讨
paras: Li Qiankun takes up a dispute over whether production or exchange has priority in Marx's critique of political economy. Since the second half of the twentieth century, the author notes, Western left theory has given exchange discourse logical priority and has tried to replace Marxism's categories of production with it. This is most visible in the New Reading of Marx and the New Dialectics school. Li argues that in the process of research Marx uncovered production as the historical basis of exchange, but in the process of presentation of the capitalist mode of production he made exchange the logical starting point. Together, Li holds, these two processes make up the distinctive method of Marx's theory of the value-form.

The article has three parts. The first surveys the turn from production to exchange in Western Marxism and Marxology (Lukács, Gramsci, Korsch, the Frankfurt School), in value-form schools (Backhaus, Reichelt, the Uno school, the Regulation school, Rancière, Arthur), and in Habermas and Baudrillard. The second traces Marx's treatment of money from On the Jewish Question through the 1844 manuscripts, the Grundrisse, the 1859 Contribution and the 1861–63 manuscripts. The third reads the opening of Capital, and the conclusion discusses Heinrich and Foucault.

Li argues that the early and middle Marx still explained money through exchange, private property and the division of labour, and left the theory of the dual character of labour and surplus value separate from the theory of value and money. In Li's account, the theories of average profit and prices of production in the 1861–63 manuscripts joined these lines. The commodity that results from capitalist production contains paid and unpaid labour, so its value cannot be measured directly and must take the money form. Li then argues that Capital still begins with exchange for three reasons: the commodity form is the cell form of bourgeois society, value can appear only through exchange relations, and the analysis of money becoming capital requires exchange, because exchange creates no value and so points to labour-power as the special commodity. Marx himself, Li notes, called this a 'circle' in the presentation.

Li concludes that the historical priority of production and the logical priority of exchange express Marx's unity of the logical and the historical, and reflect the character of capitalism itself. Production carries contradiction and antagonism, while exchange supplies a formal, normative appearance. Li says that Western approaches that start from exchange, with Heinrich as the typical case, keep the logic of presentation but lose history, and risk ending up confirming capitalism's validity. Read the original if you work on the New Reading of Marx, value-form theory or the relation between Marx's research method and his method of presentation, and want a Chinese philosophical rejoinder with close textual reference to Marx's manuscripts.
quoteEn: In the course of Marx's research for the critique of political economy, it was production, not exchange, that formed the entire foundation of his intellectual framework.
quoteZh: 在马克思的政治经济学批判研究过程中，是生产而非交换，构成了其思想构架的全部基础。

glossary.explanation: Marx's analysis, in the first chapter of Capital, of how the value of a commodity must be expressed in another commodity and finally in money. It is central to the New Reading of Marx and related schools.

A West German current from the 1960s (Backhaus, Reichelt) that reads Marx's critique of political economy as a theory of value and social form. It stresses the value-form and exchange over a production-centred reading.
An Anglophone and German current (including Christopher Arthur) that reads Capital as a systematic dialectic of categories, in which the exposition proceeds logically rather than historically.

glossary.en: unity of the logical and the historical
glossary.explanation: A methodological principle in Chinese Marxist philosophy, drawn from Engels and Hegel. It holds that the order of categories in a theory corresponds to, without simply copying, real historical development.

t: Opening up a new realm for the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
zh: 开拓中国特色社会主义政治经济学新境界
paras: Writing in the People's Daily on 3 April 2025, Zhang Yu, a professor at Renmin University of China, takes up the newly published first volume of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping. The article argues that Xi Jinping's economic thought is the latest achievement of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. In Zhang's reading, it opens a new realm for that discipline and marks a new leap in adapting Marxist political economy to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The piece first traces the Party's handling of Marxist political economy from Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then sets out Xi's requirements for developing a contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy, lists the concepts Zhang counts as original contributions, and describes the theory as a systematic whole. It closes by presenting the thought as having universal and global significance.

Zhang's central claim is that Xi's thought answers a new question of the era: how to uphold and develop a socialist economy so as to achieve more efficient, fairer, more sustainable and safer development. He lists as original contributions the Party's overall leadership of economic work, the people-centred development philosophy, the new development philosophy, high-quality development, new quality productive forces, the basic socialist economic system, the new development pattern, and balancing development with security. Zhang says the system has a clear structure: high-quality development is its theme, and the people-centred philosophy is its main thread. He also contends that Xi's guidance on drawing on Western economics only selectively, and not copying its ideological content, lays the basis for an autonomous Chinese body of economic knowledge.

Zhang concludes that Xi's economic thought is both the Marxist political economy of contemporary China and that of the twenty-first-century world. As examples of principles with general validity, he cites the people-centred philosophy, Chinese modernization, and a community with a shared future for mankind. He adds that Chinese modernization breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization. He calls on Chinese Communists to answer the questions of China, the world, the people and the times, and so to keep enriching Marxist political economy. Read the original if you want an official-line account, from a leading Renmin University economist, of how Xi's economic thought is placed within Marxist political economy and presented as a Chinese contribution to it.
quoteEn: Xi Jinping's economic thought is the Marxist political economy of contemporary China, with distinct Chinese characteristics, and also the Marxist political economy of the twenty-first-century world, with major global significance.
quoteZh: 习近平经济思想是当代中国的马克思主义政治经济学，具有鲜明的中国特色，也是21世纪世界的马克思主义政治经济学，具有重大的世界意义

glossary.explanation: The body of economic ideas and policy principles attributed to Xi Jinping since 2012, officially treated as a component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学
glossary.pinyin: Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì zhèngzhì jīngjìxué
glossary.en: political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The official name for the theoretical system that generalises China's reform-era economic practice within a Marxist framework. Xi Jinping promoted the term after 2012.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义政治经济学中国化时代化
glossary.pinyin: Mǎkèsī zhǔyì zhèngzhì jīngjìxué Zhōngguóhuà shídàihuà
glossary.en: adapting Marxist political economy to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxist theory to China's conditions and to contemporary developments, here applied to political economy.
A concept Xi Jinping introduced in 2023–24, referring to advanced productivity driven by high technology, high efficiency and high quality.
The official description of China's economic stage since around 2017, which shifts the emphasis from speed of growth to quality, efficiency and sustainability.
The official term for China's own path to modernization, led by the Communist Party and promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's slogan for China's vision of international relations and global governance.

t: Marx's critique of Western-centrism and its implications
zh: 马克思对西方中心论的批判及其启示
paras: Some Western scholars, especially on the left, now claim that Marxism is itself a typical case of Western-centrism. Andre Gunder Frank, in ReOrient, is the example Yang Shengping gives. Yang argues the opposite: historical materialism and Marx's theory of world history are the most fundamental and thorough critique of Western-centrism, though Marx's own thinking took time to free itself from its traces. Yang also draws lessons for cultural construction in China today.

The article has three parts. The first defines Western-centrism and shows why historical materialism undermines it. The second traces how Marx's critique developed, dividing his work after historical materialism into stages: before the 1850s, the 1850s and 1860s, and the 1870s until his death. The third turns to present-day implications, covering cultural subjectivity, cultural advancement and cultural national character. Long endnotes add textual evidence and conceptual clarifications.

Yang separates Western-centrism as a view of history, as political and value stance, and as a mode of thinking and discourse. Marx's materialist basis in modes of production, the author says, removes the first two, but the third persists. Yang reads Marx's early writings on India and China, which relied on Western sources, as bearing some such traces, for example the 'stagnant East' and the absence of private property. Yang holds that Marx's later work on the dual nature of the Russian village commune corrected these. Against readings that make Marx's late Russian path 'unrelated' to the West, Yang argues that this risks an 'anti-Western-centric Western-centrism'. In Yang's account the two paths, capitalist and leapfrogging, are linked. A leap past capitalism depends on Western capitalist development and on absorbing its advanced achievements, and the 'central' position of advanced countries shifts over time.

Yang concludes that criticising Western-centrism is a means, not an end, and that the aim is theory able to guide China's development. Social institutions can be leapt over, Yang says, but productive forces cannot, so learning from advanced capitalist countries is indispensable. Cultural subjectivity should be built first on cultural advancement rather than national character. It should avoid narrow nationalism and take selectively from all excellent cultures, since Western modes of thinking and discourse partly reflect real regularities. Yang describes the aim as fusing advanced culture with national character, with Marxism as scientific theory in the lead, in line with the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of the claim that Marx was Eurocentric, or want to see how that rebuttal is tied to current debates on cultural subjectivity and an autonomous knowledge system.
quoteEn: Therefore, in constructing cultural subjectivity, what must be considered first is cultural advancement, not cultural national character.
quoteZh: 因此，文化主体性的建构首先应该考虑的是文化先进性，而不是文化民族性。

glossary.explanation: Formula associated with Xi Jinping: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities (the first) and with China's fine traditional culture (the second).

t: Constructing a systematic doctrine of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy
zh: 构建了当代中国马克思主义政治经济学系统学说
paras: Writing in the People's Daily on the publication of the first volume of Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping, Pang Jinju argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party leadership has built a systematic doctrine of contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy, which took shape as Xi Jinping Thought on the economy. The commentary presents the 74-item volume as an authoritative textbook and as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The piece has three parts. It first frames the opening up of new horizons for contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy, a call first made in November 2015, as a revolution in twenty-first-century economics. It then turns to guiding economic research with Xi's economic thought in order to build an independent Chinese system of economic knowledge. Finally it reports on two new textbooks, on political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics, compiled by teams at Renmin University and Nankai University.

Pang contends that Western economics has long held a monopoly, that Marxist political economy has at times been marginalised or emptied of content even in China, and that Chinese economics still struggles to make its case heard. Against this background and the new round of technological revolution, the author holds that an independent knowledge system is required. It must combine Marxist principles with Chinese realities and traditional culture, avoid empty or label-like exposition, and rest on core categories such as the basic socialist economic system, the new development philosophy and high-quality development. From the textbook work Pang draws two lessons: keep pace with the Party's theoretical innovation, and stay grounded in the practice of socialist economic construction.

Pang concludes that economists should keep studying Xi's economic thought, use the Selected Economic Writings well and speed up building the independent system of knowledge. Read the original if you want a brief example of how an academic economist presents the official programme for Chinese economics and its textbooks.
quoteEn: Continually opening up new horizons for contemporary Chinese Marxist political economy is a revolution in twenty-first-century Chinese economics and indeed in world economics.
quoteZh: 不断开拓当代中国马克思主义政治经济学新境界，是21世纪中国经济学乃至世界经济学的一场革命。

glossary.explanation: A framework announced in 2015 stressing innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared development. It is used as a guide to economic policy.
An official goal of the economy since the late 2010s, emphasising quality, efficiency and sustainability over pure growth speed.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on the economy
glossary.explanation: The official body of economic ideas attributed to Xi Jinping, treated as a component of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义政治经济学中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for adapting Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and to contemporary developments.

glossary.zh: 社会主义基本经济制度
glossary.explanation: The official term for China's economic structure: public ownership as the mainstay alongside diverse forms of ownership, distribution according to work, and the socialist market economy.

keywords: Selected Economic Writings of Xi Jinping

t: The inner logic of Marx's view of civilisation and its Chinese context
zh: 马克思文明观的内在逻辑与中国语境
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2025 no. 2
paras: Zang asks how Marx understood "civilisation" and what this understanding offers for creating a new form of human civilisation today. The article argues that Marx grounded the emergence and development of culture and civilisation in material production and the basic contradictions of society. From this, Zang says, one can reconstruct a coherent inner logic of civilisation that bears on Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first surveys Marx's uses of the term from his early journalism and the 1843 critique of Hegel's philosophy of right through the 1844 manuscripts, The German Ideology, The Poverty of Philosophy, the Communist Manifesto, the economic manuscripts of 1857–63, Capital and the Morgan excerpts. The second organises these remarks into four dimensions. The third turns to Marx's writings on China, notably the Opium Wars, and then to China's present.

Zang's core claim is that, for Marx, civilisation is a historically relative stage of development resting on the level of the productive forces and forms of ownership. Its progress is driven by material production, and it carries an antagonistic structure: the free time of some rests on the surplus labour of others. The article stresses a double aspect of capital's civilising role. Capital greatly advances productive forces, yet it estranges people from their own essence, so that the more civilised the workers' product, the more barbarous the workers. Marx therefore measures civilisation by human development and looks to an "association of free individuals". On China, Zang reads Marx as condemning Western aggression, as treating a closed, stagnant "semi-civilised" empire as vulnerable, and as expecting revolution to renew Chinese civilisation along a path distinct from Europe's.

Zang concludes that, in the Chinese context, Marxism combined with the country's own conditions and its fine traditional culture has revived Chinese civilisation. Chinese modernization, the author argues, creates a cultural form unlike one dominated by the logic of capital and rejects both civilisational superiority and clash-of-civilisations theories. Zang cites the Global Civilization Initiative and the 2024 UN resolution on an international day of dialogue among civilizations. The author presents these as steps towards the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, a new form of human civilisation and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a text-based survey of Marx's remarks on civilisation and of how Chinese theorists link them to current civilisational discourse.
quoteEn: Marx measured the degree of civilisation by the state of human development and progress, presenting the future of civilisation as a picture of people's free and all-round development, a picture that embodies the realisation of human emancipation.
quoteZh: 马克思以人的发展进步状况衡量文明程度，将文明的未来展现为人的自由与全面发展的图景，这种文明发展的未来图景体现为人的解放的实现。

glossary.explanation: The official Party-state term for China's own path to modernisation, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models of modernisation.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilisation
glossary.explanation: An official formulation, used from Xi Jinping's 2021 speeches onwards, for the civilisational form that Chinese modernization is said to create.
A proposal announced by Xi Jinping in 2023. It calls for respecting the diversity of civilisations and for exchange and mutual learning among them.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-term national goal in Party discourse, associated with the Chinese Dream and often tied to the mid-twenty-first century.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept of international relations, promoted since 2012–13, stressing shared interests and cooperation among states.

t: The "Locke factor" in the construction of Marx's thought
st: The critique of the "theory of innate ideas" as an example
zh: 马克思思想建构中的“洛克因素”
zhSub: 以对“天赋观念论”的批判为例
paras: Nie Jinfang asks how John Locke shaped the formation of Marx's philosophy, which Marx called the "new materialism", "modern materialism" or "new philosophy". Nie argues that Locke "took part" in Marx's intellectual development, so that Marx's thought contains many "Locke factors". Existing scholarship, in the author's view, has treated the topic only in abstract, general terms, without systematic work on specific texts.

The article is one part of a larger comparison of Locke and Marx. Other parts would cover labour ownership and the labour theory of value, and liberal political theory and the "association of free individuals". Using a "textology" method, it takes only Book I of Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding, the critique of innate ideas, and traces its "traces" through Marx's doctoral dissertation, the Rheinische Zeitung and Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher writings, the 1844 manuscripts, The Holy Family and The German Ideology. Its four sections deal with innate principles, universal assent, the appeal to reason, and the testing of particular ideas against social history.

Nie's central claim is one of inheritance and surpassing. Locke denies that principles are innate through largely logical argument, and Marx accepts the conclusion but grounds it in the real conditions of capitalist society. Marx reduces religion to worldly conditions and replaces Locke's abstract rebuttal of universal assent with historical analysis of the Jewish question. That analysis yields a ladder of "political emancipation", "social emancipation" and "human emancipation". Marx also applies "reason" to the structure of capital in the Paris manuscripts, and treats identity, mathematical axioms and "substance" (the Holy Family critique of the speculative "Fruit") as products of practice and history. The article also stresses Locke's influence on French materialism, as Marx describes it.

Nie concludes that Marx replaced the "innate principle" of ideas with a "principle of reality", removed idealist accounts of where ideas come from, and found practical routes by which ideas arise and develop. In this reading, Marx's development was not just a succession of idealism, materialism and new materialism, but a gradual search within the frameworks of subject and object, spirit and matter, and idea and reality. The Locke case shows, for Nie, the inseparable link between Marxism and the Western intellectual tradition. Read the original if you study Marx's relationship to British empiricism and the Enlightenment, or want a text-based example of Chinese Marxist documentary scholarship.
quoteEn: Clearly, compared with Locke's abstract refutation of the "theory of universal assent", Marx's analysis, set within particular eras, regions and classes, is far more powerful and profound.
quoteZh: 显然，较之于洛克对“普遍同意说”的抽象驳斥，马克思置于时代、地域、阶层中的分析要有力得多、深刻得多。

t: How Marxist political economy surpasses Robbins's economic philosophy
zh: 马克思主义政治经济学对罗宾斯经济哲学思想的超越
source: Political Economy Research (政治经济学研究), 2024 no. 4
paras: Marx defined the object of Capital as the capitalist mode of production and its attendant relations of production and exchange. The British economist Lionel Robbins rejected this kind of definition and formally proposed the 'scarcity' definition of economics. Zhu and Guo ask how Robbins's economic philosophy compares with Marx's, and argue that Marxist political economy surpasses it on two counts: the dialectic of matter and consciousness, and the dialectic of ends and means.

The article first criticises Robbins's reading of historical materialism as an 'economic view of history', then examines his treatment of ends and means. It draws mainly on Robbins's Lectures on the History of Economic Thought from the London School of Economics, on his remarks about the 'rational economic man', and on Marx and Engels's account of social being and social consciousness. It closes with lessons for contemporary Chinese economics.

On the first count, the authors say Robbins calls Marx's materialism 'crude' because it supposedly ignores human needs and purposes. In their reading, Robbins is attacking old, metaphysical materialism, so he misreads Marx, whose dialectical materialism sublated old materialism and idealism. They add that Marx, and Engels's 'parallelogram of forces', rejected economic determinism, since class struggle and ideology also shape history. On the second count, they argue that Robbins treats ends as given and economics as neutral about them. In their view, those ends rest on the assumption of private ownership and the pursuit of surplus value. Marxist political economy instead aims at common prosperity and the free and all-round development of the human being. They also hold that Marxism studies the mode of production, while Western economics studies resource allocation, which is subordinate to that mode.

The authors conclude that Robbins grasped some links between matter and consciousness and between ends and means but stayed at a naive dialectic, which shows some common ground with Marxism. They propose that his scarcity definition be dialectically sublated and absorbed into Marxist political economy. This would serve the building of an autonomous Chinese system of economic knowledge, guided by Xi Jinping's economic thought and the Two Integrations. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese Marxist economists engage Western economic methodology and the definition of economics.
quoteEn: The object of Marxist political economy is the mode of production, whereas Western economics mainly studies resource allocation, and the way resources are allocated falls under the category of the mode of production and is influenced and constrained by it.
quoteZh: 马克思主义政治经济学的研究对象是生产方式，西方经济学的研究对象主要是资源配置问题，而资源配置方式从属于生产方式范畴受其影响和制约。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party theory, stressed by Xi Jinping, for combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
The body of economic ideas attributed to Xi Jinping, presented in official discourse as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
A Hegelian-Marxist term (Aufhebung) meaning to negate while preserving and elevating the rational elements of what is negated.
A socialist goal in official discourse of prosperity shared by all, emphasised under Xi Jinping.

t: Digital commodities, digital labour and digital capital in the view of contemporary Western left-wing scholars
st: An analysis based on Marxist political economy
zh: 当代西方左翼学者视域中的数字商品、数字劳动和数字资本
zhSub: 基于马克思主义政治经济学的辨析
paras: Western left-wing scholars treat digital commodities, digital labour and digital capital as the core elements of digital capitalism, yet Xu Yanru argues that they use these categories loosely and without consensus. The article returns to Marx's critique of political economy to ask whether data is a commodity, whether non-wage digital labour is productive labour, and why digital capital counts as capital. Xu's thesis is that these phenomena amount to a digital "reform" of capital's movement, not a "revolution" in value movement.

The article surveys three schools: communication political economy (Mosco, Christian Fuchs, Dan Schiller), Italian autonomism (Hardt, Negri) and left accelerationism (Srnicek, Williams). Alongside them it discusses Smythe's audience commodity, Terranova's free labour, Ritzer's prosumption, Zuboff and Varoufakis. It has three parts, each setting out how the concept was introduced and then criticising it from Marx's value theory.

On commodities, Xu holds that Mosco and Fuchs conflate raw user data, which is a means of production or consumption, with the digital commodity. Only data processed by living labour, such as that of full-time digital workers, acquires value. On labour, Xu classes full-time digital work and flexible work (gig, crowdsourcing, outsourcing) as productive wage labour, since the latter involves concealed employment and produces absolute and relative surplus value. Users' unpaid prosumption is not productive labour, because it creates no surplus value and aims at use-value.

On capital, Xu argues that Schiller, Fuchs, Srnicek and Varoufakis start from digital capital as a given. They ignore the historical premise of the relation between dead and living labour, and so separate the form of capital's movement from its content. They also treat digital capital as independent of functioning capital and interest-bearing capital. In Xu's account, platform, cloud and advertising platforms fall under commercial, industrial or interest-bearing capital, and are largely controlled by financial capital. Digital capital is therefore a digital stage of capital's total movement, not a separate form, and Xu sees analyses that reify categories as still caught in metaphysics. Read the original if you want a Marxist-orthodox critique of Fuchs, Srnicek and the autonomists on the value status of data and platform labour.
quoteEn: Whether digital capital, cloud capital or platform capital, none of them goes beyond the operating logic of functioning capital and interest-bearing capital.
quoteZh: 数字资本、云资本还是平台资本，它们都没有超出职能资本和生息资本的运作逻辑

t: Translation, dissemination and initial application of Marxism in Tianyi and Hengbao
zh: 《天义•衡报》对马克思主义的译介传播与初步运用
paras: Marxism and anarchism both reached China in the early twentieth century as socialist doctrines, and anarchist journals played a real part in Marxism's early spread. Li Yingrui examines the anarchist periodicals Tianyi and Hengbao, which Liu Shipei and He Zhen ran in Japan in 1907–1908. The article argues that, although the papers served anarchist propaganda, they objectively advanced the early dissemination of Marxism in China, while also showing clear limits in how its editors understood it.

The article has three parts. The first reviews what the journals published and how the editors glossed it: He Zhen's excerpts from the Communist Manifesto and from Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, Min Ming's translations of the Manifesto and its 1888 English preface, and Liu Shipei's excerpt from Engels's Socialism: Utopian and Scientific. The second part looks at how Liu and others applied class struggle theory and a theory of surplus value to Chinese questions. The third assesses the journals' significance and limitations.

Li makes several claims about the translations. The journals began full-text translation of Marxist works into Chinese. Liu's preface to the Manifesto is described as the first Chinese preface to a Marxist work, and the Hengbao excerpt is said to be the earliest known Chinese rendering of part of Socialism: Utopian and Scientific, earlier than the 1912 version scholars usually cite. Li also argues that a full Chinese Manifesto was probably completed, though no copy has been found. On application, Liu and others criticised the capitalist state and the 'false civilisation' of capitalism, attacked imperialism, and rejected both anti-Manchu revolution and constitutional monarchy as capitalist paths. They analysed Chinese classes, including a first call for a worker–peasant alliance. Li also credits their effort to explain Marxism in Chinese idiom and to find precedents for communism in Chinese tradition, but calls Liu's equation of ancient well-field and shared-property practices with communism a mistake.

Li concludes that Tianyi and Hengbao helped prepare Chinese revolutionaries to accept Marxism and contributed to its adaptation to Chinese conditions. Subjectively, though, the editors treated Marxism only as a 'supplement' or footnote to anarchism. In Li's account, they read class mainly in political and power terms. They also misread the Manifesto's 'communism' as democratic rather than anarchist, and they overlooked the role of productive forces and the historical conditions for the state's necessary existence and withering away. Li holds that this explains why they failed to find a correct revolutionary path. Read the original if you study the early translation history of Marxist texts in China, or the relation between anarchism and Marxism in late Qing thought.
quoteEn: Liu Shipei and the others neither saw the decisive role of the development of productive forces in eliminating economic inequality and achieving human liberation, nor recognised the necessity of the state in particular historical periods and the social and historical conditions for its withering away.
quoteZh: 刘师培等人既看不到生产力发展对于消除经济不平等、实现人的解放的决定性作用，也忽视了特定历史时期国家存在的必要性和国家消亡的社会历史条件。

glossary.explanation: An anarchist journal founded in Tokyo in 1907 by Liu Shipei and He Zhen. It published translated Marxist texts alongside anarchist writing.
An anarchist periodical started in 1908 by the same circle, which continued Tianyi's work after it was forced to stop.

t: Between philosophy and Capital: the internal evolution of Marx's theory of ideology
zh: 在哲学与《资本论》之间：马克思意识形态理论的内在嬗变
paras: Zhou Luping and Wu Ting take up a long-running dispute in Western Marxist scholarship: whether Marx's theory of ideology breaks between the early and the mature Marx, as Althusser's "epistemological break" implies. They respond to Lalande-style and Balibar-style readings that see fetishism critique replacing ideology critique after 1850. Their thesis is that Marx's theory of ideology is continuous and systematic, running from the early philosophical critiques through historical materialism to Capital and its manuscripts, where the concept is present in a "hidden" form.

The article is organised in three parts. The first reconstructs the problem-field of ideology critique in the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The second treats the historical-materialist character of ideology critique in the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology, The Poverty of Philosophy, Wage-Labour and Capital and the Communist Manifesto. The third locates ideology critique within Capital, discussing the generation, operation and destruction of capitalist ideology, with side-arguments against Max Weber, Horkheimer and Adorno.

The authors argue first that the 1844 Manuscripts already contain a "trinity" of economic, philosophical and social critique of alienated labour, with ideology critique subordinate to all three. The German Ideology then explains ideology through the spontaneous division of labour and the split between material and mental labour. Later texts treat economic categories as the "copy" of the "original" of capital's real movement. Third, they read Capital as exposing capitalist ideology through the fetishism of commodities, money and capital, which legitimise wage labour and surplus-value extraction. Weber is said to stay at the level of the Protestant ethic, and Horkheimer and Adorno at the surface of the culture industry.

The authors conclude that fetishism critique does not replace ideology critique but is its mature form inside the critique of political economy. They also take this to answer claims that Marx's ideology theory is outdated. For Marx, they say, capitalist ideology disappears only by abolishing capital and wage labour, re-establishing individual ownership and moving to socially shared production. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of ideology, the Althusser debate, or the link between the early texts and Capital.
quoteEn: In fact, Marx's theory of ideology runs through the development of historical materialism and the study of Capital, and takes the form of a profound and systematic exposition.
quoteZh: 事实上，马克思的意识形态理论贯通唯物史观与《资本论》的研究过程，呈现为深刻而系统的论述。

t: Marx and Engels's critique of modern capitalist civilization and its implications
zh: 马克思恩格斯对资本主义现代文明的批判及启示
paras: Sun Xuan asks how the value core of capitalist modern civilization shapes that civilization and drives it into crisis, a question the author says Weber, Schumpeter, Rousseau and other thinkers left unanswered. Their critiques, in Sun's reading, describe value deviation and dilemmas without systematically explaining how the core works. Sun argues that Marx and Engels, working from historical materialism, supply this explanation, and that it points to a new path of human civilization built on the free and all-round development of the human being and on community values.

The article has three parts. The first defines modern civilization and reviews Western and Chinese views of its Protestant and Enlightenment roots. The second sets out Marx and Engels's critique along five dimensions: material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. The third turns each dimension into a positive alternative.

For Sun, the value core of capitalist civilization is the supremacy of material interest and the maximization of capital's interests. Marx and Engels credit the bourgeoisie with huge productive achievements and with sweeping away feudal political and ideological fetters. The same core, Sun argues, produces overproduction crises, a representative state that is an illusory community serving capital, colonial and world-market domination, commodity and money fetishism, alienated and competitive social relations, and ecological plunder. Against the logic of 'for capital, relying on working people, developing capital', Sun proposes 'for people, relying on people, developing people'. In practice this means ownership and distribution systems that favour the majority, substantive people's democracy, plural and equal exchange among civilizations, non-commercialized cultural production, a division of labour that frees people from mechanical work, and harmony between humans and nature.

Sun concludes that capitalist civilization is being 'disenchanted', exposing structural dilemmas and signs of decline. The lesson drawn is a return from a 'material-centred' to a 'human-centred' civilizational standard. On this basis the five forms of civilization would develop together in a community of all-round development, easing disputes over civilizational values and conflicts between civilizations. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese Marxist reading of Marx and Engels on civilization, organized by the five dimensions of civilization and linked to the current Chinese debate on a new path of human civilization.
quoteEn: The human spiritual world is a more essential and deeper dimension of all-round human development.
quoteZh: 人的精神世界是人的全面发展更本质、更深层的维度

glossary.en: free and all-round development of the human being
glossary.explanation: A Marxist ideal of a society in which each person can develop their capacities fully, associated with Marx and Engels's vision of communism. In Chinese discourse it is often used as the ultimate aim of social development.

Marx's term in The German Ideology for the state and bourgeois political community, which appears to represent everyone but in practice serves the ruling class. Sun contrasts it with a 'real community' of people's democracy.

glossary.zh: 物质文明、政治文明、精神文明、社会文明、生态文明
glossary.pinyin: wùzhì wénmíng, zhèngzhì wénmíng, jīngshén wénmíng, shèhuì wénmíng, shēngtài wénmíng
glossary.en: material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization
glossary.explanation: The five-sphere framework of civilization used in official Chinese discourse, which grew from earlier material/spiritual and later political, social and ecological additions. Sun uses it to structure both the critique and the alternative.
The Marxist theory that material production and class relations fundamentally shape political and ideological life.

t: On the logic of opposition in objectified labour
st: Based on the theory of metabolism in Capital and its manuscripts
zh: 论对象化劳动的对立逻辑
zhSub: 基于《资本论》及手稿中的物质变换理论
paras: Sun Lin takes up "objectified labour" (duixianghua laodong), which the article treats as the core concept of Marx's critique of political economy. The author asks how Marx, working through the theory of metabolism (Stoffwechsel) in Capital and its manuscripts, develops a dialectic of opposition that differs from Hegel's and Feuerbach's accounts of objectivity. The thesis is that objectified labour is the "centre of gravity" of the critique, and that its logic of opposition unlocks the secret of formal change (form transformation) in capitalist metabolism.

The article has three parts. The first follows social metabolism from the external opposition of commodity and money to the internal opposition of use-value and exchange-value, and then to an essential opposition. The second argues that value, commodity and capital are each objectified labour. The third turns to the "positive sublation" of objectified labour through the natural conditions of objective activity. Sun reads these steps against Hegel's speculative logic, Feuerbach's critique of theology, and Marx's 1844 Manuscripts and Grundrisse-era texts.

Sun's central move is to say that simple circulation yields only successive external oppositions. Money circulation, and then capital circulation, introduces "simultaneity" and "identity", through which past, accumulated labour inverts and dominates living labour. Capital is thereby described as the inversion and transposition of forces, a self-valorising "fetish" that sublates both external and internal opposition. Sun adds that this identity is only ideal. In reality the sale of labour-power is an "apparent exchange", and the gap between buying and selling makes realisation contingent, which Sun links to "modern crisis" and the world-market crisis. Sun contends that Hegel's pre-established harmony becomes antagonistic contradiction under capitalism.

Sun concludes that opposition within objectified labour is a logical opposition within a non-identical reality, and that the real cause and ground is living labour and the worker who carries it. The way beyond capital's totality is to start from use-value, natural conditions, and the non-objectified labour of the human–nature metabolism, which cannot be fully dissolved into abstract value. Sun holds that recovering these conditions still matters for critiquing capitalist modernity today. Read the original if you want a close, Hegel-informed reading of Marx's metabolism, objectified labour and fetishism in Capital and its manuscripts.
quoteEn: The logic of opposition in objectified labour is the key to unlocking the secret of the changes of form and the formal transformations of metabolism.
quoteZh: 对象化劳动的对立逻辑，是解开物质变换的形态变化及其形式变换秘密的钥匙。

t: Rethinking the adaptation of Marx's labour theory of value to our times under the challenge of artificial intelligence
zh: 人工智能挑战背景下马克思劳动价值论时代化审思
paras: Does the arrival of ChatGPT and Sora make Marx's labour theory of value obsolete? Yu Tianyu takes up the view that artificial intelligence (AI) is an unprecedented qualitative leap in machinery, one that expels human labour from production and so undermines the principle that labour is the only source of value. Yu argues that this view rests on a mistaken picture of AI. In Yu's account, AI has not removed human labour from production, labour remains the sole source of value, and the theory still needs to be developed for the present.

The article first traces how machines have displaced labour in three stages: manufacture, where workers become partial organs of the "collective worker"; large-scale machine industry, where they become "conscious limbs" of the machine; and the AI era, where Yu says they risk becoming a "useless class". It then reconstructs the challenge as two linked arguments, about the value-formation process and about exploitation. Next comes a rebuttal from Marx's own categories, followed by proposals for updating the theory and a discussion of its contemporary significance.

Yu reconstructs the challenge in Marx's terms.
