If variable capital disappears, new value must arise in circulation, which breaks equivalent exchange, or AI must create surplus value, which would turn "labour creates value" into "machines create value" and leave capitalists with income that involves no exploitation. Against this, Yu makes three points. Physical labour is turning into mental labour. Concrete and abstract labour are being confused, since the disappearance of concrete labour in one process does not abolish abstract labour in society. And AI is a means of production, capital and a commodity, so it is itself a product of human labour and cannot be an independent producer. Yu adds that AI as fixed capital speeds up value formation and intensifies exploitation. In the hypothetical case of a society with no human labour, capital would lose the external source of its self-expansion.

Yu calls for extending Marx's categories: redefining productive labour to cover hidden "free labour" on digital platforms, recognising the labour of scientific and technical staff, clarifying value creation around "intelligent commodities", and grasping the capitalist use of machines. Yu holds that the theory remains relevant for understanding contemporary capitalism, for guiding the socialist market economy and for building a harmonious human–machine relationship under Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, Capital-based Chinese Marxist rebuttal of the claim that AI refutes the labour theory of value, with its proposals for updating the theory.
quoteEn: Artificial intelligence cannot replace the subject position of human beings, still less can it replace humans in creating value.
quoteZh: 人工智能不能代替人的主体地位，更不能代替人创造价值。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of development under Party leadership, promoted prominently since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
The official description of China's economic system since the early 1990s, which combines market mechanisms with public ownership as the main body of the economy.
The Marxist theory that value is created by abstract human labour. Chinese scholars treat it as the foundation of Marxist political economy.
Marx's term (Gesamtarbeiter) for the combined workforce of manufacture, in which each worker performs a partial function. Yu renders it with a stress on totality.

t: A methodological reflection on the theoretical turn in the critique of use-value
st: From the critique of political economy to the critique of alienated power
zh: 使用价值批判之理论转向的方法论反思
zhSub: 从政治经济学批判到异化权力批判
source: Teaching and Research on Marxist Theory (马克思主义理论教学与研究), 2024 no. 4
paras: Contemporary Western Left social critique, the article observes, has concentrated on exchange-value and the logic of 'abstraction becoming domination', while the critical force of use-value has been little studied. Weng argues that Marx's use-value is not merely the natural 'usefulness' of a commodity but a category with its own social-critical content. Western Left thinkers such as Debord, Baudrillard and Agamben have converted it into a critique of alienated power. In Weng's view this marks a methodological retreat from Marx's critique of political economy towards a purely philosophical critique.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Marx's critique of use-value along two dimensions: fetishism (the commodity chapter of Capital, Volume 1) and economic crisis (the Grundrisse's 'fragment on machines', Capital and the 1861–63 manuscripts). The second sets out three strands of the alienated-power approach: Debord's society of the spectacle, Baudrillard's The Mirror of Production and Agamben's Profanations. The third offers a methodological assessment, including the claim that digital capitalism intensifies these power mechanisms.

Weng argues that, for Marx, use-value covers a commodity's natural usefulness only at the level of 'production in general'. Its social meaning appears in the value-form, where a commodity's material shell makes a social relation look like a natural property of things. Crises, in Marx's account, come from the opposition between use-value and value, as in the gap between producing and realising surplus value and in the imbalance between production sectors. Weng rejects readings that locate capital's collapse in the self-negation of capital logic. The Western Left thinkers, by contrast, detach use-value from value and productive forces from relations of production. Weng says this produces three shifts: scientific theory of contradiction gives way to a critique of power, class analysis gives way to 'subject identification', and a romantic 'reality versus what ought to be' alienation critique returns, with imagined escape through Lefebvre's 'appropriation', Agamben's 'inoperativity' and Baudrillard's 'symbolic exchange'. Weng adds that this may amount to a new form of bourgeois ideology.

Weng grants that these thinkers capture real changes in capitalism since the 1960s, but holds that consumer-society power relations belong to the surface of everyday life. Citing a view that profit-seeking has shifted to financial speculation and debt-fuelled consumption, Weng locates the deeper contradiction in the imbalance between production and consumption. When crisis breaks out, the author predicts, class relations will replace the alienated relation between subject and apparatus. Weng calls for a theory of contemporary capitalist power built on Marxism's overall logic, which the author sees as especially important for critiques of digital capitalism. Read the original if you work on Western Marxism, value-form theory or critiques of the consumer society and want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Debord, Baudrillard and Agamben.
quoteEn: Marx's approach grounds the social-critical effect of economic categories in the overall theory of historical materialism, whereas Western Left social critique attributes it to a critique of alienated power and so ends up as a purely philosophical critique.
quoteZh: 马克思的思路是将经济范畴的社会批判效应奠基于唯物史观的整体理论之上，而西方左翼社会批判理论则将其归于一种异化权力批判，从而走向一种纯粹的哲学批判。

glossary.explanation: The article's label for Western Left approaches that treat use-value, via exchange-value, as alienated into spectacle, symbols or subject identities. They focus on micro-level power that shapes subjects.
Marx's term for the way social relations between producers appear as natural properties of things, as with commodities and money.
Marx's analysis of how a commodity's value can be expressed only in the use-value of another commodity. It ends in the money form.

t: The new form of human civilization from the perspective of the Marxist view of civilization
zh: 马克思主义文明观视域下的人类文明新形态
paras: This short commentary asks how the Marxist view of civilization, grounded in historical materialism, can guide the construction of a "new form of human civilization". Luo Yun argues that Marx and Engels, though they gave no unified definition of civilization, supplied a scientific framework for understanding its nature, development and succession. On this basis Luo presents the new form of human civilization as emerging from socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article has three parts. It first discusses the concept of civilization and its diversity, citing Spengler, Toynbee, Jaspers and Xi Jinping. It then sketches the historical evolution of civilization through Marx and Engels's works, including Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. Finally it turns to the new form of human civilization created under socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Luo reads Marx and Engels as treating civilization as the result of human practice in transforming nature and society, tied to the growth of productive forces. Civilization, in this account, passes through three stages: its emergence (the "savage" and "barbarian" eras), the age of civilization (slave, feudal and capitalist societies), and its high development in communism, of which socialism is the initial form. Luo contends that the new form of human civilization transcends Western capitalist civilization, which the article describes as marked by contradiction, hegemony and the sacrifice of the majority. It is also said to break the equation of modernization with Westernization and to absorb the useful achievements of world civilization through Chinese modernization.

Luo concludes that the new form of civilization upholds the basic principles of socialist civilization while offering a pattern for developing and late-developing countries. The article also calls on progressive forces to promote exchange among civilizations and a unity in diversity, and to counter the "clash of civilizations" thesis with the inclusiveness of Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Chinese theorists derive the "new form of human civilization" from Marx and Engels's view of civilization.
quoteEn: The new form of human civilization is a transcendence of the Western capitalist form of civilization.
quoteZh: 人类文明新形态，是对西方资本主义文明形态的超越。

glossary.explanation: Official term for China's path of modernization, promoted by the Communist Party especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.

A Party formulation, prominent since 2021, describing the civilization said to be created by Chinese modernization under the leadership of the Communist Party. It is presented as an alternative to Western-centred models.
The official name for China's current system and path, developed since the reform era, combining Party leadership, a socialist system and market mechanisms.
The Marxist theory that material production and social relations drive historical development.

t: Historical materialism and the Marxist conception of civilization
zh: 唯物史观与马克思主义文明观
paras: Wang Weiguang asks what 'civilization' means in Marxism and why the question matters for the 'cultural mission of the new era' put forward by Xi Jinping. The article argues that this mission cannot be properly understood without the standpoint, viewpoint and method of historical materialism and a grasp of the Marxist conception of civilization. Wang notes that the classics never wrote a dedicated work on civilization. The article therefore reconstructs their view from scattered passages and holds that this conception is a component of historical materialism.

The article is organised in four parts. The first surveys how Marx, Engels and Lenin use 'civilization' and related phrases ('civilized nations', 'civilized society') for capitalist society. The second turns to their argument that capitalist civilization produces the proletariat and will be replaced by communist civilization. The third examines Engels's periodisation, borrowed in part from Morgan, and his criticism of idealist views of civilization. The fourth distils six main tenets of the Marxist conception of civilization, drawing on texts from the Communist Manifesto to Lenin's late writings, and on Mao Zedong.

Wang argues that in the classics 'civilization' usually means bourgeois or capitalist civilization, whose progressive role ('the great civilizing influence of capital') they acknowledge while exposing its basis in class exploitation. Engels, in Wang's reading, divides the 'age of civilization' into 'ancient civilization' (slave and feudal society, and the origins in primitive society) and 'modern civilization' (capitalism), marked by the division of labour, private property, class and the state. From this Wang draws six tenets. These are that productive forces are the fundamental measure of civilization; that a civilization is judged first by its social formation; that civilization is historical, so there is no abstract, 'universal' civilization; that class analysis is required; that each civilization is progressive relative to its predecessor yet is replaced; and that idealist views of civilization must be criticised.

Wang concludes that although the classics gave no explicit definition, civilization can be understood as the mark and summary of the state, nature and degree of social progress. The text calls for historical, concrete, dialectical and class analysis of civilization. It treats Samuel Huntington's 'clash of civilizations' as a contemporary variant of the idealist conception, and 'Western-centrism' as a bourgeois idealist view. Read the original if you want a dense, citation-rich reconstruction of the classical Marxist texts on civilization and the theoretical grounding the author offers for current Chinese discussions of civilization.
quoteEn: Civilization should be the mark, embodiment and summary of the condition, nature and degree of human social progress.
quoteZh: 文明应当是人类社会进步的状况、性质和程度的标志、体现和概括。

glossary.zh: 担负新时代的文化使命
glossary.pinyin: dānfù xīn shídài de wénhuà shǐmìng
glossary.en: cultural mission of the new era
glossary.literal: shouldering the cultural mission of the new era
glossary.explanation: A formulation associated with Xi Jinping, who at the 2023 national conference on propaganda and ideological work stressed the task of developing socialist culture with Chinese characteristics and advancing Chinese civilization.
The Marxist theory that material production and the relations of production ultimately determine social development. In Chinese textbooks it includes the 'five social formations' schema.
Samuel Huntington's thesis that post-Cold War conflicts would run along cultural and civilizational lines. Chinese Marxist writers often criticise it as ahistorical.

glossary.literal: theory of Western civilization as the centre
glossary.explanation: The view that Western civilization is the standard and centre of human history. The article treats it as a bourgeois idealist outlook.

t: Lenin's exploration of preventing and curbing bureaucratism and formalism
zh: 列宁对防治官僚主义形式主义的探索
paras: Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the article notes, the Party has made improving its work style a pivot of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, targeting bureaucratism and formalism, which Xi Jinping says "kill". Lü Weizhou and Liao Bin ask what Lenin's thinking and practice on these two ills offer today. They argue that Lenin analysed their manifestations, harms and roots in Soviet state and Party organs, and devised measures whose lessons help the Chinese Communist Party raise its leadership capacity.

The article is organised in three parts followed by a conclusion. The first part reconstructs Lenin's exposure of bureaucratism and formalism and their dangers. The second part treats their political, economic and cultural roots. The third part sets out Lenin's countermeasures: socialist democracy, a sound socialist legal system, improvement of state organs, and purification of the ranks of Party members and cadres. It draws on Lenin's speeches and writings and on Soviet examples from 1918 to 1922.

On manifestations, the authors say Lenin identified three forms of formalism: endless meetings, paper-shuffling, and procrastination. They report that he saw the greatest harms as damage to the Party's image and its ties with the masses, harm to popular interests, delay to socialist construction, and, as the authors put it, ultimately the survival of Party and state; the article attributes the Soviet collapse partly to these ills after Lenin's death. On roots, Lenin is said to have traced them to tsarist autocratic survivals, a fragmented small-producer economy, and low cultural and educational levels, which limited mass participation and supervision. On remedies, the authors describe elections and recall of officials, pay not exceeding a skilled worker's wage, supervisory bodies, prosecution of exemplary cases, slimmed-down institutions, personal responsibility, fewer meetings, strict admission and the 1921 purge, and cadre training, assessment and rewards.

The authors conclude that Lenin left valuable experience, that the Party has drawn on and developed it since the 18th Party Congress, and that bureaucratism and formalism are stubborn and recurrent, requiring sustained effort. They call for further study of where they grow in the new era and of ways to curb new and hidden forms, so as to provide institutional safeguards for the Party's leadership of deepening reform and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Lenin's anti-bureaucracy measures are presented in current Chinese Party-building scholarship.
quoteEn: Lenin took promoting socialist democracy, perfecting the socialist legal system, improving the organs of state power and purifying the ranks of Party members and cadres as important measures for preventing and curbing bureaucratism and formalism.
quoteZh: 列宁把发扬社会主义民主、健全社会主义法制、改善政权机关、纯洁党员干部队伍等作为防治官僚主义和形式主义的重要举措

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Official slogan since the 18th Party Congress (2012) for stricter discipline, anti-corruption and work-style campaigns inside the Chinese Communist Party.
The official concept of China's own path to modernization, promoted in Party documents especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
In Party usage, an emphasis on form, procedure and appearances over substance and real results, such as excessive meetings, paperwork and show.

In Party usage, a work style of officials who are detached from the masses, privileged, slow and self-serving. Together with formalism it is one of the "four undesirable work styles" (四风) targeted since 2012.

t: A political-economy critique of contemporary Western theories of cognitive-capitalist exploitation
zh: 当代西方认知资本主义剥削理论的政治经济学批判
paras: Sun Liang takes up Western theories of "cognitive capitalism", which hold that knowledge, information, emotion and creativity now drive capital accumulation. The article asks what these theories identify as the objects and mechanisms of exploitation, and what they miss. Sun argues that they describe new forms of exploitation well but remain at the level of subjective experience. In Sun's reading, they do not question the capitalist mode of production that makes cognition available to capital, so resistance is reduced to individual self-liberation.

The article distinguishes three strands of theory. The first is French (Yann Moulier Boutang, Carlo Vercellone), the second Italian autonomist (Andrea Fumagalli, Hardt and Negri), and the third associated with Franco Berardi and Maurizio Lazzarato, on AI and the brain. Section one treats the objects of exploitation: general intellect, life itself (the "social factory") and the brain and nervous system. Section two treats three forms of power: "technological feudalisation" and rent extraction, psychopolitics, and machinic enslavement. Section three offers a critique drawing on Marx's Grundrisse and Capital, followed by a short conclusion.

Sun makes two central moves. First, cognitive exploitation falls within the category Marx criticised. Intellect, life and nerve activity become means of production only inside capitalist relations, under wage labour and the separation of producers from the means of production. For Sun, Marx's remark that capital does not create science but appropriates it shows that knowledge is not productive in itself. Cognitive workers are integrated into collective production and lose their products to capital. Sun reads the theorists as treating cognition directly as a factor of production, and holds that cognitive capitalism changes the form of capitalist relations but not their content.

Second, Sun places cognitive capitalism within global capitalism and what the article calls new imperialism. In Sun's account, high-value cognitive work in developed countries depends on low-end labour elsewhere, on control of global value chains, intellectual property and data. Platforms also spread consumerist and individualist values. The conclusion calls for a return to Marx's critique of political economy. Sun says such an analysis helps in grasping new quality productive forces, in guarding against capital's absorption of cognitive labour, and in balancing technological development with social fairness while pursuing independent innovation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of autonomist and post-operaist theories of cognitive, digital and platform capitalism, grounded in Marx's texts.
quoteEn: A political-economy critique of cognitive capitalism must go beyond the subjective dimension of exploitation and return to a holistic understanding of the capitalist mode of production.
quoteZh: 对认知资本主义的政治经济学批判，必须超越剥削的主体性维度，回到对资本主义生产方式的整体性理解。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2023 for advanced productivity driven by technological innovation, digital technology and emerging industries. It is used in official discourse on high-quality development.
A concept from mainly French and Italian post-operaist thought. It holds that capital now accumulates chiefly through knowledge, information and affective or creative labour.
A term from Marx's 1857–58 manuscripts for socially accumulated knowledge that becomes a direct force of production. Autonomist writers use it to ground their theories of immaterial labour.
The claim that digital platform firms act like feudal lords who collect rents from dependent users and workers. It is used by some Western critics of rent-seeking digital capital.
A notion from Italian operaismo that capitalist production relations extend into every sphere of society, such as the home, school and consumption.

t: Reconsidering some basic questions in the Marxist theory of productive forces
st: Reflections based on labour subjectivity
zh: 马克思主义生产力理论若干基本问题再认识
zhSub: 基于劳动主体性的思考
paras: Zhang Yu takes up a set of long-debated basic questions in the Marxist theory of productive forces, prompted by the current technological revolution and the rise of new quality productive forces. The article argues that the essence of this theory lies in labour and its subjectivity: productive forces must be understood from the standpoint of the active human subject, not as a collection of things, as bourgeois political economy treated them.

The article is organised in eight parts, each a question. It covers the core place of labour; the elements of productive forces, including the two-, three- and multi-element debates; whether their social character belongs to productive forces or to relations of production; the primacy of productive forces against the active role of relations of production; the productive-forces criterion and the value criterion; the ultimate driving force of productive-force development; how to measure productive-force levels; and the qualitative forms of productive forces. Zhang draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on Chinese and foreign scholars such as Wu Yifeng, Wei Xinghua and G. A. Cohen.

Zhang makes three main moves. First, the social side of productive forces, meaning division of labour, cooperation and the organisation of production, is distinguished from relations of production and treated as the mediating link in a chain running from productive forces to mode of production to relations of production. Second, Zhang holds that productive forces take primacy because they supply the standard by which relations of production count as progressive, while relations of production can act decisively back and may even precede new productive forces historically. The productive-forces criterion is fundamental but not the only one, and it is joined to a value criterion through the purposefulness of labour. Third, Zhang rejects Cohen's individualist model and the Western premise of scarcity. In Zhang's reading, the saving of labour time is Marx's primary economic law and the source of productive-force growth, taking the form of the law of value, the law of surplus value and the basic economic law of socialism.

On the current period, Zhang argues that productive forces are undergoing a third revolutionary leap, after agriculture and industry, centred on informatisation, digitalisation and intelligent production. New quality productive forces are in essence intelligent productive forces, and the matching relations of production are socialism's basic economic system and a high-standard socialist market economy. Zhang sees digital capitalism as sharpening capitalist contradictions while enlarging the material basis for human freedom, and expresses confidence in the Party-led achievement of high-quality development. Read the original if you want a systematic, theory-driven account of how Chinese Marxist economists are rethinking productive forces, relations of production and new quality productive forces.
quoteEn: Labour and its distinctive subjectivity are the essence of the Marxist theory of productive forces.
quoteZh: 劳动及其鲜明的主体性，是马克思主义生产力理论的精髓。

glossary.explanation: A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in 2023 for advanced productive forces driven by technological breakthroughs, especially digital and intelligent technologies, and by the optimised combination of production factors.
The official goal since the late 2010s of shifting from high-speed growth to growth emphasising quality, innovation and sustainability.
The principle, prominent since Deng Xiaoping, that whether something promotes productive-force development is the fundamental test of social progress and of policy.

glossary.zh: 社会主义基本经济制度
glossary.explanation: The official term for the system combining public ownership as the mainstay with diverse forms of ownership, distribution according to work, and the socialist market economy.

t: Theoretical foundations and construction logic of a high-standard socialist market economy
zh: 高水平社会主义市场经济体制的理论基础和构建逻辑
source: Studies on Marxist Theory Discipline (马克思主义理论学科研究), 2025 no. 1
paras: Zhang Xu asks what theoretical basis should guide the building of a "high-standard socialist market economy", a goal set out in the 2020 Party and State Council opinions and in the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). The article argues that the core issue is the relationship between government and market, and that existing research on it leans largely on Western political theory and Western economics while neglecting Marx. Zhang contends that the theoretical foundation must rest on Marx's understanding of this relationship, absorb useful elements of modern Western economics, and be tied to the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Marx's views on civil society, the state and its economic functions, drawing on Marx's early critique of Hegel, the Grundrisse, Capital and Engels's Anti-Dühring. It then extracts the basic logic of those views and turns to the Chinese Party's evolving understanding of government and market since reform and opening up. It closes by placing the high-standard market economy within the Party's overall logic of comprehensively deepening reform, running through congress and plenum documents from 1978 to 2024.

In Zhang's reading, Marx had no standalone theory of government and market, but his analysis of the state as the form in which the bourgeoisie secures its property and interests contains one. Zhang points to the state's role in creating the conditions for capital, such as the coercive legislation accompanying primitive accumulation, and to the dual character of government functions: directing labour required by large-scale socialised production, and supervisory labour arising from the opposition between producers and owners. From this Zhang draws four principles: government functions rest on civil society, the relationship develops as a natural historical process, restraining government power matters as much as restraining market power, and state power must be used properly, which makes ongoing reform necessary.

Zhang traces the Party's shift from the market playing a "basic" role in resource allocation to the "decisive" role announced at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), alongside "better" government. The author presents this as a major theoretical innovation and the foundation for the high-standard market economy, which is described as an enhanced and innovative version of the existing system and an important safeguard for Chinese modernization. Zhang calls for combining Marx's views on government, market and economic systems with deepened reform, so as to open new horizons for Marxist political economy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar grounds current market-economy policy in Marx's writings on the state and traces the Party's documentary lineage on government and market.
quoteEn: The theoretical basis for building a high-standard socialist market economy must rest on Marx's understanding of the relationship between government and market, absorb the useful elements of modern Western economics, and combine them with the practice of reform and development under socialism with Chinese characteristics; only then can such a system truly be built.
quoteZh: 构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制的理论基础必须以马克思对政府和市场关系的认识为依据，吸收现代西方经济学的有益成分，结合中国特色社会主义改革和发展实践，才能真正构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制。

glossary.zh: 高水平社会主义市场经济体制
glossary.pinyin: gāo shuǐpíng shèhuì zhǔyì shìchǎng jīngjì tǐzhì
glossary.explanation: A goal first formulated in a May 2020 Party and State Council document and elevated in the 20th Party Congress (2022) report. It denotes a more systematic, mature and well-established version of the existing market economy system.
The official formulation of China's development path, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022). The Party presents it as distinct from Western modernization models.

The reform programme launched at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and renewed in 2024. It covers economic, political, social, cultural and Party-building reform, with economic reform as the driving element.

t: Western perceptions of new quality productive forces: main views and an assessment
zh: 西方关于新质生产力的主要认知与评析
paras: Since Xi Jinping put forward the concept of new quality productive forces, Western media, think tanks, politicians and scholars have followed it closely. Zhang Lisi asks how the West understands the concept and why. The article argues that most Western commentary is positive or relatively objective, while a minority of views misread it out of anxiety and strategic interest. Zhang presents the survey as a way to understand the shape of Western opinion contests and to improve China's external communication.

The article has four parts. It first sorts Western definitions of the concept under four headings: development strategy, development philosophy, form of productive forces, and essential character. It then reviews Western explanations of why the concept emerged, and Western judgements of its significance, including some cautions. The longest section assesses these views, covering the reasons for Western attention, four general features and four features of what Zhang calls distorted readings. Sources include the BBC, Reuters, The Economist, the Wall Street Journal, Deutsche Welle, US ambassador Nicholas Burns and academics such as Robert Kuhn and Barry Naughton.

Zhang reports that many Western commentators link the concept to high-quality development, to a new stage of productive forces and to the new development philosophy. Some call it a Chinese-context development of Marxist productive-forces theory. Zhang identifies two reasons for Western attention: China's achievements in frontier fields, and anxiety in some Western states that China's rise in new energy vehicles, chips and photovoltaics will erode their technological dominance. On this reading, the unfavourable views share four traits: theoretical traps such as the 'overcapacity' thesis, tying the concept to national security, ideological labelling, and zero-sum thinking. Zhang rejects the overcapacity thesis as a false proposition and as a pretext for protectionism.

Zhang concludes that Western interpretations are broadly positive and growing, and that US allies are diverging from Washington. The author calls for objective, historical and comprehensive study of Western views and for stronger external publicity on high-quality development and Chinese modernization. Zhang also advises a calm search for the roots of misreadings, firm rebuttal of what the article calls smears, and the pursuit of shared interests to build a favourable international environment. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly overview of how Western media and experts have framed new quality productive forces, and how Chinese analysts interpret those framings.
quoteEn: Therefore, a stance fixed in advance and the primacy of interests are the reasons behind some Western misreadings and one-sided views of new quality productive forces.
quoteZh: 因此，立场先行、利益主导是西方对于新质生产力的一些误读和片面观点产生的原因。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping introduced in 2023 for advanced productive forces driven by technological innovation, data and new production factors. It is presented as a basis for high-quality development.
An official goal, prominent since 2017, of shifting from rapid growth to growth stressing quality, efficiency and innovation.
The official name for China's path to modernization under Communist Party leadership, set out especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
Five principles announced in 2015: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing.

t: Cultivating and expanding patient capital to empower the development of new quality productive forces
zh: 以培育壮大耐心资本赋能新质生产力发展
paras: Zhang Yang takes up a policy question raised by recent Party documents: how to build up "patient capital" (naixin ziben) so that it supports new quality productive forces. The article starts from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) and the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference, both of which call for developing patient capital. Zhang's thesis is that patient capital suits the long, risky and costly path of new quality productive forces, and that the state should deliberately foster it through policy, institutions and financial innovation.

The commentary has three parts. The first defines patient capital. The second explains why new quality productive forces need it. The third sets out measures to cultivate and expand it. Zhang draws throughout on the Plenum's decision and on statements by Xi Jinping, and the piece reads as a Party-theory explainer rather than an empirical study.

In the definition, Zhang names three features. Patient capital is long-term, since it values long-run returns over short-term ones. It is value investing, focused on a firm's intrinsic value, business model and technology path rather than price swings. It is risk-tolerant, able to accept long periods without returns, or even losses, and to invest counter-cyclically. Zhang argues that new quality productive forces need such capital for three tasks: breaking through key core technologies and achieving high-level scientific and technological self-reliance; deeply upgrading industry and building a modern industrial system, including digital and intelligent transformation of traditional industries; and speeding the allocation of advanced production factors so as to raise total factor productivity.

On measures, Zhang calls for upholding the Party's overall leadership and combining an efficient market with a capable government. Specific proposals are a package of policies, closer fiscal–financial coordination, government guidance funds and credit risk-sharing for tech firms. Zhang also wants a long-term capital ecosystem, with household savings channelled through enterprise and occupational annuities and easier exit routes for venture funds. Finally, the author proposes innovative products and relay-style financing across a firm's life cycle: angel investment at the incubation stage, convertible bonds and intellectual-property pledges during industrial transition, and smooth exit and reinvestment at maturity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary links patient capital, venture finance and new quality productive forces in policy terms.
quoteEn: Value investing is the essential attribute of patient capital.
quoteZh: 价值投资是耐心资本的本质属性。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2023, referring to advanced productivity driven by technological breakthroughs, emerging and future industries, and innovative allocation of production factors.

Long-term investment capital that does not seek quick returns and can tolerate volatility and losses. It entered Party policy language in the 2024 Third Plenum decision and the Central Economic Work Conference.

glossary.pinyin: dǎng de èrshí jiè sānzhōng quánhuì
glossary.en: the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee
glossary.explanation: A 2024 plenary meeting of the Communist Party's Central Committee that adopted a decision on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization.
An economic measure of output growth not explained by increases in labour and capital inputs, often used to represent efficiency and technological progress.

t: Bringing the roles of government and market into play to promote new quality productive forces
zh: 发挥政府和市场作用促进新质生产力发展
paras: Yin Qingshuang and Xiao Lei ask how the relationship between government and market should be arranged so that new quality productive forces can develop. They argue that the blockages in developing them are closely tied to how well government and market are coordinated in technological innovation, factor allocation and industrial upgrading. Their answer is a division of labour in which the 'visible hand' and the 'invisible hand' work together, differently at each stage of the process.

The article builds on Xi Jinping's statement that new quality productive forces arise from revolutionary technological breakthroughs, innovative allocation of production factors and deep industrial transformation. It first sets out this three-stage 'generative logic', drawing on Marx, Schumpeter and the history of industrial revolutions. It then analyses government and market roles stage by stage, citing the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). Next it diagnoses current obstacles under five headings of 'innovation': science and technology, industry, development mode, institutions and talent. It ends with six practical priorities.

The core move is stage-specific allocation. In basic research, disruptive technologies and 'chokepoint' technologies, the authors hold that markets under-invest, so government should lead through planning, funding, institutions and public infrastructure, using the new whole-nation system. In crossing the 'valley of death' from laboratory to commercial use, the authors hold that the market is decisive, with entrepreneurs, enterprises and patient capital in the lead. In industrial transformation, markets drive the replacement of old industries by new ones, while government manages the social costs of 'creative destruction' and adjusts production relations. Citing Marx on science, technology and industrial change, the authors present this as theoretical grounding. They cite patent-commercialisation rates of 36.7% and 39.6% for valid invention patents (2022 and 2023) as evidence of weak conversion outside enterprises, and cite the Silicon Valley model as an example of state–market complementarity.

The authors conclude that government should provide forward-looking guidance, correct market failures and supply institutions. Enterprises should lead innovation, regions should be coordinated according to local conditions, and a unified national market should be built. They also call for policy coordination, an upgraded innovation ecosystem and an orderly exit for declining industries. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese-economics account of how the state–market division of labour is applied to innovation policy, with extensive reference to the Third Plenum's measures.
quoteEn: Crossing the 'valley of death' depends, above all, on the market.
quoteZh: 跨越“死亡谷”,关键靠市场。

glossary.explanation: A concept put forward by Xi Jinping in 2023 for advanced productive forces driven by technological breakthroughs, new factor allocation and industrial upgrading. It is now a central theme in Chinese economic policy discourse.
A mode of mobilising state resources and coordinating institutions across the country for major scientific and technological goals, adapted to a market economy.

glossary.pinyin: dǎng de èrshí jiè sānzhōng quánhuì
glossary.en: Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee
glossary.explanation: The Party meeting held in July 2024 that adopted a decision on further deepening reform, including the economic system and the government–market relationship.

t: New forms of capital in the digital society and their distributional characteristics
zh: 数字社会的新型资本及其分配特征
paras: Zhao Yizhang asks how the digital transformation is creating new kinds of capital and how their distribution reshapes social stratification. The article argues that three new capital types (data capital, digital skill capital and attention capital) are distributed in different ways, and that these differences produce new advantaged and disadvantaged groups. It is written in the context of the 2023 plan for building a Digital China and the goal of common prosperity.

The article starts from the sociological framework of David Grusky and Katherine Weisshaar, who identify eight types of key social resource or capital. It then explains why digitalisation of information and the emergence of a virtual space make new capital forms possible. It sets out how each of the three is acquired, analyses each along three dimensions (inequality, rigidity and crystallisation), identifies the resulting social groups, and closes with policy proposals.

Zhao holds that each capital follows a distinct acquisition path: data capital through paid and unpaid digital labour gathered by firms, digital skill capital mainly through formal education and training, and attention capital through individual content creation. Data capital scores high on inequality, rigidity and crystallisation. Zhao attributes this to network effects, platform monopoly and ready convertibility into economic and even political capital. Skill and attention capital are also unequally distributed but are less rigid and less crystallised, because technology turns over quickly, attention shifts easily and algorithms are opaque. On this basis, platform owners and top executives, highly skilled specialists and influential content creators emerge as new advantaged groups. People who are disadvantaged in the traditional hierarchy and also lack digital skills or attention face a double disadvantage.

Zhao proposes three measures for an inclusive digital society: redistributing the wealth created by data capital, since it rests on the digital labour of many parties; providing multi-channel digital skill training, including in basic education; and building a social security system that covers flexible workers, with adjustable contributions. Zhao presents skill and attention capital as new channels of upward mobility, while calling for attention to the doubly disadvantaged. Read the original if you want a sociological, empirically illustrated account of data, skills and attention as capital in China's digital economy, together with the policy proposals that follow from it.
quoteEn: Data capital is high on inequality, rigidity and crystallisation, whereas digital skill capital and attention capital, though highly unequal, are at a medium or low level in rigidity and crystallisation.
quoteZh: 数据资本在不平等程度、刚性程度、结晶化程度方面都具有较高水平，数字技能资本和注意力资本虽然不平等程度较高，但在刚性程度和结晶化程度方面处于中等或较低水平。

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal that Party leaders have emphasised in recent years. It refers to prosperity shared by all, with reduced gaps in income and wealth.
The article's term for data treated as a valuable productive asset, built up chiefly by firms and platforms from users' and employees' digital labour.
The article's term for the audience attention that users, creators and firms can attract and convert into income, influence or social connections.

t: A contemporary interpretation of the identity of Marx's primitive accumulation of capital and capital accumulation
zh: 马克思的资本原始积累与资本积累同一性的当代阐释
paras: Does primitive accumulation belong to the finished prehistory of capitalism, or does it continue? Tai Lihua and Zhang Ruiqi side with the 'continuity' position and argue that, for Marx, primitive accumulation and capital accumulation are essentially identical. They hold that primitive accumulation runs through the emergence, development and demise of the capitalist mode of production, and that this has present-day relevance.

The article opens with the foreign debate. The 'termination' view (Robert Brenner, Ellen Meiksins Wood, Massimo De Angelis, Paul Zarembka) treats primitive accumulation as a completed precondition. The 'continuity' view is associated with David Harvey's 'accumulation by dispossession', which the authors criticise as reformist and as focused on distribution. They then take three steps. The first is a theoretical critique of Adam Smith's 'previous accumulation'. The second is an analysis of the shared task of the two forms of accumulation. The third is a look at the historical trend, using contemporary capitalism as illustration.

The authors make three main moves. First, they argue that Marx's term 'so-called primitive accumulation' answers Smith's idyllic story of thrift and diligence by stressing violence, the social history of wage labour, and capital as a social relation rather than a thing. Second, they argue that the shared aim of both forms is to separate labourers from the means of production. Primitive accumulation does this through direct and indirect violence, such as enclosures and the Corn Laws. Capital accumulation entrenches the separation through the relative surplus population. The authors argue that digital technology, platform work, migration and what they call 'war capitalism' reinforce this today. Third, they argue that conflicts between labour and capital, among capitals (monopoly tech firms, CDO and CDS speculation, the 2008 crisis) and between states sharpen the contradiction between socialised production and private ownership. They cite protest movements such as Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests as signs of growing class consciousness.

The authors conclude that primitive accumulation is not a closed chapter. They hold that the contradictions it generates make replacement of capitalist private ownership by socialist public ownership both theoretically necessary and practically feasible. They draw three implications for China's basic socialist economic system. The first is to uphold the dominant position of public ownership unwaveringly. The second is to protect the leading role of the state-owned economy. The third is to keep the system coherent, with a role for the non-public economy, in order to support high-quality development. Read the original if you work on Marx's theory of primitive accumulation, on the debate with Harvey and the 'termination' school, or on how Chinese Marxists link Capital to digital capitalism and China's economic system.
quoteEn: Primitive accumulation of capital is not a history that has already ended; it is continuous, present throughout the emergence and development of the capitalist mode of production, and not essentially different from capital accumulation.
quoteZh: 资本的原始积累并非已经终结的历史，它具有持续性的特点，始终存在于资本主义生产方式产生与发展的全过程，与资本积累之间没有本质的区别。

glossary.explanation: An official economic goal, prominent since the 19th Party Congress (2017), that emphasises quality, efficiency and innovation over speed of growth.

glossary.zh: 社会主义基本经济制度
glossary.explanation: The official formula for China's economic system: public ownership as the mainstay alongside diverse forms of ownership, distribution according to work, and the socialist market economy.
Marx's term in Capital for the workers made redundant by rising capital intensity. They form an 'industrial reserve army' that holds down wages and compels workers to accept exploitation.
David Harvey's concept, from the early 2000s, for the continuing use of privatisation, finance and state power to seize wealth under contemporary capitalism, extending Marx's primitive accumulation.

t: Striving to be the vanguard in innovating the Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project
zh: 勇当创新马克思主义理论研究和建设工程的排头兵
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2025, Huang Taiyan asks what role Schools of Marxism should play in the Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project, now in its twentieth year. The author's answer is that these schools should be the "vanguard" (paixingbing) of its renewal, with studying, researching and propagating Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the project's fundamental task.

The short commentary opens with Xi Jinping's instruction on the project. The instruction calls for the Two Integrations, building an autonomous knowledge system for Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and training theoretical talent. Huang then sets out three tasks for the Schools of Marxism: systematic and scholarly interpretation of Xi Jinping Thought, more effective study and dissemination of it, and the training of high-calibre theoretical talent.

On research, Huang urges schools to improve their disciplinary layout and pool resources. They should organise interdisciplinary, collaborative work, with "collective attack on key problems" rather than "fighting alone". On dissemination, Huang says winning over young people is decisive. Teaching the university course introducing Xi Jinping Thought, now offered in all universities, is described as the best form of propaganda. Teachers should combine teaching and research, "open the door" to outside teaching expertise, and use collective lesson preparation to make it a flagship ideological and political course.

Huang adds that Schools of Marxism and the related disciplines have a clearer responsibility for talent training, citing a 2021 General Office document on strengthening the schools. The author proposes adjusting programmes, curricula and student intake to give integrated undergraduate-to-doctoral training, and concludes that the schools have achieved much and can do more. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a senior university Party official frames the mission of Marxism schools and the teaching of Xi Jinping Thought.
quoteEn: Studying, researching and propagating Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is the fundamental task of innovating the Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project.
quoteZh: 学习研究宣传习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想是创新马克思主义理论研究和建设工程的根本任务。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Chinese Communist Party, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.
The formula of combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义理论研究和建设工程
glossary.pinyin: Mǎkèsīzhǔyì lǐlùn yánjiū hé jiànshè gōngchéng
glossary.en: Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project
glossary.literal: Marxist theory research and construction project
glossary.explanation: A Party-led national project launched in 2004 to promote research, textbooks and training in Marxist theory.
University schools responsible for Marxist theory teaching, research and ideological and political courses in China.

keywords: Marxist Theoretical Research and Development Project

t: The construction logic of the order of spectacle under digital capitalism and its cognitive control
zh: 数字资本主义景观秩序的建构逻辑及其认知控制
paras: Drawing on Guy Debord's idea of the spectacle, Xie Lixia asks how digital capitalism builds an "order of spectacle" and how that order controls individuals. The article argues that digital technology turns direct social existence into images and, through three layers of control, produces "data believers" whose knowledge is standardised, whose emotions are uniform and whose behaviour is docile.

The article is organised as three sections that move from cognition to emotion to behaviour, followed by a short conclusion. Each section has three sub-parts. The first covers filtering, hidden coding and preference-driven production of knowledge. The second covers emotional saturation through data, simulated intimacy and disciplinary power. The third covers the exploitation of time, the confinement of space and the governing power of discipline. Xie draws on Marx, Foucault, Marcuse, Debord and Mike Crang, among others.

Xie's central move is to treat knowledge, emotion and behaviour as successive sites where capital extracts value and secures ideological control. Platforms filter knowledge at its source and during production, then bind fragments into image chains and "tacit knowledge" attached to wearable devices. Emotion is then commodified: data "painting" spreads collective feeling, platform "walled gardens" simulate closeness, and digital labour becomes "play labour". Finally, digital devices blur work and leisure, turn every place into a workstation, and embed discipline in the individual until subjectivity dissolves. Xie also introduces "data fetishism" as a successor to the fetishism of commodities, money and capital.

In the conclusion Xie holds that nostalgia for a pre-digital age is not an option, and that digital capital also contains openings for liberation. The author calls for going beyond the order set by the logic of capital, regulating the capitalisation and privatisation of data, promoting digital sharing, and building a community with a shared future for mankind in which humans and the digital coexist. Read the original if you want a Marxist-Foucauldian critique of platform power that follows Debord's spectacle from cognition to emotion to bodily discipline.
quoteEn: The spectacle is penetrating everyday life in digital form, cultivating data believers with standardised cognition, uniform emotion and docile behaviour.
quoteZh: 景观正以数字化方式渗透人们的日常生活，培植出认知规整、情感统一、行为驯顺的数据信徒

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13, stressing shared interests and cooperation among countries. Here the author applies it to the relationship between humans and digital technology.
The author's term for individuals who, under digital capitalism, have been shaped to trust and obey data and platforms. It echoes the article's idea of data fetishism.
Derived from Debord's 'society of the spectacle'. It names a social order in which images and representations mediate and conceal capital's domination.
The author's extension of Marx's fetishism of commodities, money and capital. It describes reverence for data as the source of knowledge and the good life.

t: Marx's thought on proletarian poverty as institutional poverty
zh: 马克思关于作为制度性贫困的无产阶级贫困思想
paras: Mou Chengwen and Wang Weijun ask what Marx held to be the cause of proletarian poverty, and argue that he treated it as institutional poverty, produced by the injustice of social or state institutions. They contrast this with Hegel, for whom a 'rabble' arises 'naturally' from individual differences. In Marx's view, as the authors read him, the proletariat is an artificially created mass of poor people, produced by the sudden dissolution of society, above all of the middle estate.

The article is organised around three roots of this poverty: alienated labour as the social root, class rule as the political root, and surplus value as the economic root. It draws mainly on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Class Struggles in France 1848 to 1850, Capital and the Communist Manifesto. Before turning to Marx, the authors clarify the concepts involved, such as alienation, externalisation, reification and labour.

On alienated labour, the authors argue that it strips the labour process, the worker and even the idle appropriator of their essence as free activity. Its direct result is private property, whose forms (wages, capital, profit, rent) are all treated as outcomes of alienation. On class rule, they describe ruling power as scarce, hidden, monopolistic and dominating, and say it entrenches the position of the ruling class and fixes that of the ruled. They use Marx's analysis of the French classes to show an asymmetric structure in which the proletariat sits at the bottom. On surplus value, they follow the purchase of labour-power, the production and accumulation of surplus value, and its division into industrial and commercial profit, interest and rent. This process, they say, makes capitalists richer and wage workers poorer.

The authors conclude that alienated labour, class rule and surplus value all rest on the capitalist system, which is therefore the ultimate root of proletarian poverty. They state that proletarians can end it only by abolishing bourgeois ownership, rising to become the ruling class, winning democracy, taking over capital step by step and intervening forcibly in property relations. They present this analysis as the theoretical basis of Marx's idea of the fundamental emancipation of the proletariat and of all humanity. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based account of how Marx's early and mature works are linked in explaining poverty as a product of institutions.
quoteEn: The capitalist system must be the overall root of proletarian poverty.
quoteZh: 资本主义制度必然是无产阶级贫困的总根源。

glossary.explanation: The authors' term for poverty caused by injustice in a society's or state's institutions, as opposed to the individual differences between people. They use it to interpret Marx's account of proletarian poverty.
Marx's early concept, from the 1844 Manuscripts, for labour that has lost its character as free human activity and is estranged from the worker, from the product and from other people.
The authors' term for the process by which a ruling class controls power, whether economic, political or cultural, and keeps its dominance over the ruled classes.

t: Reflections on two important questions in the Critique of the Gotha Programme
zh: 关于《哥达纲领批判》中两个重要问题的思考
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2025 no. 2
paras: Marx wrote the Critique of the Gotha Programme in 1875 to combat Lassallean claims that the state is a community of the whole people and that its mission is to develop freedom. Yang Jianyi argues that two questions in the text still carry theoretical and practical weight: the necessity of the dictatorship of the proletariat, and the staged character of communism. Both, the author says, must be rethought as circumstances change.

The article has two main sections. The first reads Marx on the class nature of the state, on the transitional period, and on proletarian dictatorship, then follows how Mao Zedong adapted the doctrine into the people's democratic dictatorship and into the handling of contradictions among the people. It then moves through the Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao periods to the era since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second section sets out Marx's account of communism's lower and higher phases and applies it to contemporary China.

On the state, Yang argues that no supra-class state or freedom exists. The proletariat therefore cannot be emancipated through the bourgeois state and needs its own state power for the revolutionary transition. In Yang's account, Mao's people's democratic dictatorship joins democracy among the people with dictatorship over reactionaries. Under Xi Jinping, the author says, this theory has gained new content through whole-process people's democracy, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the anti-corruption campaign. On communism, Yang reads the first phase as a contradictory unity of past and future. Distribution according to labour there remains "bourgeois right", and the higher phase requires highly developed productive forces, abundant collective wealth and all-round human development. Yang warns against letting capitalist elements spread in the first phase and against importing higher-phase features into it. The move to the higher phase, Yang adds, is not automatic.

Yang concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era fits Marx's description of the first phase while adding Chinese features. The primary stage of socialism, the author says, has not changed. Studying the Critique, Yang argues, strengthens the Four-sphere Confidence, supports the Two Upholds and aids the modernization of national governance, and Marxist classics need continual study. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-school scholar links Marx's 1875 text to Mao's theory of people's democratic dictatorship and to current Party doctrine.
quoteEn: The unity of ideal and reality must begin from the present and be realised in practice.
quoteZh: 理想与现实的统一需要从当下做起，需要在实践中实现。

glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's 1949 formulation, in which democracy for the people is combined with dictatorship over reactionaries. It was later written into the Party constitution and the state constitution as one of the Four Cardinal Principles.

A concept the Party leadership put forward in the 2010s and 20s and officially defined as the essential attribute of socialist democracy at the 20th Party Congress (2022). It stresses participation across all stages of governance, not only voting.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party's disciplinary and anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The official judgement, adopted in 1981 and 1987, that China is at an early stage of socialism, which will last a long time. The Party uses it to justify its basic line and policies.
Confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics, a slogan associated with Xi Jinping.
The Party requirement to uphold the authority of General Secretary Xi Jinping as the core of the Party and the centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee.

t: Coordinating an effective market and a capable government: forming an economic order that is both "lively" and "well-regulated"
zh: 必须统筹好有效市场和有为政府的关系 形成既“放得活”又“管得住”的经济秩序
paras: Zhang Xu's short commentary, published in Qiqi (Banner) in early 2025, takes up the Central Economic Work Conference's formula that an effective market and a capable government must be coordinated, so as to form an economic order that is both "fang de huo" (liberated and lively) and "guan de zhu" (properly regulated). Zhang argues that the formula reflects the Party Central Committee's grasp of economic laws and guides the improvement of the socialist market economy.

The piece has three parts. It first explains why the market–government relationship matters, tracing it to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). It then sets out the dialectical, "two-sided" approach to market and state roles. Finally it breaks the formula into its two halves, drawing on the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024).

Zhang holds that market and government have different functions. The market, under the law of value, should play the decisive role in allocating resources, while government should change its functions, strengthen macroeconomic governance and regulation, and improve public services. Zhang stresses that the market economy develops under Party leadership and the socialist system, so the qualifier "socialist" must never be forgotten. "Liberating" means removing barriers: building a unified national market, strengthening competition policy, improving factor markets and property protection. "Regulating" means correcting market failure, countering monopoly and smoothing economic fluctuations, which Zhang says a market left alone cannot do.

Zhang concludes that both the "invisible hand" and the "visible hand" should be used, forming a pattern in which they complement each other. The author cites early results in building the unified national market and presents capable government as an institutional advantage of concentrating efforts on major tasks. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how the market–government relationship is framed in current Chinese economic policy.
quoteEn: The market is a spontaneous mechanism; if there is only "liberalizing" without "regulating", market failure and monopoly will appear, and the economy will run hot or cold and fluctuate violently.
quoteZh: 市场是一种自动自发机制，如果只“放”不“管”，会出现市场失灵、市场垄断，经济或冷或热、剧烈波动。

glossary.en: an effective market and a capable government
glossary.literal: effective market and government that accomplishes something
glossary.explanation: A formula in Chinese economic policy discourse stressing that market mechanisms and active state intervention should work together rather than against each other.

glossary.pinyin: fàng de huó, guǎn de zhù
glossary.en: "fang de huo" (liberated and lively) and "guan de zhu" (properly regulated)
glossary.literal: loosened enough to be lively, controlled enough to hold
glossary.explanation: A phrase from the 2024 Third Plenum describing an economy that gives market actors freedom while keeping effective oversight.

glossary.zh: 社会主义市场经济体制
glossary.explanation: China's official economic model, adopted in the early 1990s, combining market mechanisms with public ownership as the main body and Party leadership.
A policy goal of removing local protectionism and regional barriers so that goods, capital and factors of production flow freely across China.
An annual meeting of top Party and state leaders, usually in December, that sets economic priorities for the coming year.

t: Historic transformation of the mode of production: the practical precondition of Chinese-style cultural modernization
zh: 生产方式的历史性变革：中国式文化现代化的实践前提
source: Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2025 no. 1
paras: Liu Tongfang and Zhang Qian ask what the practical, material precondition of Chinese-style cultural modernization is. They note that existing scholarship follows a cultural-history approach and explains only its intellectual preconditions: cultural exchange, the contemporary value of traditional culture, and the advanced character of socialist culture. The authors argue that these accounts leave open what drives cultural exchange, how "contemporary" is defined and where the nature of socialist culture comes from. Their answer, from the standpoint of historical materialism, is that the historic transformation of the mode of production is the practical precondition of cultural modernization.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the dialectical relation between mode of production and cultural form, criticising economic determinism and cultural determinism. The second examines the leap in productive forces as the material basis of cultural modernization, treating the form and the content of culture separately. The third turns to changes in the relations of production and the way they gave the people a subjective consciousness of cultural modernization. Its cases include Kautsky, Bernstein and Marvin Harris on the economic side, and Max Weber, Gramsci and Toynbee on the cultural side. The Chinese material runs from the May Fourth Movement to the present.

The authors hold that the mode of production drives change in cultural form, while mature culture gains relative independence and reacts back on production. Weber, Gramsci and Toynbee are described as idealist because they treat culture as the starting point of society. On productive forces, the authors argue that new media (newspapers, radio and film, television, the internet) modernised the forms of Chinese culture. They add that machine systems and artificial intelligence changed its content, with themes of industrialisation, reflection on machines and the human predicament in the AI age. Material change alone does not bring cultural change, however, so the human subject must be explained. The authors argue that two historic changes in the relations of production did this: the move from feudal to socialist public ownership, and the later move to public ownership as the mainstay alongside several forms of ownership. These changes reshaped the people's interests and led them to criticise feudal and capitalist culture and to build socialist culture.

The authors conclude that cultural modernization is a long process led by the Communist Party in which both Chinese cultural form and cultural subjects become modern. They suggest that this approach helps identify new growth points for culture amid new quality productive forces. It also helps guard against the damaging influence of the logic of capital valorisation in a booming market economy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist journal grounds cultural modernization in the mode of production and sets itself against both economic and cultural determinism.
quoteEn: The historic transformation of the mode of production is the practical precondition of Chinese-style cultural modernization: changes in the relations of production reshape the people's interests and awaken their subjective consciousness to build socialist culture.
quoteZh: 生产方式的历史性变革是中国式文化现代化的实践前提，通过生产关系的变革重塑人民群众的利益诉求，激发其构建社会主义文化的主体自觉。

glossary.explanation: A term popularised by Xi Jinping in 2023–24 for productivity driven by technological breakthroughs and emerging industries such as AI and digital technology.
The cultural dimension of the official concept of Chinese modernization, referring to the Party-led modernization of China's cultural forms and of the people's cultural consciousness.
In Marxist theory, the unity of productive forces and relations of production that shapes the material basis of a society.

t: Upholding a systems approach: a basic principle and methodology for further deepening reform comprehensively
zh: 坚持系统观念：进一步全面深化改革的基本原则和方法论
paras: Xiao Guiqing and Lu Yang take up the principle of the systems approach (xitong guannian) set out in the decision of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on further deepening reform comprehensively and advancing Chinese modernization. They argue that this approach is both a basic principle and a methodology, and that reform must be made more systematic, integrated and coordinated if it is to go further.

The article has three parts. The first traces the systems approach to Marxist fundamental principles and to traditional Chinese thought, and reviews its role in reform since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second examines how the 2024 decision applies it: through institutional building across all fields, through the leading role of economic reform, and through balancing development and security. The third sets out three conditions for putting the approach into practice.

The authors present the approach as running from Engels's account of universal connection, through Mao Zedong's "playing the piano" method and Deng Xiaoping's call for balance, to Xi Jinping's formulations. They hold that reform has moved from local experiments to systems integration, with institution-building as the main thread. On their account the decision proposes over 300 reform measures, with economic reform pulling the others along. Measures in politics, culture, society, ecology and national security are said to interlock, producing a multiplier effect of "1+1>2". Systemic reform is said to carry systemic risk, so national security reform is described as a safeguard for the whole.

For implementation the authors name three requirements. First, the Party's overall leadership must be upheld unwaveringly, since it is said to coordinate interests and keep reform on the right political course. Second, the advantages of the socialist system with Chinese characteristics should be used, including the ability to act as "one nation, one chessboard" and to meet risks with institutional strength. Third, strategy should rest on the "two overall situations": the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the great changes unseen in a century. Read the original if you want a detailed Party-theoretical account of how the systems approach is tied to the 2024 reform decision.
quoteEn: Further deepening reform comprehensively ultimately comes down to being comprehensive.
quoteZh: 进一步全面深化改革，归根结底要落实到全面上。

glossary.explanation: A method of analysing and solving problems by looking at the whole, the links between parts and their development. It is presented in Party documents as part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought.
The official term for China's path of modernization, stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central long-term goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, closely linked to the Chinese Dream.

t: Historical materialism and the Marxist view of civilization
zh: 唯物史观与马克思主义文明观
paras: Wang Weiguang starts from Xi Jinping's call to 'shoulder the cultural mission of the new era'. The article argues that this call cannot be properly understood without answering what civilization is, and that the answer requires historical materialism and a Marxist view of civilization. Wang holds that the founders of Marxism wrote no dedicated treatise on civilization, but that their scattered statements allow a coherent view to be reconstructed, and that this view is part of historical materialism.

The article is a close reading of the classics. It surveys how Marx, Engels and Lenin use terms such as 'civilization', 'civilized nations', 'civilized society', 'ancient civilization' and 'modern civilization', with page-referenced citations from works including the Communist Manifesto, the Grundrisse, Capital, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State and Lenin's speeches. It is organised in four parts: civilization as capitalist civilization; the revolutionary supersession of that civilization; Engels's periodisation of the 'age of civilization'; and a closing list of the main tenets of the Marxist view.

Wang's central claim is that, in the classics, 'civilization' in contexts about capitalism usually denotes bourgeois or capitalist civilization, which they praise for its historical role yet expose as resting on class exploitation. Engels's 'age of civilization' is read as running from slave society through feudalism to capitalism, marked by division of labour, commodity production, private property, classes and the state. Wang adds that tool-making in primitive society marks the origin of civilization, which he distinguishes from the beginning of the 'age of civilization'. From these readings Wang derives six tenets: the productive forces are the basic standard; the social formation determines a civilization's character; civilization is a historical category, so no abstract 'universal' civilization exists; class analysis is required; each civilization is progressive relative to its predecessor yet will be replaced; and idealist views must be criticised.

Wang concludes that Marxism treats civilization as a marker of the nature, condition and degree of social progress, to be analysed historically, concretely, dialectically and in class terms. Wang presents Huntington's 'clash of civilizations' as a contemporary variant of the idealist view criticised by the classics, which in Wang's account obscures class struggle. Read the original if you want a densely documented, Chinese-language account of how a leading Party theorist extracts a theory of civilization from Marx, Engels and Lenin and uses it to frame current cultural policy.
quoteEn: Civilization should be the marker, embodiment and summation of the condition, nature and degree of human social progress.
quoteZh: 文明应当是人类社会进步的状况、性质和程度的标志、体现和概括。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory that material production and the conflict between productive forces and relations of production drive social change. Chinese texts use it as the basis for analysing history and culture.
A theoretical stance on what civilization is and how it develops. Wang reconstructs a 'Marxist view of civilization' from the classics.

glossary.zh: 担负新时代的文化使命
glossary.pinyin: dānfù xīn shídài de wénhuà shǐmìng
glossary.en: shoulder the cultural mission of the new era
glossary.explanation: A formulation associated with Xi Jinping, calling on the Party and the nation to develop socialist culture with Chinese characteristics and carry forward Chinese civilization.
Samuel Huntington's thesis that post-Cold War conflict follows cultural and civilizational lines. Wang criticises it as idealist.

t: Developing new quality productive forces with patient capital: Chinese and Western variants, dual attributes and practical paths
zh: 以耐心资本发展新质生产力：中西分野、二重属性与实践探索
source: China Economic Problems (中国经济问题), 2024 no. 6
paras: He Cheng, Gao Hepeng and Lin Peng ask how "patient capital" (long-term, steady investment capital) can be built up to develop new quality productive forces. They take up the policy call in the Third Plenum decision of the 20th Central Committee (2024) to develop patient capital. Their thesis is that Chinese patient capital differs in kind from its Western counterpart, carries both the general attributes of capital and a special long-term, steady character, and can drive technological innovation, total factor productivity and industrial upgrading, provided current obstacles are removed.

The article has six parts. It first compares Western and Chinese patient capital through the history of economic thought. It then analyses the dual attributes of patient capital in a Marxist framework, sets out its value for new quality productive forces, and identifies constraints in China's capital market. It ends with practical paths and a short conclusion. Sources include Marx's Capital, Mariana Mazzucato's work, Keynesian investment theory, and Chinese statistics on turnover, basic research spending and patent commercialisation.

The authors argue that Western patient capital rests on the factor-value theory and on Western investment theory. In their account this reduces capital to a production factor, drifts toward finance and speculation, and makes patience hard to sustain. Chinese patient capital, they say, rests on the labour theory of value and on a long-termist investment tradition. It is led by the Party, centred on state capital, and meant to serve the people. Drawing on Marx, they hold that patient capital shares capital's drive to self-valorisation, but chooses long holding periods and prudent management as a strategy. They attribute its usefulness to its role as a "fund stabiliser" for innovation and its pull of capital away from M–M′ speculation toward industrial capital.

The authors identify four obstacles: short-termism in the capital market, citing an annual stock turnover of 273% against 102% in the United States; weak long-term investment appetite among both state and private capital; blockages in the technology–industry–finance cycle, such as a 3.9% industrialisation rate for university invention patents; and incomplete exit mechanisms.
