They propose responsible (ESG) investment, a guiding role for state capital, broader sources of funds (government funds, pension funds, insurance capital, regulated international capital), and a better market environment. They conclude that only under the Party's centralised leadership can patient capital become a driver of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese economic-policy argument on patient capital, with its Marxist justification and the statistics it cites.
quoteEn: The long-term and steady character of patient capital is a concrete expression of capital's valorisation attribute under particular conditions, a strategic choice within capital's pursuit of profit.
quoteZh: 耐心资本的长期性和稳健性是资本增殖属性在特定条件下的具体表现，是资本逐利过程中的一种战略选择。

glossary.explanation: Long-horizon, steady investment capital that tolerates long payback periods. Chinese policy documents began promoting it in 2024, including in the Third Plenum decision.
A concept promoted by Xi Jinping from 2023. It refers to innovation-led, high-technology, high-efficiency productive forces, often linked to strategic emerging and future industries.
The official name for China's path of development under Party leadership, set out in Party documents since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
An economic measure of output growth not explained by increases in capital and labour inputs. Chinese policy texts treat it as an indicator of growth quality.

t: Rethinking the forms in which the "new world outlook" has been interpreted
st: An examination based on the history of the development of Marxist philosophy
zh: 重思“新世界观”阐释形式问题
zhSub: 基于马克思主义哲学发展史的考察
paras: Marx never used the term "Marxist philosophy". Zhang Dingxin asks how the "new world outlook", which Marx and Engels used for their philosophical revolution, should be understood and why its later interpretive forms matter today. The article argues that this outlook is, at root, a proletarian world outlook. Its core is the critique of political economy, not speculative philosophy alone. The successive interpretive forms (Engels's, Lenin's, Western Marxism's and Chinese Marxism's) each made real contributions.

The article first traces how Marx built the outlook, from his 1842 letter to Ruge through the 1844 Manuscripts, the Theses on Feuerbach, The German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto, the 1859 Preface and Capital. It then surveys how others presented it. Engels used historical materialism and materialist dialectics. Lenin and Stalin developed dialectical and historical materialism. Gramsci and Lukács formulated a philosophy of practice. Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping adapted it in China. A fourth section draws out principles for Marxist philosophy now.

Zhang holds that Marxist philosophy has three layers: a new theory of practice, a dialectic of social history, and the critique of political economy, with the first two serving as the philosophical basis of the third. On this reading, Engels's forms were not "pre-Marxist" but registered the shift of focus from nature to human society and "real human beings". Zhang also identifies a tension between practical subjectivity and material objective reality, and argues that Marx's texts treat the two as intertwined and unified, not antinomic. Marxism is thus neither a hostile materialism nor a "practice-only" doctrine.

Zhang draws three principles for developing Marxist philosophy today. It must keep its proletarian world-outlook identity. It must retain the dual dimension of philosophical critique and critique of political economy. It must combine responsiveness to the times with universal necessity. Zhang cites Xi Jinping's statements on common prosperity, on capital, on Chinese modernization and on a community with a shared future for mankind as embodying these principles. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Chinese philosophers trace the lineage from Marx through Engels, Lenin and Western Marxism to Chinese Marxism.
quoteEn: Holding fast to the "identity" of the proletarian world outlook remains the fundamental precondition for upholding and developing Marxist philosophy today.
quoteZh: 持守无产阶级世界观“身份”仍然是当代坚持和发展马克思主义哲学的根本前提。

glossary.explanation: A goal of socialism that Xi Jinping has stressed in recent years. It is officially described as prosperity for all the people, in both material and cultural life, and not egalitarianism.
The official name for China's path of modernization under Party leadership. It has been a central theme of Party discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations and global governance, promoted in Chinese foreign-policy and theoretical writing since about 2012.

t: How the modern age can speak of the Absolute: Hegel's interpretation of Spinoza as a case
zh: 现代如何言说绝对者：以黑格尔的斯宾诺莎阐释为例
paras: Zhuang Zhenhua asks how modern thought can speak of the Absolute without lapsing into dogmatic assertion. Taking Hegel's reading of Spinoza as the test case, the article argues that Hegel's real objection is not that Spinoza's substance is static or that his geometrical method is flawed. In Zhuang's reading, the objection is that Spinoza's Absolute cannot pass the 'test' of modern life, because it is posited directly rather than shown to be necessary from within actual things.

The article begins with the Absolute as a question that runs through modern philosophy, from Leibniz's 'why is there something rather than nothing?' to present-day speculative realism and new realism. Section one reviews Hegel's remarks on Spinoza in the Lectures on the History of Philosophy and in the two Logics, the Science of Logic and the Encyclopaedia Logic. Section two follows three chapters of the Doctrine of Essence, 'The Absolute', 'Actuality' and 'The Absolute Relation'. A closing section considers the contemporary relevance of Hegel's route.

Zhuang's central claim is that, for Hegel, an Absolute that stands beyond finite determinations must pass two further 'gates'. The first is to discern absolute necessity in actual things, moving from contingency through relative necessity to absolute necessity. The second is to see how that necessity presents itself as freedom, through the substantial relation, causality and reciprocity. Zhuang reads the chapter on 'The Absolute' as Hegel's 'rewriting' of Spinoza's substance, attribute and mode. It remains an abstract, external reflection that never examines its own dualistic positing. The next two chapters 'complete' Spinoza, producing a new kind of substance that, on Zhuang's account, fulfils Spinoza's original intention.

Zhuang concludes that Hegel 'revises' rather than 'overthrows' Spinoza, which strips the substance doctrine of its dogmatic character and offers a model for modern engagement with the Absolute. The article suggests that Meillassoux's 'necessity of contingency' echoes Hegel's move, though it says it remains to be seen whether recent realisms avoid Spinoza's predicament. Zhuang adds that Hegel's Absolute does not strengthen subjective reason or confer a 'God's-eye view'. Freedom must be preserved through renunciation of what one immediately is and has. Read the original if you work on Hegel's Logic, Spinoza reception or German idealism and want a close, text-based account of the Absolute in the Doctrine of Essence.)
quoteEn: Hegel is wary not only of all finite determinations, as Spinoza is, but also of the lofty yet abstract fervour of casting off finite determinations to embrace the Absolute directly.
quoteZh: 黑格尔不仅像斯宾诺莎那样警惕一切有限规定，也警惕人抛弃有限规定而直接拥抱绝对者这种虽然崇高却也抽象的激昂做法。

t: The shift of axial research paradigms in the emergence of Marx's philosophical revolution
zh: 马克思哲学革命出场的轴心研究范式转换
paras: Ren Ping and Fan Yun ask whether Marx's philosophical revolution and the founding of a new worldview were accompanied by a conscious change of research method, and whether that change drove the revolution. They argue that earlier scholarship studied the results, process and content of the revolution but overlooked the "axial paradigm" that structured each phase. In their account, shifts of axial paradigm were an internal methodological link in the change from old to new worldview.

The article divides Marx's path into three periods, each led by a different axial paradigm: the text-and-literature interpretation paradigm, the dialogue paradigm, and the paradigm of reflective problematics. It follows Marx from his move from law to philosophy and from Kant and Schelling to Hegel, through his break with the Young Hegelians and engagement with Feuerbach and Engels. It then follows his turn to the study of political economy, ending with Capital, the Paris Commune and the Russian question. A final section draws lessons for Marxist philosophy in China.

The authors hold that every paradigm has a limited range, and that Marx met a "methodological predicament" whenever his questions outgrew his method. Interpretation of texts, as in his doctoral dissertation, was in their view monological and stayed inside the history of ideas. Dialogue with contemporaries such as Bauer, Feuerbach and Engels gave two-way exchange and helped him leave Hegel behind. The paradigm of reflective problematics, shown in the Rheinische Zeitung's "material interest" problem, Engels's critique of political economy and the Manchester visit, moved him from criticising "copies" to criticising the historical "original". The three paradigms ended up as "one body, two wings", with problematics as the body and the other two as wings.

The authors conclude that methodological self-awareness and the founding of the new worldview advanced together. They add that paradigms alternate synchronically as well as diachronically, and that no paradigm is permanently present. Finally, they propose that the "one body, two wings" pattern can be a breakthrough point in building an autonomous knowledge system of contemporary Chinese Marxist philosophy. Read the original if you want a methodological periodisation of the young Marx's development, with detailed attention to the Rheinische Zeitung, the Manchester notes and the influence of Engels.
quoteEn: Marx's philosophical revolution contained within it a shift of research paradigms: the change in the research path Marx adopted was precisely the indispensable internal methodological link on which the transition from the old worldview to the new depended.
quoteZh: 马克思发动的哲学革命内蕴着研究范式的转换，即马克思所采取的研究路径的变革恰恰是新旧世界观转换赖以发生的必不可少的内在方法论环节

glossary.explanation: The authors' term for the research paradigm that, in a given period, breaks the balance among coexisting paradigms and takes the leading role.
A paradigm centred on real problems in history's "original" rather than on texts or ideas. The authors treat it as the third and decisive axial paradigm in Marx's development.
The authors' image for Marx's mature research pattern, with the problematics paradigm as the body and the interpretation and dialogue paradigms as supporting wings.

t: The epistemological presuppositions of Marx's critique of political economy
zh: 马克思政治经济学批判的认识论前提
paras: This short commentary asks what epistemological presuppositions underlie Marx's critique of political economy. Luo argues that, although epistemology was not central to Marx's thinking, his critique rests on premises quite different from those of mainstream natural and social science, and that Marx was fully aware of this. Marx continues the tradition of German critical philosophy and refuses to treat capitalist economic activity as a natural, eternal fact.

The article first places Marx after Kant and Hegel, then turns to his objections to classical political economy. It closes with Marx's own method of abstraction, drawing on his discussion of the concept of production.

Luo contends that Marx should not be separated from epistemology or read only ontologically. Instead, Marx's thought needs an epistemology that moves beyond the paradigm of subjectivity philosophy and grasps things themselves, so that changing the world becomes possible. Following Hegel's critique of Kant, Marx inherits the post-Kantian demand to "know things themselves". On this reading, political economy treats atomised individuals, private property and the division of labour as universal presuppositions, and capitalist reproduction then reinforces them. Its abstractions yield empty "abstract identity", while Marx's abstraction keeps what it abstracts tied to the whole and to historically specific social relations.

Luo concludes that classical economists therefore miss surplus value, the dual character of labour and commodities, and the relations of domination hidden in capital and wage labour. Marx's critique, in the article's account, grasps identity within difference and so understands capitalism more fully. It also shows the practical necessity of changing the capitalist facts it exposes. Read the original if you want a compact philosophical account of Marx's epistemology and its Kantian and Hegelian background.
quoteEn: Marx's critique of political economy is the truly scientific knowledge of modern capitalism.
quoteZh: 马克思的政治经济学批判才是真正的关于现代资本主义的科学认识

t: Foundational questions in constructing Marx's view of morality
st: An analysis based on The German Ideology
zh: 马克思道德观构建的基础问题
zhSub: 基于《德意志意识形态》的分析
paras: Zhang Yonggang takes up the long dispute between "Marxist moralism" and "Marxist immoralism", associated with Allen Wood, who calls Marx a critic of all morality, and with Rodney Peffer and Ziyade Hussami, who find moral values in Marx's thought. The article argues that neither side can be settled by quarrelling over the word "morality". In Zhang's view, Marx's moral outlook has to be read from its foundations in historical materialism, in the life of real people and in concrete social life, as set out in The German Ideology.

The article is organised in three parts. The first asks how morality can legitimately exist within historical materialism and how its normative content is formed. The second turns to the concern with human existence: the "real individual" as the practical subject of morality and the free and all-round development of the human being as its ultimate aim. The third treats morality oriented to social life, including its role as an ideological "tool of thought" in the working of society. Zhang draws on Engels, Kai Nielsen, David McLellan, Alasdair MacIntyre and Paul Blackledge.

Zhang argues first that morality is a form of social consciousness determined "in the last instance" by the economic base, but not by it alone. Fatalist and mechanical readings of historical materialism are rejected, as is moral absolutism. The apparent contradiction between Marx's condemnation of bourgeois morality and his moral language against exploitation is said to dissolve: he rejects bourgeois moral content while holding a normative vision of a communist society of human self-realisation. Humans are both "actors" and "authors" of moral norms, which resolves the tension between agency and structural determination. Second, Zhang disputes Wood's split between "moral" and "non-moral" goods. On a broad sense of morality, freedom and self-realisation are moral values, and history's direction and morality's core demand coincide.

Zhang concludes that Marx's morality is a distinct "other construction" set against traditional moral philosophy. It does not slide into moral nihilism or moral determinism, and it moves from maintaining social order to pursuing human emancipation. Clarifying these foundations, the author says, answers the objections to Marx's view and supports a Marxist moral theory grounded in the texts. Read the original if you work on Marxist ethics or the Wood debate and want a Chinese scholar's systematic reading of The German Ideology on morality.
quoteEn: Morality, as a form of social consciousness, reflects real life at the level of ideas. It has no history of its own and cannot develop by itself, and only within real society does it acquire meaningful content.
quoteZh: 道德作为一种社会意识，是现实生活在观念层面的反映，其本身没有历史也无法自我发展，只有置身于现实社会，才具有其意义的内容。

t: Marx on the "retribution" of colonialism and its contemporary lessons
st: A close reading of "The Indian Revolt" and related texts
zh: 马克思论殖民主义的“报应”及其现实启示
zhSub: 对《印度起义》等文献的研读
source: Ideological and Political Education Research (思想教育研究), 2025 no. 1
paras: Xu Qin asks what Marx meant by "retribution" (baoying) in his 1850s writings on British rule in India, and what that idea says to the present. The article argues that Marx used the word in a materialist-dialectical sense: colonialism's own crimes produce the opposition that undoes it. Xu opens with Xi Jinping's 2018 warning that trade wars and economic hegemony will end up like "lifting a rock only to drop it on one's own feet", and presents Marx's concept as an earlier warning to the colonial powers.

The study rests on Marx's New-York Daily Tribune articles on the 1857 Indian uprising, including "The Revolt in the Indian Army", "The Indian Revolt", "The Indian Question" and "Investigation of Tortures in India", together with his writings on the East India Company. After separating Marxist "retribution" from religious karma, Xu identifies three forms of it: the sepoy army that Britain built and that then rebelled; the sepoys' "atrocities" as a concentrated reflection of British conduct; and the cost of holding India, which could exceed any revenue. A final section draws conclusions for today.

Xu contrasts religious retribution, which is run by an alien supernatural power and rests on idealism, with the Marxist version, in which people themselves are the agents and cause and effect are objective. In this account Marx treated the revolt as retribution because it came from the British-trained, British-fed sepoys, not from the plundered peasantry. Xu says Marx tied the sepoys' violence to British annexations, tax torture and officers' cruelty, and criticised The Times for inflating it. On cost, Xu cites Marx's point that India's revenue never reached the British treasury, while Parliament lent the Company over £50 million. Only a small group of shareholders, officials and traders profited.

Xu concludes that colonialism's end as a system, which the author dates to Namibia's independence in 1990, did not end colonial thinking. The author charges the United States and the West with neo-colonial hegemony, citing domestic disorder and the Gaza vetoes as self-inflicted costs, and calls on them to abandon colonial thinking and follow the trend of peace, development, cooperation and win-win outcomes. The article also urges a new type of international relations built on mutual respect, fairness and justice, and win-win cooperation, and links this to the Global Security Initiative, the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Marx's India articles, or an example of how Chinese scholarship ties them to current foreign-policy language.
quoteEn: A nation that enslaves other nations is forging its own chains.
quoteZh: 奴役其他民族的民族是在为自己锻造镣铐。

glossary.en: a new type of international relations
glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping put forward in 2013 and defined in the 19th Party Congress report (2017) as relations built on mutual respect, fairness and justice, and win-win cooperation. It is presented as an alternative to Cold War thinking and power politics.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's framework for global governance, promoted since 2013, which stresses shared interests and cooperation among states.
A Chinese infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched in 2013, linking China with countries across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.
A proposal Xi Jinping announced at the Boao Forum in April 2022. It calls for common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security and opposes bloc confrontation.
Ordinarily a religious notion of karmic payback. The article argues that Marx used it in a materialist sense, for the objective causal consequences of colonial oppression.

t: The second leap over the "Caudine Forks"
zh: “卡夫丁峡谷”的第二重跨越
source: Journal of Hainan Tropical Ocean University, online first, 12 February 2025
paras: Yu Bin asks why the Soviet Union, having apparently crossed the "Caudine Forks" of capitalism that Marx discussed in his late writings on Russia, fell back into them, and what this means for China. The article argues that the Soviet Union and China completed only a first leap, which abolished the capitalist system. A second leap remains: workers must fully master the achievements capitalism created. Yu reads the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) call to raise the whole Party's "Marxist level and capacity for modernization" as the path to this second leap.

The article has four parts. It first traces the incomplete crossing, from Marx's 1881 reply to Vera Zasulich through the October Revolution, the Soviet collapse and China's reform and opening up. It then defends the claim that the first leap was completed, against two views in the scholarly literature. A third section examines the first leap's shortcomings, covering Lenin's New Economic Policy, the Soviet model, the Party's treatment of intellectuals in China and Deng Xiaoping's response. The last section names three new problems of the second leap and proposes measures for Party members.

Yu's central move is to separate two leaps. The first is the abolition of capitalist relations of production and the "two ruptures" of the Communist Manifesto, with traditional property relations and traditional ideas. The second is the real appropriation of capitalism's positive results, above all knowledge. Yu holds that the Soviet Union fell not through backwardness but because Party members' Marxist level was too low to break fully with feudal and bourgeois ideas, which left it open to Gorbachev's turn to democratic socialism and to "peaceful evolution". Yu then names three requirements. Science and labour must be directly united, so that production is not left under the control of capital. The people led by the Party must be the subject of the leap, since development must rely on and benefit them. Marxist level and modernization capacity must rise together, since either alone leads to failure.

Yu proposes theoretical study, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and practice of whole-process people's democracy. Party members are given tasks by workplace: civil servants, state-owned enterprises, private firms, individual traders and mixed-ownership companies. Yu concludes that once members have these capacities, the goal of a modernized socialist power will be reached, and other countries may then look to China as a model. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar links Marx's Russia writings to Party-building and Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: For a socialist country that aims to cross the "Caudine Forks", the "Marxist level and capacity for modernization" of the proletarian vanguard, that is, of all Party members, must be raised together.
quoteZh: 对于旨在跨过“卡夫丁峡谷”的社会主义国家来说，无产阶级先进分子或全体党员的“马克思主义水平和现代化建设能力”必须共同提高

glossary.explanation: Marx's image, taken from the Roman defeat at the Caudine Forks, for the humiliation of capitalism. In 1881 he and Zasulich discussed whether Russia could skip it by building on the village commune.

glossary.zh: 提高全党马克思主义水平和现代化建设能力
glossary.pinyin: tígāo quándǎng Mǎkèsīzhǔyì shuǐpíng hé xiàndàihuà jiànshè nénglì
glossary.en: Marxist level and capacity for modernization
glossary.literal: raise the whole Party's Marxist level and modernization-building capacity
glossary.explanation: A requirement in the communiqué of the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024). It concerns Party members' theoretical grounding and practical ability to carry out modernization.
A term in Chinese Party discourse for Western efforts to change socialist states from within through ideological and cultural influence, without force.
The official name for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, presented as distinct from Western models.
An official concept, promoted since 2019, for the claim that democratic participation in China covers every stage of governance and not only elections.

t: Clarifying the materialist foundation of Marxist epistemology
zh: 马克思主义认识论的唯物主义基础辨析
paras: This short theoretical piece, published in Guangming Daily in March 2025, asks how Marxist epistemology can keep its materialist foundation while recognising the subject's activity in cognition. Wang Xiaosheng argues that stressing subjectivity can undermine materialism, while the theory of reflection, though materialist in stance, has not explained why reflection is objectively valid. The article's answer is that the objective validity of reflection must be shown through a bodily, material basis that remains present inside sensation, reason and concepts.

The article moves in three steps under three headings: the objectivity of sensation and experience; the spiritualisation of sensation and experience; and the non-conceptual element within concepts. Wang engages Husserl's phenomenology, Adorno's critique of it, Kant's idea of the manifold of sensibility, and Hegel's concept of actuality. Examples include the bent stick in water, the pain of the body, a blind person's grasp of 'red', and a mother's 'love'.

Wang observes that both defenders and critics of reflection treat sensory experience as unreliable, yet cognition depends on it, so it must contain something objective. Husserl locates this in the indubitable fact of having an experience, which Wang calls a subjectivised objectivity. Following Adorno, Wang locates it instead in the body: objectivity in sensation comes from material interaction, not from reflection. Cognition nonetheless spiritualises sensation, making it neutral and expressible in language, and the objective content survives as a 'trace' of bodily activity. Reason is likewise both opposed to nature and an extension of it, and logic rests on a pre-logical base. Concepts therefore contain non-conceptual elements; without them they are empty words, and scientific innovation often comes when such elements break through existing concepts.

Wang concludes that Marx's concept of actuality, unlike Hegel's, contains the bodily element and connects with external reality, so that a concept 'contains' reality rather than merely referring to it. Marxist epistemology, in this reading, is dialectical materialism that sees both the objective basis of cognition and the interaction of body and mind, offering a key to the problems of traditional subject–object dualism. Read the original if you want a compact attempt to ground the Marxist theory of reflection in the body through Adorno and phenomenology.
quoteEn: The active theory of reflection shows that even if cognition is a process of spiritualisation, this process is always built on the basis of reflection.
quoteZh: 能动的反映论表明，即使认识是一个精神化的过程，这个精神化的过程始终是建立在反映的基础上的。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist-Leninist view that human cognition reflects an objective, material reality existing independently of consciousness. Wang discusses it in an 'active' (能动的) form, stressing the subject's activity.

t: Lenin's idea of the ruling party's "general leadership" and its contemporary value
zh: 列宁执政党“总的领导”思想及其当代价值
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2024 no. 5
paras: After the October Revolution the Bolsheviks became a ruling party and had to decide how it should lead a state without simply running it. Shi Weilei argues that Lenin, combining Marx and Engels's theory of party leadership with the practice of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks), developed an idea of the ruling party's "general leadership" (总的领导). In Shi's reading, this is overall, supreme leadership of the whole of national life, exercised through state power rather than in place of it.

The article has four parts. It traces the idea through three phases: an embryonic stage (1917 to spring 1919), a preliminary formation (1919 to early 1921) and a final formation (from 1921). It then sets out the idea's content, the means of implementing it, and its value today. Shi draws mainly on Lenin's writings and on resolutions of the Party congresses of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks).

Shi's central claim is that "general leadership" combines several features. It is supreme and comprehensive, covering state power, the economy, culture and the military. It is the unity of political, ideological and organisational leadership, including the principle that the Party manages cadres. It includes general supervision through independent Party control commissions. Lenin first used the term in 1920, in criticism of the Proletkult. In 1922 he used it against the confusion of Party and soviet functions, which Shi says weakened both. Shi lists the means of exercising it: guiding legislation without replacing law, Party groups and exemplary Communists inside other bodies, cadre selection, leadership of trade unions and the youth league, democratic centralism, a ban on factions, and better capacity to oversee the whole and coordinate the parts. Shi concedes that the Russian party failed to resolve the problem in practice, but holds that Lenin set out the right path in theory.

Shi concludes that the idea is a theoretical source for the Chinese Communist Party's "comprehensive leadership" in the new era. Shi claims that "general", "everything" and "comprehensive" mean full coverage and indirect, overall leadership, not meddling in detail. The article calls for upholding the authority of the Party Central Committee and its centralised, unified leadership, and for leadership over all work. It also calls for a tight organisational system from central to grassroots level, and for stronger leadership capacity, above all political leadership. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theory account of how Lenin's writings on the party and the state are used to ground the current doctrine of the Party's comprehensive leadership.
quoteEn: "General", "everything" and "comprehensive" do not mean taking charge of every detail and trivial matter; they refer mainly to full coverage of objects, fields and scope, and to leadership that is overall and indirect in method.
quoteZh: “总的”、党是领导一切中的“一切”、党的全面领导中的“全面”并不是事无巨细、细枝末节的大包大揽，主要指的是对象、领域、范围的全覆盖以及领导方式上的全局性、间接性

glossary.explanation: A phrase from Lenin's texts (a 1920 text on the Proletkult and a 1922 Party congress resolution). The article takes it to mean supreme, overall leadership by the ruling party, exercised mainly indirectly through state organs.
A formula stressed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), meaning the Chinese Communist Party's leadership over all fields and levels of work. The article links it to Lenin's idea.
The organisational principle of Leninist parties, combining discussion and election with binding discipline and subordination of lower bodies to higher ones.

t: Marx and Engels's thought on modernization and its contemporary implications
zh: 马克思恩格斯的现代化思想及其当代启示
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2024 no. 6
paras: This article asks what Marx and Engels contributed to the theory of modernization, a topic that postwar Western modernization studies took up only later. Zhou Dan argues that their theory of social development is above all a theory of modern society, and that it therefore amounts to a body of thought on modernization. In the author's reading, that thought supplies a theoretical foundation and a direction for Chinese modernization.

The article is organised in five parts. It begins with three preconditions of modernization, drawn from Engels's remark on the English industrial revolution, French political revolution and German philosophical revolution. It then treats the assertion of human agency, the value goal of the free and all-round development of the individual, the logic by which Marx and Engels confront the problems of their age, and their vision of a future communist civilisation. Each part ends by linking the classical position to Chinese modernization.

Zhou's central move is to read modernization as having three dimensions: modern persons (philosophical revolution), the modern state (political revolution, illustrated by the French Declaration of the Rights of Man) and the modern material mode of production (industrial revolution). Marx and Engels, the author notes, rarely used the word itself, and mostly in connection with modern production. Zhou then argues that they gave modernization a dialectical analysis. They credited capitalism with advancing the productive forces while criticising capitalist modernity as a process in which the valorisation of capital devalues the human being. They also held that modernization has no single prescribed pattern, since historical conditions differ between countries. Engels's theory of the resultant of historical forces and Marx's theory of world history are used to ground the claim that people, as the practical subject, drive modernization.

Zhou concludes that Marx and Engels made the free and all-round development of the individual the core value of modernization, and that this points to a 'community of free individuals' and a shared human future beyond Western centrism and 'universal values'. In the author's account, Chinese modernization is the contemporary practice of this thought and has overcome the inherent dilemmas of capitalist modernity, through a socialist market economy and a people-centred approach. Zhou calls for pursuing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and a new form of human civilisation. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese reading of how Marx and Engels's classical texts are used to legitimise Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: Marx and Engels regarded 'modernization' as the necessary manifestation and necessary result of the 'modern', reflected above all in the mode of production.
quoteZh: 马克思恩格斯把“现代化”认定为“现代”的必然呈现和必然结果，并且集中反映在生产方式上。

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of China's own path of modernization, led by the Communist Party and described as socialist in character. It has been a central theme in Party theory since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-standing official goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, closely associated with Xi Jinping's leadership.
The Chinese rendering of Marx's idea of an 'association of free men', a communist form of society. The article links it to the official idea of a shared human future.

glossary.zh: 社会主义市场经济体制
glossary.explanation: The official name for China's economic system since the 1990s. It combines market mechanisms with public ownership and state macro-regulation.

t: Marx's thought on productive forces and its implications for developing new quality productive forces
zh: 马克思生产力思想及其对发展新质生产力的启示
source: Marxism and Reality (马克思主义与现实), 2024 no. 5
paras: Sun Shaoyong asks how new quality productive forces, a concept prominent in Party policy since 2023, can be grounded in Marx's own account of productive forces. The article argues that new quality productive forces belong to Marx's category of productive forces but give it new content in technological form, historical meaning, internal requirements and strategic value. In Sun's reading, the concept amounts to a terminological and paradigm shift in Marxist productive-force theory for the twenty-first century.

The article has four parts. It first sets out three core determinations of productive forces in Marx: the creative power of 'real individuals', a combined force formed in actual production, and the capacity for metabolic exchange between humans and nature. It then interprets new quality productive forces through historical materialism, political economy and modernization. A third part draws practical implications, and a short conclusion follows. Sun cites Marx's German Ideology, Capital and his critique of List, alongside Xi Jinping's statements and the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024).

Sun's central move is to read new quality productive forces through Marx's three elements of productive forces: labourers, means of labour and objects of labour. New technologies such as artificial intelligence and data replace some manual labour, push workers towards mental labour, and create new use-values and new value. Sun treats division of labour and cooperation as the 'social labour' dimension and links the concept to Chinese modernization through technological, factor and industrial modernization. Because Marx treats productive forces as historically specific and as unity of natural and social productive forces, Sun holds that new quality productive forces are necessarily 'green productive forces'.

Sun draws four proposals. These are to train high-quality 'new quality labourers' by linking education, science and talent; to develop green technology and new energy; to adjust relations of production, including the basic socialist economic system, the Two Unwaverings, distribution by labour combined with distribution by factors, and a new nationwide system for major innovation; and to integrate the digital and real economies. Sun concludes that labourers play the leading role and that tracing the concept to Marx clarifies its features and requirements. Read the original if you want a systematic account of how Chinese scholars derive new quality productive forces from Marx's texts and what policy measures they attach to it.
quoteEn: New quality productive forces are a higher-order requirement of the development of productive forces and in essence belong to the Marxist category of productive forces.
quoteZh: 新质生产力是生产力发展的高阶性要求，本质上隶属于马克思主义的生产力范畴

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping from 2023 for advanced productive forces driven by technological breakthroughs, new factor combinations and industrial upgrading, rather than by resource input alone.
The official name for the Party's model of national modernization, presented as distinct from Western paths.
The official formula of unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector and unwaveringly encouraging and supporting the non-public sector.

glossary.en: a new nationwide system for major innovation
glossary.explanation: An official term for mobilising state research capacity, government finance and market actors under Party leadership to tackle major science and technology projects.

t: Marx's conception of revolution and its significance for the new era
zh: 马克思革命观及其新时代意蕴
paras: Gao Junhua takes up Hannah Arendt's claim that Marx, though the greatest theorist of revolution, almost wholly ignored the revolutionaries' real intention, the founding of freedom. The article treats this as a representative misreading: it denies freedom a place in Marx's theory and then pits the mature Marx against the young Marx. Gao argues that Marx's conception of revolution can be understood only through the close link between political and social revolution and through its relation to freedom. On that basis, Gao explains in what sense China in the new era speaks of continuing revolution.

The article has four parts. The first sets out the scientific content of Marx's conception, drawing on On the Jewish Question, the Communist Manifesto and Hal Draper's Karl Marx's Theory of Revolution. The second examines its value orientation, distinguishing political freedom from social freedom. The third discusses the revolutionary subject, the proletariat. The fourth turns to the new era, taking up the Party's self-reform and common prosperity.

Gao holds that for Marx political revolution is the struggle between classes over state power, and that it need not be violent: Marx allowed some countries to win power through universal suffrage. Bourgeois revolutions, in this reading, produced only formal freedom, because the split between state and civil society and private ownership left real freedom unrealised. Social revolution therefore means developing the productive forces, replacing private ownership of the means of production and so overcoming alienated labour, and it serves as the basis of political revolution. Against Arendt, Gao argues that Marx never abandoned freedom: it appears in the Paris Commune, in the later notion of the 'free individuality', and in the realm of freedom beyond the realm of necessity. The proletariat, as a universal class, moves from a class in itself to a class for itself through revolutionary practice, uniting consciousness with reality and the universal with the particular.

Gao concludes that two themes of the new era extend Marx's conception. The Party's self-reform is presented as political revolution, expressing Marx's stress on the proletarian party and his dialectic of the subject remaking itself. Common prosperity is presented as social revolution, resting on developed productive forces, adjusted relations of production with public ownership in the leading position, and the material basis for individual freedom. Gao links these in the Party's formula of leading a great social revolution through a great self-reform. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar defends a freedom-centred reading of Marx against Arendt and ties it to current Party doctrine.
quoteEn: The revolutionary spirit in Marx's conception of revolution is not the abstract freedom of liberalism, but real freedom in society.
quoteZh: 马克思革命观中的革命精神不是自由主义抽象的自由，而是社会中的真实自由。

glossary.explanation: A term stressed by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It denotes the Party's continuing effort to correct its own problems and keep its vitality as the long-term ruling party.
A goal of socialism that the Party leadership has emphasised in recent years. It means prosperity shared by all the people, with attention to development and to distribution.

t: "The masses" and "spirit"
st: Based on Marx and Engels's arguments in The Holy Family
zh: “群众”和“精神”
zhSub: 基于马克思恩格斯在《神圣家族》中的相关论断
source: Teaching and Research (教学与研究), 2024 no. 11
paras: Yang Ke and Li Zhongjun treat the relation between "the masses" and "spirit" as a basic question of historical materialism. They also present it as a precondition for advancing common prosperity in the spiritual life of the people. Their thesis is that Marx and Engels, in The Holy Family, rejected the speculative opposition of spirit to the masses and set out a dialectical unity of the two. The authors say this unity underpins the current policy goal that common prosperity cover both material and spiritual life.

The article has four parts. It first reconstructs Marx and Engels's critique of Hegel and the Young Hegelians, in particular Bruno Bauer's "critical criticism". It then sets out their positive account of how masses and spirit are unified. The third part draws out the contemporary significance of this unity, and the fourth derives practical requirements from it. It cites Xi Jinping's remarks and the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) alongside the classical texts.

In the authors' reading, the speculative philosophers made three moves. They separated spirit from the masses and made the masses mere bearers of spirit. They cast the masses as spirit's "true enemy". They then excluded the masses from history, so that history became that of a few outstanding individuals. Marx and Engels, Yang and Li argue, traced this inverted worldview back to an inverted world of minority oppression and bourgeois exploitation. Against it they held that the masses are the subjects of historical activity and thought, and that ideas which part from interests disgrace themselves. Ideas also achieve nothing unless "people who can use practical force" internalise them in the masses' thinking and carry them out in the masses' activity.

From this the authors derive three footholds for spiritual common prosperity. These are the unity of material and spiritual life, coordination between spiritual production and spiritual needs, and mutual promotion of cultural undertakings and the cultural industry. The latter requires breaking capital's grip on spiritual production while still using capital's positive role. They propose three requirements: putting the people at the centre, arming the masses with advanced theory (specifically Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era), and advancing material abundance and spiritual richness together as part of Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a close reading of The Holy Family is used to justify current Chinese policy on cultural and spiritual life.
quoteEn: For ideas to be realised, there must be people who can use practical force.
quoteZh: 思想要想得到实现，就要有使用实践力量的人。

glossary.explanation: A policy goal of shared wealth for all the people, promoted especially under Xi Jinping. Official statements say it covers both material and spiritual life.

The official term for China's own path of modernization, set out prominently in the 20th Party Congress report (2022). Its stated features include common prosperity and material and spiritual abundance.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sixiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China since 2017, written into the Party and state constitutions.

t: The value orientation of Marx's view of life and its contemporary significance
zh: 马克思生活观的价值旨趣及其当代意义
source: Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 17 December 2024
paras: Sun Min takes up the question of how Marx's view of life (shenghuo guan) relates to his philosophical revolution. The article argues that the two are inherently unified: Marx's philosophical innovation lies in the historical-materialist dimension of his view of life. Sun contends that scholars have neglected this link, which leaves Marx's philosophical revolution understood abstractly and obscures the value orientation of his view of life.

The article has three parts. It first contrasts Marx's view with the rationalist view of life of traditional philosophy, using Marx's critique of Hegel, and describes the existential reading of sensuous activity and the critique of capital. It then sets out four aspects of the value orientation of Marx's view of life. The last part names three kinds of contemporary significance, covering the development of Marxist philosophy, a new form of twenty-first-century Marxist philosophy, and the grasp of present-day human practice.

Sun's central claim is that Marx moved from abstract life to real life, from interpreting life to changing it, from the world of language to the lifeworld, and from dogmatic life to living life. In Sun's account, traditional philosophy treated life as spirit or idea and so could only explain it. Marx grounded life in practice and in the contradictions between productive forces and relations of production and between economic base and superstructure, so changing life requires changing social relations of production. Sun also criticises Husserl and Heidegger for bracketing material production, and reads Wittgenstein's return of words to everyday use as partly congruent with Marx. Sun adds that a people's life must be grasped through its own history, culture and traditions, and that otherwise historical materialism becomes dogma. Tradition itself is described as a living thing renewed through present practice.

Sun concludes that the four aspects together make up Marx's philosophical revolution and open a path to a better life for humanity. In Sun's view, grasping them helps recover the authentic spirit of Marx's philosophy and supports a new form of twenty-first-century Marxist philosophy that links China's fate with the world's. It also helps address the crises of virtual practice and of nature, society and spirit. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical account that ties Marx's view of everyday life to historical materialism and to current debates on Marxist philosophy.
quoteEn: Marx's view of life and his philosophical revolution are inherently unified.
quoteZh: 马克思生活观与他的哲学革命是内在统一的。

glossary.en: a new form of twenty-first-century Marxist philosophy
glossary.literal: new form of twenty-first-century Marxist philosophy
glossary.explanation: A phrase in Chinese Marxist theory for a Marxist philosophy said to address present-day conditions and to have both Chinese and world significance. Sun uses it to describe the goal that the study of Marx's view of life is meant to serve.
The guiding value aims or normative thrust of a theory. Sun uses it for the four turns that give Marx's view of life its direction.

glossary.literal: view of life / outlook on life
glossary.explanation: An understanding of what human life is and how it should be changed. Sun treats it as the core of Marx's philosophy and as inseparable from historical materialism.
The Marxist claim that Marx broke with earlier philosophy by basing it on practice and changing the world rather than only interpreting it.

t: Re-examining Marx's proposition on uneven development between art and material production, and its cultural implications
zh: 马克思不平衡关系命题的再辨析及其文化启示
source: Social Sciences Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2024 no. 6
paras: Bao Jin returns to a passage in Marx's 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, where Marx says that the flourishing of art is by no means proportionate to the general development of society or its material basis. The author notes that scholars still disagree. Some treat the imbalance as local and accidental, with rough proportion as the long-run rule. Others treat imbalance as absolute and balance as accidental. Bao seeks to clarify the proposition's real meaning so as to grasp the objective laws of cultural production and to inform China's new cultural mission.

The article has three parts. The first separates two forms in which the imbalance appears, synchronic and diachronic, using Greek epic and tragedy as the example. The second links the Introduction to Marx's 1861–63 manuscripts, where capitalist production is described as hostile to certain branches of spiritual production such as art and poetry. The third draws cultural lessons, discussing how Marx used the concept of culture and then connecting the proposition to Xi Jinping's statements on culture.

Bao argues that the imbalance is both synchronic (art against material production and against other civilisations of the same era) and diachronic (early art against later art and later material production). Greek art arose from an underdeveloped social stage and still serves as a model. The hostility thesis supplies the proposition's internal tension. Commodity art production follows capital's logic and is marked by capital, scale and popularity. Free spiritual production, by contrast, is self-regulating, unique and rich in ideas, so Milton writes Paradise Lost as a silkworm spins silk. Bao adds that free spiritual production is not wholly outside commodity production. It draws its means and nourishment from its own era, so its autonomy has historical limits, as Adorno also observed.

Bao draws three implications. First, culture's comparative advantage supports inheriting excellent traditional Chinese culture and shaping a cultural form of Chinese modernization, one that seeks balance within dynamic imbalance and opposes unilateralism and hegemony. Second, Marx's open appreciation of Greek culture supports mutual learning among civilisations over claims of civilisational superiority. Third, the transcendence of free spiritual production means spiritual abundance is a basic requirement of socialist modernization, and it cannot be measured in economic terms. Read the original if you want to see how a Marxist aesthetics debate is connected to current Party cultural policy and to Xi Jinping's cultural thought.
quoteEn: Free spiritual production is the objectification of the creator's essential powers and a free, conscious creation, containing the creator's own life course, emotions and ideas, consciousness and cultivated taste.
quoteZh: 自由精神生产是创作者本质力量的对象化和自由自觉的创造，包含创作者自己的生命历程、情感观念、思想意识和修养品位。

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of China's own path to modernization, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as combining material and cultural-ethical advancement.
The body of Xi Jinping's statements on culture, formally set out in 2023 as part of the Party's official ideology. It stresses cultural confidence and the Two Integrations.
A phrase Xi Jinping has used to say that socialist modernization requires cultural and moral enrichment as well as material wealth.
The official term for the parts of China's historical culture that the Party says should be creatively transformed and carried forward.

keywords: Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy

t: A systematic analysis of integrating the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture
zh: 马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合的系统分析
paras: Hong Xiaonan takes up the Party's formula, set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), of combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture. The article asks why this combination is necessary, possible and real. Using the method of unity of the logical and the historical, Hong concludes that Marxism has not failed China and China has not failed Marxism. The relationship must be guided by Marxism and by a scientific attitude to tradition, rejecting both cultural and historical nihilism and cultural restorationism or conservatism.

The article opens with a semantic analysis of the proposition. It asks why the text says "basic principles" rather than Marxism as a whole, "fine" traditional culture rather than traditional culture in general, and "tong" (with) rather than "he" or "yu" (and). Hong distinguishes traditional culture, cultural tradition, Chinese culture and Chinese traditional culture, and traces how Mao Zedong's wording of the "second integration" of 1956 developed. Sections then deal with necessity, possibility, the two directions of benefit, and the conditions for healthy interaction.

On necessity, Hong reviews how early Chinese Marxists, above all Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, chose Marxism through emotional and intellectual needs, and follows Chen's 1921 and 1923 lectures favouring communism over other socialisms. On possibility, citing Zhang Dainian, Xi Jinping and the 20th Congress report, Hong argues that fine traditional culture is highly compatible with the values of scientific socialism in four areas: cosmology ("unity of heaven and humanity"), views of the world order ("the world belongs to all"), views of society ("harmony without uniformity") and morality. Hong adds that the two are not identical. Confucian materialism, dialectics and utopianism differ from their Marxist counterparts.

Hong argues that the benefit runs both ways. Marxism gave tradition new vitality, as with the Party's reworking of "seeking truth from facts", "a moderately prosperous society", "keeping pace with the times" and "a community with a shared future for mankind". Tradition in turn gives Chinese Marxism its distinctive style and lifts its own simple materialism and dialectics to a higher level. The integration is not between equals but an organic one led by Marxism. Hong calls for creative transformation and innovative development of tradition, and presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the model. Read the original if you want a detailed account of how Chinese scholarship justifies the second of the Two Integrations, with its conceptual analysis and its historical cases from Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao.
quoteEn: The integration of the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture is not an equal, external combination but an \"organic integration\" in which Marxism holds the leading position.
quoteZh: 马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合，不是对等地、外在地结合，而是马克思主义居于主导地位的“有机结合”。

glossary.explanation: The Party's formula for adapting Marxism: combining its basic principles with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture. The second element was added to the formulation under Xi Jinping.
The part of China's traditional culture that official discourse regards as its essence, as distinct from "dross" such as feudal or outdated elements.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.pinyin: chuàngzào xìng zhuǎnhuà, chuàngxīn xìng fāzhǎn
glossary.explanation: A formula for treating tradition: giving old content and forms a modern meaning and expression, and supplementing and extending that content to suit new conditions.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations. The article presents it as drawing on the traditional notion of "tianxia" (all under heaven).
A goal Deng Xiaoping set in 1979 for modernization, borrowing a classical term from the Book of Songs.

t: The political-economy logic of developing service-oriented manufacturing
zh: 发展服务型制造的政治经济学逻辑
paras: This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2025, asks what service-oriented manufacturing means for Marxist political economy. Qi Hao defines it as manufacturers providing services across a product's whole life cycle, from design and financing to maintenance and recycling. The author argues that it is a new mode of production that carries new quality productive forces and that it calls for new relations of production.

The article has three parts. The first treats service-oriented manufacturing as a vehicle for new quality productive forces. The second examines how it raises the degree of socialisation of production. The third sets out the new production relations it requires, in data, in technology firms and in finance.

Qi holds that in Marxist terms a qualitative change in productive forces depends on a new mode of production. Smart products and the Internet of Things create a "data–service" cycle, which the author says integrates the real and digital economies, improves equipment use through leasing and pay-per-use, and eases overcapacity in durable goods. Every firm becomes a node in a denser network of data and service flows, and user data lets local innovation spread across industries. Qi therefore reads it as a leap in socialisation.

Following the principle that productive forces determine relations of production, Qi calls for three measures. These are laws that settle data ownership, cooperation between technology and manufacturing firms with curbs on monopoly over data and computing power, and "patient capital" against short-term returns. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist-political-economy framing of digital-era manufacturing within the discourse on new quality productive forces.
quoteEn: The distinctive significance of service-oriented manufacturing lies in its marked rise in the degree of socialisation of production, which reflects a qualitative leap in new quality productive forces.
quoteZh: 服务型制造的独特意义在于它显著提升了生产的社会化水平，体现出新质生产力质的跃迁。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2023 for advanced productivity driven by technological breakthroughs, new industries and digital technologies. It is a central theme of recent Chinese economic policy and theory.
A Marxist category for the growing division of labour and interdependence among producers in large-scale production. The author treats its degree as a marker of the level of productive forces.
Long-term investment capital that accepts slow returns and uncertainty. It appears in recent Chinese policy discussion of financing for the real economy and technological upgrading.

t: Viewing the cultural industry of the new era through Marx's theory of division of labour and cooperation
zh: 从马克思的分工协作理论看新时代文化产业
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 27 February 2025
paras: Prompted by the success of the domestic game Black Myth: Wukong and the animated film Ne Zha 2, this newspaper commentary asks how China's cultural industry can develop further in the new era. Xu and Wang argue that the idea of coordinated development (xietong fazhan), which they present as a deepening and extension of Marx's theory of division of labour and cooperation, explains these successes and should guide the industry.

The piece has three parts. It first traces the move from Marx's division of labour and cooperation to coordinated development. It then identifies three kinds of coordination behind industrial growth. It closes with three practical recommendations.

Drawing on Marx's Economic Manuscript of 1861–63, the authors describe division of labour as the totality of particular productive activities and cooperation as the basis of social combinations aimed at higher productivity. Coordination, in their reading, combines high specialisation with close cooperation, capturing efficiency gains while limiting the costs of excessive division. The three coordinations are cultural innovation with dissemination, internal enterprise systems with the external environment, and multiple business formats. The authors cite the game's developer, Game Science (Youke Hudong), as an example of the second, and online literature, film and games as examples of the third.

The authors call for coordinated innovation in culture and technology, including high-precision digitisation of relics and heritage. They urge stronger support for small and medium cultural-technology firms and for innovation ecosystems, and joint creation of high-quality original content for global audiences, with promotion on overseas social media. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars apply Marx's cooperation theory to cultural-industry policy.
quoteEn: Coordination is a dynamic process of coordination, cooperation and even synchronised linkage among the subsystems within a system; it is the result of a high integration of collective behaviour, and a way of organising productive forces that combines a high degree of division of labour with close cooperation.
quoteZh: 协同是系统内部各子系统间协调、合作乃至同步联动的动态过程，是一种集体行为高度整合的结果，是将高度分工与紧密协作相结合的生产力组织方式。

glossary.explanation: A concept used in Chinese policy and scholarship for the integrated, mutually reinforcing development of components within a system. Here the authors present it as an extension of Marx's theory of division of labour and cooperation.

The sector producing and distributing cultural goods and services, such as games, film, animation and online literature. In Chinese policy it is treated as a field for both economic growth and cultural development.

t: Marx's resolution of Rousseau's "paradox of freedom"
zh: 马克思对卢梭“自由悖论”的解决
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2025 no. 1
paras: Rousseau opens The Social Contract with the claim that man is born free yet is everywhere in chains. Yang He argues that this "paradox of freedom" exposes a tension between liberty and equality inside classical liberalism, and that Marx resolved it, not by refuting Rousseau but by transforming it critically through historical materialism and the theory of surplus value. The article appeared in the Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2025, no. 1.

The piece has three parts. The first reconstructs the liberal tradition (Locke, Grotius, Hobbes, Adam Smith) on natural rights, property and labour, and shows where Rousseau departed from it and why his proposed "moral and collective" community remained utopian. The second follows Marx's engagement with Rousseau, from the Kreuznach notebooks through the 1844 Manuscripts, and Hegel's influence on him. The third turns to the present: liberal adjustments (Keynesianism, neoliberalism, Hayek, Rawls) and the Chinese Communist Party's practice.

Yang's core claim is that Rousseau failed because his view of history was moralised and rooted in human nature. In the author's reading, Marx replaced this with a materialist account in four steps. Freedom is grasped through labour and the saving of labour time, and so is historical. Equality is a product of commodity exchange and cannot be an innate right, since formal equality in the market conceals exploitation in production. True community is not the political state, which Marx treated as a "false community", but arises when the means of production are socially owned. And the alienation narrative of subject, estrangement and return is replaced by the development of productive forces through class antagonism.

Yang concludes that liberal remedies remain trapped in Rousseau's paradox because they serve capital's logic. The author argues that public ownership and common prosperity are Marx's two basic requirements for resolving it, and that the Party has developed them through the basic socialist economic system, the elimination of absolute poverty and Chinese modernization. The author adds that regulating capital under the socialist market economy, while using its productive role, remains an open theoretical task. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Rousseau, Hegel and liberalism that links classical texts to the current common prosperity agenda.
quoteEn: Public ownership and common prosperity are Marx's two most basic requirements for transcending capitalist civilisation, the two most basic principles for resolving Rousseau's "paradox of freedom", and also the two most basic points of divergence between Marxism and liberalism.
quoteZh: 公有制和共同富裕,是马克思对于超越资本主义文明的两个最基本要求,是解决卢梭“自由悖论”的两个最基本原则,也是马克思主义与自由主义的两个最基本分歧

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal of shared wealth, given renewed emphasis under Xi Jinping. The article treats it as a defining institutional feature of socialism that separates it from capitalism.

The official name for China's development path under the Party, presented as distinct from Western modernization. The article lists it among the Party's contributions to Marx's ideas on the future society.

t: Methodological shifts in the young Marx's exploration of the philosophy of law
zh: 青年马克思法哲学探索中的方法论转换
source: Observation and Thinking (Guancha yu sikao), 2014 no. 1
paras: Why did the young Marx, starting from legal questions, have to take a "detour" through the critique of political economy, and how did his materialism and dialectics combine to bring about that change? Sun Meitang argues that the common explanation, which holds that the Rheinische Zeitung debates on material interests moved Marx from "copy" to "original", is not wrong but is too simple. In Sun's reading, the change in Marx's legal thought was complex, and it was accompanied by a change in method.

The article, first published in 2014, follows Marx from his university years and the Rheinische Zeitung commentaries (on press censorship and the law on wood theft), through the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right written at Kreuznach, to the critique of political economy. It sets this path against Marx's wider reading in history, politics and economics, and against the rise of capitalism in Western Europe. At each stage Sun identifies a different form of dialectics: the dialectic of the understanding, negative dialectics, and finally historical or practical dialectics.

Sun argues that in the Rheinische Zeitung period Marx measured actual Prussian law against an ideal of law, shaped by Hegel and the Enlightenment, as it "ought" to be. This opposition of ought and is remained abstract, but it exposed the economic interests behind legal relations. In the critique of Hegel, Marx then turned Hegel's own negative dialectics against him in two ways. He reversed the relation between concept and reality, so that civil society and the family become the basis of the state. He also replaced a dialectic serving monarchical absolutism with one oriented to the people and to democracy. Sun holds that this critique still worked within Hegel's logic. Only the critique of political economy, which Sun calls practical dialectics, could treat law as a product of material life. On this view, justice and legality become historical results of rising productive forces and of human liberation, and every legal form is both legitimate and illegitimate in its time.

Sun concludes that for Marx the question of law is finally the question of human emancipation. It cannot be settled by conceptual deduction, only by social transformation. The article adds that today's context differs from Marx's, so his words cannot simply be applied to the rule of law under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Sun says his guidance can be realised only by grasping that justice and legality mean human emancipation and that legal problems are solved through real social change. Read the original if you are interested in how Marx's method developed from legal criticism to political economy, or in a Chinese reading of Marx's philosophy of law in relation to Hegel and Althusser.
quoteEn: In the end the problem of law is the problem of human emancipation, and human emancipation cannot be achieved by deduction from categories of legal philosophy but proceeds through the practical dialectics of the social revolutionary movement.
quoteZh: 法的问题终究是人的解放，而人的解放不是用法哲学范畴演绎能解决的，而是通过社会革命运动的实践辩证法来进行的。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. Here it appears in the article's closing remark on the rule of law.

t: Treating reification within the dialectical relation of spirit and body
zh: 在精神与肉体的辩证关系中对待物化
paras: Since Lukács, Western Marxist critiques of capitalism have increasingly targeted reification rather than the system's internal contradictions. Huang and Wang argue that most thinkers have not found the right way to deal with it. Their thesis is that reification cannot be abolished but must be both accepted within limits and continually resisted, using Marx's materialist dialectic of body and spirit and of subject and object.

The article has four sections. It first criticises Lukács's theory of reification as idealist, then looks for the roots of reification in the opposition of spirit and body. It next compares three ways of overcoming the subject–object opposition: Lukács's Hegelian route, Heidegger's phenomenological route and Marx's route. A final section discusses the theoretical and social significance of reification, drawing on Adorno and Horkheimer, Honneth, Kant, Descartes and Baudrillard.

The authors contend that Lukács turned Marx's analysis of the economic base into a question of ideology and, through the category of totality, rebuilt Marx along Hegelian lines. They trace reification to the way humans must control external nature and so also their own bodily nature, which leaves spirit purely rationalised. Spirit that excludes the body is then avenged by nature and ends up following natural laws. On this view Lukács's strategy of subject conquering object cannot truly overcome reification, since a rationally run system stays reified. Heidegger's attempt to leap beyond the dichotomy turns Being into a thing and risks negating civilisation. For Marx the subject is a living, self-contradictory human being, and the use-value of commodities, which cannot be calculated, is the non-identical element that resists reification.

Huang and Wang conclude that reification is partly rational, because survival requires separating subject from object, but becomes harmful when it is unconditionally rationalised. They ascribe the difficulty of seeing through it to commodity fetishism, to existential and epistemological factors, and to the blending of true and false, as in Baudrillard's hyperreality. They call for reviving passions suppressed in daily life and reconciling them with spirit, without Lukács's excessive stress on the subject or Heidegger's abandonment of it. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist critique of Lukács and Heidegger on reification that rests on materialist dialectics.
quoteEn: We need to hold to Marx's materialist dialectic and approach the reification we face from the standpoint of the dialectic between body and spirit and between subject and object.
quoteZh: 我们需要坚持马克思的唯物主义辩证法，从肉体与精神、主体与客体之间的辩证法的角度来对待我们所面对的物化现象。

glossary.explanation: Lukács's term for the process by which social relations under capitalism take on the appearance of things governed by rational calculation. The article treats it as a product of the opposition between spirit and body and between subject and object.
Marx's term for the way social relations between people appear as relations between things in commodity exchange. The article presents it as a reified, inverted consciousness.
The tradition of Marxist thought associated with Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and others, which tends to stress philosophy, culture and consciousness.

t: Debates over the logical starting point of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and reflections on them
zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学逻辑起点的争论与反思
source: Studies in Political Economy (Zhengzhi jingjixue yanjiu), 2024 no. 4
paras: Chen Long and Wu Xuzhong take up a question that, in their account, remains unsettled: what should be the logical starting point (the first category) of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics? Scholars have proposed commodity, the socialist economic system, public ownership, the state, the people, surplus product and more. The authors argue that the starting point cannot be chosen in isolation from the discipline's object of study and its whole theoretical system, and that Marx's Capital is the necessary reference. They conclude that the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism is the most defensible starting point, while accepting that no single starting point is uniquely correct.

The article first sorts the existing positions into three camps. The "imitators" (for example Liu Mingyuan, Duan Xuehui and Cheng Enfu, Yan Pengfei, Zhou Shaodong and Wang Song) take commodity, in modified forms, as the starting point. The "opponents" propose the state (Qiu Haiping), the people as subject, labour productivity, particular interest relations or surplus product. The "eclectics" (Wei Xinghua, Liu Qian and Pei Xiaoge) propose the basic economic system, which the authors say leading recent textbooks also adopt. The authors then compare the approaches in three respects: methodology, object of study and level of research.

On method, the authors hold that the disagreement arises from differing readings of how Marx fixed Capital's starting point. They argue that the "ascent from the abstract to the concrete" demands a simple, cell-like category, but that this is feasible only for a mature social formation, and socialism with Chinese characteristics is still developing. They reject the state as a starting point because the principle of unity of the logical and the historical, in their reading, was not Marx's method but originated with Engels. They favour Marx's "universal light" method, which begins from the relation that determines all others. On the object of study, they contend that Capital examined mature, purely private capitalism with capital as its single thread. The socialist market economy, by contrast, has heterogeneous production relations and two regulating mechanisms, state and market. On levels, the authors say Capital is pure theory, whereas the Chinese discipline also covers historical-institutional and policy analysis, which are more concrete.

The authors conclude that the discipline's practical, problem-oriented character allows several concrete starting points and a "block-type structure" of parallel theoretical systems. They concede this is less tightly logical than Capital's "artistic whole" but call it a pragmatic route. They urge a more tolerant attitude to the debate and faster construction of the theoretical system along different starting points. Read the original if you want a structured survey of Chinese proposals on the starting point of socialist political economy, and an argument for the basic economic system drawn from Marx's methodology.
quoteEn: The theoretical system of the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics has no single correct logical starting point; there can be different logical starting points.
quoteZh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学理论体系不存在唯一正确的逻辑起点,而是可以存在不同的逻辑起点。

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学
glossary.en: the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The label for the official Chinese project of building a systematic economic theory of China's socialist path, promoted in textbooks and research since the mid-2010s.
The first, most basic category from which a theoretical system is developed, as commodity is in Marx's Capital.
The official characterisation of China's present historical stage, adopted by the Party in the 1980s, expected to last a long time.

glossary.zh: 社会主义初级阶段基本经济制度
glossary.pinyin: shèhuìzhǔyì chūjí jiēduàn jīběn jīngjì zhìdù
glossary.en: the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism
glossary.explanation: The official formulation of China's core economic institutions, with public ownership as the mainstay alongside diverse forms of ownership and a socialist market economy.

A phrase from Marx's 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy: in every social form one kind of production determines the position and influence of all others. The authors use it as a method for choosing a starting category.

glossary.en: ascent from the abstract to the concrete
glossary.explanation: Marx's method of presentation, which begins with simple abstract categories and builds up to the concrete whole.

keywords: political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics

t: New quality productive forces empowering the high-quality development of the real economy
zh: 新质生产力赋能实体经济高质量发展研究
paras: Taking its cue from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024), which called for institutions that deepen the integration of the real and digital economies, this article asks how new quality productive forces can drive the high-quality development of the real economy. Chen argues that they hold strategic value, but that three sets of difficulties must be overcome through policies aimed at factor allocation, technological breakthroughs and industrial upgrading. The piece appeared in Theoretical Horizon in December 2024.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the strategic value of new quality productive forces for consolidating the foundations of the national economy, building a modern industrial system and raising China's position in global value chains. The second identifies problems that need solving: shocks to the traditional real economy, gaps in key core technologies, and obstacles to upgrading traditional industries. The third proposes countermeasures under three headings: innovative allocation of production factors, revolutionary technological breakthroughs and deep industrial transformation.

Chen's core claim is that new quality productive forces are advanced productive forces whose carrier is industry.
