Liu sees the two as complementary: demand expansion is macro, short-term and demand-side, and works through regulation, while supply-side reform is micro, medium-term and supply-side, and works through reform. Liu therefore calls for action on both supply and demand, and on both policy and institutions, guided by high-quality development, a domestic circulation of high-level dynamic balance, and the principle of seeking progress while maintaining stability.

For practice, Liu calls for forming a complete domestic demand system and raising consumption backed by income, investment with reasonable returns, and financing subject to capital and debt constraints. Liu also calls for technological and institutional innovation to strengthen industrial and supply chains, for promoting mutual reinforcement of domestic and international circulation, and for deeper reform and opening up, including a unified national market and institutional opening-up. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how the official macroeconomic line of early 2023 links demand-side and supply-side policy.
quoteEn: Deepening supply-side structural reform and implementing the strategy of expanding domestic demand are unified, not opposed.
quoteZh: 深化供给侧结构性改革和实施扩大内需战略是统一的，不是对立的

glossary.explanation: An economic policy line announced by Xi Jinping in 2015. It aims to raise the quality and efficiency of supply through structural adjustment and reform, rather than relying mainly on stimulating demand.
A strategy centred on the domestic economic circulation, with domestic and international circulations reinforcing each other. It was put forward by Xi Jinping in 2020.
The official goal of economic development that stresses quality, efficiency and innovation over speed of growth. It was formally adopted as a priority in 2017.
The general keynote of Chinese economic work since 2012. It requires macroeconomic stability while pushing forward structural adjustment and reform.

t: Accelerating the improvement of the socialist market economy system
zh: 加快完善社会主义市场经济体制
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, argues that the socialist market economy system must be improved more quickly and understood accurately. Yang Jing holds that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core has made the system an integral part of the basic socialist economic system. In Yang's account, this has deepened understanding of market laws, advanced Chinese modernization and enriched Marxist political economy's theory of the market economy. The piece follows the 20th Party Congress (2022) report, which makes building a high-standard socialist market economy system a strategic task.

The article has three parts. The first places the market economy within the basic socialist economic system. The second deals with the relationship between market and government. The third takes up how to understand and handle capital's characteristics and patterns of behaviour. Throughout, it relies heavily on statements by Xi Jinping and on Party documents, and it presents Xi Jinping's economic thought as the guiding framework.

Yang first notes that the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) placed the market economy system alongside public ownership as the main body and the distribution principle of 'to each according to work' in a 'trinity' framework. Combining the socialist system with the market economy is described as a great innovation that unites ownership, distribution and economic operation. On government and market, Yang says the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) set out that the market plays the decisive role in allocating resources while government plays its role better. In practice this means reducing direct government interference in micro-level activity and also reforming government functions, macroeconomic governance and public services to make up for market failure. On capital, Yang lists state, collective, private, foreign and mixed forms. Yang says capital's negative effects under capitalism, such as crises, ecological damage and polarisation, are largely overcome under socialism, but its profit-seeking nature can still lead to disorderly expansion. Capital therefore needs regulation by law, with 'traffic lights', so that its positive role is used and its negative role controlled.

Yang concludes that accelerating improvement of the system, with the market and government uniting organically, accords with the law that relations of production must suit the state of the productive forces. It would, in this view, liberate and develop the productive forces and meet people's growing needs for a better life, while serving common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Party-line exposition of the socialist market economy, the government–market relationship and the treatment of capital as framed after the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: In the socialist market economy, recognising and affirming the existence of capital and its positive role, and correctly understanding and grasping its characteristics and laws of behaviour, is a major theoretical innovation of Xi Jinping's economic thought and an inevitable requirement for building a high-standard socialist market economy system.
quoteZh: 在社会主义市场经济中，承认并肯定资本的存在及其积极作用，正确认识和把握资本的特性和行为规律，是习近平经济思想的重大理论创新，也是构建高水平社会主义市场经济体制的必然要求。

glossary.zh: 社会主义市场经济体制
glossary.explanation: The economic system adopted in China from the early 1990s (the 14th Party Congress, 1992), combining market mechanisms with public ownership and Party leadership. The article treats it as part of the basic socialist economic system.

glossary.zh: 社会主义基本经济制度
glossary.explanation: Since 2019 defined as three elements: public ownership as the main body with diverse ownership forms, distribution according to work as the main body with other methods alongside, and the socialist market economy system.
The official term for China's path of modernization, prominently developed in the 20th Party Congress report (2022).
An official goal of shared prosperity for all people, emphasised in Party discourse as a defining feature of socialism.
The part of Xi Jinping Thought dealing with economic work, formally presented from 2017 as guidance for China's economic policy.

t: We must adhere to self-confidence and self-reliance
zh: 必须坚持自信自立
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in February 2023, argues that adhering to self-confidence and self-reliance (zixin zili) is an integral part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Liu Jun contends that it is a dialectical unity of theoretical, historical and practical logic.

The piece is organised along those three logics. The theoretical logic concerns firm belief in adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The historical logic presents self-confidence and self-reliance as a key instrument behind the Communist Party's century of struggle. The practical logic treats it as a requirement for what the article calls the new "road of examination" towards the second centenary goal. Liu draws throughout on statements by Marx, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping.

On theory, Liu argues that confidence rests on the conviction that Marxism works, and specifically Marxism adapted to China through the Two Integrations, with Marxist principles combined with Chinese realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Liu reads dialectical materialism and historical materialism as implying that there is no universal development model, so each country must find its own path. On history, the author claims that self-reliance opened the road to national rejuvenation, from the New Democratic Revolution through reform and opening up to the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and revitalised scientific socialism through successive theoretical innovations. Liu states that Chinese modernization rejects what the article describes as the old Western path of capital-centred, polarising, materialist and expansionist modernization, creating a new form of human civilization.

For the new journey, Liu calls for three things: firm belief in Marxism and socialism with Chinese characteristics, together with continued adaptation of Marxism; independence and a path of China's own, neither copying classic Marxist templates nor foreign models; and open opposition to historical nihilism as well as to complacency and arrogance. Liu urges vigilance towards "black swan" and "grey rhino" events and an awareness of risk. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2023 linked self-confidence and self-reliance to Xi Jinping Thought, Chinese modernization and the Party's historical narrative.
quoteEn: The most fundamental point of adhering to self-confidence and self-reliance is independence and taking our own path.
quoteZh: 坚持自信自立，最根本的就是独立自主，走自己的路。

glossary.explanation: A principle highlighted in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), stressing confidence in China's own path and independent development rather than reliance on external models.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for combining Marxist principles with Chinese conditions and contemporary developments.
The formula of integrating Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture.
The official concept of China's own path to modernization, elaborated at the 20th Party Congress (2022) and contrasted with Western models.
In official usage, a label for views seen as denying or disparaging the Party's history and the revolutionary and socialist record.

t: Socialism's transcendence of capitalism, seen from the all-round development of the human being
zh: 从人的全面发展看社会主义对资本主义的超越
paras: Dong Jianming asks why capitalism can realise only a one-sided, abstract development of human beings, while socialism contains the possibility of their all-round development. Taking its cue from the 20th Party Congress report (2022), which lists all-round human development among the goals for 2035, the article argues that capitalism's internal logic of capital limits human development. Socialism, in Dong's reading, transcends that limit, and Chinese modernization shows the possibility becoming real in practice.

The article reconstructs Marx's and Engels's notion of all-round development on three levels: the material basis of productive forces, the all-round development of labour and of human abilities, needs and individuality, and the forms of social intercourse. Each of the first three sections takes one level, first setting out the contradictory role of capitalism and then the corresponding Chinese practice. Dong draws on Marx's analysis of exploitation, alienation, the cooperative factory and the "illusory community", and on Weber, Horkheimer and Adorno, and Marcuse.

On the material basis, Dong argues that capitalism created the productive forces needed for all-round development but deprived workers of the means to realise it, and then became a fetter on those forces. Socialised ownership of the means of production is presented as the way to remove that fetter. On labour, capital shapes workers, the industrial reserve army and capitalists alike into one-sided, "one-dimensional" individuals, whereas socialism can reverse the relation between people and capital, as Marx's workers' cooperative factory foreshadows. On intercourse, capitalist world history produced a state that is an "illusory community" and an unequal order of "East subordinate to West"; the "true community" is the alternative. Dong cites as Chinese counterparts the public-capital logic, land reform from household contracting to the "three rights separation", state guidance of capital with "traffic lights", the dignity of labour, a community with a shared future for mankind, and a distinct path to modernization.

Dong concludes that capitalism cannot truly achieve all-round human development, while socialism provides its real basis and, in the author's account, this possibility is being realised under socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article presents common prosperity, a people-centred approach and adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times as the vehicles of this realisation. Read the original if you want a detailed Marxist-philosophical argument, anchored in Marx's texts, for why Chinese theorists treat all-round human development as the measure of socialism's superiority over capitalism.
quoteEn: Capitalism can only bring about a one-sided, abstract development of human beings and shapes them into one-dimensional people who meet the requirements of the logic of capital, whereas socialism provides a real basis for people's free liberation and all-round development.
quoteZh: 资本主义只能实现人的片面化、抽象化发展，并将人塑造为符合资本逻辑要求的单向度的人，社会主义则为人的自由解放和全面发展提供了真实的基础

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's path of modernization, set out prominently in the 20th Party Congress report (2022). It is presented as a path distinct from Western models.
A Party goal of prosperity shared by all the people rather than polarisation. It is described in official discourse as an essential requirement of socialism.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for international relations based on interdependence and cooperation. Official discourse offers it as an alternative to Western-dominated world order.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for developing Marxist theory in line with China's conditions and the contemporary period.

glossary.literal: taking the people as the centre
glossary.explanation: A guiding principle of Party policy under Xi Jinping, stressing that development should serve the people's interests.

t: The two dimensions of the human–nature relationship in Capital and their contemporary implications
zh: 《资本论》中人与自然关系二维向度思想及当代启示
source: Journal of Jiangsu University (Social Science Edition), 2022 no. 1
paras: Dou Ling and Geng Rumeng ask how Marx's Capital treats the relationship between humans and nature, a question they describe as both a major practical problem and a major theoretical concern in current scholarship. They argue that, unlike Marx's early philosophical reflections, Capital treats the question scientifically from the standpoint of historical materialism. In their reading, the human–nature relationship is in essence the relationship between human productive activity and nature, and it is shaped by two dimensions: the productive forces and the relations of production.

The article has four parts. The first examines the productive-force dimension, from natural conditions as the basis of production, through small-scale production, to machine industry and the double-edged effect of science and technology. The second examines the production-relations dimension under capitalism: separation of producers from the means of production, unlimited expansion, technology in the hands of capital, and private ownership of land. The third considers how the contradiction between humans and nature can finally be resolved. The fourth draws implications for global environmental governance and for building a "Beautiful China".

The authors' central move is that the productive forces determine how far humans can exploit or improve nature, while the relations of production determine which tendency prevails. They contend that capital's pursuit of profit, the capitalist use of machinery and the split between landowner and tenant farmer, who has no motive for long-term improvement, give capitalism an inherent mechanism of ecological destruction. Citing Marx's passage on associated producers regulating the metabolism with nature, they argue that most scholars read it only through production relations. In their view it requires both highly and rationally developed productive forces and public ownership of the means of production, and the contradiction can arise under any system while society remains in the "realm of necessity".

On global governance, the authors criticise Western eco-socialism and argue that capitalist states shift pollution abroad and resist environmental agreements. They call on China to cooperate internationally while uniting with others against "ecological imperialism", and they hold that a final resolution requires fundamental change to capitalist private ownership. For China, they describe the shift from passive to conscious environmental protection since reform and opening up. They treat ecological civilization and the aim of a "Beautiful China" as expressions of socialism's essence, to be advanced by institutional reform and public conscientiousness. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Capital's ecological thought that links it to current Chinese ecological civilization policy and to criticism of Western eco-socialism.
quoteEn: The relationship between humans and nature will in the end reach true harmony as society's productive forces develop and socialist relations of production are perfected.
quoteZh: 人与自然的关系，终将随着社会生产力的发展、社会主义生产关系的完善而达到真正的和谐。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy concept, written into the Party's overall plan at the 18th Party Congress (2012), that places environmental protection within the national development strategy.
A goal put forward in Party documents of the 2010s for a country with a good ecological environment, tied to ecological civilization construction.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978.

t: Heller's construction of a Marxist anthropology centred on "feelings"
zh: 赫勒以feelings为中心的马克思主义人类学建构
paras: Sun Jianyin examines "feelings", the core concept of Ágnes Heller's early philosophical anthropology, and asks how Heller used it to build a Marxist anthropology. Sun argues that, guided by Wittgenstein and Kant, Heller took elements of Marx's thought to go beyond both, and so joined Marxism with psychoanalytic and psychological analysis. Sun also holds that the result has real limits from the standpoint of Marx's historical materialism.

The article has five parts. It first sets out the context: the split between Anglo-American empirical anthropology and the continental tradition of philosophical anthropology, the question of whether Marxism and psychoanalysis are compatible, and Heller's planned series on instinct, feelings, needs, morality, personality and history, which she did not complete. It then traces the concept's philosophical sources in Wittgenstein's analysis of sensation and private language and in Kant's Anthropology from a Pragmatic Point of View. A third part reconstructs Heller's conceptual system, a fourth assesses its value, and a closing section compares it with Marx's own texts.

Sun's central claim is that Heller solved two problems. First, she joined sensation (Wittgenstein's focus) and feeling (Kant's) in one plural concept, "sensation/feeling", which rises from simple sensation through perception, memory and emotion to stable feeling and is inseparable from thought and action as forms of "involvement". Second, she rejected an a priori view of feeling by treating feelings as socially learned motivations, "built in from within" through social practice. Sun draws on her use of Marx's account of human essence and of objectification, alienation and sublation. In Sun's reading, this renews the field of philosophical anthropology, deepens the philosophical understanding of psychology, and offers a route between psychoanalysis and orthodox Marxist anthropology.

In the conclusion Sun is critical. Heller's anthropology abstracts from socialisation and never takes economic life as its basis. It draws its "experience" largely from literary depictions of individual psychology, and so yields an abstract universality that fits any social formation. Sun says this misreads the objective stance of Marx's late anthropological work, which tied ideas to historical conditions, and that it foreshadows her later turn to the "postmodern". Even so, Sun credits Heller with a dialectical account of how feelings arise and develop, and with one possible path towards a Marxist anthropology. Read the original if you work on the Budapest School, Marxism and psychoanalysis, or the history of philosophical anthropology and want a detailed Chinese critical reading of Heller's early work.
quoteEn: Heller's path of building a Marxist anthropology through sensation and feeling has limitations that cannot be avoided.
quoteZh: 赫勒通过感觉和感情建构马克思主义人类学的路径还具有不可避免的局限性。

glossary.explanation: A group of Hungarian philosophers around Georg Lukács, including Ágnes Heller and György Márkus, who developed a humanist, renewed Marxism from the 1960s and 1970s.
A continental European tradition (Scheler, Landmann and others) that asks Kant's question "What is man?" by philosophical rather than field-based means.
The article's rendering of Heller's idea that human nature, including feelings, is not given in advance but is built into the individual by social and historical factors over time.
Marx's term (Vergegenständlichung) for the process in which human powers are expressed in objects and social forms. The article links it to Heller's view of how feelings develop.
A rendering of Hegel's and Marx's Aufhebung: a process that cancels, preserves and raises a thing to a higher level. The article applies it to alienation.

t: The inherent logic of Marxism leading the system of philosophy and social sciences
zh: 马克思主义引领哲学社会科学体系的内在逻辑
paras: Han Xiping and Wang Siran take up the call to build philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, which they describe as ultimately the construction of China's own autonomous knowledge system. Their thesis is that this system should be led by Marxism, and that this follows from three sources: a historical logic, a practical logic and a theoretical logic.

The article first reviews how Marxism shaped China's revolution, construction and reform, from the Mao Zedong Thought tradition through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development to Chinese modernization. It then argues from present needs and from the state of Western social science, and from Marxism's own theoretical character. It ends with five concrete measures.

In the historical argument, the authors hold that the Communist Party's century of success rests on Marxism's continual adaptation to Chinese conditions, so that a new knowledge system should be built on the same foundation. In the practical argument, they say a China that has become strong needs social sciences that are strong and autonomous, and that liberal-led Western social science, built on market-centred assumptions and fragmented disciplines, cannot explain or solve today's interlinked problems. In the theoretical argument, they claim that Marxism's scientific, people-centred, practical and open character, with historical materialism and dialectics as method, suits the holistic study of complex problems.

The proposed measures are: strengthening Marxist theory as a first-level discipline (its doctoral programmes rose from 39 in 2016 to 104 by 2021, according to the authors) and ending its perceived marginalisation; applying Marxist standpoint and method across disciplines while drawing on traditional Chinese culture; promoting interdisciplinary "new liberal arts"; absorbing outstanding human social-science achievements critically; and shifting paradigms so that Chinese experience is turned into original theory and the habit of imitating the West is dropped. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official case for a Marxist-led autonomous knowledge system in Chinese academia, together with its policy references and proposed disciplinary measures.
quoteEn: An era of becoming strong inevitably demands philosophy and social sciences that have become strong.
quoteZh: 强起来的时代必然要求强起来的哲学社会科学

glossary.explanation: A slogan in Chinese academic policy, associated with Xi Jinping's speeches on philosophy and social sciences. It refers to building theories, concepts and discourse rooted in Chinese experience rather than adopted from the West.
The official name for China's path of modernization, stressed since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
An education-policy initiative promoting interdisciplinary integration within the humanities and social sciences and their links with science and technology.
The guiding concept of Hu Jintao's leadership, which emphasised comprehensive, balanced and sustainable development.
Jiang Zemin's theory, holding that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the people.

t: The relationship between government and market in high-quality development
zh: 高质量发展中的政府与市场关系
paras: Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2023, Fang Fuqian asks how the relationship between government and market bears on high-quality development, which the author defines at base as stable, sustained and harmonious growth. Fang's thesis is that high-quality development requires raising the "fit" (shipeixing) between government and market, so that the two combine better.

The short piece has two parts. The first sets out how to understand the government–market relationship, contrasting Western economics with the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The second discusses how to advance market-oriented reform and government reform together, drawing on the 19th Party Congress (2017) and 20th Party Congress (2022) reports.

Fang argues that neoliberal schools oppose government intervention and hold that markets stabilise themselves, whereas in Chinese political economy the two are complementary, not opposed. The author cites Xi Jinping's call to use both the "invisible hand" and the "visible hand", and treats the formula of the market playing the decisive role and the government playing its role better as a breakthrough beyond Western economics. Fang grounds the fit in China's basic economic system, with public ownership as the mainstay and distribution according to work as the main form. Markets allocate resources most efficiently, but monopoly, incomplete information, externalities and unfair income distribution cause market failure, while government can also fail through poor decisions and policy lags.

Fang concludes that China faces a double task because of its transition from a highly centralised planned economy. It must deepen market reform, including property rights, factor markets and a unified national market, and it must reform government by reducing direct intervention, placing government conduct under the rule of law and building a service-oriented government. The author stresses that government should act in a moderate, effective and scientific way, not simply more actively. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Chinese line on government and market in the language of high-quality development.
quoteEn: The socialist market economy needs the government to act positively, but it is more important that the government act moderately, effectively and scientifically.
quoteZh: 社会主义市场经济需要政府积极作为，但是更重要的是需要政府适度作为、有效作为和科学作为

glossary.explanation: An official economic goal put forward in the late 2010s, shifting emphasis from the speed of growth to its quality, efficiency, balance and sustainability.

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学
glossary.en: political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The official body of economic theory that seeks to systematise China's reform-era experience and Party economic thought.

The official definition of China's socialist economic order: public ownership as the mainstay alongside diverse ownership forms, distribution according to work alongside other forms, and the socialist market economy.
An official reform aim of shifting government functions toward public services, regulation and macro-control, and away from direct management of the economy.

t: Continuously advancing and expanding Chinese modernization
zh: 不断推进和拓展中国式现代化
paras: Writing in the People's Daily in February 2023, Chen Jin takes up Xi Jinping's description of the theory of Chinese modernization, set out at the 20th Party Congress (2022), as a major theoretical innovation and the latest major achievement of scientific socialism. The commentary asks how Party members should understand this path in order to keep advancing and expanding it. Chen's answer is that Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, and that it is inseparable from socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The piece is organised under six headings: the historical logic of Chinese modernization, its link with building a moderately prosperous society, the innovations achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012), its Chinese characteristics, its essential requirements, and its far-reaching influence on world modernization. It traces the idea from Mao Zedong's calls for industrialisation and the 'four modernizations' to Deng Xiaoping's 1979 remarks on 'Chinese-style modernization'. It then follows the stages from the 16th to the 19th Party Congress.

Chen argues that Deng used the 'xiaokang' (moderately prosperous) idea to give Chinese modernization its meaning. In Chen's reading, this idea rejects rashness and copying of the West, treats modernization as staged, and aims at social progress and all-round human development, not only economic growth. For Chen, the distinctive features are an enormous population, common prosperity, coordinated material and cultural-ethical advance, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development. Its essential requirements are Party leadership and socialism, together with the five-sphere overall plan and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Chen also contends that capital-driven Western modernization carries built-in limits such as wealth gaps, polarisation and spiritual emptiness, and that Chinese modernization overcomes them and breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization.

Chen concludes that Chinese modernization and socialism with Chinese characteristics have advanced as one process, and that Party leadership is its most prominent advantage and a principle that must be upheld. The author presents the path as a new option for developing countries that want faster growth while keeping their independence. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account, by a Party-history scholar, of how Chinese modernization is linked to earlier Party goals and to socialism with Chinese characteristics.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party, and not some other kind of modernization.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化是中国共产党领导的社会主义现代化而不是别的什么现代化。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official account of China's path to modernization, set out at the 20th Party Congress in 2022. Deng Xiaoping had used the phrase 'Chinese-style modernization' in 1979.
A Confucian-derived term for modest, comfortable well-being. Deng Xiaoping adopted it in 1979 as a staged target of modernization, and the Party declared it fully achieved in 2021.
A goal of shared wealth for all the people, which official texts call an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It has been given new emphasis under Xi Jinping.
The Party's name for its governing ideology and system since reform and opening up, which it presents as Marxism applied to Chinese conditions.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept in Xi Jinping's foreign policy thought that calls for shared interests and joint global governance. Official texts present it as an alternative to bloc politics.

t: Gaining a deep understanding of the "six musts"
zh: 深刻领悟“六个必须坚持”
paras: Writing in the China Social Sciences Today in February 2023, Qiao Maolin offers a study-guide commentary on the "six musts" set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). These are the requirements to adhere to the principle of putting the people first, to self-confidence and self-reliance, to being committed to the fundamentals while breaking new ground, to a problem-oriented approach, to a systems approach, and to thinking with the world in mind. Qiao argues that together they give a basic route to understanding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and a basic guide for continuing to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The commentary opens by presenting Marxism as an open system that develops with the times, and the Thought as the latest step in that development. It then takes each of the six musts in turn, using a similar pattern. Qiao first gives the theoretical basis, then shows how the principle runs through the Thought and the work of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and finally lists what it requires for the new journey ahead.

Qiao's central claim is that each principle joins a Marxist premise to a feature of the Thought. The people-first principle rests on the materialist view that the people create history and on the idea that Marxism is by nature a theory of the people. Self-confidence and self-reliance is tied to Chinese modernization and the Four-sphere Confidence, since China's problems must be answered by Chinese people on the basis of national conditions. The "commitment to fundamentals" is defined as holding firm to Marxism's basic tenets, the Party's overall leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics, while "breaking new ground" means saying and doing what predecessors have not. The problem-oriented approach reflects the universality of contradiction. The systems approach is linked to the coordinated overall plans Xi has put forward. Thinking with the world in mind is tied to the proposal for a community with a shared future for mankind.

Qiao concludes that the six musts form an organic whole that unites upholding Marxism with developing it. The commentary calls them a "golden key" to the essence of the Thought and a guide for theoretical innovation grounded in practice. It urges readers to understand their theoretical content, method and practical meaning so as to keep writing new chapters of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned account of how the 20th Party Congress's methodological principles are being explained to Chinese readers.
quoteEn: Only by holding to the fundamentals can one avoid losing direction and making subversive errors; only by innovating can one grasp the times and lead them.
quoteZh: 守正才能不迷失方向、不犯颠覆性错误，创新才能把握时代、引领时代。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018. It is presented as the latest stage in adapting Marxism to China.
The official name for China's path of development under Party leadership, which the Party says differs from Western models. It was given a systematic formulation at the 20th Party Congress (2022).
The official call for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy and global-governance concept, first put forward in 2012–2013. It calls for shared security, development and values among states.

glossary.en: being committed to the fundamentals while breaking new ground
glossary.literal: Upholding what is correct and innovating
glossary.explanation: A principle stressed since the 20th Party Congress: keep to the basic orientation of Marxism, Party leadership and the socialist path, while innovating in theory and practice.

t: The rich connotations and contemporary significance of the "Three Musts"
zh: “三个务必”的丰富内涵和时代意义
paras: This commentary, first published in the People's Daily on 3 March 2023, interprets the "Three Musts" set out in Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022): stay true to the founding mission, remain modest, prudent and hard-working, and dare and know how to fight. Shen argues that the formula is a major judgement grounded in historical regularities and the demands of the times. In Shen's account, it deepens understanding of how a communist party governs and how it builds itself, and it helps the whole Party unify its thinking and will on the new journey.

The article has three parts. The first traces the "Three Musts" to the Party's experience over a century, starting with Mao Zedong's "Two Musts" of 1949 and moving to the Party's recent efforts to govern itself rigorously. The second takes each of the three requirements in turn, with historical examples and statements by Mao and Xi. The third sets out what the formula means for Party building and for the national goals ahead.

Shen presents the "Three Musts" as both a whole and a set of distinct emphases. On the founding mission, Shen says the Party's understanding has widened: it now covers spiritual as well as material well-being, the influence of Chinese civilization, and contributions to human progress. On modesty and hard struggle, Shen sees continuity with the "Two Musts" and with a tradition the Party carried forward from revolution to the present. On struggle, the article holds that all of China's achievements came through struggle, and that the new journey requires "great struggle". Shen links this to the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle of rise and decline, namely self-reform, and to the long-term persistence of the "four tests" and "four dangers".

Shen concludes that the "Three Musts" deepen understanding of the laws of Communist Party governance. The article also calls them a firm grip for strengthening Party building across ideological and work-style fields, and a political guarantee for realising the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Shen proposes continued Party-wide education campaigns, a more complete body of Party regulations, and the promotion of the spirit of the Party's founding. Read the original if you want an authoritative-style account of how Party theorists connect the 20th Party Congress formula to Mao's 1949 "Two Musts" and to the self-reform agenda.
quoteEn: All the achievements we have made did not fall from the sky, were not bestowed by others, but were won through continuous struggle.
quoteZh: 我们取得的一切成就,不是天上掉下来的,不是别人恩赐的,而是通过不断斗争取得的。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) calling on all Party members to stay true to the founding mission, stay modest and hard-working, and dare and know how to fight.
Mao Zedong's 1949 warning at the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee that the Party must keep up a modest, prudent style and a hard-working style after winning nationwide power.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: An official goal, associated with the Chinese Dream, of restoring China's national strength and international standing by the middle of the 21st century.

t: The socialism of humanist Marxism
st: A review of Kevin B. Anderson's view of socialism
zh: 人本主义马克思主义的社会主义观
zhSub: 凯文·B.安德森社会主义观述评
paras: Guo Lishuang and Liu Yang present and assess the conception of socialism developed by the American Marxist scholar Kevin B. Anderson. The article reports that Anderson treats socialism as the thorough negation and transcendence of capitalism, and regards both Stalinism and democratic socialism as inadequate to present challenges. In its own assessment, the article finds Anderson's critique of capitalism comprehensive and his socialist vision insightful, but argues that his socialist vision is thin and that his reading of China under Mao Zedong is mistaken.

After a short introduction to Anderson's career as a MEGA2 researcher and author, the article is built in three parts. The first sets out his analysis of capitalism through six core features. The second covers his account of Stalinism and democratic socialism, followed by a critical response. The third reconstructs his humanist Marxist socialism and offers an evaluation, closing with remarks on foreign Marxist scholars more generally.

According to the authors, Anderson names exploitation, alienation, racism and imperialism, gender subordination, the strengthening and centralisation of the state, and environmental destruction as capitalism's defining traits. Socialism must therefore overcome alienated labour, end capital accumulation and the critique-free embrace of technology, address hierarchies of race, gender and sexuality, and tackle ecological damage. Anderson draws on Marx's three stages of communism, with the Paris Commune as a transitional form. The authors then dispute his claim that Mao-era China was wholly Stalinist: they cite decentralisation in the Ten Great Relationships and the 1957 reforms, the role of markets, and intra-Party and multi-party democracy. They also reject his claim that workers and peasants were ruthlessly exploited, arguing that workers laboured voluntarily, as in the Daqing oilfield.

The authors conclude that Anderson's negation-based method deepens understanding of capitalism, but that his socialism mainly targets capitalism's ills. They also say he does not clarify how humanist socialism differs from communism, and that his view of China rests on Western yardsticks and scarce primary sources. They see him as typical of foreign Marxist scholars whose systems are theoretically complete but weak in practical strategy, and they call for more dialogue and tolerance of socialist models that arise from different national conditions. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic's critical account of a Western humanist Marxist's theory of socialism and of his view of Mao-era China.
quoteEn: Hence they are rather weak in action and rather radical in thought, which to some extent is a common feature of many Western Marxists.
quoteZh: 因此，行动上较为无力，思想上较为激进——这在某种程度上也是不少西方马克思主义者的普遍特征。

glossary.explanation: A term for the Soviet model of centralised state planning and one-party rule associated with Stalin. Anderson applies it to Mao-era China, which the article disputes.
A socialist current favouring multi-party elections, grassroots mobilisation and a strong welfare state. Anderson sees it as opposing neoliberalism but not capitalism itself.

A 1956 speech by Mao Zedong on balancing key relationships in socialist construction, including that between the central government and the localities. The article cites it as evidence that China departed from the Soviet model.
The broad field of Marxist thought outside China, which Chinese academics study and assess.

t: "Cosmopolitanism" in Marx's perspective
zh: 马克思视野中的“世界主义”
paras: Feng Ziyi takes up a gap in scholarship on Marx. Researchers have studied his theory of world history extensively but paid little attention to his views on cosmopolitanism. Feng argues that these views cannot be reduced to the world-history theory and have a distinct value. Marx opposed false cosmopolitanism, which in Feng's reading serves narrow nationalism or capital, and upheld a true cosmopolitanism grounded in the people and in human emancipation.

The article has four parts. It first traces the origins of Marx's engagement, from Stoic and Christian universalism through Kant and Hegel to the German 'ideological fervour' of the 1840s. It then distinguishes four aspects of the concept in Marx's writings: critique of political economy, value critique, description of modern society, and the theory of the international workers' movement and human liberation. A third part sets out his method, and a fourth draws implications for today.

Feng's central claim is that Marx's cosmopolitanism differs from earlier versions in four methodological respects. It rests on historical materialism rather than reason, human nature or absolute spirit, deriving world history from productive forces and from capital's expansion. It holds a people-centred standpoint, in contrast to the Young Hegelians, 'true socialism' and bourgeois economics. It treats the universal as 'concrete' and historical, so that world culture presupposes national cultures. And it uses contradiction analysis, exposing colonial plunder and hypocritical appeals to a world-historical view, as in Engels on Poznań and Marx's writing on China.

Writing in 2023, Feng draws three lessons. The civilizational value of cosmopolitanism should be upheld against what the author describes as the false and opportunistic cosmopolitanism of some Western states, especially the United States, and against 'reverse globalization'. A new cosmopolitanism should be built on a community with a shared future for mankind, which Feng distinguishes from earlier versions by its subject (humanity, not the individual), its horizon and its goal of cooperation. The international economic and political order should also be rebuilt on mutual respect and shared global governance. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of Marx's scattered remarks on cosmopolitanism and of how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher links them to current foreign-policy concepts.
quoteEn: Whether one adheres to the people's standpoint is the watershed that distinguishes Marx's cosmopolitanism from other cosmopolitanisms.
quoteZh: 是否坚持人民立场，是马克思的世界主义区别于其他世界主义的分水岭。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny of humankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013 as the guiding idea of China's foreign policy and vision of international relations. The article presents it as the core of a 'new cosmopolitanism'.

Marx's idea that, with the world market and large-scale industry, national histories merge into a single interconnected history. The article treats it as closely related to, but not identical with, cosmopolitanism.

Marx and Engels's theory that history is shaped by the development of productive forces and relations of production. The article uses it as the theoretical basis that separates Marx's cosmopolitanism from idealist versions.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Marx's theoretical reflections on the modernization of Eastern countries and their implications
zh: 马克思关于东方国家现代化进程的理论思考及启示
paras: Ma Jun asks how Marx explained the late and stalled modernization of Eastern countries, and what that analysis offers for Chinese modernization today. The article argues that, from the 1850s, Marx's scattered writings on China, India and Russia form a second side of his theory of modernity, alongside his analysis of Western industrial capitalism. In Ma's reading, Marx located the causes of Eastern lag in internal structures, saw modernization there as started by Western pressure, and did not fall into Eurocentrism.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the historical background: the Crimean War, the Opium Wars and British rule in India as the mid-nineteenth-century divide between East and West. The second examines how modernization was set in motion in the East and how East and West interacted. The third draws three lessons for Chinese modernization. Ma draws on Marx's articles on China and India, Capital, The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte and the letter on Russia, and also cites scholars such as Luo Rongqu, Edward Said and Hannah Arendt.

On causes, Ma identifies three. One is the durability of a self-sufficient natural economy built on small peasant farming joined to household handicrafts. Another is the fusion of the feudal state and society, with no separation between political state and civil society. The third is a feudal and small-peasant mentality that favoured submission and conservatism. On interaction, Ma uses Luo Rongqu's term "transmitted great change" for modernization imposed from outside, and cites Marx's image of the mummy exposed to fresh air. Against charges of Eurocentrism, including from Said and postcolonial critics, Ma argues four points. Marx used Western Europe as a reference point on the basis of productive forces. He rejected treating the Western path as a universal model. He saw Eastern events, such as the Taiping Rebellion, as acting back on Europe. He also condemned colonial aggression morally.

Ma draws three implications. Modernization requires comprehensive reform of economy, politics, culture and society, and the remnants of peasant consciousness, official-centred culture and weak rule of law still hinder it. Marx's idea of "social revolution" as a total transformation should be kept, joining personal, national and world emancipation. China should also raise its level of opening up, while aiming to break the capitalist "centre–periphery" pattern and promote common prosperity. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of how Marx's Eastern writings are used to defend him against Eurocentrism charges and to ground Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: Innovation is the inner driving force of modernization, while citizens' participation and collective recognition are the basis on which modern states arise and develop; the absence of innovative thought and a democratic political tradition doomed Eastern countries to find it hard to launch modernization spontaneously.
quoteZh: 创新是现代化的内在动力，公民的参与和集体的承认则是现代国家产生发展的基础，创新思想和民主政治传统的缺失注定使东方国家的现代化难以自发地启动。

glossary.explanation: An official Party concept, prominent since the early 2020s, describing China's own path of modernization as distinct from the Western model.
A socialist goal of shared wealth for all, given renewed emphasis in Party policy under Xi Jinping.

t: Clarifying the concept of the "class for itself"
zh: “自为阶级”概念辨析
paras: Jia Tianyu and Zhang Youkui take up the concept of the "class for itself" (自为阶级), which Marxism uses to state the proletariat's historical mission and its relation to the Communist Party. They argue that earlier studies have identified what the concept points to (historical mission, class consciousness, Party leadership) but have not explained the dialectical logic of the concept itself. Without that, the authors say, the internal links among these three elements remain unclear. Their thesis is that these three elements together make up the concept's content.

The article first traces the concept's formation. It starts from Hegel's category of "being-for-itself" in the Logic and Marx's use of it to separate a stage of wage struggle from a stage of political class-against-class struggle. It then follows Lenin's account of spontaneity and consciousness, including his theory of "inculcation", and Mao Zedong's definition of the class for itself through the "three understandings". The three main sections then take the three elements in turn: human emancipation as the historical task, correct knowledge of class relations, and leadership by the Communist Party.

The authors argue that the class for itself is the proletariat whose class interest is universal, namely the abolition of classes and human emancipation, and that this follows from the full development of the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Class consciousness, they say, is not a subjective awakening but a correct, reflective grasp of the essence of class relations, which is both scientific and revolutionary. It can arise only from the proletarian position under developed capitalism. The Party is presented as an internal component of the class for itself rather than an external instrument: communists may differ from workers in class origin, but not in class standpoint or relation to the movement.

The authors conclude that inculcation is not the transfer of knowledge from outside. In their account, the proletariat becomes a class for itself through the practice of class struggle, and the process also reshapes the educators into Communist Party members. They criticise readings that treat the Party as external to the class, or that explain its vanguard role by members' qualities or workers' wage interests. Read the original if you want a close, Hegel-informed reading of how Marxist-Leninist-Maoist theory ties class consciousness to Party leadership.
quoteEn: It is not that the proletariat wages class struggle after becoming a class for itself; rather, the proletariat becomes a class for itself in the practice of class struggle.
quoteZh: 不是无产阶级在成为自为阶级之后展开阶级斗争，而是无产阶级在阶级斗争实践中成为自为阶级。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term, drawn from Hegel's "being-for-itself", for a class that has become conscious of its own interests and acts politically as a class, as opposed to a class merely defined by its place in production.
Lenin's view in What Is To Be Done? that socialist consciousness must be brought to workers by theory-trained communists rather than arising spontaneously from workers' economic struggles.
Mao Zedong's definition of a class for itself as a proletariat that understands the essence of capitalist society, the exploitative relations among classes, and the proletariat's historical task.

t: Capital accumulation and the inner logic of capitalist ownership
st: A theoretical examination based on Capital
zh: 资本积累与资本主义所有制的内在逻辑
zhSub: 基于《资本论》的理论考察
paras: Cai Ling argues that the theory of surplus value has become a shorthand for Marx's critique of capitalism, and that this hides how Marx reached the system's deepest structure. In Cai's reading, Marx got there by tracing the recapitalisation of surplus value, that is, capital accumulation, and this leads to the inner logic of capitalist ownership. Earlier research, the article says, has stayed with the basic nature of accumulation or its technical analysis and has not reached the question of ownership.

The article has three sections, all drawn from the three volumes of Capital. The first covers the realisation and limits of accumulation: its general law in Volume 1, the conditions of realisation in Volume 2 (circuits of capital and the two departments of reproduction), and its tendencies towards crisis in Volume 3. The second sets Marx's account of how the law of capitalist appropriation forms and consolidates against classical economics and modern political philosophy. The third examines how accumulation sustains and expands capitalist ownership. Cai also rejects David Harvey's view that the three volumes' theories of accumulation are fractured and contradictory.

Cai's central claim is that capitalist ownership is not a legal relation of persons to things, as classical economics assumes. It is an appropriation relation, reproduced through accumulation, in which capital takes the labour activity of wage workers and its value. Cai gives three steps: the conversion of the commodity-production law of ownership into the law of capitalist appropriation, through the social character of labour and labour-power becoming a commodity; primitive accumulation, with its expropriation and colonial violence, as the historical origin of appropriation; and the continuous reproduction of the capital relation itself, capitalists on one side and wage workers on the other. On this basis Cai argues that Marx's model of simple reproduction is essential, because it shows how labour-power is appropriated and the class relation reproduced.

Cai concludes that capitalist ownership is sustained mainly by expanding the scale of accumulation, which pushes capital to compete, concentrate and seek new markets. Capitalists are described as puppets of accumulation's own logic. Accumulation is limited by the opposition between capital and wage labour and by consumption, and these limits appear as crises of relative overproduction. Read the original if you want a close reading of Capital that links accumulation, appropriation and ownership, and that contests classical economics and Harvey on these points.
quoteEn: It was precisely by grasping accurately the movement of the capitalisation, or recapitalisation, of surplus value that Marx probed the inner logic of capitalist ownership.
quoteZh: 马克思正是通过对剩余价值的资本化或再资本化的运动过程的准确把握而究诘到资本主义所有制的内在逻辑。

t: An analysis of the conception of practice in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
zh: 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》实践观探析
source: Journal of Donghua University (Social Sciences), 2021 no. 3
paras: Tian Changsheng asks what view of practice is contained in Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and why it matters for understanding Marxist philosophy. The article argues that the Manuscripts, which it calls the birthplace of Marxist philosophy, contain an early form of a scientific conception of practice. In Tian's reading, this conception differs from both Hegel's objective idealism and Feuerbach's old materialism and opens the path to a "new materialism".

The article is organised around four aspects of practice, each treated in its own section. These are the precondition of practice (sensuous nature), its essential content (objectifying activity), its distorted form (alienated labour) and its moment of return (the humanisation of nature). Tian draws mainly on passages from the Manuscripts, with supporting references to The German Ideology and to Engels on nature's "revenge".

Tian first argues that practice presupposes nature. Nature supplies the means of production, the means of subsistence and the "spiritual nourishment" of practice, and the human subject is both an active and a passive natural being. Practice is then defined as objectifying activity: unlike other living things, humans realise their essence in objects, change those objects and so enrich their own nature, including their senses. Alienated labour is presented as a distorted form of this relation, arising from practice itself through surplus products, the division of labour and private property. Tian reads Marx as holding that alienation can be overcome only through practice, leading to communism as the return of the human being to itself.

Tian concludes with a dialectic of the "humanisation of nature" and the "naturalisation of humanity". The first reflects human civilisation and the capacity to transform nature, and the article notes that it risks provoking nature's counter-effects. The second is presented as a reflection on that civilisation, which the author ties to ecological damage and consumerism, and as a return to harmony with nature. Practice mediates between the two. Tian holds that the Manuscripts founded a new worldview and settled accounts with Hegel, although traces of Feuerbach's humanism remain. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based account of how the early Marx's concept of practice links alienation, objectification and the human relation to nature.
quoteEn: Humans produce alienation in practical activity, and they will necessarily escape alienation through practical activity, thereby realising communism and completing the free emancipation of humanity.
quoteZh: 人类在实践活动中产生了异化，也必将通过实践活动来摆脱异化，进而实现共产主义，完成人的自由解放。

t: Marx's idea of the "productive force of capital"
st: A study based on Capital and its economic manuscripts
zh: 马克思关于“资本的生产力”思想探析
zhSub: 以《资本论》及其经济学手稿为例
paras: Scholars disagree about whether Marx actually held a notion of the "productive force of capital". Xu Shuihua and Yang Zeguang argue that he did, that he used the concept explicitly, and that it carries two meanings: capital's power to command other productive forces, and capital's role as a real historical force that is itself a productive force.

The article proceeds in three steps. It first traces the textual basis through the 1857–58 manuscripts and Volumes I, II and III of Capital. It then sets out what Marx meant by the concept. Finally it examines how Marx weighed the concept's effects on capitalist society, both affirming and critical.

On the textual side, the authors find the phrase first mentioned in Marx's notes on Ricardo and developed in the 1857–58 manuscripts. In Volume I it appears in the treatment of relative surplus value, covering cooperation, the combination of labour, machinery, science and natural forces. In Volume II the idea is said to be implicit in the continuity and turnover of capital, and in Volume III it appears in passages on rent and on free natural forces. On meaning, the authors hold that capital's ownership of the means of production makes it the subject of production. Collective, scientific and natural productive forces therefore appear as capital's own. They also hold that capital, as a historical force, moved society from feudal "barbarism" to capitalist "civilisation" and supplies the material conditions for communism. Marx's assessment is dialectical in the authors' account. He credits capital with material abundance, the world market, scientific advance and the free time and conditions from which a revolutionary subject emerges. He also condemns it for one-sided human development and for damaging nature.

The authors conclude that Marx treated capital both as a relation of production and as a productive force with a historical limit. When capital stops advancing productive forces and begins to fetter them, history discards it. They present the productive force of capital as a mode of exercising the productive force of social labour under capitalism, one that turns against both people and ecology. Read the original if you want a text-by-text survey of where Capital and the manuscripts use the phrase, or a Chinese-language argument that capital is both a relation of production and a productive force.
quoteEn: Marx put forward this concept with two meanings: first, capital as the subject of capitalist production has the power to command other productive forces; second, capital exerts enormous power in historical development and in practice, and in this sense capital is itself a productive force.
quoteZh: 马克思提出这一概念有两层涵义：其一是指资本作为资本主义生产的主体性存在，具有驾驭其他生产力的力量；其二是指资本在历史发展和现实作用方面发挥着巨大力量，在这种意义上，资本本身就是一种生产力。

t: The value orientation, practical implications and contemporary enlightenment of Marx's thought on social relations
zh: 马克思社会关系思想的价值旨趣、实践意蕴与当代启示
paras: Bi Guoshuai asks what Marx's thought on social relations offers for improving social relations and promoting all-round human development today. The article argues that Marx's account is organised around human emancipation as the core of historical progress. It holds that this thought supplies guidance for building what Bi calls "people's relations" (renmin guanxi) in contemporary China.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the value orientation of Marx's thought: its starting point in "human beings engaged in sensuous activity", its goal of the "free individuality" of persons, and its overall horizon of social-historical development. The second sets out the practical implications, as a dual logic of transforming reified relations and constructing human relations. The third draws lessons for present-day China under three headings.

Bi contends that Marx overcame both Hegel's idealist reduction of social relations to relations of consciousness and Feuerbach's intuitive, ahistorical "natural" ties, thereby uniting their materiality and historicity. Marx's three stages of social relations (natural, reified, human) are said to correspond to the three stages of emancipation. In the reified stage, capital-dominated production and exchange invert the relation between persons and things. Changing this requires overthrowing bourgeois political rule and gradually abolishing capitalist private property, which Bi says cannot be done by ignoring the level of the productive forces. Human relations must then be built up under socialism by developing the productive forces and perfecting socialist institutions, with public ownership at their core.

Bi concludes that China, at the primary stage of socialism, has largely passed beyond the stage of transforming reified relations but lacks the conditions for human relations. Its task is therefore to build "people's relations" as a transitional form, by giving them direction, strengthening their foundation and shaping their form. In practice, Bi calls for upholding the socialist road, Party leadership and the people's principal position; pursuing high-quality development; and building institutions that combine public ownership, common prosperity and harmony between humanity and nature. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese Marxist reading of Marx's relational theory of the human being and its policy application to contemporary China.
quoteEn: In modern society, communicative practice dominated by capital inevitably generates reified social relations; only people-centred communicative practice led by the Communist Party can generate social relations that are truly human.
quoteZh: 在现代社会，资本主导的交往实践必然生成物化的社会关系，只有共产党领导的以人民为中心的交往实践才能生成真正属人的社会关系

glossary.explanation: An official Chinese Communist Party thesis, elaborated from the 1980s, that China remains at an early and long stage of socialism with underdeveloped productive forces.
The author's own term for a socialist form of social relations. It is presented as a transitional form between capitalist reified relations and communist human relations.
An official economic goal, prominent since the 19th Party Congress (2017), that stresses quality, efficiency and balance over speed of growth.
A Chinese Communist Party goal of prosperity shared by all, stressed in recent years as a defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

t: The history of rhythm and the rhythm of history
st: The Communist Manifesto's historical analysis of the bourgeoisie and its methodology
zh: 节奏的历史与历史的节奏
zhSub: 《共产党宣言》对资产阶级的历史分析及其蕴含的方法论
paras: Why does the Communist Manifesto, a political programme, open its main text with a historical account of the bourgeoisie? Liu Tongfang argues that the answer lies in the historical consciousness Marx and Engels developed in the age of the 'dual revolution'. To bring this out, the article uses 'rhythm' as an analytical lens, distinguishing a 'history of rhythm' from a 'rhythm of history'.

The article first treats history as grounded in 'social structure', meaning the mode of production and exchange, and shows how the bourgeoisie's expansion of productive forces sped up historical tempo. It then turns to the rhythm of history, understood as the recurrence of historical laws, and illustrates it through capitalist crises and changes in property relations. Finally it draws out three methods in the Manifesto: class analysis, historicity and totality. Liu engages Vico, Kant, Hegel, Croce, Collingwood, Lefebvre, Braudel and Karatani Kojin along the way.

Liu contends that Marx and Engels go beyond both speculative and analytical philosophy of history by treating all history as a history of rhythm. Class struggle repeats its essential content (exploitation and resistance) in changing forms. What recurs, in Liu's reading, is neither events (Marx's 'tragedy and farce' remark) nor structures (Karatani's view) but the necessity of laws. Capital's rhythm of production and destruction, with periodic crises, and the shifting of property relations from feudal to bourgeois and onward show that the bourgeoisie produces its own 'gravediggers'. This points to the inevitable fall of capitalism and victory of communism.

On method, Liu holds that class analysis explains how the bourgeoisie arose through class struggle. Historicity treats it as a transient product of development. Totality allows capitalism to be assessed both for its historic achievements and for its alienating effects, without denying either. The article concludes that the Manifesto's analysis retains lasting theoretical value, and it calls for close reading of the classic texts to draw out their historical-materialist methodology. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese scholars read the Manifesto's historical method, or in the 'rhythm' framing that links Lefebvre and Braudel to historical materialism.
quoteEn: The rhythm of history is generated in the interplay of historical time and space, and is the concrete manifestation of the 'repetition' of differentiated historical laws.
quoteZh: 历史的节奏在历史的时空交互之中生成，是差异化历史规律的“重复”的具体表征。

t: Re-examining Marx's thesis of the "natural history" of economic social formations
st: From the perspective of Hegel's "natural history of spirit"
zh: 马克思“经济社会形态的自然史”论断再探
zhSub: 以黑格尔“精神自然史”为视角
paras: Marx's preface to the first edition of Capital describes the development of the economic formation of society as 'a process of natural history'. Liu Zhenjiang takes up the long-running debate in Chinese scholarship over what this means. One camp (Chen Zhiliang, Yang Geng) reads it as saying that social formations are merely 'similar to' natural history in having their own laws. The other (Luo Bozhong) reads it as saying that social development is 'naturally' so, driven by the dialectic of human productive agency rather than material necessity. Liu argues that both are partial, and that the direct theoretical basis of Marx's thesis is Hegel's 'natural history of spirit'.

The article has four parts. It begins with Marx's reading of Hegel's 'pure-thought dialectic' in the 1844 Manuscripts and in Capital. It then reconstructs Hegel's natural history of spirit from the Philosophy of Right, the Lectures on the History of Philosophy, the Phenomenology of Spirit and the Philosophy of History. The third part examines Marx's concept of natural history and the negation of the negation in free labour. The last part turns to the concrete forms of the economic formations: the 'five formations', the 'three forms' of personal development and the 'three historical states' of the Capital manuscripts.

Liu's central claim is that Marx sublated Hegel's account, replacing the self-realisation of spirit with real human beings and their material productive labour. For Hegel, 'nature' includes human natural drives and needs, and history is the process in which freedom reconciles itself with natural necessity. Marx, in Liu's reading, defines natural history as the process by which nature becomes human, driven by the satisfaction of needs through labour. The first camp therefore wrongly equates human history with natural history in the sense of the natural world, while the second wrongly denies material necessity. On this account, capitalism's own 'natural laws' lead to the negation of private property based on individual labour and to the re-establishment of individual ownership on the basis of cooperation and common possession of the means of production.

Liu concludes that the development of economic formations is a natural history of human modes of production, in which the unity of lawfulness and purposiveness is realised as human freedom grows. Society cannot skip or abolish natural stages of development by decree, but knowledge of its laws can shorten and ease the 'birth pangs'. The 'realm of freedom' rests on the 'realm of necessity'. Read the original if you work on the Hegel–Marx relationship, the historical-materialist theory of social formations, or the Chinese debate over 'natural history' and want a detailed textual argument drawing on the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology and Capital.
quoteEn: In fact, the view of history as a 'natural history of spirit', which Hegel's pure-thought dialectic presents, is the direct theoretical basis of Marx's thesis.
quoteZh: 事实上，黑格尔的纯思想的辩证法展现的“精神自然史”的历史观是马克思的论断的直接的理论基础。

t: Marx's "Chapter on Capital" as a pioneering exploration of capital theory
st: With a discussion of capital theory under the socialist market economy
zh: 马克思“资本章”对资本理论的开创性探索
zhSub: 兼论社会主义市场经济条件下的资本理论问题
paras: Gu Hailiang asks what Marx's "Chapter on Capital" in the Economic Manuscripts of 1857–58 contributed to capital theory, and what it offers for studying capital under China's socialist market economy. The article argues that the chapter made three "firsts": it first explored the structure of a theory of capital, it first used "capital in general" and "many capitals" to frame the study of capital's characteristics and laws of behaviour, and it first treated capital as a "totality", disclosing its historical, social and class character.

The article has three main sections, one for each "first". The first traces Marx's successive plans: the five-part plan of the 1857 Introduction, the "six-part" and "three-part" structures for capital, the six-book plan of 1858, and the four-part structure for the book on capital. The second follows the pair "capital in general" and "many capitals" into the three volumes of Capital. The third examines the totality and then turns to Party documents from the 1990s to the 2010s on capital under the socialist market economy.

Gu reads the pair "capital in general" and "many capitals", derived from Hegel's "one and many", as the key to Capital. Volumes I and II analyse capital's nature at the level of capital in general, while Volume III moves to competition, the average rate of profit and prices of production, which Gu calls Marx's original contribution. Drawing on Marx's image of capital as the "universal light" that gives other relations their colour and weight, Gu reads Xi Jinping's concept of a "capital structure" of state, collective, private, foreign and mixed capital in the same way. In this account public capital is the "universal light" that changes the character of the other forms. Xi's call to grasp capital's "characteristics and laws of behaviour" is presented as a creative application of Marx's two themes.

Gu concludes that private capital under socialism keeps its profit-seeking nature, so that it has both positive and negative effects. The aim is orderly development, not abolition, and curbing "disorderly expansion" is not meant to suppress competition or accumulation. Marx's analysis of the limits capital meets is also said to bear on the specific limits that may arise among public and non-public, and domestic and foreign, capital, and on building an effective structure of capital governance. Read the original if you want a close reading of how the 1857–58 manuscripts' plans for capital theory are linked to current Chinese policy language on capital.
quoteEn: "It is not that capital is not wanted, but that capital should develop in an orderly way."
quoteZh: “不是不要资本，而是要资本有序发展”

glossary.explanation: The economic system formally adopted as China's goal at the 14th Party Congress in 1992. It combines market allocation of resources with public ownership as the main body of the economy.

t: On the practical character of Marx
st: In commemoration of the 140th anniversary of Marx's death
zh: 论马克思的实践品格
zhSub: 纪念马克思逝世140周年
paras: Marking the 140th anniversary of Marx's death in 2023, Jiang Yingchun asks what it means to keep Marx "alive among us". The article answers that the best way is to grasp the practical character (shijian pinge) of Marx and his thought, and to keep developing Marxism through practice. Jiang presents this character as the core and soul of Marxism's practical character in general, citing Xi Jinping's remark that Marxism seeks both to "interpret the world" and to "change the world".

The article has three sections. The first treats Marx as a revolutionary in the history of thought who settled accounts with idealism and with philosophy detached from life. The second discusses Marx as a unity of the "man of thought" and the "man of action", drawing on obituaries from 1883, Franz Mehring's biography, and Mao Zedong's 1945 remarks on the October Revolution's effect in China. The third examines Marx as leader and promoter of the practice of scientific socialism, through three activities.

Jiang argues that Marx grounded his work in practice and that idealist "conjectures" keep reappearing to defend backward social orders. Phenomenology is given as one example, described via a Chinese scholar's judgement as subjective idealism. Following Mehring, Jiang holds that the fighter in Marx always outweighed the thinker, because thought has value only when it guides human emancipation. Jiang criticises scholars who study Marx's texts in detail but will not act as he did. Marx's leadership is traced in three areas. He helped build international workers' organisations: the Communist League and the Communist Manifesto, and the First International. He defended the vanguard character and purity of workers' parties, as in the Critique of the Gotha Programme and the 1879 circular letter, with the German Social Democratic Party's later degeneration offered as a warning. He also fought erroneous currents inside the socialist movement that left private ownership of capital intact.

Jiang concludes that reactionary forces will always try to stifle socialism, so studying Marx's practical character is needed for real struggle, for acquiring the skills of struggle and for advancing the cause. Socialist China's continuing efforts to change the world in its own way are called the best way to honour Marx. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of how the unity of theory and practice is used to criticise academic detachment and to frame the lessons of the history of the communist movement.
quoteEn: Marxism has never shut itself up inside a system of concepts; its vitality is in the final analysis determined by the development of practice, and it has always aimed its edge at the contradiction-ridden practice of human society.
quoteZh: 马克思主义从来不将自己封闭在概念体系里，它的生命力归根结底决定于实践的发展，它始终将其锋芒指向充满矛盾的人类社会实践。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese Marxist writing for Marxism's orientation towards practice, summed up in the formula of both interpreting and changing the world. It is often attributed to Xi Jinping's formulations.

glossary.literal: interpreting the world and changing the world
glossary.explanation: An allusion to Marx's eleventh thesis on Feuerbach, used here to describe the unity of scientific theory and transformative practice.

t: The logic of alienation, the logic of production, the logic of capital
st: Three important shifts in the development of Marx's philosophy
zh: 异化逻辑·生产逻辑·资本逻辑
zhSub: 马克思哲学发展中的三次重要转换
paras: How should one grasp the development of Marx's philosophy from the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 to Capital? Yang Haifeng argues that a philosopher is best understood through the cognitive framework that governs each phase of their thought. On this basis Yang holds that Marx passed through three frameworks: a logic of alienation built on alienated labour, a logic of production built on material production, and a logic of capital aimed at the self-valorization of capital.

The article is organised in three sections, one for each shift.
