A Hegelian dialectical law that Marx and Engels use for historical development. For example, capitalist private property negates small-scale individual property and is in turn negated.

t: The value content of China's governance and its contribution to the world
zh: 中国之治的价值蕴涵与世界贡献
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 29 August 2022
paras: Zhang Shuhua asks what the political development of the People's Republic over more than seven decades, which the author labels "China's governance" (Zhongguo zhi zhi), offers to China and to the wider world. The commentary, published in 2022, argues that this experience has broken the "myth" that Western-style liberal democracy and free markets are the only successful model. In Zhang's view it has opened a new realm for scientific socialism and given other developing countries a new option.

The piece is a short newspaper commentary. It places China's governance within Chinese modernization, identifies its distinctive features and the principles behind its success, draws out two theoretical products, and ends with the vision of a community with a shared future for mankind.

Zhang names three keys to success: not copying other countries' political models but following a path rooted in China's own history and culture; adhering to the leadership of the Communist Party, which gives governance a stable political core; and keeping the people's principal position. Chinese politics, the author says, integrates democracy, order and efficiency, and unites Party leadership, law-based governance and the people as masters of the country. Its path is marked by stability, developmental orientation, continuity, coordination and practical effectiveness. Zhang rejects abstract and simplified debate on "democracy, freedom and human rights". The theoretical result is a "new view of democracy" and a "view of comprehensive development".

Zhang presents the community with a shared future for mankind as the step from one country's comprehensive development to "common governance" worldwide, going beyond the unilateralism and "own country first" attitude of some major powers. The author calls for global governance based on consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, together with multilateralism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a CASS scholar frames the general principles and international significance of China's political model.
quoteEn: China's governance is rooted in Chinese soil and is, in essence, autonomous and endogenous.
quoteZh: “中国之治”深植于中国大地，本质上具有自主性、内生性特点。

glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Party-state discourse for the Chinese system of governance and its record, here used by the author for China's political development under Chinese modernization.
The official term for China's own path to modernization, promoted by the Party since 2021 as an alternative to Western models.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept advanced by Xi Jinping since 2012–13, stressing shared development and multilateral global governance.
The Marxist theory of socialism developed by Marx and Engels, which Chinese official writing says is developed further by socialism with Chinese characteristics.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: The value content of China's governance and its contribution to the world
zh: 中国之治的价值蕴涵与世界贡献
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, Zhang Shuhua asks what is distinctive and universally meaningful in what he calls "China's governance" (zhongguo zhi zhi), the political development that accompanies Chinese modernization. The author argues that it contains elements specific to China but also general principles that other countries can compare and learn from.

The short commentary begins with the leap from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong" over more than seven decades. It then sets out the sources of China's governance, the features of its political development path, and its two theoretical products, before turning to its international significance.

Zhang names three keys to success: no copying of foreign political models, leadership by the Communist Party of China, and the principal position of the people. He lists five features of the political path under socialism with Chinese characteristics: stability, developmental character, continuity, coordination and effectiveness. The author says this path integrates democracy, order and efficiency and rejects abstract, simplified debates on "democracy, freedom and human rights". Its theoretical crystallisation, in Zhang's account, is a "new view of democracy" and a "comprehensive view of development", which treat political stability, order, performance, capacity, mobilisation and integrity as parts of political development.

Zhang contends that this experience broke the "myth" that Western-style liberal democracy and free markets are the only successful model, and offers other developing countries a new option. He presents a community with a shared future for mankind as the extension of "comprehensive development" into "common governance", surpassing the unilateralism of some major powers. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a CASS scholar frames China's political model and its claimed global relevance.
quoteEn: China's governance is deeply rooted in Chinese soil and is essentially autonomous and endogenous in character.
quoteZh: “中国之治”深植于中国大地，本质上具有自主性、内生性特点。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–2013 as China's vision for international relations, stressing common development, multilateralism and shared global governance.
The official description of China's own path to modernization, which the Party presents as distinct from Western models.
The official name for the Party's theory and system since the reform era, combining Marxism with China's conditions.
A phrase in official discourse, prominent since 2019, for China's system of governance and its record of stability and development.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Common prosperity and the intelligent revolution
st: Reflections starting from Marx
zh: 共同富裕与智能革命
zhSub: 从马克思出发的思考
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2022, Gao Qiqi asks how the intelligent revolution (AI and digital technology) bears on common prosperity. Starting from Marx's critique of alienated labour and theory of surplus value, Gao argues that common prosperity cannot be realised under capitalism because of surplus-value exploitation. The article's thesis is double-edged: the intelligent revolution may deepen inequality and exploitation, yet it is also a necessary condition for common prosperity.

The piece begins with the Chinese Communist Party's adoption of common prosperity as its value choice for social justice, and with its practical exploration of the concept. It then sets out the risks of the intelligent revolution, turns to its enabling potential, and ends with a proposal for "common labour".

On the risks, Gao says intelligent technology may replace workers across industries, lower the weight of labour and land in production, and widen income inequality and "social exclusion". Under the dominance of financial and monopoly capital, the author argues, digital exploitation produces digital labour alienation. Algorithms turn a "digital proletariat" into an appendage of machines, shift exploitation from other-directed to self-directed, and extend it to emotions, which prompts "lying flat". On the other side, Gao holds that the sharing and digital economies support high-quality development and can erode private-ownership concepts, creating new conditions for public ownership of the means of production. Gao adds that they can also improve state precision in governance and resource allocation, and strengthen political participation and information processing.

Gao concludes that common labour, built on public ownership, is the key to overcoming digital alienation. It would reunite workers with the material conditions of labour, expand use-value, and let individuals find self-fulfilment and "poetic dwelling". Its final aim is the free and all-round development of the human being, for which the intelligent revolution saves labour time. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese scholar links Marx's alienation theory, digital labour and common prosperity.
quoteEn: The common labour established by the intelligent revolution is the key to overcoming digital labour alienation.
quoteZh: 智能革命建立起的共同劳动是克服数字劳动异化的关键。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese Communist Party goal of prosperity shared by all, presented as a defining feature of socialism. It has received renewed emphasis in Party policy in recent years.
An official economic guideline, prominent since 2017, that stresses quality, efficiency and innovation over speed of growth.
A popular term for young people's withdrawal from intense work and competition by choosing minimal effort and consumption.
A term for the social transformation driven by artificial intelligence, big data and digital technologies.

t: Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization and the building of an ecological civilization
zh: 习近平生态文明思想与生态文明建设
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (August 2022), Huan Qingzhi argues that since the early 21st century, and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012), China's ecological civilization construction has become a relatively independent and complete system of discourse and theory, institutions and policy, and social practice. In Huan's account it forms part of Chinese modernization and of a "new form of human civilization".

The short commentary is organised around three levels: theory, institutional policy and social practice. It then turns to the global significance of this construction, outlines three "green story" narratives, and ends by asking what stays the same and what changes for ecological civilization in the post-pandemic period.

At the level of theory, Huan reads Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization as a political-philosophical justification whose core is modernization marked by harmony between humanity and nature. He describes this as a conscious union of "green" ecological sustainability and "red" socialist politics, tying ecological priority to socialist fairness and justice. At the institutional level, he cites the "eight systems" of the Overall Plan for Reforming the Ecological Civilization System and four requirements from the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019). He holds that institutionalisation will be long and gradual. In practice, he points to pilot zones and indicators such as GEP accounting. He sees the Party and government leading from above, while the broad masses increasingly become the "self-conscious" main actors.

Huan holds that this construction has global universality, because it answers worldwide demands to rebalance humanity and nature and would raise global environmental work as China moves from participant to contributor and leader. He concludes that its foundations and goals are unchanged, but that since the 2020 pandemic its international environment has changed. He expects the "low politics" advantage of ecological issues to fade and competition to become more visible. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic summary of how ecological civilization is framed theoretically, institutionally and globally.
quoteEn: It can be said that this is a conscious union of ecological sustainability ("green") and socialist politics ("red") in the course of continuously advancing economic and social modernization.
quoteZh: 可以说，这是在持续推进经济社会现代化建设的过程中实现生态可持续性（“绿色”）与社会主义政治（“红色”）的自觉结合。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy and theoretical concept, prominent since the early 2000s and written into Party documents from the 17th Party Congress (2007), that aims to integrate environmental protection into economic, political and social development.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization
glossary.explanation: The body of Xi Jinping's statements on ecology and environment, formally articulated in 2018, and presented as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
The official name for China's path of modernization under Party leadership, which official texts distinguish from Western models.

glossary.literal: harmonious coexistence of humans and nature
glossary.explanation: An official formulation of the intended relationship between society and the natural environment, used as a defining feature of China's modernization.

glossary.zh: 生态文明体制改革总体方案
glossary.pinyin: Shēngtài wénmíng tǐzhì gǎigé zǒngtǐ fāng'àn
glossary.en: Overall Plan for Reforming the Ecological Civilization System
glossary.explanation: A 2015 Party and State Council document setting out eight institutional systems for ecological civilization.

t: Strengthen Party building as the lead and consolidate the cornerstone of epidemic prevention and control
zh: 强化党建引领 夯实疫情防控基石
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 22 June 2022
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary published in June 2022, Qin Jingran and Guan Suye ask how grassroots governance can be strengthened in light of China's experience with COVID-19. They argue that the most important lesson of the response has been Party-building-led reinforcement of the grassroots defence line of joint and collective prevention and control. They treat this as a marker of modernising the system and capacity of social governance.

The piece focuses on the 'smallest unit' of grassroots organisation, described as the 'last kilometre' of governance and the 'last metre' of serving the public. It is organised around four measures, each tied to a function of grassroots Party organisations: leadership and linkage, a combat-ready organisational structure, personnel support, and coordination.

Qin and Guan call for clear working areas, staff groupings and duties, and for villages and communities to act as self-governing bodies in early warning and emergency response. They propose a tiered structure of village or community Party organisations, neighbourhood (grid) organisations and building-level Party groups. In peacetime this structure handles publicity, information and services, and in an outbreak it is reorganised into flatter task-based groups. They also urge mobilising Party members, grid workers, volunteers, retired soldiers and enterprise staff, and setting up Party member shock teams and vanguard posts. The authors add that information should be shared among grid workers, medical staff and police, and that channels for residents' concerns should be kept open, drawing on the 'Fengqiao experience' and 'Tongxiang experience'.

The authors conclude that grassroots Party organisations are the 'lead geese' of epidemic control, and that strengthening the smallest unit is key. They hold that the Party's political, organisational and mass-work advantages should be turned into practical results under a 'grassroots Party building+' approach. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-building language was applied to community-level epidemic management in 2022.
quoteEn: Grassroots Party organisations are the 'lead geese' of epidemic prevention and control, and strengthening the smallest grassroots unit is the key.
quoteZh: 基层党组织是疫情防控的“领头雁”，强化基层最小单元是关键。

glossary.explanation: A model of grassroots conflict resolution that originated in Fengqiao, Zhejiang, in the 1960s. It stresses mobilising local people to settle disputes locally, and has been revived in recent Party discourse on social governance.

A system of grid-based management in which communities or villages are divided into small units, each with assigned workers responsible for monitoring, services and reporting. It is widely used in Chinese grassroots governance.

t: The third industrial revolution and management change
zh: 第三次工业革命与管理变革
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 24 April 2013
paras: Writing in 2013, Wang Qin asks what the so-called third industrial revolution means for management and for enterprises. The commentary argues that the revolution should not be understood only as a change in technology, production organisation and lifestyle. In Wang's view its deeper content is institutional and managerial change, a transformation in how social resources are allocated.

The piece first distinguishes two readings of the third industrial revolution: an energy-based view (renewables, distributed energy, hydrogen storage, new-energy vehicles) and a view centred on structural technologies (big data, artificial intelligence, robots, digital manufacturing). It then describes how big data, intelligent manufacturing, 3D printing and wireless networks are altering relations inside and between firms, and closes with two contrasts: enterprise manufacturing versus social manufacturing, and large enterprises versus platform enterprises.

Wang's central claim is that the logic of management change is now the "rebalancing" of social resources. For about a century, the author says, management change followed Fayol's five functions, adding, removing or recombining them, and this logic can no longer guide firms whose boundaries are shifting. Firms must instead treat user resources as strategic, seek complementary resources from other firms, focus on newly created rather than existing resources, and push resources down through organisational layers. Wang argues that consumers become co-creators of value through "micro-manufacturing" and open, parallel innovation, and that competition will be between platforms, citing Apple's App Store as an example.

Wang concludes that firms worldwide stand at a new starting line and must look for management and institutional innovation suited to the era. The author suggests that classical bureaucratic theory, scientific management and divisional organisation, drawn from the first two revolutions, face challenges to their applicability. Read the original if you want a brief 2013 Chinese management-studies view of how digital manufacturing and platforms were expected to reshape firm organisation.
quoteEn: The logic of future management change is the "rebalancing" of social resources.
quoteZh: 未来管理变革的逻辑是社会资源“再平衡”。

t: The implications of building China into a country of strong civilization
zh: 中国文明强国建设的意蕴
paras: This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks what kind of civilizational power China should become. Starting from the 19th Party Congress (2017) goal of a modern socialist country that is prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious and beautiful by mid-century, Xin Xiangyang argues that a strong civilization has several defining features, and that it requires the balanced advance of five civilizations.

The article moves through a series of marks of a civilizational power: a flourishing cultural sector and cultural industries, a rich and uplifting spiritual life for the people, stronger cultural communication abroad, and the modernization of the human being. It closes by discussing the coordinated development of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization.

Xin ties each feature to Chinese modernization and common prosperity. Western modernization, the author says, is marked by expanding materialism, so Chinese modernization must coordinate material and spiritual civilization. Common prosperity, in this reading, covers spiritual as well as material life. Xin follows Xi Jinping in treating the modernization of people as the essence of modernization. The author argues that advanced socialist spiritual civilization can resolve the "Adam Smith problem" and "Rousseau's question". Both, in Xin's view, reflect the basic contradiction of capitalist society and cannot be solved within it.

Xin concludes that a civilizational power means the integrated development of all five civilizations by mid-century, not excellence in one field. The author also calls for China's own philosophy and social science, scholar-thinkers versed in Chinese, Western and Marxist thought, and wider global dissemination of Xi Jinping's ideas on governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese theorists in 2022 linked civilizational strength to Chinese modernization and spiritual common prosperity.
quoteEn: A strong civilization does not mean the high development of civilization in one respect, but the common, integrated development of all civilizations.
quoteZh: 文明强国不是一个方面文明的高度发达，而是所有文明的共同整体性发展。

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's own path of modernization, promoted in Party documents especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A long-standing socialist goal of prosperity shared by all, given new emphasis under Xi Jinping. The article extends it to spiritual as well as material life.
Official shorthand for material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization, whose coordinated development is presented as the aim of national construction.

t: The materialist conception of history and the construction of civilisation
zh: 唯物史观与文明建构
paras: Writing in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper (August 2022), Li Jingyuan asks what lies at the base of Deng Xiaoping Theory. Li argues that its foundation is Deng's restoration of the correct understanding of historical materialism. The piece is a short commentary, and despite its title it concentrates on Deng rather than on civilisation as such.

Li begins from two questions Deng posed: what has changed since Marx's death more than a century ago, and how Marxism should be understood and developed under changed conditions. Li then sets out three parts of Deng's view of Marxism, which Li calls the theories of the system, of the essence, and of development. The piece closes by linking these to the Party's basic line of the reform period.

Li contends that setting right the traditional view of Marxism is the soul of Deng Xiaoping Theory, and setting right the traditional view of socialism is its core. Both rest on clearing up the conception of history. In the first part, Deng held that Mao Zedong Thought must be grasped as a whole system, and Li presents the "Two Whatevers" as a product of an idealist view of history. In the second, seeking truth from facts is the essence of Marxism and of Mao Zedong Thought, and the ideological line underpins the political line. In the third, Marxism develops by solving China's pressing problems, so that it becomes sinicised.

Li concludes that Deng, guided by historical materialism, set the basic line of "one central task, two basic points" and turned historical materialism towards everyday life. In Li's view, restoring historical materialism gave philosophical grounding to replacing "class struggle as the key link" with economic construction as the centre, and to the line of reform and opening up. Read the original if you want a brief statement of how a Chinese philosopher links Deng Xiaoping Theory to historical materialism.
quoteEn: Facts have shown that Deng Xiaoping's setting right of the ideological line and the political line was in essence a setting right of the conception of history.
quoteZh: 事实证明,邓小平对思想路线和政治路线的拨乱反正,本质上都是对历史观的拨乱反正。

glossary.explanation: The body of ideas associated with Deng Xiaoping on reform, opening up and socialism with Chinese characteristics. It was written into the Party constitution in 1997.
A slogan of 1977 holding that whatever policy decisions Mao made and whatever instructions he gave must be upheld. Deng and others criticised it as dogmatic.
A principle taken up by Mao and made central by Deng. It calls for starting from actual conditions and testing theory in practice.
The policy of domestic economic reform and opening to the outside world begun in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.

glossary.pinyin: yí gè zhōngxīn, liǎng gè jīběndiǎn
glossary.en: one central task, two basic points
glossary.explanation: The Party's basic line from the 1980s. The central task is economic development; the two basic points are the Four Cardinal Principles and reform and opening up.

t: The task of our times: building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics
zh: 构建中国特色哲学社会科学的时代任务
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (August 2022), Wu Xiaoming argues that building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics is a major task entrusted to Chinese scholarship by the age. The author holds that the era is changing so deeply that it can only be understood once those changes become objects of scholarly theory.

The short piece has three numbered parts. It first defines what kind of scholarship "Chinese characteristics" refers to, then considers the task from the side of theory, and finally places it within a new historical position and the world-historical significance of China's practice. Wu draws on Hegel, Marx and Xi Jinping's remarks at the 2016 symposium on philosophy and the social sciences.

Wu contends that Chinese characteristics concern the nature and standpoint of scholarship, not its form: adding Chinese elements or topics misreads the task. What is required is scholarship that has left its "apprenticeship" and developed its own claims, with subjectivity and originality. Apprenticeship, the author says, was necessary but is dependent and imitative, and tends towards Hegel's "external reflection", which Wu equates with dogmatism: applying abstract principles to any content without engaging its substance.

Wu concludes that scholarship must be freed from external reflection and enter social-historical reality, above all that of present-day China, while continuing to learn from others. Because China's practice has reached a new historical position, the author says, it generates a theoretical need that falls to this generation of scholars. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher frames the "subjectivity" of Chinese scholarship.
quoteEn: Unless our scholarship can shake off its apprenticeship and gain its own voice, it cannot possess "subjectivity" or "originality" and can only "follow others step by step".
quoteZh: 除非我们的学术能够摆脱其学徒状态并获得自我主张，否则的话，它就不可能具有“主体性”“原创性”，就只能“跟在别人后面亦步亦趋”

glossary.zh: 中国特色哲学社会科学
glossary.en: philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: A programme, stressed by Xi Jinping from 2016, to build Chinese disciplinary, academic and discourse systems with their own subjectivity and originality, guided by Marxism.
Hegel's term for reasoning that applies general principles abstractly to any content without entering its substance. Wu equates it with dogmatism or formalism.
Wu's term for the long phase in which Chinese scholarship learned from and depended on foreign, mainly Western, theory.

keywords: philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics

t: Finance capital and the financialization of contemporary capitalism
zh: 金融资本与当代资本主义金融化
paras: Since the 1970s, financialization has become a defining feature of contemporary capitalism. Yet Rudolf Hilferding's systematic account of finance capital has received little attention, and some scholars deny that it has any contemporary relevance. Liu asks whether finance capital still has explanatory power for Marxist economics. The article, a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2022, argues that Hilferding's concept remains the theoretical foundation for understanding financialization, and that it in turn needs the test of present-day developments.

The article first sets out three dimensions of Hilferding's finance capital: the monopolisation of bank and industrial capital, their fusion, and the dominant position of bank capital. It then reviews objections from Paul Sweezy, John Bellamy Foster and Costas Lapavitsas. Finally it turns to the Monopoly Capital school and its account of financialization since the 1970s, which Liu criticises.

Liu reads Hilferding as treating monopoly as the precondition for finance capital, since without it ownership and use of money capital cannot be structurally separated. Bank capital then merges with industrial capital and dominates it through loan capital and fictitious capital. Industrial capital does not vanish but becomes one moment in the accumulation of finance capital. Finance capital's internal structure must therefore be grasped through both productive and non-productive accumulation. The Monopoly Capital school keeps Hilferding's split between production and finance but treats the two as absolutely opposed, equating financialization with fictitious capital. Liu calls this one-sided. In Liu's view, the school concentrates on circulation and on how surplus is absorbed, neglects how it is produced, never defines finance capital ontologically, and so cannot show why finance capital arises as the highest form of capital.

Liu concludes that only a dual understanding of accumulation, in the real and the fictitious economy, reveals finance capital's structure and so grounds a theory of financialization. This would allow Marxist finance-capital theory to be developed into a world system combining economics, politics and international relations. Liu also holds that contemporary financialization should be used to renew the theory's modern relevance. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese Marxist statement of why Hilferding's Finance Capital still matters in debates with Sweezy, Foster and the Monopoly Capital school.
quoteEn: Defining the concept of finance capital in an ontological sense is the primary question for understanding financialization.
quoteZh: 而从本体论的意义上对金融资本概念的界定是理解金融化的首要问题。

t: A critique of biopolitics in the context of digital capitalism
zh: 数字资本主义背景下的生命政治批判
paras: This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks how biopolitics, a hot topic in Marxism outside China, should be understood once data has become the organising principle of society. Qu argues that data-based identity and "general data" mark a turning point that changes how political power reaches individual lives, and that this turning point is best analysed through Marx's critique of political economy.

The article draws on Western thinkers: Agamben, Deleuze, Foucault, Dan Schiller, Cass Sunstein, Byung-Chul Han and Roberto Esposito. It first treats data identity as the condition of the new biopolitics, then distinguishes types of the "control society", and finally compares critical and affirmative accounts of biopolitics.

Qu describes data identity as combining biometric data, records of social activity and algorithmic profiles of preferences. Without it, the author says, citizens cannot access travel, medical care or shopping, and individuals become "transparent", a society-wide Foucauldian panopticon. Control also works through performance metrics that split workers into competing units, and through "information cocoons" that isolate groups from each other. Qu reads Han's "psychopolitics" as a further extension of biopolitics. Agamben's "bare life" and "form-of-life" are set against Esposito's affirmative biopolitics of community and openness to others.

Qu concludes that data becomes a new ruling force only when it acts as a general equivalent and operates as capital, just as the mere appearance of money did not create capitalism. Critical and affirmative biopolitics share one aim: a more complete society, with new technology bringing both challenges and possibilities. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how Western biopolitical theory is being reframed around digital capitalism.
quoteEn: Only when data, as a general equivalent, can abstract all differences into quantifiable differences in data, and unfolds through the operation of capital to become the ruling force of society, does a new mode of control emerge in biopolitics under data capitalism.
quoteZh: 只有当数据作为一般等价物可以把各种差别抽象化为数据上的可量化的差别，并以资本运作的方式展开，从而成为社会的统治力量之时，数据资本主义视域下的生命政治才出现了新的控制方式。

t: An interpretation of Marx and Engels's constitutional thought
st: An examination based on the drafting of the Communist Manifesto, 1843–1848
zh: 马克思恩格斯宪法思想诠释
zhSub: 基于1843至1848年《共产党宣言》创作过程的考察
source: Journal of Xiangtan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2022 no. 4
paras: Liu and Wu ask whether the Communist Manifesto, usually read as a programme of class struggle and a landmark of Marxist jurisprudence, also contains a developed theory of the constitution. Tracing the document's roughly ten-year drafting history and Marx and Engels's sustained attention to constitutions from 1843 to 1848, they argue that it does. They support this with the German and English editions of the Manifesto.

The article sets out four propositions. These are that a constitution should recognise human rights and civil rights and reflect the people's demands; that the working class needs a democratic constitution to achieve political emancipation and establish political rule; that a constitution is determined by, and must suit, the material conditions of life of a given society; and that each country must follow a constitutional path suited to its own national conditions. The evidence ranges from Marx's early critiques of Hegel and his notes on the French and American constitutions to the programmes of the League of the Just and the Communist League, Engels's draft credo and Principles of Communism, and the polemics against 'true socialism'.

In the authors' reading, Marx held that democracy is the 'solved riddle of all constitutions' and that new constitutions arise through revolution. In On the Jewish Question, Marx distinguished the rights of man from the rights of the citizen and judged political emancipation both a real advance and not yet human emancipation. Liu and Wu stress that this critique did not reject individual freedom or equality as such. Next, they argue that Marx and Engels tied constitutions to the rise of the bourgeoisie, large-scale industry and free competition. Where the bourgeoisie had not yet won power, as in Germany, communists should support its revolution against absolutism while preparing the struggle against it. Where it ruled, as in Britain, France and the United States, workers should use constitutional rights for lawful class struggle. After a proletarian revolution, a democratic constitution is the first step in establishing proletarian rule.

The authors conclude that the Manifesto's general principles must be applied according to historical conditions, which they take as a constitutional lesson: no country should copy another's constitutional path. They present Marx and Engels's criticism of 'true socialists', who transplanted French texts into Germany, as the model case. They also cite Lenin's continuation of the same democratic-constitution theory. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the drafting history of the Manifesto bears on Marxist constitutional and legal theory, including the rights debates of the 1840s.
quoteEn: A constitution is determined by the material conditions of life of a given society and must be suited to them.
quoteZh: 宪法由一定社会的物质生活条件决定并须与之相适应

t: Making historical materialism concrete: Marx's exploration and its significance
zh: 唯物史观具体化：马克思的探索及其意义
source: Journal of Sichuan University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2022 no. 3
paras: Western scholarship has recently returned to Marx's two early-1850s political histories, The Class Struggles in France, 1848 to 1850 and The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, often reading them as a politics of action or a history of events set against economic determinism. Tang Zhengdong argues instead that they are Marx's first attempt to make historical materialism concrete (具体化), meaning to apply it to the real problems of a particular country. The article claims this reading clarifies the preconditions, theoretical marks and methodological features of such concretization.

The article takes the two texts in three steps. It first shows that the inherited ideas and illusions Marx describes are products of social relations not yet sharpened into acute class antagonism. It then identifies two theoretical results of Marx's concretization, and finally draws out implications for the history of Marxism and for the adaptation of Marxism in China. Tang compares Marx with Victor Hugo and Proudhon, and with Engels's The Peasant War in Germany.

Tang's first result is that Marx treats France's apparently farcical political struggles as the outward, mediating form of the internal contradictions of the French mode of production. Because France's development was atypical and lagged behind Britain's, its classes were underdeveloped, so class struggle could not take the pure form of capital against labour. Marx therefore traces the June defeat, the incoherent conduct of the parties and the peasants' support for Bonaparte to class position, not to tactics, party principles or the autonomy of state power. The second result is that Marx lifts this history to the level of laws of political struggle. He argues that small-holding peasants and the petty bourgeoisie would be driven towards the proletariat, and he formulates the idea of permanent revolution and the class dictatorship of the proletariat, which Tang says sets the texts apart from ordinary event history.

Tang concludes that Marx's post-1848 thought should be read as an exploration of concretization, not merely an application of historical materialism, and that concretization is as central to the theory as its basic content. In Tang's view this marks what counts as success in combining basic principles with the analysis of a specific country. The article ties this to Mao Zedong's 1938 call to make Marxism concrete in China and to the Party's later study of principal contradictions and development laws under socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a close reading of these two Marx texts that challenges event-history interpretations and links them to debates on adapting Marxism.
quoteEn: Seeing and grasping that the intricate political struggles were the mediating, outward form of the internal contradictions of the French mode of production was the first theoretical result Marx achieved in advancing the concretization of historical materialism.
quoteZh: 看出并抓住错综复杂的政治斗争是法国生产方式内在矛盾性的外部表现的中介形式，是马克思在学理层面推进唯物史观具体化时所取得的第一项理论成果。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term for the combination of productive forces and relations of production in a society. The author treats it as the basis from which political struggles must be explained.

The Party's long-standing formula for applying Marxism to Chinese conditions, developed from Mao Zedong's 1938 call to give Marxism a national form. The article presents it as a case of concretization.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

t: Enriching and developing the Marxist theory of productive forces: scientific guidance for accelerating the building of an innovation-oriented country
zh: 丰富和发展马克思主义生产力理论 为加快建设创新型国家提供科学指引
paras: This short commentary, first published in the People's Daily in 2022, asks how Xi Jinping's statements on innovation-driven development relate to the Marxist theory of productive forces. Liu Yapin argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) these statements have enriched and developed that theory and give scientific guidance for accelerating the building of an innovation-oriented country.

The piece sets out four propositions of Xi's, each paired with a claimed theoretical contribution. They are: innovation as the "primary driving force" of development; scientific and technological innovation as the strategic support for raising productive forces; the "three-stage leap" of scientific and technological achievements; and innovation as an important driver of world development.

Liu's reasoning follows a repeated pattern. Each proposition is anchored in a Marxist premise: productive forces are the fundamental driving force of social development, science is part of productive forces, and science becomes a real, direct productive force only when applied in production. Xi's formulations are then presented as extending these premises. The author reads the "primary driving force" formulation as building on the earlier thesis that science and technology are the primary productive force. The "three-stage leap", from scientific research through experimental development to popularisation and application, is described as a path for turning technology into real productive forces.

Liu concludes that Xi's expositions deepen the Party's understanding of how productive forces relate to scientific and technological innovation, and offer a global perspective for countries facing shared risks and challenges. The author credits the innovation-driven development strategy, guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, with raising China's productive forces and comprehensive national strength. Read the original if you want a brief, official-style example of how Xi's innovation discourse is tied to the Marxist theory of productive forces.
quoteEn: General Secretary Xi Jinping's important expositions have enriched the content of the Marxist theory of productive forces, provide a guide to action for comprehensively promoting China's sustained and healthy economic development and the change of economic growth drivers in the new era, and are a major innovative development of that theory.
quoteZh: 习近平总书记的重要论述，丰富了马克思主义生产力理论的内涵，为新时代全面推动我国经济持续健康发展、全面推进经济发展动力变革提供了行动指南，是对马克思主义生产力理论的重大创新发展。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name of the Party's guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.
A national strategy set out in the early 2010s that makes scientific and technological innovation the main source of economic growth.

glossary.zh: 科学技术是第一生产力
glossary.en: science and technology are the primary productive force
glossary.explanation: A thesis associated with Deng Xiaoping in the post-1978 reform period, stressing the role of science and technology in economic development.
An official goal of making innovation the main driver of national development, with strong independent innovation capacity.

t: Guiding the correct handling of the relationship between production and distribution: the contemporary significance of Marx's labour theory of value
zh: 指导正确处理生产与分配关系马克思劳动价值论的时代意义
paras: Huang Shao'an, writing in the People's Daily in 2022, asks what Marx's labour theory of value offers for handling the relationship between production and distribution today. The author argues that, although the theory arose from analysis of private-ownership commodity economies, its account of general laws of commodity production and exchange still guides the building of a socialist market economy in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The short commentary first summarises the theory's main distinctions and then draws three practical implications. These are that labour creates wealth and value, that productive labour strengthens the country, and that income distribution should reflect labour's contribution.

Huang identifies four distinctions in Marx's theory: concrete and abstract labour; necessary and surplus labour; social and private labour; and productive and non-productive labour. From these the author derives policy points. Because labour creates value, diligence and hard work should be promoted at the stage of promoting common prosperity, and labour's share in primary distribution should rise. Because productive labour creates material wealth, the real economy should be strengthened, avoiding what the author calls the 'shift from the real to the virtual' seen in some countries, and factor markets reformed so that factors are rewarded by their market-assessed contribution. Huang adds that productive labour now includes producing knowledge, technology, information and data, so the creative and complex labour of scientists, technicians and managers should be rewarded in line with its contribution.

The author concludes that Marx's theory remains relevant to economic development and to distribution policy under common prosperity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese economist links Marx's labour theory of value to current policy on distribution, the real economy and technical labour.
quoteEn: In modern society the scope of productive labour has expanded greatly, covering not only labour that produces material goods but also labour that produces knowledge, technology, information or data products.
quoteZh: 在现代社会，生产性劳动的外延大大扩展了，不仅包括生产物质产品的劳动，而且包括生产知识、技术、信息或数据产品的劳动。

glossary.explanation: A goal of shared affluence for all, stressed in Party policy under Xi Jinping, especially since 2021. It is linked to distribution policy and narrowing inequality.
The official name for China's path and system since reform and opening up. The 18th Party Congress (2012) and later documents speak of it entering a 'new era'.
The part of the economy that produces goods and services, such as manufacturing, as distinct from finance and speculation. Official discourse stresses it as the foundation of national strength.
The first round of income distribution among factors of production, mainly wages and returns on capital, before redistribution by taxes and transfers.

t: The critical, revolutionary and practical logics of Marx and Engels's thought on spatial justice
zh: 马克思恩格斯空间正义思想的批判逻辑、革命逻辑与实践逻辑
source: Ideological and Political Education Research (思想教育研究), 2022 no. 8
paras: Western spatial theorists such as Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja, the authors report, treat classical Marxism as a 'spaceless' and closed system with four defects: an epistemological gap, an outdated critique, a useless theory of revolution and a hopeless vision of the future. Yuan and Zhang answer that Marx and Engels did hold a thought on spatial justice, and that Marxism is a 'double helix' of time and space, not a one-dimensional theory of time. They call on scholars to 'return to Marx and Engels' against the tendency to belittle or discard Marxism.

The article first establishes that Marx and Engels's thought on space was present, drawing on the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, Capital and Engels's writings on English cities. It then organises the argument in three logics: critique (how spatial injustice arises), revolution (how it is overcome) and practice (how it is realised). The last section turns to socialism with Chinese characteristics and ends with a brief afterword.

On critique, the authors argue that Marx and Engels traced capitalism's spatial divisions to capital itself at three levels. These are class segregation within cities, the rural–urban rupture, and a global 'centre–periphery' structure. On revolution, they argue that Marx and Engels required a three-part programme: a revolution in productive forces, an ethical revolution and violent revolution. They hold that dialogue with capital and the reformist 'right to the city' leave the capitalist mode of production intact. They credit the Communist Party of China with adapting this to China through 'encircling the cities from the countryside'. On realisation, they say spatial justice means productive, distributive and ethical justice. They argue that China's land system, the rural revitalisation and targeted poverty-alleviation strategies, 'people's cities', ecological civilization and shared human values have put these into practice. In their view this refutes Harvey's claim that the communist prospect is spatially vague.

The authors conclude that Xi Jinping's ideas, including 'lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets', the new development philosophy and 'joint contribution, joint governance and shared benefits' in social governance, uphold and extend Marx and Engels's thought on spatial justice. They present these ideas as a guide for building socialist equal space, regulating the production of urban space and realising spatial human rights. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja, or an example of how Chinese urban and rural policy is framed as spatial justice.
quoteEn: Marxism is not a one-dimensional theory of time, but a 'double-helix' theory combining time and space.
quoteZh: 马克思主义不是时间的单向度理论，而是时空复合的“双螺旋”理论。

glossary.explanation: A framework set out by Xi Jinping in 2015 that calls for innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared development.
The official name for China's path since reform and opening up, which combines Party leadership, public ownership as the mainstay and a market economy.
A national strategy announced in 2017 to develop agriculture, villages and farmers' incomes and to narrow the urban–rural gap.

A concept from Western critical urban theory, associated with Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja, about the fair distribution of resources and rights across space. The authors reinterpret it as a Marxist idea rooted in the mode of production.

t: Marx's view of capital and its contemporary significance
zh: 马克思的资本观及其现实意义
paras: Yao Manlin asks what Marx's analysis of capital, developed in the era of free-competition capitalism, offers for understanding and using capital in China today. The article argues that Marx's view of capital rests on three claims: capital is a production relation, it has both a barbaric and a civilising face, and the capitalist is the personification of capital as an economic category. Yao holds that each claim yields practical guidance for how capital should be regulated and guided under socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article has four sections. The first treats capital as a socio-historical phenomenon and sets Marx against bourgeois economists. The second examines the two faces of capital. The third examines the relation between capital and the capitalist, and the fourth sums up the theoretical contribution and present relevance of Marx's view. Each of the first three sections ends with implications for contemporary China, drawing on texts such as Capital, the 1857–58 manuscripts, Wage Labour and Capital and The Communist Manifesto.

Yao reads Marx as showing that money becomes capital only where the objective conditions of labour are separated from labour itself and labour-power becomes a commodity. Capital is therefore a relation of unpaid appropriation of surplus value, not a mere thing. On the second claim, Yao says capital's barbarism lies in primitive accumulation, in alienation driven by the pursuit of profit, and in the inherent limits of capitalist production. Its civilising role lies in advancing productive forces, dissolving feudal bonds and preparing the conditions for socialism. Yao insists that barbarism dominates and that the civilising side must not be stretched into a defence of exploitation. On the third claim, Yao says Marx held that capital implies the capitalist, but did not blame individuals for the system. From this Yao draws the conclusion that entrepreneurs in China are not capitalists.

From these arguments Yao draws policy lessons. These include systemic thinking, with the market playing the decisive role in allocating resources and the government playing its role better. They also include bottom-line thinking against the disorderly expansion of capital, and rule-of-law thinking that sets "traffic lights" for capital. Yao adds that labour creates value, that wealth should be understood as use value, and that entrepreneurship should be promoted. Yao concludes that Marx's view of capital also offers a method that joins philosophy, political economy and socialism, a critical spirit that bears on Frankfurt School and ecological critiques, and resources for handling capital in an era of globalisation. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar derives current policy on regulating capital from Marx's texts.
quoteEn: It can be said that Chinese Communists have always deepened their understanding of capital from the standpoint of production relations, upholding the unity of theory and practice.
quoteZh: 可以说，中国共产党人总是从生产关系的高度来深化对资本的认识，坚持理论与实践相统一

glossary.explanation: A phrase in Chinese official discourse, prominent from around 2020–21, for private capital's unregulated growth in areas such as platform economy and finance. It is used to justify tighter regulation and antitrust measures.
A term the Party leadership has promoted in recent years. It praises private entrepreneurs' patriotism, innovation, integrity, social responsibility and international vision.

t: Did Marx really believe the circulation process creates value?
st: Upholding the monism of "productive labour creates value" and its implications for the new era
zh: 马克思真的认为流通过程能创造价值吗？
zhSub: 坚持“生产劳动创造价值”一元论及其在新时代的启示
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2022 no. 5
paras: Does circulation, including transport and commerce, create value? Wang Xianpeng takes up a dispute that has run in Chinese scholarship since the 1960s and was revived by the growth of the tertiary sector. Through a close reading of Marx's texts, the article argues that Marx never held that circulation creates value. In Wang's account, Marx held a monist position: only productive labour creates value.

The article has four parts. It first shows that productive labour creating value is the foundation of Marx's critique of political economy. It then examines the passages in Volume 2 of Capital that are most often cited to support value creation in circulation. Next it sets out four judgements on how to read Marx correctly. It ends with the significance of the monist position for contemporary China.

Wang's first move is to read Marx's Economic Manuscripts of 1861–63 and the Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy as limiting the "labour" that creates value to labour that is directly exchanged with capital in capitalist production. In this reading, services and "total labour" fall outside that concept. The second move is a re-reading of the Capital passages on transport, storage and the "total circuit". Wang stresses Marx's wording: "adding" value rather than creating it; "for the individual capitalist" circulation costs may "act as value-creating", which concerns price mark-ups; and what transport sells is a "useful effect", not a commodity. Wang adds a logical test: if circulation created value, the same commodity transported short, long or not at all would have different values, and the "created" value would have nowhere to go. Wang also treats transport profit as a transfer of surplus value from industrial capital.

Wang concludes that circulation labour is unproductive but still important, since it enables the realization of value and use-value. The author holds that abandoning the monism would split theory from practice, damage the theoretical legitimacy of a socialist state and open the door to claims that Marxism is outdated. Wang calls for upholding fundamental principles while supplementing them for new conditions, as an aid to strengthening the real economy, curbing the disorderly expansion of capital and advancing common prosperity. Read the original if you want a text-based case against value creation in circulation, or want to see how this debate is tied to current Chinese economic policy.
quoteEn: In Marx's work, the sphere of circulation does not create value.
quoteZh: 流通领域在马克思那里是不创造价值的

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy goal of shared wealth for all, stressed in Party documents and especially under Xi Jinping.

t: Always upholding the value pursuit of putting the people first
zh: 始终坚持人民至上的价值追求
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Wan Guangxia comments on Xi Jinping's speech at a seminar for provincial and ministerial leaders held ahead of the 20th Party Congress. Wan reads the speech's call to serve the people wholeheartedly as a restatement of the historical lesson of "putting the people first", and as an expression of the value pursuit of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article argues that the Party must keep to this principle on the new journey.

The short piece is organised under three headings: placing the people's interests in the highest position, respecting the people's principal position, and promoting all-round human development and common prosperity for all.

On the first, Wan holds that the people's stance is the Party's basic political stance, that the Party has no special interests of its own, and that the people are the foundation of its governing position. Wan cites the 19th Party Congress's adoption of "putting the people at the center" as a basic principle. On the second, Wan invokes historical materialism, Marx and Engels, and Mao Zedong to present the masses as the decisive force in history, and calls for using the mass line, respecting people's initiative and learning from them. On the third, Wan links human development to the aim of common prosperity.

Wan concludes that common prosperity is an essential requirement of socialism and a feature of Chinese modernization. Wan describes it as prosperity of all, material and cultural, and neither the wealth of a few nor egalitarian levelling. Wan calls for high-quality development, social fairness and justice, and the balanced handling of competing interests. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's "people first" principle was presented to a general readership just before the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Common prosperity is the prosperity of all the people, prosperity in both the material and the spiritual life of the masses; it is neither the prosperity of a few nor uniform egalitarianism.
quoteZh: 共同富裕是全体人民的富裕，是人民群众物质生活和精神生活都富裕，不是少数人的富裕，也不是整齐划一的平均主义。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. It is presented as Marxism adapted to China's conditions.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping. It was written into the Party constitution in 2017.
A Party working method associated with Mao Zedong: gathering the views of the masses, refining them, and returning them as policy ("from the masses, to the masses").
A goal of socialism that the Party stresses under Xi Jinping. It is described officially as prosperity shared by all, not egalitarian levelling.
The official term for China's path of modernization, which the Party presents as distinct from Western models.
An official economic goal emphasising quality, balance and sustainability over speed of growth alone.

t: The people's standpoint is the fundamental standpoint for promoting the spirit of historical initiative in the new era
zh: 人民立场是新时代弘扬历史主动精神的根本立场
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 24 August 2022, asks why the Communist Party of China has been able to hold the "historical initiative" through more than a century of changing tasks and crises. Li Yuyan argues that the root answer is the Party's consistent adherence to the people's standpoint, and that promoting the spirit of historical initiative in the new era requires keeping to it.

The article defines the spirit of historical initiative as a state of mind: grasping historical laws under Marxist guidance, following the main trend of history, acting proactively and innovating. It is organised in three parts, treating the people's standpoint as, in turn, the logical premise for understanding historical laws, the greatest source of confidence for shouldering historical responsibility, and the solid foundation for recognising the people's status as the subject of history.

In the first part, Li reads modern Chinese history as showing that earlier patriots failed to change the nation's fate because they did not stand with the people and so could not grasp historical laws. Marxism-Leninism, in Li's account, moved Chinese people from passivity to initiative because it takes the people's standpoint. In the second, Li surveys the Party's stages from the New Democratic Revolution to the new era, presenting each as responsibility borne for the people. In the third, citing Engels and Xi Jinping, Li contends that only this standpoint sees the masses as creators of history, and illustrates it with poverty alleviation and epidemic control.

Li concludes that promoting historical initiative means keeping close ties with the people, applying a people-centred philosophy of development, developing whole-process people's democracy, pursuing common prosperity, and relying on the people. Read the original if you want a short, representative example of how Party theorists in 2022 linked the spirit of historical initiative to the people's standpoint.
quoteEn: The people's standpoint is the greatest source of confidence for shouldering historical responsibility and demonstrating historical initiative.
quoteZh: 人民立场是担当历史责任、彰显历史主动的最大底气

glossary.explanation: A phrase stressing that the Party grasps historical laws and acts proactively rather than reactively. It gained prominence in Party discourse around 2021–2022, notably in Xi Jinping's speeches.
The Party's stated principle of taking the people's position, interests and perspective as its basis. It is presented as the fundamental political stance of the Party.

A concept introduced by Xi Jinping in 2019 describing China's democracy as covering every stage of political life, not only elections. Officially presented as a distinctive form of socialist democracy.
A goal of shared wealth for all, tied to socialism in Party discourse and given renewed emphasis under Xi Jinping.
Mao Zedong's term for the Chinese revolution led by the Communist Party from about 1919 to 1949, before the founding of the People's Republic.

t: Leading social revolution through the Party's self-reform
zh: 以党的自我革命引领社会革命
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily on 22 August 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, Li Xiaodong argues that the Communist Party of China can carry out a great social revolution only because it is also capable of great self-revolution. The commentary takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at a seminar for provincial and ministerial leading cadres, to use the Party's self-reform to lead social revolution. Li presents this as the key to consolidating the Party's long-term governing position and keeping the people's support.

The piece is organised in three numbered sections. The first presents the principle as an inherent requirement of a Marxist party's historical mission. The second reads it as the accumulated experience of revolution, construction and reform, from the Gutian, Zunyi and Yan'an episodes to the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) and the post-2012 period. The third treats it as the key to meeting the changes in the world, the times and history.

Li defines social revolution, on Marxist premises, as grounded in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, covering both the overthrow of the old political superstructure and the building of a new society. Self-revolution means continual self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation. Citing Engels and Lenin on the value of internal struggle and of openly admitting mistakes, Li holds that the two processes are organically unified and reinforce each other. Li cites the fall of dynasties and of long-established parties abroad as evidence that failing to confront internal problems is fatal. For the new era, Li points to the Central Committee's eight-point regulations, the anti-corruption campaign and the cases it brought down, and Party education campaigns as a set of measures that, in the article's account, helped the Party escape the historical cycle of rise and fall.

Li concludes that the Party's work is unprecedented in breadth, depth, sharpness, difficulty and complexity, and so calls for greater urgency, initiative and foresight in self-revolution. Li stresses that the "four dangers" and "four tests" remain severe, that problems of impurity in thought, politics, organisation and style are unresolved, and that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is never finished. The article ends with confidence that a Party able to break an old world and build a new one will keep winning victories. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party's official line on self-reform was framed for a general readership on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Self-revolution has only a present continuous tense and no completed one; full and rigorous self-governance of the Party is always on the road.
quoteZh: 自我革命只有进行时没有完成时，全面从严治党永远在路上。

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed by Xi Jinping since 2012, meaning the Party's continual purification, renewal and correction of its own problems. The article itself uses the word "self-revolution" (自我革命).

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party-building and anti-corruption drive promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering discipline, supervision and conduct of members.
Rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb formalism, extravagance and bureaucratic style among officials.

glossary.pinyin: sì zhǒng wēixiǎn, sì dà kǎoyàn
glossary.explanation: Official formula: the dangers are lack of drive, inadequate ability, detachment from the people and corruption; the tests are governing, reform and opening up, the market economy and the external environment.

glossary.en: the historical cycle of rise and fall
glossary.literal: jump out of the historical cycle
glossary.explanation: A reference to a 1945 exchange between Huang Yanpei and Mao Zedong about how regimes decline after rising; the Party presents self-reform as its answer.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: The natural yardsticks and spatial dimensions of common prosperity
zh: 共同富裕的自然尺度与空间维度
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 20 July 2022
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary of July 2022, Chen Huixiong asks how common prosperity can be given a concrete measure and an internal structure. Drawing on Marx's definition of wealth as a thing that satisfies human needs, Chen defines prosperity as the degree to which wealth adequately meets needs. Common prosperity is then a shared but differentiated sufficiency across people's different levels of need. The article proposes two "natural yardsticks" and three "spatial dimensions" for realising it.

The piece is organised in two parts. The first sets out the two yardsticks: meeting people's reasonable needs as the goal, and the carrying capacity of natural resources as the limiting boundary. The second applies a systems perspective to divide common prosperity into three levels: harmony between humanity and nature, prosperity among people, and prosperity of body and mind. A short conclusion ties the two parts together.

On the first yardstick, Chen distinguishes needs ("needs") from wants or desires ("wants"). Citing the economic happiness equation (happiness = utility/desire), Chen argues that no growth in productive forces can satisfy ever-rising desires for money, so common prosperity must be measured by reasonable needs. On the second, Chen calls for abandoning growth that ignores ecological capacity and for using the dual carbon goals and high-quality development to advance common prosperity. Of the three dimensions, Chen treats harmony between humanity and nature as the premise, holding that without it there can be no prosperity among people. Prosperity among people is to come from individuals' "productive effort", fair distribution and a mix of government-led design with market competition. Chen adds that psychological poverty now needs more attention than physical poverty. Chen links this three-level structure to the traditional Chinese idea of the unity of heaven and humanity.

Chen concludes that common prosperity is an essential feature of socialism and that the two yardsticks and three dimensions are all indispensable. Only by taking people's growing need for a better life as the goal and natural carrying capacity as the limit can a more sustainable common prosperity be achieved. Chen presents this as the way to sustainable development of people, economy, society and ecology together. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of how ecological limits and spiritual well-being are being built into the concept of common prosperity.
quoteEn: Meeting people's reasonable needs as the goal and the carrying capacity of natural resources as the limiting boundary are the two natural yardsticks for achieving common prosperity, while shared prosperity of heaven and humanity, of people with one another, and of mind and body are its three spatial dimensions.
quoteZh: “以满足人的合理需要为目标、以自然资源承载力为约束边界”是实现共同富裕的两个自然尺度，“天人共富、人人共富、心身共富”是实现共同富裕的三大空间维度。

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal of prosperity shared by all, given fresh emphasis in Chinese policy from 2021. Chinese discussions treat it as a goal of reducing polarisation and poverty rather than equal outcomes.
An official formula, prominent since 2017, that shifts emphasis from speed of growth to efficiency, innovation, environmental sustainability and fairness.
China's pledge to peak carbon emissions before 2030 and reach carbon neutrality before 2060, announced in 2020.
A traditional Chinese philosophical idea that humans and nature form a harmonious whole. The author invokes it as the cultural basis of the three-level model.

t: On accelerating the construction of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics
zh: 关于加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学
paras: This commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's remarks during his inspection of Renmin University of China. Xi Ge and Shu Yating argue that these remarks raise basic questions about the standard, substance and path of building philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, and that they call for systematic study and elaboration.

The article is organised around three paired relationships. The first is between "Chinese characteristics" and "world-class" status, which the authors treat as the question of standards. The second is between building Chinese-characteristic philosophy and social sciences and building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system, which they treat as the question of substance. The third is between philosophical and social science work and the training of talent, which they treat as the question of path.

On standards, the authors invoke historical materialism: universal laws of civilizational progress are realised through particular national paths. They argue that a universal standard detached from particulars is a "pseudo-universal", so world-class university standards must be internalised and creatively transformed to fit China's conditions. On substance, they contend that answering the questions of the times and upholding the Two Integrations are the guiding requirements. Citing Xi, they hold that the field's main task is to build an autonomous knowledge system. In their view, whether the field has Chinese characteristics depends less on the "outward forms" of disciplinary, academic and discourse systems than on the "substantive core" of an original, autonomous body of knowledge.

On path, the authors call on scholars to be "great teachers" (da xiansheng), combining teaching and research and uniting the roles of "teacher of classics" and "teacher of conduct". They conclude that a new path to a Chinese-characteristic, world-class university lies in unifying the building of Chinese-characteristic philosophy and social sciences with the fundamental task of fostering virtue through education. They present this unity as an expression of the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-aligned account of how Chinese academics interpret Xi Jinping's 2022 remarks on academic autonomy and university building.
quoteEn: Whether our philosophy and social sciences have Chinese characteristics depends not only on such "outward forms" as the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems, but even more on whether there is an autonomous and original knowledge system as their "substantive core".
quoteZh: 我们的哲学社会科学有没有中国特色,不只要看学科体系、学术体系和话语体系这些“外显形式”,更要看有没有自主性和原创性的知识体系这一“实质内核”。

glossary.explanation: Formula associating the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture. It is prominent in Xi Jinping-era Party theory.
Confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is a slogan of the Xi Jinping era.
Xi Jinping's 2022 formulation for the core aim of building Chinese philosophy and social sciences: knowledge developed independently from Chinese practice rather than borrowed from foreign models.
Official term for the fundamental task of education in China: moral formation alongside knowledge and skills.

t: Deepening full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to keep it vigorous
zh: 深化全面从严治党 永葆旺盛生命活力
paras: Published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, this short commentary asks why the Communist Party of China must keep deepening full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Wang and Yang argue that governing the country requires first governing the Party, and that strict governance affects the fate of the Party, the state and the nation. They conclude that it is the necessary road for the Party to stay vigorous and to pass what the text calls the "new examination".

The article is organised in three sections: a historical summary, the theoretical support, and practical requirements. The first traces the principle of strict Party governance from the Party's founding through the democratic revolution, the early People's Republic and the period of reform and opening up, to the new era. The second sets the policy within the "Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy" and Marxist Party-building theory, and the third lists concrete tasks.

In the authors' account, strict governance has been a constant of Party history. It is credited with winning popular support, strengthening Party unity and discipline, and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), with ending lax and soft Party governance and securing an overwhelming victory in the anti-corruption struggle. Theoretically, Wang and Yang hold that the nature of a proletarian party decides what kind of party must be built. They hold that its fundamental purpose, serving the people wholeheartedly, requires strict discipline, since slack discipline and unpunished corruption would cost popular support. They also say the Party still faces the "four tests" and "four dangers", and that political building must come first.

For practice, the authors propose four tasks: strengthening ideals and convictions education, improving conduct by tackling formalism, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance, enforcing political discipline and rules, and building a rule-based system of Party regulations. They call for Party members to uphold the Two Upholds, for zero tolerance in anti-corruption work, and for discipline that binds everyone without exception. They also call for integrating rule-based Party governance with law-based national governance. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated scholars in 2022 presented the historical logic, theoretical basis and practical agenda of Party discipline.
quoteEn: Governing the Party through institutions makes Party building more stable, standardised, scientific and long-term.
quoteZh: 制度治党，能使党的建设更具稳定性、规范性、科学性和长期性。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: Official slogan since the 18th Party Congress (2012) for a campaign of stricter Party discipline, anti-corruption work and rule-based Party management, led by Xi Jinping.
A strategic framework put forward by Xi Jinping in 2014–2015: building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform, advancing law-based governance, and strict Party governance.

The requirement to uphold the core position of General Secretary Xi Jinping in the Party Central Committee and in the Party as a whole, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.

t: Accurately grasping the theoretical character and practical logic of "people-centredness"
zh: 准确把握“以人民为中心”的理论特质和实践逻辑
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 28 July 2022
paras: Writing in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) in July 2022, Gao Fengni asks what the "people-centred" development philosophy advanced by Xi Jinping consists of, and how it works in practice. The author argues that it draws on three sources: the historical-materialist view of the masses as makers of history, the "people as the root" (minben) tradition of Chinese culture, and the Chinese Communists' own view of the people. In Gao's account, Xi creatively developed these into the principle of upholding the people's principal position.

The piece is a short commentary in three parts. It first traces the idea's historical lineage from Mao Zedong's 1945 call to serve the people wholeheartedly, through Deng Xiaoping, to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012), citing the 2021 Resolution on the Party's century of struggle. It then sets out the idea's theoretical character, and finally its practical logic.

On theory, Gao names three features. The first is the Marxist view of the masses as the creators of history, which the author says has been carried forward through the Party's purpose of serving the people and the Scientific Outlook on Development. The second is traditional minben thought, from the Shang and Zhou notion of protecting the people to the image of the ruler as a boat and the people as water. Gao treats this as compatible with historical materialism and as a cultural gene that Xi's formulation lifts to a higher level. The third is the value of people's free and all-round development, in which Gao reads the Party's concern with raising living standards and, since 2012, with people's sense of fulfilment and common prosperity. On practice, Gao argues that putting the people first means ranking the people's interests above all else, mobilising their initiative to raise labour efficiency, and using the people's own judgement as the measure of the Party's work. Pursuing common prosperity is presented as the route to realising those interests.

Gao concludes that, with the principal social contradiction having changed in the new era, work must shift from meeting material and cultural needs to meeting the people's needs for a better life.
